headline: Today in history, August 24
body of the article: Aug. 24 Today in history Today is Aug. 24. On this date in: 79:Mount Vesuvius erupted, destroying Pompeii and Herculaneum, killing what is believed to be thousands. The Aug. 24 date comes from a medieval copy of a letter by Pliny the Younger. But some copies of the letter have other dates, and botanical, graffiti and other evidence point to a possible fall date for the disaster. 410:An army of Visigoths led by Alaric sacked Rome. It was the first time in 800 years that Rome had been invaded, and it came to symbolize the fall of the Western Roman Empire. "Sobs choke me. The city which had taken the whole world was itself taken," wrote Jerome, later a saint. 1682:The Duke of York deeded William Penn the "Three Lower Counties" that make up the present state of Delaware. Penn wanted the land for Atlantic access for his colony of Pennsylvania. 1814:British troops captured Washington, DC, and set fire to several government buildings. Most notable were the Capitol and the Executive Mansion, now called the White House. What they didn't confiscate, however, was a portrait of George Washington painted by Gilbert Stuart. First lady Dolley Madison instructed 15-year-old Paul Jennings to "Save that picture, if possible," allegedly refusing to flee until the 8-foot portrait was unscrewed from the wall; for speed, she ordered the frame broken. 1821:Spanish Viceroy Juan de O'Donojú signed the Treaty of Cordoba, granting Mexico independence from Spain. The Mexican War of Independence had started 11 years earlier. 1949:NATO entered into force following the signing of its treaty four months earlier. The founding treaty pledged that the members would "promote stability and well-being in the North Atlantic area" and "unite their efforts for collective defence and for the preservation of peace and security." 1950:Judge Edith Sampson became the United States' first Black representative to the United Nations. She was named as an alternate delegate. Sampson was a woman of many firsts, including being the first Black woman to be elected to the judiciary. 1968:France became the world's fifth thermonuclear power, exploding a hydrogen bomb in a test on French Polynesia. The 2.6-megaton explosion contaminated the uninhabited atoll to such an extent that people could not set foot on the island for six years. 1981:Mark David Chapman was sentenced to 20 years to life in prison for the murder of John Lennon. He pleaded guilty, saying devils told him to shoot the former Beatle and God told him to confess. 1987:Civil rights leader Bayard Rustin died at 75. A chief organizer of the March on Washington, he was often kept behind the scenes because he was gay. 1996:Four women enrolled at the Citadel, a South Carolina military college that had lost a court fight to remain all-male. One of them, Nancy Mace, later successfully ran for Congress. 2006:The International Astronomical Union voted to demote Pluto to a "dwarf planet." The decision was highly controversial, with some influential scientists criticizing the definition of a planet and noting that only about 4% of the world's astronomers attended the conference. 2011:Steve Jobs resigned as CEO of Apple, saying he could no longer meet his "duties and expectations" due to health issues. He died of cancer less than two months later. – USA TODAY Network This article originally appeared on USA TODAY:Today in history, August 24

headline: Heatwave hits evicted families sleeping rough in Rome
body of the article: For hundreds of people recently kicked out of a social centre in Rome, extreme heat is proving an added strain on top of a dispute highlighting the Italian capital's housing crisis. The centre, occupied since 2013 despite an eviction order and threats from far-right Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's government, was evacuated last month following a minor fire and seized by police. Now, families, elderly residents and pets are sleeping in tents and on camp beds outside the chained gates of Spin Time Labs, as temperatures in Rome near 40C. "As the days go by, we are seeing increasing psychological distress; people are at their limit, they are exhausted," Anastasia Destro, a 33-year-old doctor helping the evictees, told AFP. "We've seen all the health issues associated with living on the street and spending the entire day exposed to the sun," said Destro, part of a team offering medical and psychological aid. The fate of the building and its 400 or so residents, including children and disabled people, has generated a groundswell of support. Volunteers from across Rome have donated clothing, food and toys, while the left-wing city council has supplied tents, air-conditioning units, portable toilets and a drinking water truck. Film directors from Italy's Paolo Sorrentino to Britain's Ken Loach have called for the residents to be allowed back, while Matteo Garrone put on a showing of his film "Pinocchio" for the children. Spin Time, which over a decade grew to include a food bank, canteen, carpenter studio, newspaper and theatre, became a high-profile symbol of solidarity towards the marginalised. It even won the support of the pope: in 2019, Pope Francis's charity czar -- a cardinal -- climbed down a manhole to restore electricity after it was cut off. The community has provided sanctuary for those who found themselves "in an emergency situation", said Marco Perilli, a 60-year-old Italian construction worker who has lived there since 2013. - 'Life changed' - "The building was home to 27 different ethnic groups, cultures, and religions" who found a way to get along as "one big family", said Perilli, who moved in after separating from his partner. Perilli said it pained him to see residents "forced into unsanitary conditions, facing major health issues and serious illnesses". The evictions have thrown a spotlight on the Italian capital's housing emergency. More than 17,000 households are on the waiting list for council accommodation in Rome, almost half of whom applied at least a decade ago, according to city data. Mayor Roberto Gualtieri -- who wants the city to buy the building -- hoped the residents could be allowed back in while negotiations were underway. But the owner, the privately owned asset and investment management company Investire SGR, has so far refused. And Meloni's far-right Brothers of Italy party has accused Gualtieri of wasting public money and rewarding illegal behaviour in offering to buy the squat. Supporters say Spin Time has provided essential support to hundreds of vulnerable people. While the most vulnerable residents have been moved into alternative accommodation, others keep waiting outside, hoping they'll be allowed back in. Among them was Patience Sare, a 40-year-old from Nigeria, who ran a restaurant in Libya before fleeing to Europe when the war broke out in 2011. "Spin Time has taken me in, my kids in," said Sare, who has two children and tried to make a life in France, Switzerland and Malta before coming to Spin Time. "My life changed. It was as if I found my home," she said with tears in her eyes. "I wish we could stay." ide/ams/sbk

headline: Over 16,000 civilians detained by Russia during the war in Ukraine are still held, UN estimates
body of the article: UNITED NATIONS (AP) — The United Nations estimates that more than16,000 civilians detainedby Russia during itswar in Ukraineare still being "deprived of their liberty," many held incommunicado and on grounds that don't comply with international law. "Widespread and systematic torture and ill-treatment" of both Ukrainian civilian detainees and prisoners of war by Russia are continuing, includingsexual violence, said Claudia Fuentes Julio, the U.N. assistant secretary-general for human rights. She spoke at an informal meeting of the U.N. Security Council called by Latvia and the United Kingdom on Monday to spotlight the plight of civilians and soldiers taken during the war that Russia launched with a full-scale invasion of its neighbor in February 2022. The council, which counts Russia as a permanent member, heard the accounts as both Russia and Ukraine haveescalated attacksin the four-year conflict. Since the invasion, Julio said, U.N. human rights staff have interviewed 910 Ukrainian prisoners of war and 403 civilian detainees following their release. The U.N. has not been able to visit detention facilities in Russia, and its estimated figure of those held does not break down how many are adults or children. More than 95% of theUkrainian prisoners of warand 85% of the civilian detainees reported being tortured or ill-treated, often repeatedly, the U.N. official said. They also reported sexual attacks and inhumane conditions, including food deprivation and inadequate medical services. The Geneva-based human rights office "has documented the execution of 129 Ukrainian prisoners of war at the beginning of their captivity, and the deaths of 48 Ukrainian prisoners of war in custody, resulting from torture, denial of medical care, or other inhumane conditions of detention," Julio said. The U.N. Security Council also heard emotionally wrenching accounts from Crimean Tatar human rights activist Leniie Umerova, who called herself a "political prisoner" of the Russians for almost two years, and Khuan Leyva Garsiya, a Ukrainian soldier who was among the hundreds thatheld out for months at the Azovstal steel plantin thebesieged city of Mariupolbeforeturning themselves overto the Russians in May 2022. Garsiya, who was born in Mariupol to a Ukrainian mother and Cuban father, spent 1,183 days as a POW. He said he weighed 55 kilograms (120 pounds) when he was freed, pulling out a picture of his emaciated body to show the council. He said he was tortured, beaten harder and humiliated more than other prisoners because the Russians suspected that he was a foreign mercenary due to his Cuban ancestry or an American spy because he went to college in the United States. "Russians were outraged that someone with a connection to Cuba, whom they consider an ally, would fight against their occupation army," said Garsiya, who is still in the Ukrainian military. He said the Russians tried to break the prisoners mentally and force them to confess to falsified crimes through tortures including freezing, beatings, electrocution and sexual abuse, he said. "Two of my friends were beaten to death in detention centers in the Donetsk region," Garsiya said. "Two of my friends died because of the conditions they were put in in Russian prisons and were returned in plastic bags to the homeland." For Umerova, her captivity began when she tried to enter Russia from Georgia to visit her seriously ill fatherin Crimea, which is part of Ukraine but has been occupied by Russia since 2014. She said she was placed in detention on "fabricated charges." But unlike many others, she was able to contact an attorney. In the third month, she said, her attorney obtained her release through a court order. "But as soon as the prison gates opened, a bag was put over my head and I was taken away again." In six months, she said she was moved to seven different facilities, calling it "a carousel of repression." What happened to her, Umerova said, is part of a system Russia uses to unlawfully detain, isolate, torture and fabricate charges against civilians. She named half a dozen women in Russian prisons today and said at least 84 women have faced criminal prosecution. U.N. human rights experts also interviewed 816 Russians and 57 third-country national prisoners of war from over 45 countries who were members of the Russian armed forces in Ukraine, said Julio, the assistant secretary-general. About half reported torture or ill-treatment, primarily during the initial stages of captivity and interrogation by Ukrainians, she said. But U.N. monitors reported that once they arrived in Ukrainian detention facilities, "the conditions generally comply with international humanitarian law and have improved since 2022." Russia's deputy U.N. Ambassador Maria Zabolotskaya told the council the Russian armed forces are complying with international humanitarian law, which includes the treatment of prisoners. She claimed Russian prisoners in Ukraine faced "torture and degradation, and moral and physical abuse." She called the Security Council meeting part of "a disinformation campaign against Russia," funded by NATO countries involved in the Ukraine conflict. The aim, she said, "is to derail efforts towards a peace settlement and to justify strikes on the territory of Russia and against civilians." Ukraine's deputy U.N. Ambassador Volodymyr Pavlichenko said he was struck that during Monday's meeting, Russia was not ready to discuss the return of POWs — "including their POWs" — and all civilian detainees including abducted children.

headline: Russia using North Korean missiles to strike Ukraine, Zelensky says
body of the article: Ukraine and Russia have continued striking each other overnight, with President Volodymyr Zelensky accusing Moscow of using North Korean missiles. Ukraine said strikes on the southern city of Zaporizhzhia - which killed seven people and injured at least24 - involved ballistic missiles from Russia's ally. In Voronezh, western Russia, warehouses of the biggest online retailer Wildberries were hit by Ukraine. The company, known as Russia's Amazon, has been repeatedly targeted in recent weeks. The attacks come a day after at least 13 people were killed, including one child, in Ukrainian drone strikes on the Russian republic of Tatarstan, more than 1,100 km (680 miles) from the Ukrainian border. In a video address on Monday evening, Zelensky said "for the first time" Russia "cannot wage war without reinforcements from North Korea". "The more North Korean strikes there are here in Ukraine, in Europe, the more their missiles and soldiers are used, the more they correct their shortcomings and blind spots", Zelensky said, adding that this poses a danger to the rest of the world. He has not presented any evidence to back up his comments. It is not the first time Zelensky as well as other senior Ukrainian and Western officials have accused Russia of receiving military assistance from North Korea. Ukraine's military has said that says dozens of North Korean missiles have been fired by Russia into its territorysince Moscow's full-scale invasion in February 2022. The Ukrainian president warned over the weekend that as many as 50,000 North Korean soldiers were being sent to fight with Russian forces. Some 11,000 North Korean soldiers were deployed to help Moscow push Ukrainian troops out of the western Russian region of Kursk following their cross-border incursion in August 2024. In January 2025, Western officials told the BBC that North Korean troops had suffered nearly 40% casualties in the fighting there in just three months. In his Monday's address, Zelensky also hailed a successful air strike on a Russian petrochemical plant in western Siberia on Monday as a "very significant achievement" by the Ukrainian military. He promised "more Ukrainian deep strikes, which should demonstrate to Russia and the Russians that peace is necessary". Zaporizhzhia regional head Ivan Fedorov posted photos of vehicles and buildings on fire, saying Moscow had struck the city using missiles and guided bombs. All seven casualties were employees of Ukraine's Metinvest metallurgical plant, which later halted all its operations. One person was injured in strikes on the capital Kyiv, where air raid sirens sounded twice during the night. Explosions could be heard on the outskirts of the capital, triggering fires. Local officials later said a children's hospital was damaged - but there were no injuries as staff and patients were sheltering. Two women have been injured in a Russian drone strike on the north-eastern Ukrainian city of Sumy, according to regional head Serhii Kryvosheienko. He later said that one person was killed when Russia attacked the city with gliding bombs in the afternoon. Meanwhile, strikes on substations in Kherson and Kharkiv resulted in power outages. Ukrainian officials say Russia fired 120 drones overnight and a range of different missiles, but for the first time they have not given a number of missiles fired or intercepted. It follows an Air Force statement on Monday urging the media not to write "sensationalised headlines" or "spread pessimism" about the shortage of air defence interceptors. Separately, there have been reports of a fire and explosions at a logistics centre of Wildberries in the Voronezh region. Wildberries has not yet confirmed the attack, but said that its facilities in the region, which borders Ukraine, have been evacuated. In July, Ukrainian drone attacks on several retail warehousesbelonging to Wildberriesdisrupted the operations of a large number of small and medium-sized Russian businesses. Kyiv said at the time it was targeting logistics hubs used by Russians to buy military equipment, and disrupting supplies to the Russian army. The attack on Tatarstan this weekwas one of the deadliest single attacks on Russia since the start of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. At least 75 people were injured in the strikes, with Ukraine's Armed Forces saying it had hit the city's Tanevo oil refinery. Verified images on social media showed large plumes of smoke and flames rising into the sky in daytime, with air raid sirens howling in the background. The Uzbek consulate in Tatarstan said seven of those killed were citizens of Uzbekistan. At least 13 killed in Ukrainian drone strike deep into Russia Russia's businesses under strain from Ukraine's attacks on Wildberries How Ukraine is taking the war 'deeper' into Russia

headline: Europe Plunged Into Darkness With Solar Eclipse Wednesday
body of the article: Mainland Europe will see its first total solar eclipse in nearly 30 years on Wednesday. The rare celestial spectacle will begin in northern Russia before the moon's shadow sweeps across Greenland, Iceland, and the Atlantic, eventually reaching northern Spain and a small section of Portugal before disappearing into the Mediterranean, according toThe New York Times. Millions more across Europe, northwest Africa and parts of North America will experience a partial eclipse. The eclipse occurs when the moon passes directly between Earth and the sun. Those within the narrow path of totality will see the moon completely block the sun, revealing its corona and briefly plunging daytime skies into darkness. Most locations will experience less than two minutes of totality, according to NASA information cited by the Times. Spain is expected to be a prime viewing destination. Totality will become visible there around 8:26 p.m. local time, sweeping across the Balearic Islands before leaving land around 8:33 p.m., shortly before sunset. The Associated Press reported that the eclipse's shadow will travel about 5,130 miles, with maximum totality occurring off Iceland's western coast. Wednesday will mark mainland Spain's first total solar eclipse in more than 100 years. Anticipation has produced a rush for protective glasses across Europe. AFP reported pharmacies, opticians and other retailers have struggled to keep certified eclipse glasses in stock. Spain's government organized the distribution of 2 million free pairs, but some locations have already exhausted supplies. Demand at Carrefour's Spanish stores reportedly increased 20-fold in recent days. Experts stress that ordinary sunglasses are not adequate protection. Looking directly at even a partially obscured sun can cause permanent eye damage. Only during totality — when the sun is completely covered — is it safe to view the eclipse without approved eye protection. Those unable to travel to the eclipse's path can still follow the event online. TheEuropean Space Agencywill broadcast live from Spain's Observatorio Astrofísico de Javalambre beginning at 7:30 p.m. Central European Summer Time. Europeans outside the path of totality will still get an impressive show. The Guardianreported London should see about 92% of the sun covered, while parts of Cornwall will reach roughly 96%. The celestial show won't end with the eclipse: The Perseid meteor shower is expected to peak overnight Wednesday into Thursday. © 2026 Newsmax. All rights reserved.

headline: Turkey’s Kurdish region greets a conditional PKK pardon with relief, joy and doubt
body of the article: DIYARBAKIR, Turkey (AP) — Residents in Turkey's mainly Kurdish-populated southeastern region reacted with a mix of relief, joy and uncertainty on Tuesday after parliament approved aconditional pardon for thousands of Kurdish militants, offering them a potential path toward integration into normal life in Turkey. Lawmakers on Monday voted overwhelmingly in favor of the legislation that is aimed at advancing a peace effort between the Turkish state and theKurdistan Workers' Party, or PKK, which waged a long-running insurgency before announcing last year that it would lay down its weapons. The measures, however, will only come into effect after Turkish authorities have verified that the group has fully disarmed. Residents in Diyarbakir, the region's main city, expressed hope the new law will bring peace — as well as prosperity to a region that has lagged behind economically. "I was really very happy. I even applauded (the result) in my own home," said 70-year-old retiree Ali Akdogan. "The economy will improve, good things will happen, people will start doing business." "I believe it will bring peace," he continued, noting that since the start of the peace process there have been no deaths related to the conflict, which killed thousands of civilians, soldiers and militants over more than four decades. Hasan Gecti, a 56-year-old shop owner, also said he believes the stability and lack of violence will benefit the region's people economically and socially but suggested that other matters, such as greater Kurdish rights, have not been addressed. Among other issues, Kurds have been calling for broader use of their language in education and public services, along with greater political rights, including an end to the government's practice of ousting elected mayors and replacing them with government-appointed officials. "Has the Kurdish issue been directly solved? That's a bit of a question mark. In my opinion, only the terrorism problem has been solved," Gecti said. "Unfortunately, the Kurdish issue still remains where it is." The PKK declared a decision to dissolve itself last year in response to a call from its imprisoned leader,Abdullah Ocalan. The group then staged a symbolicdisarmament ceremonyin northern Iraq, where it is based, and announced that it was withdrawing fighters from key locations in Turkey to Iraq. The PKK launched the insurgency in the 1980s, initially with the aim of establishing a Kurdish state in the southeast of the country. Over time, the objective evolved into a campaign for autonomy and rights for Kurds within Turkey. Kurds are estimated to make up around 15–20% of Turkey's population. The new legislation will suspend some prison sentences for convicted PKK members and postpone ongoing investigations and trials against others for five or 10 years, depending on the severity of the alleged offenses. If no terror-related crime is committed within the time frame, the cases will be dropped. Turkish media reports said thousands of PKK members are likely to benefit, including those in exile in Europe and those who are based in Iraq and Syria. Militants convicted of intentional killings and those sentenced to life terms before 2005 are excluded from the bill's provisions. This applies to Ocalan and other senior PKK figures. Mehmet Kaya, head of the Diyarbakir Chamber of Trade and Industry, welcomed the fact that the legislation was passed with an overwhelming majority. "It signals that violence is ending and the doors of politics are opening," he said. However, the law alone does not solve the Kurdish issue and that further reforms will be needed, he added. "If the step taken from now bring sustainable democratization, social policies, and economic policies develop — which is the expectation — then the region will go through an important phase," Kaya said. In a statement carried by the PKK-linked ANF news outlet, the group on Monday described the Turkish legislation as a "beginning" to resolving outstanding issues but "has serious shortcomings and deficiencies." It called for Ocalan's release from prison, for democratic reforms and Kurdish rights. ——— Fraser reported from Ankara, Turkey.

headline: Torment of Afghan fathers as daughters deprived of education
body of the article: Father after father AFP spoke to in Afghanistan about the education ban that stops their daughters going beyond primary school choked up in despair. The pain and anguish it is causing behind closed doors is clear from interviews AFP conducted across the country, with even deeply religious fathers questioning the ruling. The Taliban authorities justify the ban -- the only one of its kind in the world -- on their interpretation of Islamic law. But "you will never find in the Quran that education is only for men," said one devout father, while another -- who praised the Taliban government for restoring security and reducing corruption -- said he couldn't "find any proper justification for this". All the men -- whose identities AFP is protecting -- described the emotional turmoil the bar is causing, with fathers losing sleep over what to do to help their bright and frustrated daughters. Nine out of 10 Afghan men questioned in a UN survey last year said it was important for girls to go to secondary school, with nearly two thirds considering it "pious" for a father to support his daughter's education. Some men have gone to prison for protesting the ban. Girls were barred from secondary schools in March 2022 after the Taliban authorities returned to power, with universities closed to young women later that year. The Taliban government did not respond to AFP questions about the ban. Officials insist the ban is temporary. But the UN's education wing UNESCO said Tuesday that an estimated "2.4 million girls have been excluded from secondary education since 2021" as it called for "an immediate and unconditional restoration of their right" to go to school. - Dreaded day approaches - Engineer Ahmad -- whose wife is a secondary school maths professor who is no longer allowed to teach -- said he never imagined that "one day my daughters would be illiterate". The father of four girls said "stopping at the sixth grade" will leave them effectively "illiterate" for the demands of "the 21st century". "Every day and every night, my wife and I... are getting closer to the moment when our daughters will have to stay home," he said. With his eldest nearing the end of her time in primary school -- and clandestine courses in their northern city costing more than half his salary -- he sees no option but to leave. As an ex-employee of an international organisation, he was well on track to get his family to the United States before President Donald Trump slammed that door shut. Despite European countries regularly denouncing the restrictions Afghanistan puts on women, Sweden, Denmark and Germany have also refused them visas. The children "do not know that we are losing our hope," Ahmad, 40, told AFP, adding that leaving illegally was "too risky". "Every day" the children ask, "'When do we leave?'" They try to keep their spirits up whatever way they can. Their eldest might fail her final year after breaking a bone during her exams. "She was sad, but I said to her: 'If you have to repeat, you'll have an extra year at school.'" - They can't go abroad - Mohammad, a doctor in a small town in Kabul province, said he always dreamed of sending his two daughters to one of the best universities. "For the development of Afghanistan we need women, not only for the home," he said. His two daughters -- aged 12 and 14 -- are in their last year of primary, the older one having started school later. For the last four years he has been trying to come up with ways around the ban -- including sending them to school in neighbouring Pakistan, now impossible since the land border was sealed after hostilities intensified between the two countries. Then he was told about a school that secretly teaches general subjects alongside its religious curriculum. "It's a private school" that charges higher fees of "around 10,000 Afghanis ($153)" a month for the two girls because "they are taking more risk". And there is no graduation certificate. But Mohammad is afraid officials might inspect the school and "take my daughters into custody". "The most important... is that they go on learning," the 42-year-old told AFP, adding that he told his daughters: "'While I'm alive, I will find a solution for your education.'" - 'How can I learn?' - N -- who only wanted to be identified by an initial -- is from Kandahar province in the south, a bastion of the Taliban movement, where he said girls can be excluded from school even before the end of primary if they are tall. He has three sons and a 12-year-old daughter. She "is very interested in astronomy. The other day, she did a collage of the solar system. She asked me a lot of questions, on gravity for example, and I told her that... 'You will learn.' "'How can I learn... if I cannot go beyond grade six,' she told me." He moved his family to Kabul to find work and told AFP that "we have to be patient" and explore ways around the "poison" of the ban, like underground schools and online design or computer courses. "Now I am working, I can afford the education of my children. But the opportunities are decreasing day by day and I may not be able to support that," with international aid also dwindling, he said. In the meantime, he tries to shield his daughter, with her school days already numbered. "She does not know that there is this other stress on us," he said. - 'I hide to cry' - It was a feast day and everyone was celebrating, but M's daughter stayed in her room crying. At 13 she could no longer go to school. "Beside the school (ban), girls are not allowed to go to parks for sightseeing or refreshments, it's really stressful," M told AFP, clearly shaken by his child's plight. He tries to take her to a restaurant once a week just to get her out. A devout logistics manager from a poor background, he worked hard to educate and improve himself, and praises the Taliban authorities for restoring security and fighting corruption. But "I cannot find any proper justification for" barring girls from secondary education, he said. "Sometimes when she gets so disappointed at home," he cannot bear it, he admitted. "I go to another room and... I hide to cry." M wants his daughter to go to university, and saved every cent so they could move to Iran so she could study there. But the war put an end to that. So she could have some "social interactions", he enrolled her in a Quranic school, "because staying at home all the time is stressful." However, recently she has refused to go. "Even if I continue, there will be no future for me," she told him. - Home schooling - "My daughter and her classmates were in a very bad mood" on the last day of primary school. "It was tragic," said Nasir, who had already witnessed the pain his 15-year-old went through when her education was cut short. The trophies the girls won for excellence at school sit alongside the books on the shelves of the home library he and his wife, a teacher, have proudly put together for them. They tutor their daughters at home with secondhand high school textbooks they salvaged, making them stick to a strict weekday routine going "early to bed, wake up at the same time as if you were going to school." But alone in the living room, Nasir, 47, confided that his younger daughter "is depressed and does not always have strong morale to continue learning on her own at home." He gives her novels to soften the blow, as she loves to read. The girls -- who help others in their building with their homework -- have recently started going to classes outside in secret. "We have sleepless nights" about it all, Nasir admitted. "This regime does not want educated people," he sighed. "When will we go back to a normal life?" iw/rsc/dp/fg/st

headline: UNESCO: Afghan school ban affects 2.4 million girls
body of the article: Around 2.4 million girls are currently excluded from secondary schooling in Afghanistan as a result of Taliban government policy, according to an estimate published by the UN's Paris-based cultural organization on Tuesday. "Women have been erased from public life, and as a new generation of girls grows without an education, their future becomes increasingly dark," it said. That figure could rise to almost 4 million by 2030, UNESCO predicted. The estimate is based on the number of girls who already enrolled in secondary school and had to leave after the Taliban took power, as well as girls currently completing primary school. Afghanistan is the only country in the world to ban girls and women from receiving education beyond primary school. Two decades of progress were being undone as a result, UNESCO said. After taking power in 2021, the Taliban drastically restricted women's rights. They are not allowed to attend secondary schools or universities. They are also largely being pushed out of the workforce. UNESCO sees these restrictions as a serious human rights violations and forecasts that the exclusion of girls from education will worsen poverty in the country and leave potential untapped. "At a time when nearly half of Afghans live below the poverty line, denying girls and women access to education and restricting their employment further undermines their ability to support their families and contribute to the country's economic future," it said. The UN body believes that girls run the risk of marrying at a younger age and says the ban on continuing their education harms their well-being. UNESCO estimates that the country could lose around $9.6 billion in income by 2066, as numerous highly educated women are likely to have left the workforce by then. UNESCO is working in Afghanistan to provide alternative learning opportunities. More than 69,000 people have participated in these programs since 2021, 70% of them girls and women.

headline: Watch: Man spins 33 hula hoops while upside down to break world record
body of the article: Aug. 11 (UPI) -- A Chinese man managed to spin 33 hula hoops around his body while suspended upside down to break a Guinness World Record. Yan Yanjia was suspended upside down from playground equipment in Guilin, Guangxi, and two friends then helped pull the hula hoops over his head and down to his hips. Yanjia was able to keep the hoops spinning for the time required by Guinness World Records, earning him the title for themost hula hoops spun while suspended upside down. He beat the previous record by 10 hoops. Yanjia said he started hula hooping eight years ago as a means of losing weight. "In 2018, I was diagnosed with fatty liver due to obesity, and my doctor advised me to lose weight. At that time, I bought a 2-kilogram [4.4-pound] hula hoop for exercise, and in a month, I went from 80 kg [175 pounds] to 63 kg [132 pounds]," he told Guinness World Records. "Of course, the main factor in successful fat loss is gradual control of diet." Yanjia said the next record his has his eye on involves spinning hula hoops while doing pullups. "This exercise consumes many times more force than dozens of hula hoops upside down, requiring much greater core stability," he said.

headline: Colombia earthquake is a test for de la Espriella, Taiwan learns from Ukraine on the battlefield, India-Bangladesh rivalry spills on and off the wicket
body of the article: A 7.4 magnitude earthquakestruckColombia yesterday – at least 160 people have died, though officials expect the toll to rise as rescue efforts continue. The quake's epicenter was in the Chocó region – one of Colombia's poorest areas that has also been wracked with clashes in recent years between the country's powerful armed groups. But damage to roads, buildings, and other infrastructure was reported across the country, including in Cali, Bogotá, and Medellín. The earthquake hit just three days after PresidentAbelardo de la Espriellawas sworn into office, and the disaster will prove to be an earlytestfor the right-wing leader, who now has to make good on his tough-on-crime pledge while also providing disaster relief. His budding friendship with US PresidentDonald Trump,who endorsed him back in June,could prove useful: Washington has alreadyofferedaid and support for the recovery, marking a sharp contrast with the often tense relationship between Trump and former Colombian PresidentGustavo Petro. Taiwan conducted its annual war games on Monday with a new twist: For the first time, itslowedhigh-speed mobile internet service across a large part of the island to simulate disruptions from a Chinese attack or natural disaster. The drill was designed to encourage Taiwan's 23 million residents to find other ways to communicate if mobile networks fail. It's one of several lessons Taiwan appears to be taking from Ukraine, where Russia hastargetedcommunications infrastructure since its full-scale invasion in 2022. Taiwan is also studying Ukraine's use of agile drones on the battlefield, building fleets of unmanned aircraft and attack boats to help deter a potential invasion. The island also aims to become a drone manufacturing hub, with agoalof producing 100,000 drones a month by 2030 and exporting half of them. An India-Bangladesh cricket series is atriskas diplomatic tensions between the two neighbors continue to simmer. The six-match series, featuring two of the sport's biggest powers, was originally scheduled for August 2025. Officials postponed the matches after relations deteriorated in 2024, when a student-led anti-government uprising forced then-Prime MinisterSheikh Hasina, a longtime Indian ally, to flee to New Delhi. Bangladesh's interim government has repeatedly criticized India for sheltering Hasina, who hascontinuedto make public appearances and hold press conferences. Politics have spilled onto the pitch of the world's second most popular sport before: in February, Bangladeshdeclinedto send a team to the Cricket World Cup in India, citing safety concerns for its players due to the political tensions.

headline: Paris tightens rules on electric scooters and other rideables
body of the article: Paris is cracking down on rules for users of rideables such as electric scooters, Segways, and electric skateboards, as crashes involving such devices continue to rise in the French capital. Police officers have launched a targeted operation in the city to enforce a new order for riders to wear helmets and reflective gear that took effect on 7 August. Those caught without a helmet will now be hit with a €135 fine, while riders spotted without reflective gear face a €35 fine, according to police. Hélène Denéchère, a spokesperson for the Paris police prefecture, highlighted the need for the new measures. "Since the start of the year, 136 personal injury accidents have involved vehicles of this kind, an increase of 12%. This is therefore the only category of road users in Paris for which personal injury accidents are on the rise," Denéchère said. She noted that while some riders already comply, others see the rules as an added burden. But she stressed that "wearing a helmet reduces the severity of these accidents." Public reaction in Paris remains divided, however. Rider Pierre Thoribé acknowledged the necessity of the gear despite being caught without it. "It's perfectly natural for me to have a helmet, which I don't have today… It's exceptional. I forgot my helmet," he said. Software developer Igor Monteiro, who already wears head protection, praised the enforcement. "I think it's very good. It's normal if you want safety. I've always used it... To me it's normal," he said, adding he was unaware of the new rules. Youssef Mourgui, a tattoo artist, urged fellow users to consider the risks of riding without protective gear. "Honestly, for yourself, it's good for safety. Because I know someone who works in a hospital; he told us he gets loads of people coming in, every time with their skulls smashed. There are even some now who are in wheelchairs," Mourgui said. "Not because of the police, but honestly, it's better for our health to wear a helmet." For others, the fine seems to be too hefty. One female scooter rider said the €135 fine for those caught with no helmet was in particular "a bit expensive," adding that users are getting "used to it now with everything that's going on." Those opposed to the new rules have criticised them as overly restrictive, arguing that it should be left up to personal choice. "I think it's better to let people be free and do what they want. If they have an accident afterwards, that's just tough luck for them," cyclist Romaric Bouton said. "We're not going to start holding everyone's hand and forcing them to wear a vest, a helmet, just because there are so many accidents every year. After that, we're no longer free to do what we want."

headline: Warship earmarked as River Clyde museum threatened with destruction
body of the article: A former Royal Navy warship which served in the Falklands War could be destroyed if campaigners fail to raise £2m to bring it back to Scotland. HMS Ambuscade was built at the Yarrow shipyard in Glasgow in 1975 and was part of the Royal Navy's fleet until 1993 when it was sold to Pakistan. It was used to rescue 377 tourists in the Maldives during the Indian Ocean tsunami in 2004, by which time it had been renamed PNS Tariq. The charity Clyde Naval Heritage (CNH) wants to bring the Type 21 frigate back to the River Clyde and turn it into a floating museum - but the Pakistan Navy has now ordered the vessel to leave Karachi by the end of September amid soaring transfer costs. The £2m required is nearly double the figure originally needed, largely because insurance costs have gone up due to the conflict between the US and Iran. Shipping has been significantly impacted since Iran blocked the Strait of Hormuz earlier this year, and there have been a number of attacks on vessels on the alternative waterway through the Red Sea. CNH chief executive David O'Neill said the Pakistan Navy told him they would "dispose" of HMS Ambuscade if she is not removed by September and the immediate circumstances were not looking hopeful. "We cited the continuing attacks on shipping, UK government advice and international shipping advice not to transit, but they don't accept this," he said. [BBC] O'Neill signed a deal with the Pakistan Navy in September 2023, transferring the ship to him on the basis that he took Ambuscade back to Scotland. His vision was to have the ship permanently berthed near the Beacon Arts Centre in Greenock and turn it into a museum paying tribute to the Clyde shipbuilding industry. He also wanted to give the Pakistani community a cultural landmark in Scotland. O'Neill said he is still engaged with both Inverclyde Council and Glasgow City Council, both of which have endorsed his museum plans. But he warned it is unlikely he will be able to raise £2m in such a short period of time, as conflicts have put an end to a previous sponsorship branding plan. If Ambuscade is destroyed, O'Neill said it would represent a "quiet fading" of Scottish heritage. "For the Clyde, it would mean the loss of a new tourism site with all of the heritage, cultural, jobs, economic benefits and education prospects," he added. In 2014, HMS Plymouth - another of the last surviving warships from the Falklands War campaign - wastowed out to sea from the River Mersey to be destroyeddespite a campaign to save it. The ship, which played a key role in the recapture of South Georgia from Argentinian troops in April 1982, was decommissioned in 1988. At the time Peel Ports, which owned the dock in Birkenhead where the ship was berthed for years, said it had "no practical choice but to dispose of her responsibly" but did not confirm the vessel's final destination. Ambuscade is the second Clyde-built ship O'Neill has attempted to rescue in recent years before running into difficulties. He campaigned to bring the Falls of Clyde back to Scotland from Hawaii, where the Victorian sailing ship had been moored as a museum in the 1960s before falling into disrepair. However, O'Neill ran into legal complications before the pandemic put his plans on hold. The ship was scuttled by the Honolulu Harbour Board last year. The tall ship was built in 1878 in Port Glasgow and spent many years carrying various cargoes to and from east Asia and Australasia before it moved to Hawaii. Could this warship return to the Clyde for good? Anger as historic Clyde ship towed out to sea and sunk in Hawaii Hormuz talks positive, Oman says, as Iran warns deal would not open strait

headline: Colombia Earthquake Death Toll Reaches 224 as Rescue Crews Rush to Free Trapped Survivors
body of the article: At least 224 people have been confirmed dead after a 7.4 magnitude earthquake struck eastern Colombia on Aug. 10 In addition to those who have died, more than 2,700 people have been reported missing and at least 600 have been injured Rescue teams have been working to free trapped survivors more than 24 hours after the earthquake first hit At least 224 people have been confirmed dead after a 7.4 magnitudestruck eastern Colombia. On Monday, Aug. 10, a devastating earthquake struck the South American country at about 7:34 a.m. local time, causing the collapse of dozens of buildings in its third-largest city, Cali, according to reports fromReuters,CNNandThe New York Times. One day after the natural disaster, theAustralian Broadcasting Corporation(ABC) reported that the death toll has risen to 224, with more than 2,700 people having been reported missing.CBS Newsalso reported that at least 600 people have been injured. Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella has declared a national disaster and announced that he was traveling to Bogotá, the country's capital, to "focus on addressing the emergency that our country faces." A collapsed house is pictured after an earthquake in Pereira, Colombia, on Aug. 11, 2026Credit: Jaime SALDARRIAGA / AFP via Getty "I have convened a United Command Post at the UNGRD from where I will personally lead the actions to assist communities in Choco, Eje Cafetero, and all affected areas," hewrote on X. He added, "To the Colombians who are today facing hard times, I want to say: you are not alone. You have a President who hurts for his people and who will do whatever is necessary to protect them, stand by them, and get through, together, all the affected regions." Never miss a story — sign up forPEOPLE's free daily newsletterto stay up-to-date on the best of what PEOPLE has to offer, from celebrity news to compelling human interest stories. While the epicenter of the quake was located in San Jose del Palmar, approximately 174 miles west of Bogotá, the powerful earthquake was felt in nine departments and all 32 departmental capitals, after which it triggered mass evacuations, according to Reuters. It was also felt in neighboring Ecuador and Panama. Alejandro Eder, the mayor of Cali, said that at least 20 buildings had collapsed in the city with people trapped inside. "We are already managing this emergency alongside all of Cali's rescue agencies," heshared on X. "I ask the public to remain calm. Please check your buildings for any visible structural damage. If you do not feel safe, or if you see large cracks, please evacuate the building." A woman looks at inside a collapsed house after an earthquake in Pereira, Colombia, on Aug. 11, 2026Credit: Luis ACOSTA / AFP via Getty On Tuesday, Aug. 11, firefighters shared a video of rescue crews pulling a 35-year-old man from the wreckage of a collapsed building nearly 24 hours after the earthquake hit. "We have found life under the debris," theywrote on X. "Every minute counts!" According to theTimes, the United Nations humanitarian agency said that preliminary reports indicated that 1,684 homes were damaged and 77 were destroyed. It also said that 61 buildings had collapsed. Colombia's armed forces sharedimagesof a search underway in Cali around 11 p.m. on Monday night. After a structure collapsed, they used dogs and drones equipped with thermal cameras to assist in finding and identifying victims under the rubble. Read the original article onPeople

headline: Welcome to the new digital divide
body of the article: In 2019, GZERO reported ona brewing backlashagainst AI's facial recognition and surveillance capabilities. Seven years later, opposition to the technology, which has advanced dramatically since then, is intensifying. Asurveyof more than 18,000 people in 15 countries found that over one-third ranked AI development among their top concerns over the next five years, ahead of immigration, energy security, and geopolitical rivalry. But attitudes toward AI vary sharply around the world.Ipsospolling found that people in Asia and Latin America are more likely to believe AI's benefits outweigh its risks and to express enthusiasm for AI-powered products and services. By contrast, North Americans are far more likely to say AI makes them nervous and are less convinced that its benefits justify its costs. North America says "not in my backyard."The AI backlash in North America centers heavily on environmental costs. The data centersneededto train and operate AI models consume enormous amounts of electricity and large volumes of water for cooling. A large data centeruses upto 5 million gallons a day, equal to the daily needs of a town of 10,000 to 50,000 people. In Canada, a recent survey found that68% of respondentswould oppose a large AI data center near their home, citing concerns about higher energy costs, environmental damage, and neighborhood quality.Seven in ten Americanshold similar views. And politicians are responding: Mississauga, Canada's seventh-largest city, voted last month totemporarily pausenew AI data center construction. In the US, New Yorkimposeda one-year moratorium in July on permits for large data centers, and voters of Monterey Park, California, approvedan outright banin June. In the US, data centers have become a political issue ahead of the November midterms. Democratic Senate candidateAbdul El-Sayedcriticized plansfor a data center in Michigan, while fellow Democratic House candidateWilliam Lawrencemade opposition to four local data centersa key plankin his platform after public outcry.In Ohio, both Republican nominee for governor,Vivek Ramaswamyand Democratic candidate for governorAmy Actonhave both pledged to restrict data centers. Fears of job losses also fuel opposition in North America.Arecent Gallup surveyfound that among Americans ages 14 to 29, excitement about AI fell 14 percentage points over the past year, to 22%, while anger rose nine points, to 31%.Two factorsappear to be driving that concern. First, North America has large white-collar sectors, including law, finance, and media, where generative AI isautomatingparts of entry-level work. Second, the US is home to many companies building AI systems, which gives citizens greater exposure to news about AI and its disruptive potential. But so far, those lossesappear limited: Research from Stanford University found that employment in occupations most exposed to AI fell by 0.2% year over year in June 2026, while employment in the least-exposed occupations grew by 0.6% over the same period. Asia and the Global South embrace AI.By contrast, polling suggests people in parts of Asia and Latin America are far more enthusiastic about AI.Overall,64% of respondents across Asia Pacific and 56% of respondents in Latin America say that using AI products and services excites them, compared with just 29% in North America. Why the difference? Opportunity. A recentstudyby the World Bank found that generative AI threatens far fewer jobs through automation in low- and middle-income countries (about 4.5%) than in advanced economies (over 14%), because fewer people in those countries work in knowledge-intensive professional services. Despite the controversy surrounding them in the West, many developing countries—including somevery small states, as GZERO reported last week—welcome data centers as a means of economic development. Although countries such as Thailand and Indonesia are concerned about environmental impacts, 69% and 65% of their citizens, respectively,believethat AI's benefits outweigh its environmental costs. In India, 71% share that view, although activists recently protested Google's planned $15 billion AI data center complex in Visakhapatnam, the largest city in the Indian state of Andhra Pradesh.Marchingunder the banner "We cannot drink DATA," they warned that the project could worsen an already fragile local water supply. China's all in on AI.China is the world's most bullish country on AI, with 80% of its population sayingthey are excitedabout its prospects.Several factorshelp explain that optimism. Over the last three decades, rapid technological progress has raised living standards and improved infrastructure. China has also built leading chip and electronics industries, which many view as a source of national pride. Meanwhile, the Chinese one-party system makes it very difficult toorganize political oppositionto AI data centers, unlike the democratic systems in the United States and Canada. China also has thehighest percentageof citizens—77%—who believe AI's potential benefits or society outweigh its environmental costs. The country has about one-tenth the number of data centers as the US: 449, compared to 5,427 in the US. As a result, fewer Chinese citizens have been exposed to the negative impacts of those facilities. The new digital divide.Ultimately, the AI backlash is not about the technology itself, but about its impact. In North America, many people fear that AI will threaten white-collar jobs and damage the environment. In China and parts of the Global South, many see AI as a path to higher productivity and faster growth. The key question is whether those countries can overcome the hurdles to implementation—and whether states with the capacity to deploy AI choose to pause.

headline: Lebanon parliament votes to abolish death penalty
body of the article: Lebanon's parliament has voted to abolish the death penalty, a move that would make it the first country inthe Middle East to formally end capital punishment. A majority of MPs in the 128-seat parliament backed the measure on Tuesday, while Hezbollah's parliamentary bloc voted against it. The legislation will now go to the cabinet before being passed to President Joseph Aoun for signing. The government has already expressed its support for the measure. Lebanon has not carried out an execution since January 2004, although courts have continued to hand down death sentences. Rights groups estimate that more than 78 people remain on death row. Under the new legislation, capital punishment will be replaced with life imprisonment with hard labour. However, the legislation does not yet set out in detail how the new sentence would be enforced. Hard labour is alreadywritten intoLebanese law but has rarely been implemented in recent years. The country's financial crisis and overcrowded prisons have limited the authorities' resources and capacity. The latest legislation follows years of campaigning by civil society groups and lawyers for the removal of capital punishment from Lebanese law. "We cannot solve a crime with a crime or end violence with violence," Oragit Younan told the BBC. As co-founder of the Lebanese Association for Civil Rights, she led a nearly three-decade campaign to abolish the death penalty in Lebanon. "We are in a war, and people [have been] killed every day, so even in this situation, we can fight, we can struggle for human rights, and we can win. We can be a model for others," she said. Tuesday's vote in parliament follows more than two decades of a de facto moratorium on executions. An execution required a decree signed by the president, prime minister and justice minister - but no such decree has been signed since 2004. Under Lebanese law, the death penalty could previously be imposed for some of the country's most serious offences, including aggravated murder, certain terrorism-related crimes resulting in death, treason, espionage and offences against state security. Previous attempts to abolish the death penalty have failed, including legislation introduced in parliament in 2004 and a proposal from the justice ministry in 2008. Lebanon's move comes as the use of the death penalty remains contested elsewhere in the Middle East. Jordan resumed executions in June, carrying out its first since 2017. In Israel, its parliament has approved legislation that allows for the expansion of the circumstances in which capital punishment can be imposed. Israeli MPs passed a new law in May to impose the death penalty and conduct public trialsfor those involved in the Hamas-led attacks and mass hostage-taking in Israel in October 2023. Elsewhere, the UN human rights chief has said he is alarmed by the rise in executions in Iran, with capital punishment continuing to be used "to instil fear among the population and suppress dissent". In Iran, at least 56 people had been executed on national security-related charges since 19 March,including 27 in cases linked to January's nationwide anti-government protests, UN human rights chief Volker Türk said earlier this month. headline: King Charles' Death Mistakenly Announced In Radio Show Mix-Up
body of the article: Like this article? Keep independent journalism alive.Support HuffPost. King Charles'death was mistakenly announced on a radio show back in May, Ofcam, the communications regulator for the United Kingdom,said in a new report on Monday. Ofcam released the case regarding the radio station, Radio Caroline, and spelled out the violations against the radio show and staffer who played the erroneous message "out of curiosity" during "The Barry Marsh Show." Buzz:'Kimmel' Guest Host Anthony Anderson Brutally Trolls Trump With 'Silent' Melania Joke The Ofcam report said that "a member of staff carrying out maintenance on the studio computer accessed three sound files which had been pre-recorded to use in the event of the death of King Charles III." While "these files are accompanied with 'a set of strict instructions to presenters and managers' to follow before being aired," the staffer played them "out of curiosity" which interrupted the radio program. In an all-too-relatable moment, the report said that "once the individual realized what had occurred," the staffer " topped the files and then 'panicked and left the premises.'" Though Ofcam only received two complaints about the messages played in error, anyone listening would've certainly thought the king had died, as the three announcements read: Buzz:John Oliver Makes A Total '*******' Out Of GOP Senator Who Caved To Trump "This is Radio Caroline; we have suspended our normal programs until further notice as a mark of respect following the passing of His Majesty King Charles III." "This is Radio Caroline, His Majesty King Charles III has passed away, as a mark of respect we will now be playing suitable continuous music until further notice." "This is Radio Caroline, the news media has confirmed that His Majesty King Charles III has passed away, consequently as a mark of respect, Radio Caroline is suspending its normal programs." In addition to the announcements, the national anthem was played after the first statement, which was then followed by 16 minutes of silence. Buzz:Jon Hamm And Wife Anna Osceola Are Expecting Their First Baby Together Some 30 minutes after Charles' death was mistakenly announced, the radio show presenter apologized to listeners. "I've just been informed that we've played in error some information a little earlier, I didn't hear this myself, but it is incorrect, it's a technical issue, and of course we apologize," the presenter said at the time. The late Queen Elizabeth notably faced a false death rumor in recent years, though it circulated far faster ― and further ― than King Charles' fake death announcement. The U.S. blog Hollywood Unlockedfalsely reported that the queen diedin February 2022. Shedied a few months later, in September 2022. headline: Divers discover wreck of warship lost 118 years ago
body of the article: By Dean Murray The wreck of a Royal Navywarshipsunk off the Isle of Wight 118 years ago has been discovered by divers. HMS Tiger was cut in two after she strayed into the path of the 10,000-ton cruiser HMS Berwick in 1908. Fewer than half of the 400-ton destroyer's 57-strong crew survived as she sank. The ship was considered lost at sea until Aug. 10, when their discovery was announced by the ProjectXplore dive group. It comes as the Government is changing the law to strengthen protections forshipwrecksthrough the Armed Forces Bill. (Guy Trees via SWNS) The graves of thousands of sailors and marines at sea will receive automatic legal protection through expanded powers. Under the Armed Forces Bill, potentially thousands of shipwrecks, such as HMS Tiger, will be safeguarded from the moment they are found by a 'protected place' designation. This will make it an offense to disturb or remove items from military wreck sites without permission, while permitting divers to visit freely, as long as they apply the principle of 'look but don't touch'. Minister for the Armed Forces Louise Sandher-Jones MP said: "As well as protecting UK national security, Defence has a role to play in preserving our maritime heritage and the memory of those who gave their lives serving their country. (Joe Colls Burnett via SWNS) "These protections go further to ensure that these vulnerable and nationally significant monuments are protected from day one of discovery, giving lost sailors the dignity and respect they deserve. "This Armed Forces Bill is wide-ranging in the measures it proposes – from protecting our rich cultural heritage, to transforming the lives of military families by upgrading and improving the Defence housing estate." While dozens ofmilitary shipwreckshave been safeguarded against illegal activity since the mid-1980s under the Protection of Military Remains Act, only vessels lost within the last 200 years can currently be protected. Expanding the Act to include wrecks more than 200 years old would mean that military vessels dating as far back as the Armada, including those of former foes, would qualify for protection. The same would go for merchant ships sunk while on military service under Admiralty orders. The proposed regulations have been welcomed by ProjectXplore, the team of divers and historians who discovered HMS Tiger's shattered remains. The team, who also found the wreck of cruiser HMS Nottingham in the North Sea last year, spent five years in the archives piecing together all the relevant data to help pinpoint the wreck's location. (Royal Navy via SWNS) Leo Fielding and Dan McMullen, co-organizers of ProjectXplore said: "It has been the privilege of a lifetime to research, discover and document the wreck of HMS Tiger. We sincerely hope that our work will ensure that HMS Tiger, her story and the memory of those connected with her endure for future generations. "ProjectXplore welcomes the proposed amendments in the Armed Forces Bill. We believe they represent a constructive step forward in protecting the United Kingdom's maritime heritage and ensuring that wreck sites of historical and archaeological significance are appropriately safeguarded." Royal Navy Deputy Fleet Wreck Officer Lieutenant Commander Jen Smith said: "Protecting military wrecks helps to ensure they are preserved for future generations. This is beneficial for our rich maritime heritage and the diving community who keep the stories of our lost shipwrecks alive. "Divers are still able to visit these sites and witness history first-hand, which is key to ensuring that these ships and their crews are not forgotten. "All we ask of divers is this – enjoy looking, learning and paying your respects at these incredible sites, but do so in a manner that does not disturb them." The postDivers discover wreck of warship lost 118 years agoappeared first onTalker.

headline: Colombia earthquake: Dozens dead, people trapped in collapsed buildings
body of the article: At least 224 people are dead after a 7.4-magnitude earthquake rocked western Colombia on Monday, Colombia's Public Ministry said. The country's new president, Abelardo de la Espriella, has declared a national disaster, with destruction reported in multiple cities. The earthquake's epicenter was 5 kilometers, or about 3 miles, east of San José del Palmar, Colombia, according to the U.S. Geological Survey. Santiago Saldarriaga/AP - PHOTO: Residents and rescue workers search through the rubble of a collapsed building after an earthquake struck Cali, Colombia, Aug. 10, 2026. Along with the 224 dead, at least 572 others have been injured, officials said. Alejandro Eder, the Mayor of Cali, said in asocial media poston Tuesday morning that of the people killed in the earthquake, 95 perished in Cali, the second-largest city in Colombia with more than 2.2 million residents. Eder said at least 86 people have been rescued in Cali so far. Preliminary reports indicate that at least 239 people are believed to be trapped in rubble and 949 people injured in the city, according to Eder. Additionally, 93 structures have been damaged and another 45 have partially or wholly collapsed, he said. "Today more than ever, we need to be united and help each other," Eder said in the post. The U.S. State Department said in a post on X that the Trump administration is committing $15.5 million for the Colombia earthquake response that will go towards emergency shelter, food, protection and earthquake assessments. Some of the hardest-hit regions include the cities of Pereira and Cali. Dozens of people have been reported dead in their respective departments. De La Espriella, who was just sworn in as president on Friday, said more than 1,600 homes across the country collapsed in the earthquake. He said dozens of health centers, community centers and roads were also damaged. A rescue effort was ongoing in a building where people are believed to be trapped, according to officials. A hospital in Cali experienced severe damage, with one of the wings partially collapsing, and patients were being relocated, the local governor said. Eder announced a curfew from 8 p.m. Monday to 6 a.m. Tuesday to "ensure safety in the city and to provide sufficient space and conditions for rescue workers to continue their efforts." Joaquin Sarmiento/AFP via Getty Images - PHOTO: People look for survivors amid the rubble of a collapsed building after an earthquake in Cali, Colombia, Aug. 10, 2026. The governor of Chuco said there were injuries and "severe damage" to buildings in the department's capital city of Quibdo. Seven airports have suspended service in the cities of Armenia, Cali, Manizales, Pereira, Quibdo, Buenaventura and Cartago. Jonh Bonilla/AFP via Getty Images - PHOTO: Rubbles on a street are pictured after the earthquake in Manizales, Colombia, Aug. 10, 2026. There have not been any reports of collapsed buildings in the capital of Bogota, officials said. The earthquake was the strongest recorded in the country in a decade, according to the Colombian Geological Survey. It was widely felt throughout Colombia and in neighboring countries, including Venezuela, Ecuador and Panama, it said. The Colombian president said in a video on social media that he was headed to Bogota to "focus on addressing the emergency facing our country" and has convened a unified command post to respond to the affected areas, including what's known as the Coffee-Growers' Axis. The Trump administration is "closely monitoring" the earthquake and stands "ready" to support the people of Colombia, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a statement.

headline: UK Radio Station Mistakenly Aired King Charles Death Report ‘Out of Curiosity’
body of the article: A British radio station mistakenly announced King Charles III's death after a staffer played pre-recorded announcements "out of curiosity," according to the U.K.'s media regulator. Radio Caroline aired three statements declaring the King dead during "The Barry Marsh Show" on May 19, according to anOfcom ruling released Monday. The national anthem was also played before one of the statements was repeated. The station then went silent for roughly 16 minutes for listeners on DAB+, while AM listeners continued to hear music. Radio Caroline told Ofcom that an employee performing maintenance on a studio computer discovered three audio files pre-recorded for use in the event of the King's death. Despite "strict instructions" governing when they could be aired, the staffer played them "out of curiosity." The recordings interrupted the feed from the show's remote presenter and went out over the air. After realizing what had happened, the staffer stopped the files, "panicked and left the premises," according to the station. The presenter did not immediately realize the show had been knocked off the air. Programming eventually resumed, with an apology and correction airing roughly 30 minutes after the false report. Ofcom found Radio Caroline in breach of two provisions of its Broadcasting Code, including requirements that news be reported with "due accuracy" and that significant mistakes be corrected quickly. The regulator called the report a "very significant inaccuracy," pointing to the repeated announcements, the claim that news media had confirmed the King's death and the playing of the national anthem. Radio Caroline said it took the incident "very seriously." The staffer was reprimanded and apologized, while the recordings were removed from the studio computer to prevent another accidental broadcast. The postUK Radio Station Mistakenly Aired King Charles Death Report 'Out of Curiosity'appeared first onTheWrap.

headline: At least 169 killed in Colombia's largest earthquake in years
body of the article: Contains some scenes which some viewers may find upsetting. - Watch: Moment powerful earthquake shakes Colombia and crumbles buildings At least 169 people are dead and a state of emergency has been declared after Colombia was hit by one of its largest earthquakes in years. The death toll is likely to rise, with more feared trapped under collapsed buildings. The magnitude 7.4 quake struck at 07:34 (12:34 GMT) at a depth of 103km (64 miles) in Chocó province, the country's geological service said. It was felt across an enormous area, stretching for hundreds of miles across western Colombia. Many of the deaths have been concentrated in Cali, Colombia's third most populous city. At least 900 people were injured in the quakes, Colombia's Association of Capital Cities (Asocapitales) wrote in an update on Tuesday. The epicentre of the quake was near the village of San José del Palmar, in Chocó province, but local mayor León Fabio Marín Moncada said that there had miraculously been no deaths or injuries - despite the roads in and out being damaged. According to Asocapitales, most of the fatalities where in cities. Cali, located about 200km from the epicentre, was the worst affected with 85 dead. Dan Cutler, 29, is from London but has been in Colombia for about two months as part of a big trip with his partner, and is currently in Cali. Being woken by the earthquake, he told the BBC: "I've never experienced anything like it." "We sprinted outside in our pyjamas. There's no major structural damage to the hotel, but there are surface cracks in the walls, and paint and plaster have peeled off," he says. In Pereira, in Colombia's coffee-growing region, 66 people died. Videos verified by the BBC show at least one building collapsing in Plaza Bolívar, Pereira's main square, with scattered debris and dust across the open space where many people had gathered. Buildings were destroyed in the city of Manizales [EPA] Dozens of buildings have collapsed in the city of Cali [Reuters] At least five people also died in Manizales, another city in the coffee-growing region, which is popular with local and foreign tourists. Speaking to BBC World Service, Angélica Ávila said she had been staying in a hotel in Manizales. She said as the earthquake hit, cracks appeared in the walls. "Everyone was screaming... I saw dust coming out of the neighbouring buildings, and bricks were falling off the walls," she said. Journalist and meteorologist Luis Felipe Molina, from Manizales, was at home when the earthquake struck - about 150km from the epicentre. He explained that due to previous earthquakes, the city has "very strict seismic-resistant building regulations" - so his building was able to resist the impact. "I have 450 books and only a few were left standing on the shelves. You could hear glass breaking and people screaming," he told BBC Mundo. "It was a terrible and terrifying experience." The country's aviation authority has reported damage at several regional airports, including those in Pereira, Manizales, Quibdó, Armenia, Cartago and Buenaventura. In the capital, Bogotá, trees and traffic lights shook violently, with reports of cracks in buildings but so far none of any serious damage to the city's infrastructure. Tremors were felt as far away as neighbouring Venezuela, Ecuador and Panama. The quake comes less than two months after twin quakesdevastated the north of Venezuela, killing more than 6,300 people. [BBC] [BBC] Colombia's President Abelardo de la Espriella has declared a national disaster situation, creating special powers to react to the emergency, including to reallocate budgets. Having only taken up the role on Friday, the new president is immediately faced with a potentially legacy-defining event. As the extent of the damage has begun to emerge, world leaders have come forward to offer support. A spokesman for Pope Leo XIV said the pontiff was "deeply saddened to learn the painful news of the earthquake". US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the US was "closely monitoring" the earthquake, and stood "ready to support", while EU chief Ursula von der Leyen said the EU's Copernicus satellite was being used in the rescue operation. The president of El Salvador, Nayib Bukele, sent a message of solidarity to the Colombian people and offered personnel and equipment for rescue efforts. According to the US Geological Survey, an estimated 1.5 million people felt shaking close to magnitude seven. It stated that deep earthquakes, like the one which hit on Monday, are usually less dangerous than earthquakes which break closer to the Earth's surface. But they can release energy in a way which is damaging to buildings, with fewer but potentially stronger aftershocks.
