headline: Lebanon parliament votes to end death penalty, 1st in Middle East to do so
body of the article: Lebanon's parliament has passed a law to abolish capital punishment, making it the first country in the Middle East to do so. The Lebanese parliament's speaker's office said lawmakers signed off on the legislation Tuesday after making several amendments. A majority of the 128-member assembly voted in favour of ending the death penalty, with the exception of the parliamentary bloc of Hezbollah. Justice Minister Adel Nassar, who was in parliament, called it a "historic step" for the country. The new system replaces the death sentence with life imprisonment with aggravated hard labour. While Lebanon has observed an unofficial moratorium on executionssince January 2004, courts have continued to issue dozens of death sentences. At the end of 2025, 85 people were facing death sentences, according to the Lebanese Ministry of Justice's Directorate of Prisons. Rights group Amnesty International's Middle East and North Africa director, Heba Morayef, praised Lebanon's move to end capital punishment as "a major milestone and a victory for human rights in the country". "After more than two decades without executions, today's step transforms a precarious hiatus in executions into lasting legal protection upholding the right to life and bringing Lebanon in line with the global trend towards abolition," Morayef said. It is unclear how aggravated hard labour would be enforced, with some legislators saying the terms of the new punishment are not yet clear. Lebanon does have the punishment of hard labour written into law and court decisions, but even those have been rarely enforced in recent years due to cash-strapped Lebanon's lack of resources and capacity within its overcrowded prisons. Lebanon's abolition of the death penalty comes as parliament also debates a controversial general amnesty law, the largest since the end of its 15-year civil war in 1990, that could reduce sentences or even release some people convicted of violence offences. Family members of Lebanese soldiers and servicemen killed in attacks have repeatedly protested against the law, some saying they had hoped to see the perpetrators who killed their family members executed rather than be issued reduced prison sentences.

headline: Germany's Hanover Airport suspends flights after drone sighted
body of the article: Flight operations at Germany's Hanover Airport were suspended for more than an hour at around dawn on Tuesday after a drone was spotted at the site. Runways were closed between around 4:00 am (0200 GMT) and around 5:20 am, an airport spokeswoman told dpa. Six passenger flights were delayed, and a cargo plane from Paris was diverted. Flight operations have been running normally again since the morning, the spokeswoman said. Federal police said that criminal police in Hanover are investigating the incident, and declined to provide further comments due to the ongoing investigation. The incident occurred just days after an explosives-laden drone was spotted at Leipzig/Halle Airport in eastern Germany last week. The drone was found late Tuesday near a Ukrainian Antonov An-124 cargo aircraft, according to security sources. Specialists from Germany's federal police later defused the device. It was initially unclear whether the two incidents are linked.

headline: Lebanon abolishes death penalty in first for region
body of the article: BEIRUT, Aug 11 (Reuters) - Lebanon's parliament on Tuesday abolished the death penalty and replaced all existing ‌death sentences with life imprisonment, the speaker's office ‌said in a statement. The move makes it the first country in ​the Middle East to formally end capital punishment, after maintaining a de facto moratorium on executions since 2004, although dozens of people had remained technically on death row. ‌Crimes that were ⁠punishable with a death sentence included murder and treason. Last year, Lebanese lawmakers submitted a law ⁠to abolish capital punishment. Parliament's statement on Tuesday did not include a vote count. The European Union welcomed the ​move, saying ​Lebanon was setting "a powerful ​example for other countries" ‌in the Middle East and beyond. "Lebanon's decision to abolish the death penalty marks a major milestone and a victory for human rights in the country," said Amnesty International's Regional Director for the Middle East and North Africa ‌Heba Morayef. "After more than two ​decades without executions, today's step ​transforms a precarious hiatus ​in executions into lasting legal protection upholding ‌the right to life and ​bringing Lebanon ​in line with the global trend towards abolition," Morayef said. Lebanon's parliament is separately discussing legislation on a ​general amnesty for ‌some crimes, partly as a way to relieve ​overcrowding in prisons. (Reporting and writing by Maya ​Gebeily; Editing by Hugh Lawson)

headline: Thailand suspends new gun permits after mass shooting
body of the article: Thailand's government will immediately stop issuing gun permits after a shooting incident last week in which a 14-year-old killed eight people and himself. Existing gun owners are already banned from carrying their weapons in public. The South East Asian country has one of the highest rates of civilian gun ownership in the region, with around 10.3 million firearms in civilian possession, and high levels of gun crime. In response to the recent shooting, the prime minister has promised to pass tough new gun control laws with severe penalties, suspending new permits in the meantime. Last Friday, a pupil at Debsirin Nonthaburi School outside Bangkok shot his grandparents using a handgun owned by his grandfather, before opening fire at teachers and students at school, authorities say. Both grandparents, five staff members at the school and one 12-year-old girl died. Policebelieve the shooter may have taught himself to use a gun via social media. They say there is evidence that the boy watched violent content online, and that he showed a strong interest in learning how to handle guns. His consumption of this content as well as anxiety over studies and family issues might have also fuelled his actions, they add. Officials paid their respects to the victims on Tuesday at a Nonthaburi temple [AFP] Until further notice, no new permits to purchase or own guns will be issued. Existing purchase permits will not be renewed but it is unclear what will happen to existing gun ownership permits. Permits to carry guns were suspended in late 2023 - owners must keep their weapons at home or at a shooting range. The government is also considering measures to persuade the owners of an estimated four million unlicensed guns to hand them over in the wake of the school shooting. Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul has said the announced measures will remain in place as the government works to pass new gun control laws, with stronger controls and significantly harsher penalties. Gun control advocates have called for mental health assessments as part of the permit process, and for permits to be periodically re-evaluated. Anutin has said stricter ammunition controls are in his sights, while the education minister has proposed screening at the entrance of schools to stop students from bringing in weapons. headline: Congo Ebola deaths surpass 2,000 as spread shows no sign of slowing
body of the article: DAKAR, Aug 11 (Reuters) - Democratic Republic of Congo said on Tuesday that confirmed Ebola deaths had reached 2,011, the latest grim milestone in what health officials have described as the fastest-spreading ‌outbreak on record. The latest data from Congo's public health institute, seen by Reuters, also reported 4,381 ‌confirmed cases across five provinces. Delayed detection, conflict and strained health services have helped the virus spread more rapidly than in previous outbreaks. The current ​outbreak, Congo's 17th, is caused by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, for which there are no approved vaccines or treatments. The World Health Organization has declared the outbreak, which has also led to cases in neighbouring Uganda, a public health emergency of international concern. A study published last month in the journal Science found that transmission may have begun in ‌January or earlier in Ituri province, identifying ⁠more than 500 suspected cases between mid-January and May 15. Shortages of medical supplies and insecurity in affected areas have complicated efforts to trace contacts, isolate patients and curb transmission. The ⁠Congolese government data shows that the current outbreak is dwarfed only by West Africa's 2014 to 2016 Ebola outbreak in which 28,616 cases and 11,310 deaths were recorded across Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone, according to the World Health Organization. It took ​nearly ​five months from the declaration of that outbreak to hit ​1,000 deaths, whereas Congo's current outbreak has ‌hit 2,000 deaths in less than three months. In an Ebola outbreak in Congo from 2018 to 2020, it took a little over 12 months to hit 2,000 deaths. In the current outbreak, deaths have jumped from 1,000 to 2,000 in less than a month, further underscoring how quickly the virus is spreading. LOCAL GROUPS, MILITIAS DEPLOYED TO SUPPORT CONTAINMENT As in past outbreaks, community resistance and persistent mistrust have complicated the containment effort, at times putting response ‌workers at risk during disputes over burial practices. On Monday, local ​officials in North Kivu province launched a government-backed task force in the ​city of Butembo that brings together pro-government militia ​fighters and civil society groups to help protect Ebola responders as they carry out ‌their duties. The task force will assist authorities in ​protecting health workers and treatment ​facilities and enforce quarantine measures for people suspected of having been exposed to the virus. At a press conference on Monday, one of its leaders, Guy Ngavo, said people found handling the bodies of Ebola ​victims or refusing quarantine orders could ‌be forcibly taken to Ebola treatment centres and, in cases of repeated non-compliance, subjected to whipping. (Reporting ​by Fiston Mahamba; Writing by Ayen Deng Bior; Additional reporting by Clement Bonnerot and Ilham Sougue: ​Editing by Robbie Corey-Boulet, Sharon Singleton and Toby Chopra)

headline: Anti-Muslim posts misrepresent old footage of lightning-sparked Canadian church fire
body of the article: A dramatic video of a Quebec church in flames has resurfaced online in social media posts falsely claiming it shows a 2026 blaze sparked by a Muslim immigrant to Canada. But the fire took place in July 2025 and was caused not by arson, but a lightning strike that ignited the building, the local government confirmed. "SHOCKING: Another church is burned down in Canada by Muslim immigrant," says an August 7, 2026postsharing the video to X from anaccountcalled "Khan Fatima," which resembles asuspended profilethat previously spread otherfalse claimsabout immigrants starting church fires (archivedhere) . The clip shows a fire engulfing a church spire, causing it to collapse. Conservative US commentator David Harris Jr, who hasalsosharedseveralfalse claimsdebunkedby AFP, amplified the claim onFacebookand implied the fire had just taken place. The video and screengrabs of it spread acrossFacebook,X,InstagramandThreadsin several languages, includingFrench,Spanish,VietnameseandHaitian Creole. Somepostsclaimed the supposed arson was the result of "Islamization," while others called for a stop to alleged "Christian genocide." Screenshot of an X post taken August 10, 2026 Screenshot of a Facebook post taken August 10, 2026 AFP has repeatedly fact-checked similar misinformation about "Islamists" and migrants starting church fires in theUnited KingdomandCanada. Some August 2026postspushing the claim about "Islamist immigrants" burning a church misused different footage of a 2024 incident in Quebec -- an allegation that AFP previouslydebunkedafter officials ruled that fire an accident. The video of the crumpling spire is similarly misrepresented. Reverse image searchesrevealed that theclipis over a year old and shows the Église de l'Immaculée-Conception, whichburned downJuly 17, 2025 inSaint-Ours, Quebec, about 80 kilometers (50 miles) northeast of Montreal (archivedhere). The city of Saint-Ours rejected the claim that the blaze was started intentionally by a Muslim immigrant. "The fire was caused by a lightning strike during the severe thunderstorms that hit the region that evening" Saint-Ours general directorPascale Dalcourttold AFP in an August 10, 2026 email (archivedhere). A Saint-Ourspress releaseandnews reportsfrom the time further confirm that lightning started the fire (archivedhereandhere). Dalcourt also shared a screenshot of a weather map showing the observed lightning activity from July 17, 2025, with a strike blasting the church'sformer locationat the center of town (archivedhere). Several Canadian churches havesufferedserious damage fromfiressince 2021, with the most recent incident taking place inApril 2026at a deconsecrated structure in Saint-Romain, Quebec (archivedhereandhere). Multiplefireswerereportedfollowing the 2021revelationthat ground-penetrating radar detected possible human remains at the formerKamloops Residential Schoolin British Columbia, one of several Catholicboarding schoolsset up a century ago in Canada to forcibly assimilate Indigenous children (archivedhereandhere). A CBC Newsinvestigationfound 33 churches had burned down between May 2021 and December 2023, withonly tworuled accidental. Fourteen of those fires took place on reserves and in First Nations. Datafrom Statistics Canada shows a peak of 155 police-reported hate crimes targeting Catholics in 2021, but it does not indicate that Christians have been the main target of such offenses in recent years. In 2025, the government agencyreportedthat about 3 percent of religiously motivated, police-reported hate crimes in Canada targeted Catholics, while 71 percent were directed at Jews and 18 percent at Muslims (archivedhere). Read more of AFP's reporting on misinformation in Canadahere.

headline: Sharp rise in girls hospitalized in Germany for eating disorders
body of the article: The number of girls aged 10 to 17 hospitalized in Germany for eating disorders more than doubled over the 20 years up to 2024, the Federal Statistical Office reported on Tuesday. The number rose from around 2,800 in 2004 to approximately 6,000 in 2024, it said. The sharp rise meant that the proportion of girls in this age group treated for an eating disorder in 2024 was almost half of all patients treated at 48.1%, whereas 20 years earlier, it had been 24.9%. The number of people overall treated for eating disorders increased by 2.2% between 2023 and 2024 to 12,400 cases. The office said the most common diagnoses in 2024 were for anorexia, with 9,000 cases requiring treatment, and binge-purge disorder, or bulimia, with 1,300 cases. "Across all age groups, girls and women are more frequently treated as inpatients for eating disorders than boys and men," it said. Two years ago, 92.9% of people treated with this diagnosis were female. In 2004, the proportion of female patients was 88.5%.

headline: Commonwealth visitors restore listed country house
body of the article: Twenty-four architects and heritage specialists from across the Commonwealth are helping to restore part of a Grade II*-listed country house. Attendees from countries such as Barbados, India, New Zealand and Trinidad and Tobago are taking part in repairs to the stable block at Wentworth Woodhouse in Rotherham to learn heritage craft skills. As part of the three-week summer school, which is part of the Commonwealth Heritage Forum and the City & Guilds of London Art School, the students will work on the Grade I-listed stables alongside experts. Karishma Nanhu, from Trinidad and Tobago, said: "When I get back I'm going to share as much information as possible with my colleagues." The aim is for the visitors to learn transferable skills that can be used to protect heritage sites in their own countries. Nanhu, who works at the National Trust of Trinidad and Tobago, said: "It's such a privilege to be here because we don't have the opportunity to learn these skills in my country and as a result of that, the craft skills are dying out." Wentworth Woodhouse was chosen for its national architectural and heritage importance and because it is undergoing a major restoration requiring specialist skills. Most of the participants are working in heritage [BBC/Tom Ingall] The Commonwealth delegation includes a lime specialist, archaeologists, architects, conservationists and construction specialists. They were repairing sash windows more than two centuries old, cleaning statues from the early 1800s, and lime pointing. Rebecca Austin, 26, from New Zealand, said: "I usually work in an office typing on a computer, so it's been really fantastic to come and learn hands-on in this beautiful place with amazing, passionate people who know so much knowledge and so much expertise." The policy advisor for the New Zealand Ministry for Culture and Heritage said her country's stately homes were smaller so it had been "quite mind-boggling" to see the scale of the restoration required. "I want to learn more about the actual crafts and the hands-on expertise because the craftspeople are the backbone of our heritage sector." Peter Sandiford was cleaning one of the statues [BBC/Tom Ingall] Peter Sandiford, 55, an architect from Barbados, was cleaning one of the statues. He said: "It's basically just learning how to use what solvents to dissolve the pollutants without damaging the marble itself." He said it was "a lot of fun" and also important to learn the skills to "protect" heritage when they returned home. Krishna Priya Panicker is an architect in India and said: "The way we conserve our buildings is also very different." She said she wanted to "know how the conservation actually worked" because in India the communities near heritage sites were less connected to them compared to in the UK. "When I came here to Wentworth, I saw a lot of community engagement happening. We are trying to engage with the community back there [in India]," she said. Simon Gill said it was an amazing opportunity to share skills [BBC/Tom Ingall] Head of heritage at Wentworth Woodhouse, Simon Gill, said: "It's such an amazing opportunity to work with all these people from every corner of the world. "They're applying the skills that we're teaching them here back at home, but they're also bringing in their skills." He said these skills could be used in places like Trinidad and Tobago where the British had an architectural legacy and colonial-era buildings needed to be maintained. The Commonwealth Heritage Forum provided full bursaries to the successful 24 applicants from Commonwealth member states, covering course fees, accommodation, a stipend, and travel and visa costs. headline: Colombia earthquake death toll rises to 181 as rescue efforts continue
body of the article: Aug. 11 (UPI) -- Colombia entered a second day of search-and-rescue operations Tuesday after a magnitude-7.4 earthquake struck the country a day earlier, killing at least 181 people, injuring hundreds and destroying numerous buildings, according to local authorities. The Colombian Association of Capital Cities said the number of injured had risen to 1,310 and 153 buildings had collapsed, primarily in the country's Coffee Region and the western department of Valle del Cauca. Cali recorded the highest death toll, with 95 fatalities, followed by Pereira with 72, Quibdó, nine, and Manizales, five. Local authorities warned the death toll could rise as rescue crews continue searching damaged and collapsed structures. The powerful earthquake caused extensive damage to healthcare facilities and other infrastructure across western Colombia. In Cali, the capital of Valle del Cauca, parts of the facade of the University Hospital of Valle partially collapsed, forcing the urgent evacuation of patients. Emergency crews are focusing their efforts on buildings that completely collapsed, where an unknown number of people may remain trapped. In Cali, authorities said at least 193 people remained trapped beneath the rubble of 56 residential and commercial buildings that collapsed. The Cali mayor's office said rescuers had pulled 37 people alive from the rubble in recent hours. In one rescue, emergency crews found a mother and her 6-month-old baby alive beneath a concrete slab that collapsed inside their home. Rescuers were guided to them by a search dog's alerts and the woman's faint cries. Video posted by InfoMundo on X showed emergency crews rescuing the baby alive from the rubble as search operations continued across the city. In Pereira, the mayor's office said 53 people remained trapped in 58 structures that were destroyed in the urban area. Rescue crews prioritized 15 buildings where search dogs and acoustic detection equipment identified possible signs of survivors. Authorities in Pereira also coordinated a complex operation to evacuate 16 people trapped inside cabins of the city's Megacable aerial cable car system. The cable cars were left suspended dozens of feet above the ground immediately after the earthquake. After six hours of rappelling and vertical rescue operations by specialized personnel, all passengers were brought to safety, the mayor's office said. The national government and the Colombian Association of Capital Cities said more than 2,500 people remained missing or out of contact across the affected areas. Interior Minister Rodrigo Lara told Radio Bli that more than 300 rescuers had been deployed to the most critical collapse sites. An additional 45 rescuers from Bogotá were also sent with canine search teams. International assistance began arriving Tuesday. The U.S. government announced $15.5 million in humanitarian aid, while a 47-member urban search-and-rescue team from Ecuador, accompanied by canine units, joined the Colombian Red Cross and Colombian Civil Defense in rescue operations. The Colombian Geological Service said the main earthquake struck at 7:34 a.m. local time, with its epicenter near the municipality of San José del Palmar in Chocó department at a depth of about 60 miles. The agency described the earthquake as the longest-lasting seismic event recorded in Colombia in the 21st century, with intense shaking perceived for 40 to 50 seconds. The earthquake's intermediate depth allowed seismic waves to travel long distances through rigid rock inside the Earth without rapidly losing strength, prolonging the shaking at the surface. In parts of western Colombia, residents reported feeling the earthquake for as long as two minutes. The Colombian Geological Service has recorded more than 60 aftershocks, the strongest with a magnitude of 4.8. President Abelardo de la Espriella formally declared a national state of disaster to accelerate the deployment of financial assistance and logistical resources to the affected areas.

headline: Radio Station Falsely Declares King Charles’ Death On-Air, Blames Staffer’s ‘Curiosity’
body of the article: A staffer's curiosity turned into a genuine broadcasting crisis for one U.K. radio station this year. BBCreported on Monday, August 10, thatKing Charles III, 77, was falsely declared dead on air after Radio Caroline aired three pre-recorded statements duringThe Barry Marsh Showon May 19. The third of the three false announcements claimed "news media" had confirmed the King's death. The station then played the national anthem, played one of the three audio files again, and then a long silent pause for roughly 16 minutes. One of themessagesat the time read: "We have suspended our normal programmes until further notice as a mark of respect following the passing of His Majesty King Charles III." James Whatling / MEGA When the staffer realized what had happened, they paused the files and walked out of the office. The host, who was on a call at that time, had no idea the false announcement had already aired. It wasn't until he noticed the wrong program running that he called a station engineer, who was already aware of the incident and investigating it. HostBarry Marshaddressed the error the same day on air roughly 30 minutes later. "I've just been informed that we've played in error some information a little earlier. I didn't hear this myself, but it is incorrect. It's a technical issue, and of course we apologize," he said, according toExpress UK. After more than two months, the Office of Communications (Ofcom)released its reporton August 10, ruling the incident a breach of broadcasting standards following two formal complaints. Ofcom determined the incident violated two rules under the Broadcasting Code, one requiring news to be reported with due accuracy, and another requiring significant errors to be corrected quickly on air. King Charles visits Thurso, Caithness, UK, on the 28th July 2025. 28 Jul 2025 Pictured: King Charles visits Thurso, Caithness, UK, on the 28th July 2025. Photo credit: James Whatling / MEGA TheMegaAgency.com sales@mega.global (Mega Agency TagID: MEGA1343963_022.jpg) [Photo via Mega Agency] In their defense, Radio Caroline said the pre-recorded files are meant to be used only in the event of an actual royal death and normally come with safeguards. "These files are accompanied with 'a set of strict instructions to presenters and managers' to follow before being aired, but, out of curiosity, the member of staff played the files, which stopped the stream from the presenter's remote location, and broadcast the files on air," Ofcom's report reads. Radio Caroline said it took the matter seriously and acted as quickly as it could once the mistake was discovered. The staffer responsible was reprimanded and has since apologized, and the files in question have been moved to an external hard drive to prevent a repeat, according to the BBC. headline: Ousted Syrian dictator Bashar al-Assad sentenced to death in absentia
body of the article: A Syrian court has sentenced ousted dictator Bashar al-Assad to death in absentia, after convicting him of committing war crimes and crimes against humanity during the country's civil war. It is the first conviction against Assad,who fled from Damascus to the Russian capital, Moscow,with his family after his regime was overthrown in December 2024, ending his family's five-decade grip on power. Assad's cousin and the former head of political security in southern Syria's Deraa province, Atef Najib, was also sentenced to death. He appeared wearing a striped prison uniforminside a cage in the courtroom as the judge read out his sentence. Deraa is widely seen as the birthplace of the uprising against Assad's rule. In March 2011, the detention and alleged torture of a group of teenagers accused of writing anti-government graffiti sparked protests in the city, which were met with a violent crackdown by security forces. That response helped ignite nationwide demonstrations that escalated into civil war in which hundreds of thousands of people were killed. Syria's interim government began trying officials associated with the Assad regime, which ruled the country for more than 50 years, earlier this year. Najib is one of the highest-ranking officials to be put on trial. He was convicted of crimes including murder, "the intentional killing of children under 15" and "torture leading to death". The court also sentenced six former military and security officials in absentia to death, including Bashar al-Assad's younger brother, Maher. He ran the army's elite Fourth Division and also fled to Moscow when the regime fell. The others convicted include former defence minister Fahd al-Freij. Atef Najib appeared in a cage in court during his sentencing on Tuesday [NurPhoto via GettyImages] Outside the courthouse after the ruling, hundreds of people of all ages gathered holding pictures of their loved ones who were killed by the regime. Crowds were clapping and chanting, while cars drove by excitedly honking their horns. A group of men passed out flags. "The joy is indescribable," one man told the BBC, hoisting up a photo of his late father. "God willing we will see Bashar al-Assad and all his aides hanging on the gallows." Another woman told the BBC everyone is feeling a mix of "victory and liberation." "The voices of the victims are finally heard. Justice has been achieved!" she exclaimed. Nouha al-Masri, a prosecutor in the case, lost her brother during the March 2011 crackdown and massacre at al-Omari Square in Deraa. "We have been waiting for 15 years to reclaim even a small part of our rights, for all those who have spilled our blood, committed crimes, violated our rights, killed, and tortured us," Masri - now a member of the prosecution team, told the BBC. "Our demand is that this not be the end of the trials... In the new Syria, there will be no impunity from this day forward." Syria trial seen as first step on long road for Assad's victims The phone book that led us to Assad's spy chief in hiding Calls for justice and accountability in Syria grow after Assad's fall Itremains unclear whether Syria's new authorities will be able to secure Basharand Maher al-Assad'sextraditions from Moscow. It is not the first move against Assad by Syria's new leadership. An arrest warrant was issued against him last December on charges of murder and torture. He left for Russia as forces underAhmed al-Sharaa- now Syria's president - swept to power in a rapid, 11-day campaign that brought down the Assad dynasty. Since then, the new government has detained numerous former officials and security personnel, though most senior figures from the old regime, including Assad himself, remain out of reach in Russia. Attempts by Syrian opposition figures to pursue Assad through courts in Western countries during the final years of his rule did not lead to any convictions. Assad came to power in 2000 after the death of his father. The second son of Hafez al-Assad, he was not destined to be Syria's ruler until his brother, Basil, died in a car crash in 1994. Part of the Alawite minority, he continued to favour their dominance in many roles in the military, security and intelligence agencies. Much of his rule was defined by the civil war. Additional reporting by Lana Antaki in Damascus and Leen Alsaadi in Deraa. Bashar al-Assad: Sudden downfall ends decades of family's iron rule

headline: Investigators say Myanmar's military has escalated airstrikes against civilians
body of the article: BANGKOK (AP) —Myanmar's military has increasingly used low-cost aircraft such as motorized paragliders and gyrocopters in escalating aerial attacks that kill civilians inits conflictwith armed, anti-government groups, a U.N. investigation said in a report Tuesday. Separately, a major ethnic armed group fighting the government in Rakhine state said 20 civilians had been killed in strikes by the military so far this month. Myanmar's military government did not immediately respond to either the U.N. probe or the allegations bythe Arakan Army. In the past, the military has said it only attacks legitimate targets of war, accusing the resistance forces of being terrorists. The report by the United Nations-established Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar, or IIMM, details a yearlong investigation into alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity committed by Myanmar's military and affiliated militias, as well as the opposition armed groups. It found that abuses escalated around the country's army-organizedelectionsin December and January. The IIMM said it observed a notable escalation in aerial attacks in the months preceding the elections and that they have continued unabated afterward, with investigators also documenting a pattern of deliberate arbitrary detention, torture and sexual violence. The IIMM said civilian casualties are worsened by the military's increasing use of "double-tap" aerial attacks, in which a second strike follows the first, apparently targeting first responders, people helping the wounded and those trying to flee. The IIMM said the Myanmar military was increasingly using motorized paragliders — also known as paramotors — as well as gyrocopters and drones to carry out low-altitude airstrikes with unguided explosives. In several recent incidents in the upper Sagaing region, paramotor pilots allegedly cut their engines as they approached targets, allowing them to glide silently and leaving civilians little or no warning to flee or seek shelter, the report said. The IIMM's report came asthe Arakan Army, a powerful ethnic armed group fighting the army in Rakhine, said that about 20 civilians were killed and 22 injured in airstrikes across three townships from Aug. 1-11, including one attack involving up to eight aircraft that lasted about an hour. The military-backed government has not publicly commented on the alleged attacks. According to the Assistance Association for Political Prisoners, an independent organization that keeps detailed tallies of arrests and casualties linked to the civil war, more than 8,000 civilians have been killed and more than 31,000 arrested by Myanmar's security forces since 2021. The IIMM, which was established by the U.N. Human Rights Council in 2018 to monitor violations of international law in Myanmar, said it gathered evidence from more than 1,600 sources and witnesses that can be used in future prosecutions of those responsible. "Behind every piece of evidence we collect are people whose lives have been devastated by these crimes," group leader Nicholas Koumjian said in the report. "Communities across Myanmar are not only living under the constant threat of violence but are also coping with the profound and lasting impact of what they have endured." The IIMM said it is also investigating serious crimes allegedly committed by armed groups opposed to the military, including members of the Arakan Army, who have been accused of rape and other sexual violence against Rohingya Muslim women, summary executions, child recruitment and the destruction of mosques in Rakhine. The report said numerous people were also arrested underan electoral lawthat carries up to 20 years in prison or the death penalty for acts such as criticizing the elections online or distributing "anti-election" leaflets. The election was dismissed by the critics as a sham designed to consolidate the military's grip on power after its 2021 takeover that ousted the elected government ofAung San Suu Kyi, triggering deadly civil war.

headline: UK media regulator rebukes radio station over false King Charles death report
body of the article: (NewsNation) — A radio station in the United Kingdom breached broadcast standard when it mistakenly reportedKing Charlesdied. Radio Caroline aired three prerecorded statements that King Charles died in May,according to People Magazine. Brad Pitt breaks 7-year sobriety, now drinks in moderation In the third statement of Charles' passing, the station claimed the media confirmed the news. According to Ofcom, theU.K.national anthem played after one of the statements, which was then followed by over 15 minutes of silence. "I've just been informed that we've played in error some information a little earlier, I didn't hear this myself, but it is incorrect, it's a technical issue, and of course we apologize," "The Barry Marsh Show"host said 30 minutes after the statements aired. Britain's King Charles III meets with President Donald Trump in the Oval Office of the White House, Tuesday, April 28, 2026, in Washington, during a State Visit. (AP Photo/Alex Brandon) "News, in whatever form, must be reported with due accuracy and presented with dueimpartiality," Ofcom said in a statement Monday. "Significant mistakes in news should normally be acknowledged and corrected on air quickly. Corrections should be appropriately scheduled…" the media regulator continued. A Radio Caroline staffer was reportedly performing a maintenance on a computer when they found files made for Charles' death. Defense faces challenge from Keffe D's own words in Tupac Shakur case, attorney says Ofcom's report on the incident stated the station "explained that these files are accompanied with 'a set of strict instructions to presenters and managers' to follow before being aired, but, out of curiosity, the member of staff played the files, which stopped the stream from the presenter's remote location, and broadcast the files on air." headline: Istanbul overtakes Heathrow as Europe’s busiest airport after London hub sees passenger numbers fall
body of the article: Heathrow has lost its crown as Europe's busiest airport, with Istanbul welcoming almost 300,000 more passengers than the London hub in July. The shift comes asHeathrowhas seen a summer dip in passenger numbers, particularly on Middle East routes, while its long-running push for a third runway gathers pace. Figures, released annually by the trade body Airports Council International, reveal that Heathrow was Europe's busiest airport from 1996 to 2019. In 2020, it lost its top spot as coronavirus travel restrictions took hold. It regained its title in 2023 and held onto it until this year. Now, though, the latest figures released by the airport show that 7.86 million passengers passed through its four terminals in July – a relatively low amount. In contrast,Istanbulairport recorded 8.15 million passengers over the same month, traditionally among the busiest dates for the hubs. In simple terms, that means Heathrow's July passenger total saw a 1.5% decrease compared with the same month last year, while Istanbul saw a 2.3% boost when compared to last July. Heathrow was particularly badly hit by the ongoing Iran-US conflict, with passenger numbers across Middle East routes down 20.2% year-on-year in July. In a statement, representatives for the airport said the "case for expansion has never been clearer". It currently operates its two runways at almost full capacity, and has been seeking government permission to build a third runway for some time now. Heathrow's expansion proposal would see it able to process some 150 million passengers per year, up from just under 85 million in 2025. It's not clear when – or if – the proposal will be given the go-ahead, though. Recently sacked Chancellor of the Exchequer Rachel Reeves said she'd hoped for a third runway by 2035, but the UK's new Prime Minister Andy Burnham seems to be less keen. He previously said the plans would divert investment "away from the North and traps it in London". Despite the dip in passenger numbers,Heathrowis still very busy and popular. 19 July was its busiest day so far this year, with 267,000 passengers recorded. New airlines have also started serving the airport from July, including Italy's ITA Airways, Alaska Airlines and Riyadh Air.

headline: Ten police and 17 ‘bandits’ killed in firefight in northwestern Nigeria
body of the article: At least 10 police officers, 17 "bandits" and two civilians have been killed in clashes with a group of armed men in northwestern Nigeria. Police said on Tuesday that officers confronted a heavily armed group of around 240 bandits on more than 200 motorcycles in Kebbi State, which, like other northwestern and central states, is plagued by armed criminal gangs who carry out cattle rustling and kidnappings for ransom. The incident happened on Monday as the group of suspected bandits was travelling from Zamfara State to Kebbi, police spokesman Bashir Usman told AFP. "Tragically, we lost 10 gallant police personnel in the engagement, while two others sustained injuries and are receiving medical attention," Usman said. Two civilians were also killed in the clashes, in which 17 "bandits" were killed, although the final figures are still being assessed, he added. Northwestern Nigeria has long struggled with insecurity, with armed groups carrying out kidnappings for ransom and stealing livestock. Last month, at least 20 people were killed when bandits attacked villages in Zamfara. More than half a million people have been displaced by the violence in Katsina, Sokoto and Zamfara, according to a report published by the United Nations Institute for Disarmament Research in March.

headline: Lula's lead over Flavio Bolsonaro narrows in Brazilian election second-round, CNT/MDA poll shows
body of the article: SAO PAULO, Aug 11 (Reuters) - Brazil's President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's ‌advantage over Senator Flavio Bolsonaro in ‌a potential runoff ahead of October's general election narrowed, ​a CNT/MDA poll showed on Tuesday. Lula would receive 48.0% of the votes in a runoff, compared with 39.1% for Flavio ‌Bolsonaro, son of ⁠former President Jair Bolsonaro, according to the poll. In a June survey, ⁠Lula was seen with 49.3% of the votes, and Bolsonaro with 36.8%. In a ​first-round scenario, ​Lula would lead ​with 42.4% of the ‌votes, virtually unchanged from the June survey, followed by Bolsonaro's 28.7%, Ronaldo Caiado's 4.0%, Romeu Zema's 3.3% and Renan Santos' 2.8%. If no candidate wins more than 50% ‌of valid votes in ​the first round, the ​two frontrunners ​advance to a runoff. CNT/MDA interviewed 2,002 ‌people from August 5 ​to 9 ​in 140 Brazilian municipalities. The survey's margin of error is 2.2 percentage ​points in ‌either direction. (Reporting by Isabel Teles; Writing by ​Fernando Cardoso; Editing by Chizu ​Nomiyama and Keith Weir)

headline: Spectacular photos: Wehrmacht motorbike from Danube almost 'like new'
body of the article: The photo of the Wehrmacht motorbike recovered in Budapest is travelling around the world: from "Times of India" and "Vietnam.VN" via British media such as the "Daily Mirror" through to US platforms like Yahoo Autos, media are reporting on thespectacular find. According to Hungary's Institute and Museum of Military History, the recovered motorbike is a DKW NZ 350-1. Among motorcyclists at the time, the DKW NZ 250 and NZ 350 models were considered particularly tough and reliable. In 1944, therefore, the NZ 350-1 was introduced as a version developed specifically for wartime use. The motorbike from the Second World War is being cleaned and restored in the hangar of the Museum of Military History in Budapest. - Volksbund Deutsche Kriegsgräberfürsorge e. V. / Simone Schmid The Hungarian museum recovered the machine on 2 August at Batthyány Square, opposite the parliament. The motorbike is almost completely preserved. Saturated with water and mud when it was raised, it weighed in at more than 200 kilograms. It is currently being cleaned and conserved in the museum's hangar in Budapest. From 1944 onwards, the NZ 350-1 came as standard with metal panniers mounted on the sides, unlike earlier NZ models. - Volksbund Deutsche Kriegsgräberfürsorge e. V. / Simone Schmid The DKW NZ 350-1 was produced between 1944 and 1945, with just under 12,000 units built by the end of the war. One of the intriguing features is a small detail that is easy to overlook today: there was a kind of fin or mud and snow scraper on the rear frame. It was designed to prevent slush and snow sticking to the tyre and then getting into the chain drive. This modification apparently drew on experience of the Russian winter. Another striking feature was the engine block made of grey cast iron, an iron casting alloy with a high graphite content. One reason was the wartime shortage of aluminium. On the basis of the information published so far, however, this particular find still cannot be dated to a specific day or month of production. The company DKW traces its origins back to Danish engineer Jørgen Skafte Rasmussen. In 1907 he first established a firm for mechanical engineering and steam technology in Zschopau in Saxony. The brand name DKW was coined later and originally stood for "Dampfkraftwagen", literally "steam-powered vehicle". In 1922 the first DKW two-stroke engine was produced in Zschopau. Over the following years the company developed into one of Germany's most important motorcycle manufacturers. Even now it is clear how impressive the machine will look once restoration is complete. - Volksbund Deutsche Kriegsgräberfürsorge e. V. / Simone Schmid In 1932 DKW merged with Audi, Horch and Wanderer to form Auto Union AG. Within the new group, the DKW plant in Zschopau remained the hub for motorcycle and engine production. In the 1930s DKW was increasingly drawn into Germany's rearmament. The NZ 350 was also produced in large numbers for the Wehrmacht. The importance of the Zschopau plant is reflected in its output figures: as early as 1934, the 350,000th DKW motorcycle rolled off the production line, followed by the 500,000th in 1939. With the outbreak of the Second World War, civilian motorcycle production was gradually scaled back and manufacturing shifted more and more towards military needs. Related Mystery solved: story of Wehrmacht motorbike found in the Danube TheDKW NZ 350-1, now recovered from the Danube, comes from this late phase of the war. After the end of the Second World War, the Zschopau DKW plant was dismantled by the Soviet occupying forces. Machinery and equipment were shipped to the Soviet Union, and DKW engineers from Zschopau were also taken to Izhevsk to help rebuild motorcycle production there. The story of the NZ 350 did not end there: from 1946 the IZh-350, which was largely based technically on the DKW NZ 350, was produced in the Soviet Union. More than 127,000 units were built by 1951. The saddle, once made of leather, is surprisingly well preserved. - Volksbund Deutsche Kriegsgräberfürsorge e. V. / Simone Schmid In recent days, parts of the original equipment have also been found alongside the Wehrmacht motorbike in the dried-out bed of the Danube, including a petrol can, a Y-strap and a bayonet frog. A Y-strap was a leather harness worn over the shoulders and connected at the front and back to additional straps. It served to fasten equipment to the body, such as bread bags, ammunition pouches or water bottles. The designation 'Y' comes from the shape of the shoulder straps. A bayonet frog is the holder for a bayonet, attached to the belt or other gear. It carries the bayonet when it is not fixed to the rifle. A look at the speedometer of the old Wehrmacht machine. - Volksbund Deutsche Kriegsgräberfürsorge e. V. / Simone Schmid Beneath the motorbike, the remains of two German soldiers were discovered. Their identity tags, which are fully preserved, could now, for the first time in more than 80 years, provide information about who they were and what happened to them. A so-called 'Kuban' sleeve shield was also found. The Kuban shield was awarded in 1943 to German soldiers who had fought in the Kuban bridgehead. - Volksbund Deutsche Kriegsgräberfürsorge e. V. / Simone Schmid This badge may indicate that its wearer had previously served at the Kuban bridgehead in the Caucasus. At present it is assumed that the remains of the two men are those of the motorbike's rider and passenger. However, there is a possible alternative explanation: theHungarian Military History Institute(source in German)(source in Hungarian)believes that this spot may be a pit used for war rubble or waste that was created after the end of the siege. Apparently ammunition and items of equipment were among the things dumped there. The finds alone therefore do not yet allow any definitive conclusion as to whether the two men were on the DKW at the time of their deaths. headline: Four crew members killed in Houthi attack on Yemeni commercial vessel
body of the article: Four crew members have been killed in a Houthi attack on a Yemeni commercial vessel that was hit by three ballistic missiles while sailing through the Bab al-Mandab Strait, the Yemeni Transport Ministry said on Tuesday. The Tahama, which was carrying food supplies, came under attack on Tuesday morning, causing a fire to break out on board and damaging the ship, the ministry said in a statement. Four crew members as well as a member of a rescue team were injured, it added. The ministry said rescue teams were also targeted as they attempted to reach the vessel and evacuate the injured. The ministry identified the four fatalities as "three Pakistanis and an Indonesian sailor." The ministry condemned the targeting of civilian commercial vessels, ports and maritime facilities as "a flagrant violation of international law and international conventions and rules governing the safety and security of maritime navigation." The Iran-backed Houthi rebels have so far not commented on the attack. The Houthis seized large parts of Yemen, including the capital Sana'a, in 2014, plunging the impoverished Arabian Peninsula country into civil war. They have since been fighting the internationally recognized government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia. The attack comes amid rising tensions in the Red Sea and the Bab al-Mandab Strait, one of the world's most strategically important maritime corridors that connects the Gulf of Aden with the Red Sea.

headline: Somalia malnutrition response hit by more than 80% funding drop as child hunger surges, MSF says
body of the article: By Abdirahman Hussein and Edwin Okoth BAIDOA, Somalia, Aug 11 (Reuters) - Funding to tackle acute malnutrition in parts of Somalia has dropped by more than 80% this year, Médecins Sans Frontières said on Tuesday, even though one in every four children screened in displacement camps in ‌the southwest is severely malnourished. MSF Health Adviser Mitchell Sangma said the United States had cut its support to aid agencies in the country from $70 ‌million last year to no funding this year, leaving aid groups struggling to respond as needs rise. Other Western donors have also cut funding. "This year we have admitted 22,000 nutrition cases, more than ​80% higher than last year. When we need this massive scale-up in intervention measures, we are seeing less interest from donor support," Sangma said. At the Elbet 1 camp, a collection of makeshift tents constructed by a patchwork of tarpaulins in the southwestern town of Baidoa, parents bring their children to a clinic under a corrugated iron roof. They are weighed and measured for height and the thickness of their arms, which is an indicator of malnutrition. A July survey by MSF of 888 households in 14 displacement ‌sites in Baidoa found that one in four children was severely ⁠malnourished. One third of families said they were surviving on one meal a day, while only 2% could afford three meals. At the nearby Bay Regional Hospital in Baidoa, which treats people from the town, semi-nomadic communities and the camp for displaced, a ⁠dozen gaunt children lay on beds in one ward, some with drips in their hands as others were given oxygen to help them breathe. "My child had been sick for a month and a half, and we kept her at home. God knows we did not know that we could get medical assistance. We gave her a small amount of ​medicine, ​but it did not help," said Abdi Isse, who lay next to his child, now ​admitted for malnutrition. FAILED RAINS, CONFLICT, EXACERBATE CRISIS Somalia is facing a worsening ‌hunger crisis after repeated failed rainy seasons devastated crops, killed livestock and depleted water supplies. Conflict and insecurity have compounded the crisis, disrupting livelihoods and limiting access to food, healthcare and aid. In February, the Somali government and the United Nations said about 6.5 million people in the country faced acute hunger due to drought. MSF said it had screened more than 21,000 children under five in Baidoa since the start of the year, finding acute malnutrition rates of about 50%. Acute malnutrition is less extreme than severe malnutrition but still involves sudden weight loss and is life-threatening. The organisation said it had tripled the number of beds in its Baidoa facility, ‌which provides therapeutic feeding to patients, to 150 in recent months due to the number ​of malnourished patients. Sangma said teams were having to make difficult decisions over who to admit and ​who to discharge. The lack of food and water means those discharged ​often end up being re-admitted due to complications, he said. 'THE WORLD CANNOT WAIT FOR FAMINE' According to the United Nations, more than ‌half a million people were displaced in Somalia in the ​first three months of 2026, with drought driving ​virtually all of the movement. Women and children accounted for about 85% of those displaced. The crisis is reviving fears of a repeat of Somalia's 2022 near-famine, but aid agencies say the response is being constrained by severe funding shortfalls. MSF says there is only about $300 million available for Somalia from ​donors, compared to $2.2 billion that was provided by donors ‌in 2022 when a similar drought situation was experienced. "The world cannot wait for a famine declaration before acting," said Allara Ali, MSF's project ​coordinator in Somalia. "Action is needed now to prevent loss of lives." (Reporting by Abdirahman Hussein in Baidoa and Edwin Okoth in Naiorbi; Writing ​by Vincent Mumo Nzilani and David Lewis; Editing by Aidan Lewis and Sharon Singleton)

headline: Colombia crews search for quake survivors; Trump's secret Air Force One switch in Turkey
body of the article: A powerful earthquake has killed more than 160 people in Colombia, with rescuers still searching collapsed buildings for survivors. Plus, President Donald Trump says the Strait of Hormuz is open despite Iran's refusal to back down from its demands. And Jackie, the beloved Big Bear bald eagle whose nest captivated viewers around the world, has died after weeks of intensive care. These stories and more highlight your Unbiased Updates for Tuesday, Aug. 11, 2026. The search for survivors continues after Colombia's most powerful earthquake this century killed more than 160 people and left others trapped beneath collapsed buildings. The earthquake struck western Colombia on Monday, damaging about 1,600 buildings across the country. At least 61 totally collapsed. Just after the7.4-magnitude earthquakehit, video shows part of a building giving way as debris crashed into the street, followed by a wall of dust. But amid all that destruction, other videos show moments of hope, like when rescue crews pulled a woman alive from the rubble in Manizales, carrying her out on a stretcher and into a waiting ambulance. Now, as of Tuesday morning, the search continues, with people still believed to be trapped. Gabriel Aponte/Getty Images Alexis Munera/Anadolu via Getty Images Alexis Munera/Anadolu via Getty Images Alexis Munera/Anadolu via Getty Images Str/Xinhua via Getty Images Alexis Munera/Anadolu via Getty Images Alexis Munera/Anadolu via Getty Images Jonh Bonilla / AFP via Getty Images AP Photo/Sebastian Barros The quake was centered near San José del Palmar in Chocó, but the shaking was felt throughout Colombia and into neighboring Ecuador and Panama. The death toll has now reached at least 164,according to Reuters, with dozens more injured. Those numbers could still rise as crews reach some of the hardest-hit areas. Colombia has declared a national emergency as troops, specialized rescue teams and equipment are now moving into the disaster zone. For crews on the ground, the priority hasn't changed: find the people still buried in the rubble and, hopefully, rescue them alive. Trump said the Strait of Hormuz is open andclaims the U.S. now controls the critical shipping lane. The president told reporters Monday the U.S. controls the strait "100%" and called the navy's blockade of ships heading to or from Iran "infallible." REUTERS/Stringer Iran disagreed, insisting it controls security in the strait and refusing to fully reopen it unless the U.S. meets a list of demands, including lifting sanctions and paying Iran for war-related damage. Trump's response?Iran should pay the U.S. instead. "They asked for reparations, you might say, or they asked for money for the damage that we've done. I said, that's a good idea," Trump said. "Well, we're going to ask for money for that damage they've done over a 50-year period, whether you go SS Cole or whether you go all of the people that were so badly hurt, so badly wounded or killed, many thousands of people." Trump also said Iran should compensate the families of protesters killed by the Iranian government, including what he claims are 52,000 people killed over the past five months. He said he has instructed his negotiators to make compensation a part of any future talks. Trump publicly boarded Air Force One in Turkey last month, but he never left the country on it,according to The Washington Post. Trump had flown to Ankara for the NATO summit on the newer, Qatar-donated presidential jet. Before leaving, he said he would switch to the older Air Force One "for old time's sake," and then boarded that plane in front of cameras. But minutes later, Trump secretly got off on the other side. AP Photo/Patrick Semansky The Post reported that an airport catering truck took the president and a small group of aides across the tarmac to a third plane, an Air Force C-32A, which flew Trump to Britain. The older Air Force One also took off, with reporters and some White House staff aboard who believed the president was still with them. So why all the secrecy? U.S. officials previously told CBS News they had detecteda credible plot by Iranand its proxies to launch a missile at the plane carrying Trump. The Secret Service then moved to a backup plan. The White House said that such precautions are necessary because enemies of the U.S. have their sights set on the president. Trump hassigned an executive ordercalling for major changes to the childhood vaccine schedule, including spacing out shots and splitting theMeasles, Mumps, Rubella (MMR) vaccine. The order calls for separating the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine into three individual shots, something that is not currently available in the U.S. It also calls for childhood vaccines to be given at separate appointments whenever possible. While announcing the changes, Trumponce again raised the possibilityof a connection between vaccines and autism. "Decades ago, children received only a small fraction of the vaccines required today. In those times, people were much healthier, and of course, the high rates of autism now observed did not exist. While we do not know exactly what the cause is with respect to autism, it is essential to our research efforts that we have the very best vaccine recommendations in the entire world. So we're reducing them, we're changing it to visits over a period of a year, a year and a half, so they get 20% of what they would have gotten in one big shot - like the large glass of something." But decades of research involving millions of children have found no link between childhood vaccines and autism. The order also directs the Health and Human Services Department to conduct more vaccine research and develop a plan to make separate measles, mumps and rubella shots available. Medical groups are pushing back. The American College of Physicians called the order part of a "troubling pattern by the administration to attempt to unilaterally change vaccine guidance, rather than relying on the transparent, scientific review." And one of the sharpest responses came from within Trump's own party. Republican Sen. Bill Cassidy, who is a doctor and chairs the Senate health committee, said flatly, "This executive order is wrong." He added: "Vaccines are overwhelmingly safe. Vaccines are effective. Vaccines do not cause autism." Vaccine requirements for schoolchildren are still governed by states, not the federal government. The U.S. has a new attorney general as Todd Blanche wassworn in Mondayby federal appeals court judge Emil Bove, a former Trump attorney. Blanche won Senate confirmationearly Saturday in a razor-thin 50-to-49 vote, with every Democrat and two Republicans, Susan Collins and Lisa Murkowski, voting against him. Blanche has already overseen investigations into several Trump opponents, including former FBI Director James Comey. But Blanche said he feels no pressure to placate the president. At the same time, he said the president has both the "right" and "duty" to involve himself in Justice Department matters. Blanche had already been leading the Justice Department on an acting basis since Trump fired Pam Bondi in April. Jackie, the beloved bald eagle seen by millions around the world,has died. She was about 14 years old. For years, people watched Jackie and her mate, Shadow, build their nest, weather snowstorms, care for their eggs andraise their young, all through a livestream high above Big Bear Lake in California. People truly fell in love with them. Rescuers saved Jackie last month after she was found weak and unable to fly following a fight with two younger eagles. She spent more thanthree weeks at the Ojai Raptor Center, where veterinarians discovered she was severely anemic. They gave her a blood transfusion and round-the-clock care, but never found what was making her so sick. She died early Monday morning. Jackie leaves behind a lasting legacy. She and Shadow raised several eaglets, including Luna and Sandy, who fledged just this summer. The Ojai Raptor Center via Facebook The Ojai Raptor Center ended its message about Jackie with this: "To everyone who cared about patient 26-519, thank you. Thank you for your messages, your prayers, your encouragement, and for standing beside our team throughout these past weeks. We are deeply grateful for the way patient 26-519 brought people together through a shared love of wildlife." For anyone who spent years checking in on that nest - this one hurts. So we'll borrow the words from the people who knew her best: soar free, Jackie. Raul Ortin/Getty Images Social media is unrecognizable from the era of status updates, "it's complicated" relationships and "tag yourself" memes. Now, users are more likely to see a carousel of strangers' divorces than a cousin's wedding photos, or to read a 400-word personal essay aboutB2B salesthan a status update from a friend "on my way to softball practice!" Feeds are flooded withShrimp Jesus, "verified" artificial intelligence"doctors" selling supplementsand "viral" trendsthat might actually serve to gather data for their hosting platforms. Anestimated 41% of long-form content on LinkedInis AI-generated, TikTok and Instagram are rife withundisclosed paid political contentand randomPR, and platformscontinually roll outAI integrations that no one asked for. headline: 7.4-Magnitude Earthquake Strikes Colombia: Death Toll Rises as Survivors Search Through the Ruins
body of the article: A powerful 7.4-magnitude earthquake tore through western Colombia on Monday morning, killing more than 100 people, collapsing buildings across several cities, and turning the first days of a new presidency into a national emergency. The earthquake struck at around 7:34 a.m. local time, with its epicenter near San José del Palmar in Colombia's Chocó department, sending strong shaking across western Colombia and into neighboring countries, including Ecuador and Panama. The tremor was felt in major cities such as Cali, Pereira, Quibdó and Manizales, but the heaviest destruction was concentrated in areas closer to the epicenter. Authorities reported thatthe death toll climbed as rescue teams reached more affected areas, with at least 111 people killed and dozens injured. More than 1,600 buildings were damaged, including 61 that completely collapsed,leaving communities searching through rubble and waiting for answers about missing relatives. For President Abelardo de la Espriella, who had taken office only days earlier, the disaster became his first major test of leadership. He declared a national emergency response and coordinated rescue operations as officials attempted to reach the hardest-hit communities. For people living through the earthquake, the first moments were defined by confusion, fear, and the desperate search for somewhere safe to stand. Residents across western Colombia described buildings shaking violently, furniture falling and people rushing into streets as the ground continued moving beneath them. In Cali, one of Colombia's largest cities, residents gathered outside damaged buildings as emergency crews inspected structures and searched for people trapped inside. Some volunteers joined rescue efforts, helping remove debris while officials assessed the damage. One survivor, Álvaro López, described watching his building suffer severe damage while a neighboring structure collapsed. He remained nearthe scene with his dogas rescue workers searched through the destruction around him. Across affected communities, many residents chose to stay outdoors after the earthquake because they fearedweakened buildings could collapseduring aftershocks. The earthquake did not affect every region equally. Some cities became the center of Colombia's rescue operation as officials counted casualties and searched damaged buildings. Image Credit: stockvideo24/ Shutterstock The city of Pereira, in Risaralda department, was among the hardest-hit areas. Reports indicated dozens of deaths there, along with widespread structural damage and collapsed buildings. Rescue workers searched damaged areas while hospitals treated injured residents. In Valle del Cauca, where Cali is located, authorities reported major destruction, including collapsed buildings and residents trapped inside damaged structures. Early assessments indicated that Cali alone had around 20 collapsed buildings. The earthquake also hit Chocó, where the epicenter was located. The region's remote geography made rescue operations more difficult because some communities were harder to reach after roads and communication systems were affected. Among the images that showed the scale of the earthquake's power was the damage to one of Colombia's most recognizable religious landmarks. In Manizales, theCathedral Basilica of Our Lady of the Rosarysuffered major damage when its spire collapsed. The church, known for its towering structure, became one of the most visible symbols of the destruction left behind. The damage was not limited to historic buildings. Homes, schools, health facilities, and transportation infrastructure were also affected as engineers began checking whether structures remained safe. The earthquake arrived at the worst possible moment for Colombia's new government, placing President Abelardo de la Espriella in charge of a national emergency only days after taking office. De la Espriella announceda coordinated government response, directing emergency agencies and local authorities to focus on rescue operations, medical assistance and support for families who lost homes or loved ones. The president's government established emergency coordination efforts as officials worked to determine the full scale of the disaster. The challenge was greatest in rural areas around Chocó, where difficult terrain slowed access for emergency teams. In some locations, rescuers faced damaged roads and limited communication while trying to reach affected residents. International assistance was also offered, including support from countries such as the United States, Mexico, Brazil, Ecuador and others as Colombia began the recovery process. The earthquake lasted only minutes, but for families waiting for news, the uncertainty continued long after the shaking stopped. Emergency workers, firefighters, and volunteers moved through damaged neighborhoods searching collapsed structures and helping peoplewho had lost homesor family members. Authorities continued updating casualty figures as teams reached more areas, especially communities near the epicenter where access was more difficult. Thedamage assessmentalso revealed the scale of the rebuilding challenge ahead. Thousands of residents faced damaged homes, disrupted services, and questions about whether they could safely return. The earthquake exposed not just the power of nature, but also the challenges of protecting communities in regions where geography and infrastructure can determine how quickly help arrives. The disaster was driven by forces that have been building beneath Colombia for millions of years. The country sits alongthe Pacific Ring of Fire, one of the most active earthquake zones on Earth, where several tectonic plates continue to interact beneath the surface. Colombia's location places it between theNazca Plate, which lies beneath the Pacific Ocean, and the South American Plate. The Nazca Plate is slowly forcing its way beneath the South American Plate in a process known as subduction. Over time, this movement creates enormous pressure along faults deep underground. When that pressure is suddenly released, the energy travels through the Earth as seismic waves, producing an earthquake. For survivors, however, the science behind the earthquake mattered less than what happened in those first moments: homes damaged, families separated, buildings collapsing and communities forced to wait for help. As Colombia moves from rescue operations into recovery, officials will continue assessing the damage while thousands of residents begin the difficult process and cost of rebuilding. The earthquake serves as another reminder that Colombia's greatest challenge is not just thepossibility of powerful earthquakes, but also preparing communities to withstand them when the ground suddenly moves. After seeing how quickly an earthquake can change thousands of lives, how do you think communities can be truly prepared for a disaster of this scale? headline: Assad’s death sentence is a reminder of Ed Miliband’s betrayal. He must atone for his sins
body of the article: Formillions of Syrians, and for the relatively small band of us who tried to help them during the darkest years of the war, this week marks a remarkable landmark. An autocratic tyrant has finally had his day in court, even if, true to form, Bashar al-Assad was too much of a coward to face it himself – choosing instead to shelter beneath the coattails of another dictator,Vladimir Putin, in Moscow. A Syrian court hassentenced the ousted dictator to death in absentia, after convicting him of war crimes and crimes against humanity during Syria's brutal civil war. It is the first conviction against Assad, who fled Damascus with his family after his regime finally collapsed in December 2024, bringing to an end more than half a century of Assad family rule. After 12 years of bloody conflict, and the murder of hundreds of thousands of Syrians who had the temerity to question his dictatorship, there is at least some comfort in knowing that those who eventually deposed him might yet see justice done, should he ever be foolish enough to leave Russia. I confess to taking particular satisfaction at the unceremonious departure of most Russian forces from Syria following Assad's fall. Rather strangely,Russia Todaytried to suggest that I had somehow been responsible. I wish I could claim such influence, but the reality is rather more straightforward: it was the Syrian people who finally overthrew Moscow's puppet, and that must surely weigh heavily on Putin. Bashar al-Assad and his brother both fled to Russia after they were swept from power in 2024 - Gavriil Grigorov The parallels are uncomfortable for the Kremlin. Syrians endured decades of repression before finally turning against Assad. Russians, increasingly impoverished by lies, corruption and a disastrous war in Ukraine, may eventually decide that they have had enough of Putin too. Dictators often imagine that fear will last forever. History suggests otherwise. I had the enormous privilege of returning to Syria and Damascus in January 2025. To see a country emerging, however painfully, from the shadow of Assad and his Russian backers was extraordinary. Travelling with some of the heroic British and Syrian medics with whom we worked in Idlib over the years, and witnessing the delight of ordinary people in Damascus and Homs, is something I will never forget. For those of us who witnessed theconsequences of Assad's brutalityfirst-hand, the chemical weapons attacks remain particularly seared into the memory. These weapons are outlawed for very good reason. Yet Assad repeatedly used them against his own people, while the international community repeatedly failed to impose consequences. The sarin attack on Ghouta on Aug 21, 2013, which killed more than 1,500 people, should have been a red line. Instead, the Western world decided to do nothing. In fact that decision was basically made by one man:Ed Miliband. As Labour leader at the time he ensured that Parliament voted against any British intervention. This caused support for action to collapse in other nations and Assad's murderous campaign continued. That failure matters today because Putin has watched and learnt. Russia has repeatedly used chemical agents on the battlefield in Ukraine, exploiting precisely the weakness that Assad discovered. There will, understandably, be scepticism about Syria's new government. Its roots are complicated, including connections to jihadist movements, and nobody should pretend that bringing down an authoritarian system magically produces liberal democracy overnight. Syria is now under the control of Ahmed al-Sharaa, a former al-Qaeda militant who spent time in US military detention in Iraq and allegedly had links to Islamic State - Omar Sanadiki But perfection is not the test. After decades of dictatorship, torture, chemical attacks and Russian interference, an 80 per cent solution is better than the 100 per cent catastrophe that preceded it. I have watched Syrian friends whom Britain gave sanctuary from Assad return to Damascus to help rebuild their country, some now holding senior positions in government. Britain has an extraordinary opportunity here and seems to be failing to seize it. If Ed Milibandwants to atone for his sins of 2013, there is an obvious place to start: now that he is Foreign Secretary he should reopen the British Embassy in Damascus and put serious diplomatic weight behind Syria's attempt to rebuild. Given the depth of British experience and influence among Syrians, it would be both practical and morally right. And if the Foreign Secretary is looking for an ambassador, I have one or two names in mind. Assad's sentence should finally send a message that dictators must hear. War crimes and crimes against humanity do not simply disappear because the perpetrator has an army, a palace or a powerful friend. Eventually, they catch up with you. Assad may be hiding in Moscow today, but history has a very long memory. Assad's protector Vladimir Putin would do well to remember that. headline: France bans unsolicited telemarketing calls
body of the article: France has banned unsolicited telemarketing phone calls, in what a consumer group is hailing as a "small revolution" for the sales industry. From Tuesday, unsolicited calls are prohibited for businesses in all sectors - but there are some exceptions. Calls will only be permitted if they relate to a contract a person has already entered into or the company has obtained prior consent to be contacted for marketing. "It cannot be stressed enough that peace and quiet is a right, and it is time to stop exposing consumers to unwanted solicitations," consumer advocacy group Que Choisir Ensemble, said in a statement. "This observation also holds true online and on the street, which are saturated with demands to consume," group president Marie-Amandine Stévenin added. She said the group had long been advocating "for an end to the automatic assumption that someone in their home or private life is a potential customer." "This is a victory for consumers, the vast majority of whom do not want to receive sales calls," she said. But the law change has riled some business groups, and officials in Morocco, where the call centre sector is heavily reliant on the French market. One government minister estimated the telemarketing restrictions could lead to the loss of up to 50,000 jobs, according to a report in Moroccan newspaper Le Matin. The head of France's direct-selling trade association, the Fédération de la Vente Directe (FVD), also criticised the reforms for adding what he said were administrative burdens for businesses. "You'll have to obtain written consent from your customer, and you'll also have to keep proof of that consent," Frédéric Billon said in comments reported by the New York Times. According to a 2025 parliamentary report, 97% of people are annoyed by telemarketing calls, with the authors wryly noting it is "one of those rare issues that unites people in France". The same report found 72% of French people reported being contacted on their mobile phones at least once a week, while 38% said they were called once a day. Germany, Austria and Italy are among the European countries that impose significant restrictions on telemarketing calls, often referred to as cold calls. In the UK, most telemarketing calls are legal provided the recipient has not objected to the call and their number is not on a statutory list of people or businesses who do not want to receive calls.
