headline: At least 169 killed and more than 600 injured in Colombia's biggest earthquake in years
body of the article: Colombian volunteers and rescuers sifted through rubble with bare hands and buckets on Tuesday, hunting for survivors following a massive 7.4-magnitude quake that has claimed the lives of at least 169 people and injured more than 600 others. The quake struck several cities across Colombia's picturesque coffee region and Pacific shortly after 7:30 am on Monday, sending panicked residents onto the streets and damaging at least 1,500 buildings. "People ran out naked, people jumped from the second floor of their homes" Wilmer Cuesta, a law student in Quibdo told the AFP news agency, recounting violent temors. Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella, just three days after being sworn into office, declared a state of emergency and vowed a concerted rescue effort. In Cali, volunteers quickly went to work with picks, basic tools and their own hands to try to find survivors. Andres Felipe Mejia was among those who joined a makeshift crew. "We are trying to get everyone out alive," he told AFP. "One of the rescuers asked anyone trapped to whistle and someone whistled back." Rescue workers and residents search through the rubble after an earthquake struck Cali, 10 August, 2026 - Santiago Saldarriaga / AP "They pulled out a man and a baby, but the wife is still in there," he said near a pancaked multi-storey building. Rescuers formed human chains to remove bricks and masonry, stopping every few minutes to listen for signs of life from those trapped below. "A lot of people have come, with supplies, with food, helping the firefighters, helping the people," he said. There were scenes of destruction in several cities, with furniture and fabrics sandwiched between concrete, walls and floors tossed into irregular angles and cabling strewn across roads. The devastation comes less than two months after powerful twin quakes rattled neighbouring Venezuela, killing over 6,300 people and leaving tens of thousands homeless. Colombia's President Abelardo de la Espriella leaves after leading an earthquake response meeting in Bogotá, 10 August, 2026 - AP Photo Hospitals in five Colombian cities were put on red alert on Monday and a nighttime curfew was declared in Cali, according to local authorities. At least six local airports suspended operations, the civil aeronautics agency said. Authorities warned the toll could rise as rescuers searched collapsed buildings across several cities. In Manizales, an AFP journalist saw many damaged buildings, including the crumpled tower of the city's beloved neo-Gothic cathedral. Dentist Julian Pena was at home in Quibdo when he felt "very, very strong" shaking. "People were praying in the street. It was overwhelming," he told AFP. "I ran outside carrying nothing and found hundreds of people there." "There are many buildings with gaps, with cracks. There are others that have completely collapsed." The quake was felt across Colombia, including the capital Bogotá, where crowds of people rushed out into the street in their pyjamas. At a depth of 110 kilometres, the quake was also felt in neighbouring Ecuador and Panama. Rescue workers and residents search through the rubble after an earthquake struck Cali, 10 August, 2026 - AP Photo Experts at the US Geological Survey said the quake was likely caused by movement along a deep fault within the Nazca tectonic plate. All upcoming professional football matches have been postponed. Messages of support came in from countries across the region and the world. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the United States was "closely monitoring" the situation and "stands ready to support the people of Colombia." The US later announced $15.5 million (€13.4 million) in emergency relief. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the EU had mobilised Copernicus, the bloc's satellite service, to help with rescue operations. France, Mexico, Ecuador and Israel also offered assistance.

headline: Released hostage Sagui Dekel-Chen performs songs written in captivity at Kibbutz Nir Oz concert
body of the article: The Israel Festival event, titled "From Captivity to the Lawn: Stories and Songs," drew 3,000 attendees, including bereaved families and other former captives. In an emotional homecoming, formerhostageSagui Dekel-Chen performed a special concert on Monday night on the central lawn of Kibbutz Nir Oz, the community from which he was abducted during the October 7 attacks. The Israel Festival event, titled "From Captivity to the Lawn: Stories and Songs," drew 3,000 attendees, including bereaved families and other former captives. The concert marked the first public debut of nine songs Dekel-Chen authored, composed, and mentally cataloged throughout his 498 days of captivity in the Gaza Strip. Flanked by a live band and joined by prominent Israeli artists – includingIdan Raichel, Marina Maximilian, and the band Hatikva 6 – Dekel-Chen detailed the psychological role music played during his confinement. "In captivity, the music I knew kept playing in my head," Dekel-Chen told the audience. "Initially, it served as a sedative. Later, it became a weapon to maintain sanity." Dekel-Chen described nightly routines where he held imaginary conversations and storytelling sessions with his daughters. Morning routines involved pacing the corner of his cell while visualizing dancing with his wife to tracks by Israeli singer Rita. Sagui Dekel Chen sends message to the remaining hostages, February 15, 2025. (credit: IDF SPOKESPERSON'S UNIT) The debut material captures a stark juxtaposition between trauma and domestic hope. In "Song of Songs," Dekel-Chen sings, "We used to sing at the top of our lungs, now I sing in silence." Another piece, "Don't Know Your Name Yet," is dedicated to his youngest daughter, who was born while he was in Gaza. In "The Song for Me," Dekel-Chen articulates his psychological struggles post-release, noting that while he fears nightmares and lingering trauma, his primary fear was "returning to an empty house." During the performance, Dekel-Chen recounted the events ofOctober 7, detailing his engagement with the kibbutz civilian response team, his wound, and his abduction. He admitted that because he witnessed explosions and gunfire at his residence during his capture, he spent nearly his entire captivity believing his family had been killed. To survive, Dekel-Chen said he deliberately maintained a falsehood in his own mind that his children were alive. When informed by captors on February 12, 2025, that he was scheduled for release within three days, he ceased the self-deception and began mathematically planning funerals for his daughters, assuming the worst. Upon his release, he discovered his family had survived. Kibbutz Nir Oz suffered severe casualties and abductions during theOctober 7 attack. The concert's artistic director, Itay Mautner, rejected the notion that the musical event was a form of escapism, framing it instead as an essential, public processing of ongoing regional trauma. Speaking after the event, Prof. Jonathan Dekel-Chen, Sagui's father and a professional historian, characterized the concert as dual-purpose. "On one hand, it is a prayer of gratitude that Sagui returned on his own two feet," he said. "On the other, it is a prayer for everything that was lost here in Nir Oz. The grief, the loss, and the difficulty of the abandonment remain with us forever."

headline: Key Amazon cases reach Brazil’s Supreme Court following Lula's defeats in Congress
body of the article: SAO PAULO (AP) —Brazil'sSupreme Court is set to weigh a series of cases in the coming days that could reshape protections for the Amazon rainforest and theIndigenous communitiesthat depend on it. The cases span from Indigenous land rights, recent rollbacks on environmental safeguards and infrastructure projects. Despite their differences, they share a common path to the court. In recent years, a mostly conservative Congress approved measures that environmentalists say violate constitutional rights.President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva,whose administration has pursued a more environmentally focused agenda, vetoed some measures outright and parts of others. But lawmakers overrode those objections, and the disputes ultimately reached the Supreme Court, which environmental advocates increasingly view as the last line of defense against the weakening of environmental protections in Brazil. The cases illustrate the constraints facing the Lula administration. Despite notable achievements inreducing deforestationanddirecting resources to foster ecological investments, the government has often struggled to counter a conservative Congress where agribusiness interests wield significant influence. "The government is very weak in the legislative arena," said Suely Araújo, a policy coordinator at the Climate Observatory, a network of environmental nonprofits. "It often opposes anti-environmental bills, but it lacks the political strength to persuade Congress to vote with it." The Lula administration is not only outnumbered in Congress, but also has less leverage to negotiate than previous Brazilian governments. In recent years, lawmakers have gained greater control over the federal budget, a key tool of political bargaining. Agribusiness, one of Brazil's most powerful economic sectors, also holds a majority in Congress and has pushed through measures that weaken environmental protections. As a result, the Supreme Court has emerged as a check on Congress, helping preserve parts of Lula's environmental agenda when lawmakers push in the opposite direction. The office of the president's chief of staff, which coordinates the government's relations with Congress, said in a statement to The Associated Press it would not comment on cases pending before the Supreme Court. Brazil is the world's largest producer of soybeans and beef. While most Brazilian beef is consumed domestically, most soybeans are exported. From January through July 2026, China, Brazil's largest trading partner, bought 50% of its beef exports and 70% of its soybean exports, according to official trade data. The expansion of Brazil's agricultural frontier, particularly for cattle ranching and soybean production, is the country's leading cause ofdeforestation, much of it in the Amazon. The Parliamentary Agricultural Front did not respond to a request for comment. Agribusiness groups have long said they oppose illegal deforestation and point to increased agricultural productivity even as forest clearing has declined. Protecting the rainforest is critical to tacklingclimate change. The Amazon helps regulate climate and rainfall patterns and stores vast amounts of carbon that, if released, could further accelerate global warming. On Friday, Brazil's Supreme Court began reviewing final motions seeking clarification of a 2025 ruling that rejected the"time limit" thesis,a legal theory backed by the agribusiness caucus that would restrict Indigenous land claims to territories they occupied or were under legal dispute when the Constitution took effect on Oct. 5, 1988. Supporters say the cutoff provides legal certainty for landowners. Indigenous groups argue it disregards decades of expulsions and forced displacement, particularly during Brazil's agricultural expansion in the 20th century. The justices are considering motions filed by the government, political parties, farmers and Indigenous organizations, with votes due by Aug. 18. Among other issues, they are expected to address compensation rules and possible deadlines for completing Indigenous land demarcations. Ricardo Terena, a lawyer with the advocacy organization Articulation of Indigenous Peoples of Brazil, said some of the proposals could effectively stall future demarcations by adding administrative hurdles and broadening compensation rights for non-Indigenous occupants, allowing them to remain on disputed land until payment is made. The Kawahiva Indigenous people, who remain isolated and uncontacted in the Amazon, is one of the many communities who may be affected by the proceedings. Authorities confirmed their presence in Mato Grosso state in 1999, but only completed the physical demarcation of their territory, mapping it out earlier this month. According to the nonprofit Survival International, the remaining Kawahiva are nomadic hunter-gatherers who survived attacks and disease and continue to avoid contact with outsiders. On Wednesday, Brazil's top court is also scheduled to consider two other significant sets of cases: state laws that led tothe end of the soy moratoriumand anew environmental license lawthat fast-tracked approval of strategic infrastructure projects. In January, major grain traders withdrew from the soy moratorium, a nearly 20-year-old pact credited with reducing Amazon deforestation by barring soy grown on cleared land. The agreement collapsed after top soy-producing states passed bills revoking tax benefits for participating companies. Justice Flávio Dino issued an injunction temporarily halting the state legislation, and the full court is now set to review his order. Also on Wednesday, the court is expected to consider a challenge to the new environmental licensing law that took effect in February. The law fast-tracks permits for projects with significant impact, including mines, highways, and industrial plants. Araújo of the Climate Observatory said she expects the Supreme Court to strike down at least what environmentalists consider the law's most clearly unconstitutional provisions, including those allowing self-licensing for projects with moderate environmental impacts. She added the law is already having tangible consequences in the Amazon, citing thepaving of a controversial highwayand plansto dredge a major riverwithout adequate prior environmental review. The environment ministry has defended the soy moratorium, saying it helped reduce Amazon deforestation even as Brazil expanded production. On the environmental licensing law, the ministry said the government had sought to veto provisions it considered problematic and remained concerned about maintaining minimum national standards. "Brazil needs an environmental licensing system that is more efficient, predictable, technically robust and capable of addressing the challenges of an economy that must expand infrastructure investment while confronting climate change and biodiversity loss," the ministry said. ___ The Associated Press' climate and environmental coverage receives financial support from multiple private foundations. AP is solely responsible for all content. Find AP'sstandardsfor working with philanthropies, a list of supporters and funded coverage areas atAP.org.

headline: Emerging anti-immigration sentiment in Japan obscures a surprising history of strategic engagement with Islam
body of the article: A recent increase inanti-immigrant sentiment in Japanhas led people from some religious and ethnic groups who were not born in Japan to face hostility. Hate speech has spread on social media, and some mosques have been targeted with abusive messages. Over the past five years,the number of Muslims in Japan has nearly doubled, from 230,000 in 2019 to 420,000 at the end of 2024. Most Muslim immigrants areworkers from Southeast Asia and South Asia. All this has been unfolding amid a larger demographic change. The population of mixed-race Japanese children, known as "hafu," or half, has also increased in Japan over the past three decades. The number of children born in Japan who have one or two non-Japanese parentsreached 4.66% in 2023, up from just 1.3% in 1987. A long-standingmyth that Japan is a homogeneous society, which has often been linked to Japanese "racial purity," has exacerbated anxieties over demographic change. This is despite the reality that Japan has its own indigenous population in the north of the archipelago,known as the Ainu, as well as generations of Japanese of ethnically Korean, Chinese and Ryukyu, or Okinawan, heritage to complicate the landscape. Along withJapan's falling birthrate, these immigration patterns have accelerated fearsamong politicians and ordinary Japanesealike about racial purity andwhat constitutes "Japaneseness." What many don't know is that Japan has a largely forgotten and complex relationship with Islam and Muslims that predates contemporary immigration patterns. As aJapanese scholar of Islam, I have studied how Muslims perceived Japan during the 19th and early 20th centuries. In the early 20th century, the Japanese government used positive perceptions of Japan among Muslims to build alliances with Muslims across Asia as part of its geopolitical strategy. Unlike much of Asia,Japan was never colonized. Instead, in the late 19th century, Japan started tobuild its own empire, exerting influence over Korea as well as Manchuria, an important area of modern-day China that borders Korea, Russia and Mongolia. Japan's victory over Russia in theRusso-Japanese War of 1904-05established it as a major world power. An illustration of the Russo-Japanese war.PHOTOS.com/Getty Images Plus For the Muslim-majority regions that had once seen themselves as centers of learning and power, European domination over parts of Asia – including South Asia and Southeast Asia, Africa and the Middle East – was seen as humiliating. Muslim thinkers debatedhow to revitalize their societies and overcome colonial domination. For some Muslim intellectuals and travelers, Japan's modernization and its victory over Russia was proof that Asian nationsneed not be subservient to Europeor abandon their own cultural traditions. Japan's victory over Russia inspired such admiration that it gave rise to an unlikely, false rumor around the time of the Russo-Japanese War:the Japanese emperor would soon convert to Islam. According to these circulating reports, the Japanese population too would also convert out of loyalty to their emperor. These rumorsmay have started in Indiaand subsequently circulated in Indonesia, then a Dutch colony. People believed that a newly MuslimJapan would lead the Muslims of Asiain anti-colonial resistance against the West. At the time,steamships and the printing pressenabled people and ideas to travel farther and faster across the globe than ever before. Newspapers in Arabic, Urdu and Persian, published in cities such asBombay, now Mumbai, Calcutta, or Kolkata, Istanbul, London and Cairohelped in spreading religious and political ideas across the globe. Despite this publishing boom from the 1860s to the 1920s, however, most people in South Asia, Southeast Asia and the Middle East still hadlittle direct knowledge of Japan. That lack of firsthand knowledge made it easier for the rumors to spread and seem credible. For many Muslim reformers, Japan represented a non-Western model of modernity. Egyptian activist and lawyer Mustafā Kāmil Pasha described Japan as the "rising sun to Egypt's sun that has already set." Hesaw Japan as an emerging global power, at a time when Egypt had fallen behind economically, militarily and intellectually. The rumors, while untrue, did offer Japan an opportunity to position itselfas an anti-colonial leader. Japanese military intelligence seized on the potential of finding allies among the world's Muslims. Important figures in Japanese military intelligence supported anideological movement called Pan-Asianism. This movement sought to promote the political, cultural and economic unity of Asian peoples under Japanese leadership by stressing their common Asian heritage. Yamaoka Mitsutaro.Yamaoka Kōtarō, 山岡光太郎 via Wikimedia Commons Secretive Japanese Pan-Asianist organizations cultivated alliances and met with Muslims to build networks with Muslims in China, Russia and India. Japan sought to build alliances against Russia, Great Britain and other European nations. One notablePan-Asianist group was the Kokuryūkai, or Black Dragon Society, founded in 1901. Black Dragon Society members forged relationships with Muslim nationalists in Russia and in the Ottoman Empire in order tobuild a pro-Japanese network. One of the members of the Black Dragon Society wasOmar Yamaoka, born Yamaoka Kōtarō. Yamaoka was among a handful of Japanese Muslims who had converted to Islam as a political and strategic act, while remainingideologically committed to Japanese imperialism, the Japanese emperor, and Shinto as a religion. Japanese Muslims like Yamaoka could travel throughout Muslim majority countries without attracting unnecessary attention. They could build networks and report their findings back to the military in Japan. For decades, Japan continued with this strategy and evendeveloped an Islam policy in the 1930s. The goal of Japan's Islam policy, or "Kaikyō Seisaku," was to build Japan's sphere of influence across Asia. It fostered alliances with Muslims in China, Russia, Central Asia and the Caucuses, Southeast Asia and India as part of this policy. Japan's empire expandedin the decades leading up to World War II. However, it collapsed when Japan experienced a catastrophic defeat in 1945. Japan wasoccupied by the United States, and the emperor was stripped of his semidivine status. In the decades since then, Japan haslargely adopted a pacifist stancethat disavows its imperial past. Today, amid Japan's shrinking population and anti-immigrant sentiment, it might be jarring to remember that there once were hopes that Japan would be the anti-colonial leader of the world's Muslims and that some of Asia's Muslims dreamed of an Islamic Republic of Japan. headline: Urgent help needed to restore fire-ravaged reserve
body of the article: The public's help is "urgently" needed if a fire-ravaged heathland habitat described as a "jewel in the crown" of nature reserves is to be restored. Large parts of RSPB Minsmere, on the Suffolk coastline, were damaged by a wildfire which broke out on 29 July. It also tore through neighbouring Dunwich Heath. Firefighters spent about two weeks tackling the inferno, which engulfed an area the size of 210 football pitches. The landscape could take as long as 25 years to recover. The RSPB has launched an "emergency fundraising appeal", which its area manager for Suffolk, Adam Rowlands, said could make all the difference. "Minsmere has an incredible track record of habitat restoration, and, with public support, we can now begin helping nature recover," he said. "We urgently need people's support - the quicker we can raise the funds needed, the sooner we can start restoring this precious landscape and giving wildlife the best chance of recovery." Adam Rowlands, from the RSPB, is hoping the public will help fund the restoration of Minsmere [Jamie Niblock/BBC] The blaze destroyed about 150 hectares (370 acres) of heathland, making it one of the "most significant incidents" to ever impact the reserve and neighbouring land. While many birds – including Dartford Warbler, Woodlark and Nightjar - were able to escape the flames, the habitats they rely on were severely damaged. Slower-moving wildlife such as adders, invertebrates and rare butterflies, meanwhile, may have suffered significant losses as a result of the "devastating" fire. "The scale of the damage is heartbreaking. Recovery will take decades," added Rowland. "Whilst some species will have escaped the fire itself, the destruction of their habitat will be felt for many years to come." Do you have a story suggestion for Suffolk? Contact us below. headline: Former Syrian President Assad sentenced to death in absentia
body of the article: A Syrian court sentenced ousted Syrian PresidentBashar Assadalong with his younger brother to death in absentia on Tuesday for crimes against humanity and war crimes during Syria's 14-year conflict that left about half a million people dead. The sentences at the Fourth Criminal Court in Damascus are the first against Assad or members of his inner circle since the Assad family's five decades in power came to an end 20 months ago. "Bashar Assad used state agencies to commit war crimes and crimes against humanity," said Judge Fakhareddine al-Aryan during a court session that was aired live on state TV. Former Assad-era Prison Chief Convicted Of Torture In Us Federal Court, Marking A Historic First In this Dec. 9, 2010 file photo, Syrian President Bashar al-Assad arrives at the Elysee Palace in Paris for his meeting with French President Nicolas Sarkozy. Also sentenced to death in the same case was Assad's maternal cousin Atef Najib, who was convicted of overseeing a crackdown in the southern province of Daraa that led to the uprising and later thecivil war. Amid tight security, Najib stood inside a cage wearing a prisoner's uniform as the judge read the sentence. A crowd of people gathered outside the courthouse in central Damascus to hear the verdict. Syria's new rulers have asked Russia to hand the Assads over. Brief Alcohol Ban In Damascus Sparks Concerns About President Al-sharaa's Vision For Syria Najib, who wassanctionedby the U.S. Department of the Treasury in April 2011, was later detained and is one of the highest-ranking officials to be put on trial. Najib is a former Syrian army brigadier general who was head of the Political Security Branch in southern Syria's Daraa province under Assad in 2011. During his tenure, more than a dozen teenagers who scrawled anti-government graffiti on a school wall in Daraa werearrested and tortured. The case became a catalyst for mass protests against the repressive policies of Assad's security forces. Syrian soldiers assemble near Sweida on July 15, 2025, as black smoke rises following deadly sectarian clashes in the southern province. The protests were met by a brutal government crackdown and spiraled into a 14-year civil war that ended with Assad's ouster in a lightning rebel offensive. headline: Ebola outbreak in DR Congo kills more than 2,000
body of the article: Ebola has killed more than 2,000 people in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) in the latest outbreak, which is nearing the country's deadliest ever. The current outbreak, which has hit the DRC's conflict-plagued eastern and northeastern regions, was declared on May 15 but is thought to have already been spreading for several weeks. It is the DRC's 17th surge of the highly contagious disease and is already considered the largest in the country's history "and could well become the largest outbreak ever", Sania Nishtar, chief executive of the Gavi global vaccine alliance, has said. According to figures released on Tuesday by Congolese health authorities, 2,011 people have died in the latest outbreak, out of 4,381 confirmed cases of the virus. The latest toll puts it close behind the DRC's deadliest Ebola outbreak in 2018 to 2020 when nearly 2,300 people died out of 3,500 recorded cases. The surge began in northeastern Ituri province and spread to several other provinces, notably North Kivu, regions where health infrastructure and a state presence are largely lacking. The case fatality rate of the current outbreak is estimated by Congolese health authorities to be 45.9 percent. "We haven't reached the peak yet," Health Minister Samuel Roger Kamba said in an interview shared on X by his ministry on Tuesday. "Within the next three months, we expect to have already brought the spread under control and to start seeing it decline," he added. - 'Slow' response - Insecurity due to the presence of armed groups and mistrust of the local population have hampered the response to the outbreak in the affected regions. "We are only seeing 30 percent (of infected people), where 70 percent of people are dying at home. This is why this Ebola is different," Mohamed Yakub Janabi, the World Health Organization's regional director for Africa, told reporters in Ituri's provincial capital, Bunia, on Monday. Congolese virologist Jean-Jacques Muyembe, who helped discover Ebola in 1976, said in an interview with Tuesday's Le Monde newspaper that the response had been "slow and ineffective". "There is an internal problem at the level of the national coordination of the response," he said. "Everyone wanted to show they were doing something, even though nothing had actually been organised," he added. - Clinical trials - On Friday, WHO vaccine experts recommended a full-scale human trial of the only existing approved Ebola vaccine to see if it offered cross-protection against the strain of Ebola currently spreading in the DRC against which no specific vaccine currently exists. The Ervebo vaccine has proved safe and efficacious against the more common Zaire strain of Ebola virus and WHO experts said that early data, notably from animal trials, showed it may also give some protection against the rare Bundibugyo strain exploding in the DRC. The Gavi global vaccine alliance -- set up in 2000 to help developing countries acquire affordable vaccines -- maintains a stockpile of 500,000 Ervebo doses. It said doses from the stockpile were to be made available for the trials, with some already in the DRC. Two potential Bundibugyo vaccines are in the early stages of clinical trials on humans, while a third is being worked on to bring it to that stage. Ebola is spread by contact with bodily fluids and causes a haemorrhagic fever. It has killed more than 15,000 people in Africa in the last 50 years. clt/kjm/rh

headline: Off sick for up to ten years: What lies behind Germany's teacher shortage
body of the article: Germany's schools are facing a structural staffing crisis. More teachers have been hired and the federal states are trying to counter this by creating additional posts, recruiting lateral entrants and offering financial incentives. Yet in many places there are still not enough staff to cover all lessons in full. There is a particularly chronic shortage of teachers in the STEM subjects – mathematics, computer science, physics and chemistry. There is also a continuing nationwide or regional need in special needs education as well as in art and music. According to the latest projection by the Standing Conference of the Ministers of Education (KMK), there is a calculated shortfall of around 27,000 fully qualified teachers in Germany. How dramatic the situation can become in individual regions is currently illustrated by Brandenburg. Education Minister Gordon Hoffmann (CDU) warned in June that the state would probably no longer be able to guarantee the standard timetable everywhere in the coming school year. The situation is particularly difficult in rural areas and in subjects such as biology and chemistry. The situation also remains tense in North Rhine-Westphalia. Although the state now has more than 166,000 teaching posts, more than 7,770 positions were still unfilled most recently. Berlin is an example of how sickness-related absences exacerbate the already strained staffing situation. According to the city's education administration, 380 teachers have been on sick leave for at least a year. This emerges from a reply by the Senate to a parliamentary question from the MP Alexander King (BSW), first reported by the Berliner Morgenpost. Related Education comes in different forms: How do Europeans feel about vocational training? They include 225 civil servants and 155 salaried teachers. In total, Berlin employs around 35,000 teachers. More specifically, 143 civil servant teachers have been absent for at least a year, and a further 50 for at least two years. According to the education administration, 18 teachers have even been on sick leave for at least ten years. Primary schools are particularly hard hit, with 98 teachers out on long-term sick leave. Secondary schools are missing 54 teachers, grammar schools 34 and vocational schools 27. Related From playing games to building rockets: Portugal's Ubbu brings coding to primary school There are also long-term absences among salaried teachers: five of them have been on sick leave for at least ten years, and 16 for at least five years. The BSW MP Alexander King attributes this development, among other things, to the tight staffing situation: inadequate staffing levels increase the workload on those still in post and can in turn encourage further sickness-related absences. In Hesse, according to the Ministry of Education, around 225 of the approximately 67,000 teachers have been ill for at least a year, 16 of them for more than five years. Common causes cited include psychological strain and physical complaints. Related 'It will be easy to employ me' - Portugal pushes vocational training to fill skills gap In North Rhine-Westphalia, teachers in 2025 were on sick leave on average for 8.43 per cent of working days – more than in the state administration as a whole. Secondary modern schools (Hauptschulen) were particularly affected, with a sickness rate of 9.83 per cent. In Saxony-Anhalt, around 8.6 per cent of lessons in the 2024/25 school year were cancelled because no cover could be provided. It is impossible to say how many teachers nationwide have been off sick for at least a year. Why? The federal states collect and publish different sets of data. North Rhine-Westphalia, for example, distinguishes according to the duration of illness, while other states use other categories. The term "long-term illness" is also defined differently and in some states can apply to sick leave lasting more than 30 days. Surveys in individual states nevertheless show that there are at least several hundred such cases. Many teachers are over 50. According to the Federal Statistical Office, in the 2024/25 school year exactly 35.4 per cent of teachers at general education schools were at least 50 years old. Some 25.4 per cent were between 50 and 59, and a further 10 per cent were 60 or older. The German education system is therefore facing a major wave of retirements in the coming years. At the same time, it takes several years to train additional teachers. Demand for teachers is likely to continue rising for the time being. According to the Standing Conference of the Ministers of Education, there were just under 11.2 million pupils in Germany in 2024. By 2032 the number is set to rise to almost 11.8 million, an increase of around 5.3 per cent. After that it is expected to fall slightly again because of smaller birth cohorts. By 2040, however, around 11.3 million pupils are still expected. This text was translated with the help of artificial intelligence. Report a problem : [feedback-articles-en@euronews.com].

headline: Lebanon becomes first Arab country to abolish the death penalty
body of the article: In a landmark change to Lebanon's penal system, the country's parliament on Tuesday approved legislation abolishing the death penalty, replacing it with life imprisonment with aggravated hard labour, the state-run National News Agency (NNA) reported. The vote makes Lebanon the first Arab country to formally abolish the death penalty. Justice Minister Adel Nassar, who attended the parliamentary session, described the vote as a "historic step" for Lebanon. The measure was approved by a majority of the 128-member parliament, though Hezbollah's parliamentary bloc opposed it, according to parliamentary sources. The draft legislation, submitted to parliament in October 2025, was backed by seven lawmakers from different parliamentary blocs. The proposal, put forward by member of parliament (MP) Abdul Rahman al-Bizri, was amended before it was approved. Under the amended law, crimes committed before the legislation takes effect will be punished by life imprisonment, while offences committed after it takes effect will carry aggravated life imprisonment, NNA reported. The abolition follows years of campaigning by Lebanese and international human rights organizations. Human Rights Watch had urged parliament in July to pass the legislation, saying Lebanon should formally end its long-standing practice of retaining death sentences despite an unofficial moratorium on executions since 2004. Lebanon's National Human Rights Commission had also repeatedly called for the abolition of capital punishment. In June, the commission welcomed progress on the draft law and urged lawmakers to remove both the death penalty and hard-labour sentences from Lebanese legislation, arguing that punishments should respect human dignity and serve rehabilitation.

headline: ‘Maybe You Want to Revise the Way You Say That’: Woman Approached an Indian Man at a Restaurant to Tell Him He Did Not Smell Like Curry, He Responded With Perfect Composure
body of the article: An X post from @RajeevSharma00 shared a video showing a woman approaching an Indian man eating with his family at a restaurant. In the exchange that follows, the woman interrupts the meal by saying, "Excuse me sir, you smell quite nice for an Indian man." When the man asked her to repeat herself, she said, "You smell quite nice for an Indian man. You don't smell like curry." The woman made a racist remark referencing a stereotype about Indian people's scent. The man asked, "Is that intended to be a compliment?" The woman replied, "Yes, quite." He responded, "It's actually not," to which she said, "No, that's odd. You smell quite nice for an Indian man." He told her, "Okay, that's very odd the way you say that. Maybe you want to revise the way you say that." She replied, "Okay," before walking away from the table. The X user who shared the video said the comment was disrespectful regardless of the woman's claim that it was a compliment. He said the man was dining with his daughters and remained composed throughout the interaction, adding, "You can tell that hurt him a little bit." The man's response showed restraint he didn't think he would have been able to match himself, saying, "He's trying to be a good example in front of his kids," and adding that he believed most people would have reacted less calmly to being approached that way in front of their children. Several replies questioned the basis of the stereotype altogether. One commenter wrote, "Where does such things even come from!?!? What smelling got to do with Indians who bath daily!?!? It doesn't even make sense. Internet slop has emboldened idiots whose own family and friends don't even care about. Just stupid folks." Another traced the stereotype to colonial times. They wrote, "That accent sounds like a Brit. That's where the curry slur took its birth [sic]. Funny thing there's nothing called curry in any of cuisines in subcontinent. It's above and beyond time we keep giving sharp responses. I'm glad he did." The X user then talked about similar racist remarks aimed at Indian people, describing the "over lived" nature of such comments toward Indian people generally. The user suggested the woman sought attention online through such interactions, though this characterization could not be independently confirmed. Another praised the man's composed reaction. They wrote, "It's commendable how he responded. In a restaurant, people would be the relaxed self and would fumble this. I would have fumbled and then got the perfect retort in the shower the next day!" The Daily Dot was unable to independently verify the identities of those involved in this video, or confirm the claims made about the woman's other online content referenced by the person who shared the clip.

headline: King Charles’ Death Was Mistakenly Announced by British Radio Station
body of the article: A U.K. radio station has been reprimanded by media regulator Ofcom after mistakenly broadcasting a pre-recorded announcement falsely claiming thatKing Charles IIIhad died. The Office of Communications (Ofcom) hasreleased its reporton the incident that occurred on Radio Caroline on May 19 duringThe Barry Marsh Show. The regulator said it received two complaints about the situation, in which regular programming was interrupted by three pre-recorded statements claiming that King Charles (77) had died. According to the Ofcom report, the third statement said that "news media" had confirmed the passing of King Charles. The U.K.'s national anthem then played, followed by one of the statements being repeated. This was followed by about 16 minutes of dead air. Regular programming then resumed, with the host apologizing to listeners. "I've just been informed that we've played in error some information a little earlier, I didn't hear this myself, but it is incorrect, it's a technical issue, and of course we apologize," the host said. Radio Caroline explained how the situation happened, noting that the host was streaming his show from a remote location. At the same time, a staffer was performing maintenance on a studio computer when they came across the files prepared for King Charles' death. "These files are accompanied with 'a set of strict instructions to presenters and managers' to follow before being aired, but, out of curiosity, the member of staff played the files, which stopped the stream from the presenter's remote location, and broadcast the files on air," the station said. After the staffer realized what had happened, they stopped playing the files and, in a panic, left the building. Meanwhile, the show's host was on a call and hadn't noticed that the messages had mistakenly aired. Once the host realized, he contacted a station engineer, who confirmed they were investigating the situation. Related Ofcom said the station breached two rules under the Broadcasting Code, including "News, in whatever form, must be reported with due accuracy and presented with due impartiality" and "Significant mistakes in news should normally be acknowledged and corrected on air quickly." Radio Caroline added that they "took the matter very seriously, and much activity was taking place during those 30 minutes leading up to the apology." They also noted that the staffer who played the files was "reprimanded" and has "since apologized." King Charles revealed hiscancer diagnosisin February 2024 and has been undergoing treatment. In December 2025, the monarch shared an update, saying, "Thanks to early diagnosis, effective intervention and adherence to 'doctors' orders', my own schedule of cancer treatment can be reduced in the new year." The type of cancer has not been identified, but King Charles added, "Early diagnosis quite simply saves lives." Read the latest entertainment news onTV Insider.

headline: Germany drops probe into sabotage of naval vessel for lack of evidence
body of the article: A probe into sabotage of a German naval vessel in a Hamburg shipyard has been dropped for lack of evidence, prosecutors in the northern port city said on Tuesday. Spokeswoman Mia Sperling-Karstens told dpa that Hamburg prosecutors remain convinced that corvettes were tampered with. "However, it could not be established with the degree of certainty required to justify bringing charges which of the two suspects carried out the alleged act," she said. A 38-year-old Romanian and a 55-year-old Greek were released in March after their arrest warrants had to be lifted. They had been arrested in Hamburg and Greece in early February. The men were alleged to have carried out acts of sabotage on several corvettes last year while working at the Blohm+Voss shipyard in Hamburg. They were suspected of putting more than 20 kilograms of abrasive blasting grit into the engine block of one of the vessels, puncturing fresh-water supply lines, removing fuel-tank caps and disabling circuit breakers for the electronics on the corvette Köln. It remains unclear who was behind the tampering. In its latest annual report, the Military Counterintelligence Service (MAD) warned of espionage and sabotage activities originating from Russia. The German armed forces are among the institutions in Germany considered most at risk. In January, laws targeting so-called disposable agents who carry out acts of sabotage for foreign powers were tightened. "Disposable agent" refers to an untrained person recruited, for example, through social media and paid a small sum to cause damage.

headline: Syrian court sentences Bashar al-Assad in absentia to death
body of the article: More than a year and a half since the overthrow of former Syrian president Bashar al-Assad, a Damascus court on Tuesday sentenced him, his brother and several close associates to death, finding them guilty of premeditated murder, torture and crimes against humanity. Outside the courtroom, people erupted in cheers, even though it is unclear if or when al-Assad will face justice, as he is currently in exile in Russia, which has refused to date to extradite him. His brother Maher al-Assad, known as "The Butcher" and several other associates are also in Russia. But al-Assad's first conviction is a long-awaited moment for Syrian society in coming to terms with its own history after nearly 14 years of a brutal civil war that saw millions leave the country, many seeking refuge in Germany. "This is not the end of the road, but rather an important milestone on the path to justice, reparations for the victims and the upholding of the rule of law," officials in the courtroom said. Al-Assad's government was overthrown by a rebel alliance led by the Islamist group Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS), or the Organization for the Liberation of the Levant, which Syria's current interim president, Ahmed al-Sharaa, had led. Syria has been struggling to find its footing ever since. The transitional justice system also faces challenges. One the few former officials who could face punishment in Syria is a cousin of the former president, Atef Najib. He was head of the political security service in the southern province of Daraa when the protests first erupted in March 2011. Najib was also sentenced to death. Daraa is considered the cradle of the uprising against al-Assad. The first mass protests were triggered by the arrest of young people who had sprayed anti-government graffiti on the walls of their school. Security forces violently suppressed the protests, igniting the civil war. The court unanimously decided to impose the harshest sentence on Najib, sentencing him to death, Judge Fakhr al-Din al-Arian said. According to the indictment, Najib was accused of "systematic mass murder" and arbitrary arrests. Dozens of people gathered in front of the Palace of Justice in Damascus during the announcement of the verdict, which was televised live. Cheers and shouts of joy erupted after Najib's sentencing. Expressions of jubilation were also reported in Daraa. The trials are part of Syria's new transitional justice system. Following the political upheaval, the new leadership began prosecuting high-ranking officials of the former government. Since the end of April, trials have been taking place before the newly established Fourth Criminal Chamber of the Palace of Justice in Damascus, where Tuesday's sentences were handed down. These trials are intended to clarify, among other things, who ordered violence, who was involved in torture, and where mass graves are located. At the same time, the justice system is meant to deliver justice to the victims in the country and strengthen the rule of law in the new Syria. For a long time, a fair prosecution of those responsible was not possible in Syria. Proceedings against Syrian nationals were therefore conducted abroad, including in Germany and France. Now, Syrian courts must deal with the long civil war's legacy that cost more than 500,000 people their lives, according to estimates. In many cases, the trials concern the prosecution of crimes including systematic torture, mass murder, violent suppression of peaceful demonstrations, and torture resulting in death, often involving minors. Critics note that so far the proceedings have focused primarily on representatives of the former government, while crimes committed by other armed groups, including jihadist factions and rebel militias, have largely been ignored. Others see the trials as an attempt to appease the population and foreign partners politically. The next hearing will be in the case of Wassim al-Assad, another cousin of the former president.

headline: Colombia scrambles to find survivors as quake kills 169
body of the article: Colombian volunteers and rescuers cleared rubble with their bare hands to search for survivors early Tuesday after the country's strongest earthquake in a decade killed at least 169 people and smashed dozens of buildings. The 7.4-magnitude quake struck cities across Colombia's western region shortly after 7:30 am (1230 GMT) on Monday, sending panicked residents onto the streets, AFP journalists saw. The quake killed 169 people and injured more than 600, according to an association of Colombian city mayors. The deaths were concentrated in Cali, Pereira, Manizales, and Quibdo. The mayors also reported that 165 buildings collapsed. Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella -- just three days after being sworn into the job -- declared a state of emergency and vowed a concerted rescue effort. The city of Pereira, which was among those hit hardest, was mostly plunged into darkness amid power outages on Monday night as volunteers probed for signs of life under collapsed buildings. "We're without power. This seems honestly like a zombie city," resident Juan David Gaitan told AFP. Tattoo artist Andres Hernandez said he was worried about his family and friends, adding that he would stay awake because structures around him were "on the verge of collapsing." Hernandez recalled being asleep at home when the quake happened and rushing into the street for safety, as the quake devastated the city in the heart of Colombia's coffee-growing region. "It was a movie scene, because I saw the poles, the cables, everything moving. I'm worried about my family, my friends," he said. There were scenes of destruction in several cities, with furniture and fabrics sandwiched between concrete walls, floors tossed into irregular angles, and cabling strewn across roads. In Manizales, the quake crumpled a tower of the city's beloved neo-Gothic cathedral. In Quibdo, the capital of Colombia's Choco department, local official Jenny Rivas said public services and communications "have been virtually shut down." "People ran out naked, people jumped from the second floor of their homes," Quibdo resident and law student Wilmer Cuesta recalled. Dentist Julian Pena said he "ran outside carrying nothing" after feeling strong tremors and found hundreds doing the same. "People were praying in the street. It was overwhelming," he told AFP. "There are many buildings with gaps, with cracks. There are others that have completely collapsed." - Overnight searches - The quake was felt across Colombia, including the capital Bogota, where crowds rushed out into the street in their pajamas. At a depth of 110 kilometers (68 miles), the quake was also felt in neighboring Ecuador and Panama. Experts at the US Geological Survey said the quake was likely caused by movement along a deep fault within the Nazca tectonic plate. Hospitals in five Colombian cities were put on red alert Monday and a nighttime curfew was declared in Cali, according to local authorities. At least six local airports suspended operations, the civil aeronautics agency said. Colombian pop megastar Shakira led the calls for unity. "All my strength and love to my homeland. Let's hold each other tight," she said. In Cali, Colombia's third-largest city, volunteers quickly went to work with picks, basic tools and their hands to try to find survivors. "Getting here was unbelievable. It felt like the end of the world -- cars and motorcycles driving the wrong way, everyone searching for their loved ones," said volunteer rescue worker Nelson Moreno. "What we need now are flashlights and goggles" to keep working through the night, he said. Rescuers formed human chains to remove bricks and masonry, stopping every few minutes to listen for signs of life from those trapped below. "We are trying to get everyone out alive," said Andres Felipe Mejia, another volunteer. "A lot of people have come, with supplies, with food, helping the firefighters, helping the people," he said. - International support - The devastation comes less than two months after powerful twin quakes rattled neighboring Venezuela, killing over 6,300 people and leaving tens of thousands homeless. Messages of support came in from countries across the region and the world. Pope Leo XIV is "deeply saddened" and "raises his prayers to the Lord for the prompt recovery of those affected by this tragedy," the Vatican said Tuesday. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Monday the United States was "closely monitoring" the situation and "stands ready to support the people of Colombia." The US announced $15.5 million in emergency relief. European Union chief Ursula von der Leyen said the EU had mobilized Copernicus, a satellite service, to help with rescue operations. Israel, Mexico, Ecuador and France also offered assistance. bur-arb/hol/ane/msp/gv

headline: As Deforestation Falls in Brazil, It Surges in Neighboring Bolivia
body of the article: As Brazil cracks down on the illegal clearing of forests, farmers and ranchers are moving into Bolivia, helping to fuel a wave of deforestation in a country where land is cheap and enforcement lax. As Bolivia faces high inflation, waning revenues from natural gas, and widespread unrest, the government is looking to soybeans and other commodity crops to drive growth,Bloombergreports. A recent influx of growers from Brazil and other countries has expanded the agricultural footprint, at the expense of native forests. In Bolivia, the acreage of original vegetation lost yearly has nearly doubled, increasing from less than 900,000 acres in 2022 to nearly 1.8 million acres in 2024, a record high, according todatafrom MapBiomas. While Brazil has stepped up monitoring and enforcement, Bolivia is still "in the first stages" of forming conservation policy, Stasiek Czaplicki, a Bolivian economist, toldBloomberg.Bolivia has imposed few constraints on the clearing of forest. According to oneestimate, the production of one ton of soy in Bolivia is associated with seven times more deforestation than the same amount in Brazil. In Brazil, deforestation in 2026 ison trackto hit its lowest level since 1988. The sharp decline comes amid a push to stem the clearing of forest by miners, loggers, and farmers under President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who returned to office in 2023. Brazil is aiming fornet zero deforestationby the end of this decade. After Decades of Drought, Water Is Rising in the African Sahel

headline: Putin Humiliated as His Vacation Home Defenses Go Up in Flames Following Ukrainian Attack
body of the article: Ukraine has dealt Vladimir Putina chastening blow. The Russian president's allegedprivate holiday residencein the southern Russian region of Gelendzhikon the Black Seacoast is thought to have cost north of $1 billion, is mired in controversy, and has become a symbol of the corrupt decades of Putin's rule. The Residence at Cape Idokopas, an Italianate complex, known widely as "Putin's Palace," is surrounded by a square-mile no-fly zone and a broader 27-square-mile buffer zone. Ukraine has now chipped away at that safety net, striking Putin's S-400 "Triumph" anti-aircraft missile launch pad, which was left "ablaze and sputtering for three hours," Ukraine's unmanned systems forces Major Robert Brovdi said, according to theTelegraph. The system was built to shoot down drones, missiles, and aircraft, but Brovdi said it had since been repurposed to fire missiles at Ukrainian cities. He added it had been used as such on Saturday. This is particularly painful for Kyiv as Ukraine has a shortage of Patriot missile defense systems, which are designed to intercept incoming missiles and drones. The shortage comes from Ukraine's European partners having too few to donate, while the U.S. is running low due to its war in the Middle East with Iran.Politicoreports that only 29 ballistic missiles out of 195 fired at Ukraine in July were intercepted. "Over the last few months, Russia fires more missiles a week at us than we get from partners over months," former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorovsaid. Russia is pressing this advantage, using the Gelendzhik instalation to capitalize on Ukraine's vulnerability. Speaking to the Telegraph, University of Oslo missile expert Fabian Hoffmann said: "While less accurate and lethal, they still represent a threat to civilian infrastructure, particularly when launched at densely populated areas." Putin's movement between his residences has become a source of intrigue during the war. Sources cited byThe Financial Timesand Russian outletIStoriesclaimed in May that the 73-year-old has stopped visiting some of his boltholes around the country and had instead opted for the safety of specific compounds and bunkers to conduct his war. Radio Free Europereported in March that he was using three separate bunkers that all looked identical due to his paranoia about assassination attempts and long-range drone strikes. The latest strikes come amid a consistent blitz being carried out by Kyiv, which has struck key logistics and energy hubs around Russia. Images of huge columns of smoke above e-commerce centers and oil refineries have circulated widely, while several Russians are thought to havebeen arrested and forced toapologize for taking the images. The ownership of Putin's Palace has long been a source of controversy. Putin insists that the immensely expensive compound does not belong to him, and was not built for him specifically in 2005. In 2021, Russian oligarch Arkady Rotenberg, a close pal of Putin, claimed that the palace belonged to him, not Putin, after a video by Kremlin critic and political activist Alexei Navalny exploring alleged corruption around it went viral in Russia. The video alleged a $1.37 billion price tag and said it was the product of "the largest bribe in history." During the video, Navalny says "[They] built a palace for their boss with this money," and claimed that the FSB owns 27 square miles around the complex, according to theBBC. Navalny's team released the video after he was arrested. He later died in a prison camp in Siberia in 2024.

headline: Opinion - Indonesia and India are jointly planning a hydrocarbon-powered future
body of the article: Amillennium ago, India's Chola Kingdom commanded the seas of Southeast Asia, forming deep mercantile and cultural ties with the Indonesian archipelago. The two developed a shared economic destiny that lasted for hundreds of years. In the 21st century, these two giants are again engaging in complementary roles on the global stage. India is now the world's most populous nation, and Indonesia the fourth. Together, they represent 1.8 billion people intent on basic survival, industrial growth, and ascending the global economic ladder. Both countries are moving deeper into manufacturing, and both must serve an upwardly mobile middle class. That means more electricity, more refined fuels, more petrochemicals, more steel, more freight, and more industrial heat. It also means more coal, oil, gas, and nuclear power — energy sources that can deliver reliable, affordable power. It is a reminder that hydrocarbons are still the future of energy. The need for fossil fuels took center stage when Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto met in Jakarta Jul. 7 to forgecloser economic ties. At the top of their agenda sat a massive expansion of energy trade and an Indian request for more Indonesian coal to feed a ravenous power grid. This is a logical arrangement in a fast-growing industrial relationship. Bilateral trade has grown more than fivefold since 2005, from less than $5 billion to nearly $25 billion. India remains Indonesia's second-largest buyer of coal and the biggestimporter ofIndonesian crude palm oil, while also sourcing minerals, rubber, hydrocarbons, pulp, and paper. In return, India supplies refined petroleum products, vehicles, telecom equipment, steel products, and agricultural goods. The Steel Authority of India and Indonesia's Krakatau Steel just agreed to ajoint venturefor making stainless steel in Indonesia. Around 90 percent of India's primary steel outputstill depends on coal. Indonesia's steel industry is similarly coal-dependent, withalmost 80 percentof production relying on the fuel. Indonesian Energy and Mineral Resources Minister Bahlil Lahadalia reported that India has expressed interest in participating in Indonesia's oil and gas sector. Once one of the largest producers of gas in the world, Indonesia recently awarded multiple exploration contracts to international oil firms. The two governments discussed cooperating on peaceful nuclear projects. Like fossil fuels, nuclear power offers dependable baseload electricity that the intermittent sources of solar and wind cannot match. Both sides also signed multiple agreements on critical minerals and supply chain technology, medical product regulation, disaster management, telecommunications, and agriculture. Recentrolling blackouts in Sumatra and Javaexposed severe vulnerabilities in Indonesia's national electricity system. State utility PLN openly admitted that constrained coal supplies were responsible for Java's crippling outages. It is impossible to grow a manufacturing hub on solar and wind, which are subject to the whims of weather. Faced with the catastrophe of energy starvation, Indonesia is rejecting green propaganda. Jakarta has delayed its timeline for retiring coal-fired power plants. In December 2025, the government quietly but firmlyabandoned plans to close the Cirebon-1 plant. India finds itself in the same boat and is making equally rational choices. Coal continues togenerate nearly 80 percent of its powernationwide. When severe weather devastated hydroelectric facilities across the subcontinent this year, India turned to coal as a substitute. India's heavyreliance on coalis projected to continue well beyond 2047. In a declaration of energy sovereignty, Indiawithdrew its bid to host the 2028 United Nations climate summit. Take it as a sign that no amount of U.N.-inspired fearmongering will deter the mission to secure affordable energy for the Indian populace. The India-Indonesia trade relationship is dismissing the apocalyptic fantasy of the climate industrial complex. These two nations, together comprising more than one-fifth of the world's population, are determined to secure the energy sources their people need to improve their lives. Vijay Jayaraj is a Science and Research Associate at theCO2 Coalition. He holds an M.S. in environmental sciences from the University of East Anglia and a postgraduate degree in energy management from Robert Gordon University, both in the U.K. He served as a research associate with the Changing Oceans Research Unit at University of British Columbia. headline: Madagascar forced to divide and share mpox vaccine as epidemic takes off
body of the article: Authorities in Madagascar are being forced to split single vaccines into fifths to try to protect as many people as possible during an ongoing mpox outbreak. The method, known as "fractional dosing", is authorised by the World Health Organization (WHO) in emergencies when there are critical vaccine shortages, but is not routinely recommended and carries a level of risk. Madagascar, the African island with a population of roughly 33 million people, is currently battlingits largest-ever outbreak of the virus formerly known as monkeypox, with at least 4,000 cases recorded so far. Another one million people are thought to be at risk of contracting clade 1b mpox, a fast-spreading strain of the virusthat emerged from the Democratic Republic of the Congoin late 2023. High risk groups include sex workers, young children, and people living with HIV/Aids. Medical workers are also at risk. "Public health authorities in Madagascar have been given too few doses to protect the at-risk population; they were initially given 30,000 doses in May, and a subsequent 30,000 have just arrived at the end of July," said Akhil Bansal, a doctor of internal medicine working on the mpox response in Madagascar and a policy fellow at the Centre for Global Development. "However, we need to vaccinate more than one million people, so we have been "fractionally dosing", or splitting vaccines, into fifths, to stretch the supply as far as we can. "This is a somewhat established approach for vaccines, but even then, the number of doses we have is insufficient," said Dr Bansal. Mpox vaccines can be difficult to procure in countries like Madagascar, which is the world's fifth-poorest country. - Simon Townsley The WHO has previously endorsed fractional dosing, where vials of vaccine are divided into smaller parts, during health emergencies. The approach – which was used in the UK during Covid – is generally considered a safe and effective way of protecting populations when vaccine supplies are limited. The method was authorised during yellow fever outbreaks in Angola and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and was also used for mpox vaccines in the US and UK in the summer of 2022, during an outbreak involving a different strain of the virus that primarily affected gay and bisexual men. Several clinical trials have found that, when administered correctly, fractional doses of mpox vaccine can provide protection comparable to full doses. But the approach also carries associated risks. One concern is the need for thousands of extra needles and syringes, increasing the risk of accidental needle re-use and the transmission of blood-borne infections such as HIV. "Madagascar has had to acquire many more needles and syringes because normally one dose is attached to one vaccine," said Dr Bansal. Fractional doses of a standard vaccine must be administered intradermally – into the top layer of the skin – rather than into the muscle. The skin contains specialised immune cells that can trigger a strong immune response, allowing smaller quantities of vaccine to be used. But intradermal injections are considerably more difficult to administer than injections into the muscle. They require skilled vaccinators to ensure the vaccine is delivered at the correct depth. They are also more likely to cause local reactions, including swelling and itching, and can sometimes leave a distinctive raised "wheel" on the skin – similar to the scars left by the BCG vaccine for tuberculosis which many people received as children before the disease was eradicated in the UK in 1980. Public health officials within Madagascar remain hopeful that they will receive additional vaccine supplies in the coming months, helping to curb an epidemic that has overwhelmed local hospitals and clinics over the past four months. But mpox vaccines are expensive, costing between $50 and $140 per dose, and can be difficult to procure in low-income countries such as Madagascar, which is the world's fifth-poorest country. The 60,000 doses delivered to the island so far have been funded largely by Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, and the WHO. Both organisations have faced significant funding shortfalls over the past year as governments, including those of the UK and US, have reduced their spending on global health. Mpox typically causes flu-like symptoms and a painful rash of swollen lesions that can spread across the entire body. For people living with HIV, the virus is particularly dangerous and can lead to severe complications, including brain inflammation, severe bacterial infections of lesions and, in rare cases, can result in death. It spreads mostly through very close physical contact, including sexual contact and through sharing towels and bed sheets. In poor countries, where people often live in closer quarters and have less access to simple infection control measures like soap and clean water, outbreaks can be particularly difficult to control. headline: Death toll rises after 7.4 Colombia earthquake, rescuers search rubble
body of the article: More than 200 people are now believed dead as rescuers entered their second day ofsearching for survivors in the rubble after a powerful magnitude 7.4 earthquake struck Colombia. The earthquake hit just after 7:30 a.m. local time on Aug. 10, with an epicenter near San José del Palmar in western Colombia, and it was felt in cities around the country. According to the U.S. Geological Survey, an estimated 10.5 million people felt the quake. Multistory buildings and homes tumbled, trapping people underneath. At least 164 people have been confirmed dead, according to authorities in multiple cities. Scores more were injured. Police, soldiers and volunteers have been combing through wreckage. Overnight, they used excavators and sometimes their bare hands to search for survivors. WATCH:Video shows moment magnitude 7.4 earthquake strikes Colombia The death toll rose to over 200 as of midday on Aug. 11 as crews continue to search. At least 85 people have been confirmed dead in Cali, about 150 miles south of where the earthquake was centered, Mayor Alejandro Eder said. Eder said more than 800 people were injured. In Pereira, capital of the Colombian state of Risaralda, authorities said 66 were dead. Whole sections of residential neighborhoods were reduced to broken slabs of concrete and exposed rooms. Residents and volunteers formed human chains, while others stood silently nearby, listening for tapping sounds or cries from below. "They've already pulled several people out, some alive and some dead. I still can't believe it — yesterday at this same time I said hello to them, and today they're gone. It's very painful," said Fernanda Gaviria, 33, speaking from a grocery shop opposite a collapsed building. Gaviria said she spent the night sleeping in a park after her own apartment building was badly damaged. In Choco, the sparsely populated province where the earthquake was recorded, 13 were reported dead. People remain trapped in debris, and teams have been working through the night looking for survivors. Eder, the mayor of Cali, said in a post to social media that at least 25 people were trapped under a collapsed building. He posted video to social media showing the response at sites with the mangled remains of buildings in the streets. Responders won't rest until everyone is found, Eder said. Carmen Yasmin Garcia, 43, a Cali resident volunteering with rescue teams, told Reuters Aug. 10 that her group helped free seven people from one collapsed building, but they were still working to free four people and a dog trapped within. "A moment ago there was scratching, but now we can't hear anything. We still have faith that the dog is alive and we can get these people out," Garcia told Reuters. "We need people with sticks and spades − the more people lending a hand the better." Contributing: Reuters This article originally appeared on USA TODAY:Death toll rises after 7.4 Colombia earthquake, rescuers search rubble

headline: Orphaned seal pup being cared for by charity
body of the article: A Guernsey animal charity says it is caring for an orphaned common seal pup which, despite its name, is a creature rarely seen around the island. The 10kg (1.5 stone) pup is believed to be no more than a couple of weeks old and was spotted between the bathing pools and the site of the old aquarium by the GSPCA's head of marine mammals Geoff George on Monday. There was no sign of its mother and "the decision was made torescuethe pup due to concerns for its welfare and weight". George said: "Common seal pups are incredibly rare visitors to Guernsey and this little one is underweight for its age. When we arrived there was no sign of its mother and it was clear the pup needed assistance." The young seal was underweight for its age when it was found alone [GSPCA] The last common seal pup which needed rescue washed ashore in poor condition in 2018, theGSPCAsaid. Unlike grey seals, which are often seen in local waters, they are seldom born in Guernsey and the animals which arrive "have often travelled considerable distances and can be exhausted, underweight and vulnerable," according to the charity. The team at the GSPA planned to asses the pup's condition and oversee its recovery. Common seals are one of two native species and can swim almost immediately after birth. They rely on their mother's milk during their first few weeks of life and can become weak and dehydrated rapidly if they do not feed regularly, the GSPCA said. GSPCA manager Steve Byrne added: "Although this young pup is very underweight, we are hopeful that with expert care and monitoring it can regain strength." headline: Afghan former Army translator raped teenage girl
body of the article: A former translator for the British Army in Afghanistan has been sentenced to seven years in prison after raping a teenager. Abdul Nabizada was sentenced at the High Court in Edinburgh on Tuesday after being found guilty at a trial last month. The 36-year-old, who has indefinite leave to remain in the UK after moving from Afghanistan, became a taxi driver and attacked a female passenger in November 2021. He detained the 19-year-old against her will after driving her to a secluded area of Joppa, near Edinburgh, then seized her mobile phone and raped her. The victim managed to escape from the vehicle and contacted friends, who found her distressed and frightened a short time later. CCTV footage from Queens Bay Crescent then showed Nabizada repeatedly returning to the area after the attack. Mr Justice Morris called it a "crime of opportunism", saying: "The jury has unanimously convicted you of committing a serious sexual assault on a vulnerable woman. The offence is an extremely serious one." Mr Justice Morris told Nabizada that his crime had a "long-lasting impact" on the victim, which she had described in a victim impact statement. "[She] was particularly vulnerable because she was intoxicated, and that should have been obvious to you," he continued. "The [assault] occurred when you were responsible for transporting her home." Nabizada continued to deny his guilt, and David Taylor, his defence lawyer, told the court how he had come to Scotland after working for the US, Danish and UK militaries – primarily as an interpreter – in Afghanistan, his homeland. The court was told that he had applied for British citizenship, and was now concerned about the possibility of deportation in light of his conviction. Mr Justice Morris said Nabizada was described in positive references submitted before sentencing as a "family man" with four children. Nabizada was sentenced to seven years and placed on the sex offenders' register indefinitely. He was also ordered not to contact or approach the victim. He attended the sentencing accompanied by a translator. Faye Cook, procurator fiscal for High Court sexual offences, said the conviction was the result of the victim's courage in coming forward and the determined work of police officers. "Officers had to piece together evidence from a range of sources to identify the offender and build the case that was presented in court," Ms Cook said. "The victim should have been able to trust that her journey home would be safe. Instead, she was seriously sexually assaulted by a taxi driver who took advantage of her vulnerability and abused his position resulting in a deeply traumatic experience." Ms Cook added: "While stranger offending is rare, Scotland's prosecutors treat every report of sexual abuse with the utmost seriousness, recognising the profound and lasting impact these crimes have on victims and communities. "I hope this conviction provides reassurance that reports will be thoroughly investigated and that [the Crown Office and Procurator Fiscal Service] will work with policing partners to ensure offenders are held accountable." Det Insp Kirsty McArthur said: "This was a shocking attack on a woman in the city, and Nabizada will now face the consequences of his despicable actions. "We remain committed to tackling sexual crimes and bringing those responsible to justice. I'd encourage anyone who has been a victim of such crimes to come forward and report it to us. "We'll thoroughly investigate and have specially trained officers and partner agencies to support you throughout to ensure those responsible are brought to justice." headline: UK Learner Drivers Are Facing Long Wait Times for Driving Tests
body of the article: Since the COVID-19 pandemic, there has been a huge backlog of learner drivers waiting to book driving teststhroughout the UK. Young drivers have often been waiting weeks, sometimes months, to be able to do their practical test after passing their theory test. Areport from the BBCrecently revealed the plight that those in Northern Ireland have been facing, with some having to search multiple times a day to even have a chance to find a test. The search is massively frustrating for those involved. The BBC highlighted the cases of some of those who have been searching for tests, and what the Driver and Vehicle Agency (DVA) has had to say about the ongoing situation. Applications have also been much higher in 2026 than they were during the February to June period of 2025, which has also contributed to the problem. In fact, such is the demand that test slots are now being made available on Sundays and bank holidays to try and ease the pressure on those looking for a test. But it is still a long waiting game for those looking to get behind the wheel. Image Credit: Bas Peperzak/Unsplash The BBC reported on Toby, from Tamnaherin, Northern Ireland, who had been attempting to get a driving test. Mother Kerryann Barr said her 17-year-old son had been checking up to five times a day to find cancellations so he could book a driving test. Toby had been looking for a driving test in Londonderry, which is relatively local to him and his family. However, thanks to the lengthy delays that he had been facing, Toby had been forced to look for tests at the centre that was 30 miles away. That is something that can cause logistical issues for the student and instructor as they try to get to a different testing centre. The DVA said that applications for driving tests had actually risen by 13 percent for February to June 2026 compared to the same point in 2025. With such high demand, test slots have now been opened up for Sundays and bank holidays to meet the demand. "Customers are advised to book the earliest available appointment and check regularly for cancellations and newly released test slots," a spokesperson for Stormont's Department for Infrastructure (DfI) said. Yet for some students, that could mean checking at various points throughout a whole day. Image Credit:Andraz Lazic/Unsplash Toby's mum Kerryann said it was becoming a nightmare for her son. "Sometimes he's been on to book the test; it's been up to 12 weeks," she told BBC Radio Foyle's North West Today. That led them to consider finding a test in the town of Coleraine, 30 miles away. However, doing so meant extra travel, and extra lessons as Toby was not familiar with the roads around the town. Some of her son's friends had also been forced to do the same to get a test. The DFI said that from April to June, there were 18,092 tests taken in Northern Ireland. That is an increase of 5.4 percent from the same period in 2025. "Demand for driving tests continues to rise," the department spokesperson said. The month of June saw a record 6,844 tests taken in Northern Ireland, and it seems like there is no sign of this demand slowing down anytime soon. However, while it is frustrating for learners, demand is still lower than it was just after the COVID-19 pandemic, when young drivers all over the UK struggled to book a test.
