headline: TV reporter films her home in ruins as massive earthquake rocks Colombia
body of the article: Credit: Instagram/@rossylemos Rossy Lemos is one of Colombia's most prominent television journalists. But on Monday, she found herself at the heart of the story after a7.4-magnitude earthquakehit the west of the country and destroyed her home. "My soul hurts," the RCN Noticias reporter said as she shared footage of her house. The roof had collapsed onto her bed. Notebooks, photo frames and computers were strewn across the carpets. She was one of the luckier ones. More than 220 people have died after Colombia's biggest earthquake of this century struck on Monday morning. More than 3,000 are still missing. The epicentre was concentrated in the western Choco region, where Lemos lives. But the impact was felt as far away as Ecuador, Panama – and Venezuela, which is still reeling from earthquakes in June that left 6,000 dead. In Colombia on Monday, many were still asleep when disaster struck at around 7.30am local time, leaving residents in their pyjamas to fumble their way out of crumbling buildings. Rescuers search for victims in a collapsed building in the La Alameda neighbourhood of Cali - Samir Rojas/Getty Images Terrified people burst out of universities, hospitals and homes, some falling over from the tremors and into strangers' arms as the ground moved beneath them. Laura Alvarez was on the eighth floor of a block of flats in Medellin, and woke up with a jolt. She said: "I almost felt like the bones of the building were rubbing against each other. I could hear all of these other sounds. "I walked out of my bed, into the living room, and everything was shaking. I thought: 'I need to get the F out of here.' "I've never felt that before. It's like I couldn't grab my keys, because my hands were so frozen. It was just this feeling of whether this building was going to collapse on me and that nobody could help me." Ms Alvarez added: "Thankfully I'm ok, but it was probably the most terrified I've ever been in my entire life." In the Valle del Cauca region, the city of Cali – known for its vibrant salsa music – has become the scene of disaster. People look for survivors in the rubble of a collapsed building in Cali - JOAQUIN SARMIENTO/AFP via Getty Images More than 188 people are missing under the rubble. The mayor said 85 had been confirmed dead. Nicol Debia, 24, told The Telegraph from Cali: "It was violent, the movement was incredible. I was lying down, I was in shock, I felt paralysed – my friends had to help me snap out of it and go to the stairs." Health centres have been overwhelmed, said Dilian Francisca Toro, Valle's regional governor, after the University Hospital collapsed, with some patients evacuated and others trapped under the rubble. Footage shows newborns in incubators being treated on the sunny streets, while patients in wheelchairs sit exhausted under the shade of trees. For Abelardo de la Espriella, the president, the earthquake is a monumental challenge in his first week in office. Known as "El Tigre" or "The Tiger", he has been keen to be seen on the front foot after the government inVenezuelawas criticised for an inadequate response to that country's earthquakes. Inaugurated last Friday, the president leapt on a private jet and announced he would personally supervise recovery efforts and install emergency centres, as well as visit suffering areas. "You are not alone. The state is present and taking action," he said, as support came in from allies in the US, El Salvador and Ecuador, among others. The worst of the impact was concentrated in Colombia's mountainous coffee region, with the highest number of deaths so far, 60, in the city of Pereira. Credit: Social Media Angie Valero Romero, of the northern town Cucuta, told The Telegraph: "It felt like strong ocean waves. I'm scared, stressed and worried about my whole family. "The death toll is doubling every hour. We're still trying to find out about friends in other cities whom we haven't been able to contact. "My uncle lost his entire veterinary practice when it collapsed. He had lots of fish tanks, and they burst because of the earthquake." For a country where nearly 80 per cent of the population is Roman Catholic, there was deep symbolism in the spire of the tallest cathedral in the country falling. Credit: Social Media "God is punishing Colombia," one social media user said as a cloud of dust filled the sky around the Cathedral Basilica of Our Lady of Rosary, in Manizales. Above Ms Lemos's destroyed bed, a rosary remained intact, along with a message above the headboard: "God is who writes our story." The devastation to Ms Lemos's home after the earthquake As night fell, rescue operations continued. Volunteers used their mobile phone torches to illuminate the rubble as rescuers picked through breeze blocks and bricks in silence, hoping to hear any sign of life. Amid tragedy, there have been some glimmers of hope. In Cali, a six-month-old baby was pulled from the wreckage, to cheers and tears of elation from the rescuers. The mother, bloodied and grey, appeared to have been shielding her child with her body. For some, the echoes of Venezuela were much closer to home. Winder and Dedivi Delfin, teenage brothers, lost their mother, younger brother and grandmother in the back-to-back quakes in June before they moved to Colombia, seeking a fresh start. But having moved with their father to Cali, the 15-year-old and 17-year-old brothers again found themselves in the middle of a deadly earthquake as their home began to shake, they told The New York Times. "Right now we're outside the house, just sitting here," their father said on Monday afternoon. The boys were too scared to go inside, he added. "But we're OK. We're here, alive." headline: North Korea Now Leans on Crime Networks to Launder Stolen Crypto: RUSI
body of the article: North Korea is increasingly pushing stolen cryptocurrency through the same money-laundering networks used by scam syndicates and organised crime, blurring the trail investigators follow, according to a research paper published this month by the Royal United Services Institute, a British defence and security think tank. The regime stole at least $2.8 billion in virtual assets between January 2024 and September 2025, funds the paper says are assumed to support its weapons programme. Authors Allison Owen and Noémi També focus on the point where that money turns into cash, rather than the well-documented journey through decentralised services. Ownership frequently changes hands before conversion, with a third party sometimes buying the stolen coins outright at a discount. One investigator told the authors that such a handover can be inferred when funds turn up mixed with proceeds from activities like "pig butchering" investment scams, or at addresses tied to entities such as Cambodia's Huione Group, whose infrastructure the Justice Departmentseized in June. Elliptic, which supplied data for the research, believes that handover often happens on the Bitcoin blockchain. DOJ Seizes Huione Infrastructure Linked to Billions in Crypto Laundering After the February 2025Bybit hack, incident responders at ZeroShadow found the regime relying on a network of launderers, over-the-counter desks and peer-to-peer traders, often Chinese nationals working around the clock. TraderTraitor, the North Korean group behind the theft, used Chinese organised crime groups to move the money and hand back cash. That overlap is the problem the paper puts to compliance teams, because once the regime's proceeds enter criminal ecosystems the markers of proliferation finance become hard to separate from ordinary laundering. The accounts doing the cashing out usually belong to someone else, with mules recruited mainly in the Philippines, Indonesia and China, where credentials sell cheaply enough to buy in bulk and open accounts at scale. Interviewees said mules told whom they are actually working for generally want no further part in it. Conversion happens in small pieces, with actors selling roughly $7,000 of stablecoins at a time on peer-to-peer marketplaces, under the thresholds that trigger bank review, while ZeroShadow found larger sums broken into $30,000 chunks so that a freeze "would not be overly impactful." Behaviour at the exchange itself offers further signals, from Astrill VPN logins to the 50 to 70 support tickets launderers now file to get a single held transaction released. Fiat rarely arrives by simple bank transfer, with proceeds from over-the-counter brokers often deposited into North Korean-controlled accounts using UnionPay cards issued by Chinese banks. The paper lists 19 Chinese banks that the Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team identified last year as used by the regime and its proxies. Of the roughly $1.5 billion taken from Bybit, 95% moved through decentralised services, and the monitoring team reported that all of it had been converted into fiat or hard currency by September 2025. Bybit Sues North Korea Over $1.5B Hack, Wins Order Freezing Assets The authors call for regulatory guidance on correspondent relationships between exchanges, standardised onboarding questionnaires, secure intelligence-sharing channels, and a VASP identifier in payment messages so receiving banks can spot them. What that leaves for victims is clear from Bybit's own accounts: the exchangeannounced Monday that it had sued North Koreaand won an order freezing identified assets, having recovered $48.4 million and frozen $30.5 million more, together about 5% of what was taken.

headline: Bashar al-Assad Convicted of Crimes Against Humanity, Sentenced to Death
body of the article: Nearly two years afterBashar al-Assad's brutal, bloody reign over Syria came to an end, a Syrian court convicted the disgraced ruler in absentia of crimes against humanity, sentencing him and his younger brother to death. The Tuesday ruling against Assad, 60, was the first from a Syrian courtagainst the dictator and his family, which ruled for five decades until a December 2024 rebel uprising. The court proceedings, which lasted four months, were aired live on state television,the Associated Press reported. "Bashar Assad used state agencies to commit war crimes and crimes against humanity," said JudgeFakhareddine al-Aryan, according to the AP. Assad's younger brother,Maher al-Assad, a former Syrian military official, was also sentenced to death during the proceeding. The two Assad brothers escaped to Russia when their heinous regime — which killed more than 200,000 civilians over 14 years, including more than 23,000 children,according to the Syrian Human Rights Network— finally collapsed. The pair were given political asylum but Syria's new leaders have asked Russia to return the two former leaders to the country. Maher al-Assad, 58, once lead the regime's Fourth Armoured Division — a group which cracked down on protesters and allegedly lead a drug trade that enriched his older brother,Reuters reported. Atef Najib, a cousin of the brothers who served as a security official in the southern part of the country, was the only family member to be tried in person and was given the same sentence, according to reports. Clad in a prison uniform, Najib, 66, was kept in a cage during the sentencing, according to the AP. As word of the death sentence rippled through Syria, crowds gathered and celebrated — with many carrying photos of loved ones killed or taken by the Assad regime. One critic slammed the dramatic sentence as "performative" and said it did little to actually bring the Assads to justice. "There is a huge problem, which is that no one will hand over a criminal to a country that issues a death sentence. This will cut off the ​road to Assad, and many other criminals, ​being handed over to Syria,"Anwar ⁠al-Bunni, head of the Syrian Centre for Legal Studies and Research, told Reuters. "This is performative justice, not transitional justice," he added. The postBashar al-Assad Convicted of Crimes Against Humanity, Sentenced to Deathfirst appeared onMediaite.

headline: Israel demolishes home of slain Palestinian involved in deadly West Bank clash
body of the article: Israeli forces on Tuesday demolished the home of a Palestinian who died in July in the most lethal clash in months in the occupied West Bank, residents and the army told AFP. The clash broke out on July 24 when a group of Israeli settlers approached the town of Tell, leaving dead one settler, one soldier and four Palestinians including Farouq Ramadan, whose home was demolished. "At around 8:15 am (0515 GMT), the Israeli army blew up the apartment where the martyr Farouq Ramadan lived with his wife and five daughters," Tell Mayor Walid Zaidan told AFP. Zaidan said that about 30 Israeli military vehicles and engineering teams entered the village Monday evening, evacuating residents of 30 houses surrounding Ramadan's home before the demolition. AFP journalists saw army engineers set up explosives and detonate the second-floor apartment where Ramadan had lived, after troops amassed from Monday evening. The army in a statement said troops "demolished the house where the terrorist who carried out the shooting" had lived. "We will continue to take proactive and offensive action to thwart terrorism throughout Judea and Samaria and to bring to justice terrorists who sought to harm the citizens of the State of Israel," it said, using a biblical name for the West Bank. Israeli army radio said the two-week timeline to demolish the house was an "unprecedented record time". Israel routinely demolishes family homes of Palestinians it accuses of being involved in attacks, seeing the policy as a deterrent, but critics say it amounts to collective punishment that leaves innocent family members homeless. Palestinians say the villagers in Tell came under attack from settlers. On July 24, footage showed Ramadan seizing an Israeli's weapon during a clash with settlers, leading an emergency response team from a nearby settlement to rush to the scene with ensuing gunfire. A military probe last week said that the soldier was killed by Palestinian fire, but could not conclusively determine whether the settler was killed by Palestinian or friendly fire. Ramadan was killed in the exchange of gunfire, but it was unclear who by. Israel has occupied the West Bank since 1967, but in recent years the number of settlements in the Palestinian territory -- which are illegal under international law -- has soared. Excluding east Jerusalem, more than 500,000 Israelis live in settlements in the West Bank, home to around three million Palestinians. According to an AFP tally based on data from the Palestinian health ministry, Israeli soldiers or settlers have killed at least 1,097 Palestinians, including both militants and civilians, since the start of the Gaza war. Israeli figures over the same period show that at least 48 Israelis, including civilians and security personnel, have been killed in the West Bank in Palestinian attacks or during Israeli military operations. if-lba/sct/jfx

headline: Many people feared trapped under rubble after earthquake in Colombia
body of the article: The death toll in the Colombian earthquake has risen to 132, the Asocapitales association, an alliance of the country's largest cities, said on Tuesday. On Monday evening, newly sworn-in President Abelardo de la Espriella put the death toll at 111. Hundreds have been injured in the 7.4-magnitude quake, one of the strongest in decades. A state of emergency has been declared. In the affected region in western Colombia around the epicentre near San José del Palmar, the quake caused numerous buildings either to collapse completely or to sustain damage. People are still believed to be trapped under the rubble. In the city of Cali alone, which lies to the south, 188 people were reported missing, de la Espriella said at an evening press conference at the scene. "This is where all our efforts will now be focused," he said. In addition to Cali, the cities of Pereira and Manizales were also badly affected. Pereira alone had recorded 66 deaths according to the latest figures from the city administration, making it the city with the highest number of victims. Eleven more people were reported missing, while 53 were believed to be trapped under the rubble, according to a post on the platform X. Fifty-eight buildings had completely collapsed. De la Espriella put the death toll in Cali at 35, with around 700 people injured. Three hospitals and around 40 buildings had completely collapsed, he said. Operations at the city's airport were also restricted. The government and local authorities had mobilized all available resources and were working together despite political differences, de la Espriella said. The quake is the first major test for the right-wing politician backed by US President Donald Trump. He visited several badly affected cities one after another. The earthquake occurred on Monday at 7:34 am (1234 GMT) near San José del Palmar in the western region of Chocó, at a depth of around 103 kilometres. Numerous aftershocks were subsequently recorded. The tremors were also felt in Bogotá, farther to the east, as well as in the cities of Medellín, Popayán and Armenia. Reports said the earthquake was also felt in Ecuador, Venezuela and Panama. "At first I thought it was something minor. But when it kept getting stronger and wouldn't stop, I thought we were going to die," a woman from Manizales told broadcaster La FM. "Part of the roof of my house collapsed, and the walls are cracked," said Juan Bernal from Armenia. In Bogotá, several hundred kilometres away, the tremors were clearly felt. "We have a four-storey building here that has completely collapsed. We have already managed to rescue three people alive," the acting fire chief in the La Alameda neighbourhood of Cali told broadcaster Caracol. The electricity supply as well as telephone and other communications networks have been disrupted. Six airports are currently closed to commercial air traffic due to damage to their infrastructure, according to the president. The cathedral in Manizales was also severely damaged. On June 24, two quakes measuring 7.2 and 7.5 struck neighbouring Venezuela within a matter of seconds. Thousands were killed. Colombia's Geological Service said there was no connection between the events. The two quakes were caused by movements of different tectonic plates: In Venezuela, the Caribbean Plate was involved, while in Colombia it was the Nazca Plate, located off the Pacific coast. The strongest quake previously recorded occurred in 1958 off the coast between Ecuador and Colombia, measuring 7.6. According to the Geological Service, only 15 people were killed. In 1999, however, more than 1,000 people were killed in the city of Armenia and nearby municipalities in a magnitude 6.1 quake.

headline: EU provides emergency funding after Colombia earthquake
body of the article: The European Union has allocated €100,000 ($115,386.5) as a first response to support emergency operations on the ground after a 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck Colombia, while the need for additional help is being mapped out. The European Commission has been working with the German Red Cross in the affected region, a spokeswoman said on Tuesday. The EU has also made available its satellite mapping services to Colombia to support rescue and relief operations. The Colombian authorities have requested additional help from the EU and the commission is gathering information on "the scope of the disaster, the needs, what is necessary on the spot," the spokeswoman said, as more support is mobilized. "Our thoughts are with the victims, their families, the injured, and all those affected," EU top diplomat Kaja Kallas said earlier on Tuesday.

headline: Ukrainian troops are buying war robots from their digital marketplace in record numbers
body of the article: Ukrainian soldiers are buying uncrewed ground vehicles from a digital marketplace in record numbers. They purchased more than 640 units in July, a 680% increase over 2025's monthly average. It reflects the surging popularity of the robots as Kyiv aims to replace troops with machines. Ukrainian troops are rushing to a digital weapons marketplace to buy record numbers ofground robots, reflecting the surging popularity of these combat machines on the battlefield. Brave1, the Ukrainian state-backedinnovation platform, said on Monday that the military has ordered more than 3,000 ground robots from its digital marketplace since it launched last year, including over 640 units in July alone. That latter figure represents a 680% increase over 2025's monthly average, Brave1 said in a statement. Yuliia Myrna, product manager for theBrave1 Marketdigital site, said in remarks shared with Business Insider that ground robots andinterceptor drones"are among the fastest-growing categories we are seeing in 2026." Ukraine launched the Brave1 Market in April 2025, granting soldiers access to anAmazon-style websiteto buy military technology, such as drones, robots, and electronic warfare systems, from thedefense industry, streamlining the procurement process. In October 2025, uncrewed ground vehicles became eligible for purchase with"ePoints,"which Ukrainian troops collect for verified kills of Russian soldiers or military hardware, and the completion of other battlefield tasks. Brave1 said the military has ordered more than 3,000 ground robots from its online market.Genya SAVILOV/AFP via Getty Images Various drone types, includingfirst-person-view(FPV) quadcopters, interceptors, andheavy bombers, are among the most popular items on the Brave1 Market by quantity. While ground robots can cost tens of thousands of dollars — typically making them far more expensive than these other drones — they serve in drastically different roles and have a longer operational lifecycle. Myrna said Ukraine is "deliberately accelerating" the integration of ground robots into combat operations, particularly for logistics andcasualty evacuation. "Military units now earn ePoints for successfully completing these missions with robotic systems, creating an incentive to replace personnel in high-risk tasks wherever possible," she said. "This creates a powerful development cycle," Myrna added, explaining that "more battlefield use generates more operational feedback for manufacturers, which leads to faster product improvements and ultimately helps us move people away from missions that can be performed by machines." Only a few Ukrainian companies produced ground robots at the start of Russia'sfull-scale invasion. Today, there are roughly 280 firms that make hundreds of different products, Andrii Hrytseniuk, Brave1's CEO, told Business Insider. Ukrainian officials have set out to replace soldiers with robots in dangerous front-line roles.Diego Fedele/Getty Images The growing popularity of uncrewed ground vehicles on the Brave1 Market reflects Ukraine's broader push toreplace soldierswith robots and drones in dangerous missions, particularly front-line supply runs. Ukrainian officials have said they want robots to handle 100% of battlefield logistics, missions that have become particularly deadly asthe "kill zone"— the drone-saturated area that surrounds the front line — continues to expand. Ukrainian commanders told Business Insider that the robots allow their units to perform critical tasks while keeping troopsout of harm's way. Grek, a UGV company commander with the 21st Unmanned Systems "Kraken" Regiment, who asked to only be identified by his call sign, said that "the stakes of removing humans from dangerous missions are significant." "Every time a person is exposed to a high-risk environment, there is a possibility of injury, loss of life, or reduced combat effectiveness," he said. "Protecting personnel means preserving experience, training, and leadership that cannot easily be replaced." If you enjoyed this story, be sure to followBusiness Insideron Yahoo.

headline: $580 million undersea cable rerouted to avoid the grave of Dobby the House Elf — company caves to fan deman...
body of the article: When you buy through links on our articles, Future and its syndication partners may earn a commission. Credit: Getty Images The Greenlink Connector, which costs $580 million (GBP 430 million) and connects Ireland to Wales via an undersea power cable, was rerouted after scores of Harry Potter fans complained that it would go through the grave of the beloved house elf "Dobby." According toThe Guardian, project manager Simon Ludlam pointed out in a BBC interview that the cable would transition underwater at Freshwater West. Unfortunately, Ludlam was unaware that this was the filming location for the site where the Harry Potter character was buried in the movie franchise. When the BBC aired the clip, the project began receiving hundreds of calls about the site. Ludlam recounted toThe Guardiana discussion with a colleague when they told him, "Apparently, we're going to go straight through Dobby's grave." He answered, "Dobby? Who's Dobby? I don't know Dobby." It seemed that the project manager was in disbelief when it was finally explained that Dobby is the freed house elf who was killed in the process of rescuing Harry Potter and his friends in the last book. "He is a fictitious character in a fictitious book — the whole thing is fictitious. What are you talking about?" Ludlam said, after which his colleague replied, "No, it's very, very serious." In the end, the company working on the project acquiesced to the demands and concerns of the Harry Potter fans and rerouted it. "A lot of people were very happy about that, and the project is now going [ahead], and Dobby's happy," the project manager said. The Shell Cottage, where Dobby is buried, is on the outskirts of the fictional town of Tinworth, in Cornwall, but the original film series shot the scene in Freshwater West. Many Harry Potter fans leave stones marked with "Here lies Dobby, a free elf," as a nod to the epitaph that the titular hero left on his grave. The National Trust, which owns the land, has previously warned pilgrims not to do so, as the area is ecologically sensitive, but it seems that people still do so. The fans' resistance to having Dobby's "grave" desecrated seemingly prevented the undersea cable from going through the area. It was instead rerouted in an area that was close to some Bronze Age remains and urns, which, ironically, are associated with human burial. Undersea cables are crucial infrastructure connecting distant locations for sending information, power, and other crucial resources. Many of them face increasing threats, especially in areas that face geopolitical pressure, likeTaiwanand the Baltic Sea, which is why companies are creating technologies to helpdetect intentional tampering. However, it seems that the one thing that the planners of this particular project did not take into account is the passion of Harry Potter fans.

headline: Bat Yam couple arrested for allegedly posing as insurance representatives, defrauding at least 75
body of the article: In exchange for their services, the couple allegedly demanded a "fee" ranging from NIS 2,000 to NIS 5,000, and in some cases up to NIS 10,000. An undercover investigation conducted over the past several months went public on Sunday after a couple fromBat Yamwere arrested on the suspicion of posing as insurance company representatives and defrauding at least 75 people. According to police, most of Periel Ben-David and Sahar Shmuel Abutbul's victims are Arabs. During the conversations, they provided victims with personal information before claiming that money owed to them was being held by theinsurance companyand that they could help them withdraw it. In exchange for their services, the couple allegedly demanded a "fee" ranging from NIS 2,000 to NIS 5,000, and in some cases up to NIS 10,000. The victims were then asked to provide a code allowing cash to be withdrawn from an ATM without a card. Police suspect the codes were used to withdraw the money, after which contact with the victims was cut off. Man in handcuffs - illustrative (credit: INGIMAGE / ASAP) During the search, police seized 10 different phones and believe that information stored on them could lead to the identification of additional victims beyond the 75 already linked to the case. Ben-David is suspected of obtaining something by fraud under aggravated circumstances, impersonation with intent to defraud, conspiracy to commit a felony, invasion of privacy, and processing personal information from a database without authorization. She is also suspected of possessing or using drugs not for personal consumption.Policesuspect the couple acted together as part of the alleged fraud scheme. Ben-David exercised her right to remain silent during questioning, a police representative said at the hearing. Her partner, Abutbul, denied the allegations against him during his initial questioning. During the hearing, Ben-David's attorney raised allegations regarding the conduct of police officers at the time of her arrest. According to the attorney, she was told that "if you cooperate, you'll get off lightly, you have children at home, we know about the six-month-oldbabywho recently underwent surgery at Wolfson." The defense attorney then asked the police representative to explain why the statement had been made. They asked for their client to be released to house arrest at her father's home, citing, among other factors, the baby's condition following the surgery. They also argued that Ben-David was not the person who went to the ATMs and physically withdrew the money. Police, however, requested that her detention be extended by nine days. Judge Zivon Alimi ruled that there was reasonable suspicion against Ben-David and that releasing her at this stage could interfere with the investigation. At the conclusion of the hearings, the court ordered that the couple remain in custody until August 12. Police are continuing to examine the seized material and determine whether there are additional victims. Ben-David's attorney is also expected to file an appeal with the Central District Court in Lod on Tuesday seeking her release.

headline: The CEVA Logistics data breach is having major knock-on effects across Europe - here's what we know
body of the article: When you buy through links on our articles, Future and its syndication partners may earn a commission. Credit: Shutterstock CEVA Logistics hack disrupted European warehouses and exposed some customer data Retailers and Valve reported compromised delivery information and service delays Clients warned of targeted scams while awaiting fuller incident details from CEVA CEVA Logistics, one of the biggest shipping and logistics companies in the world, has suffered a major cyberattack, the effects of which are trickling down to many of its clients. The details of the hack itself, however, are not yet publicly available and what little information is out there came from the affected clients themselves. CEVA has not yet issued an official statement, or filed a report with the regulators, but confirmed toTechCrunchthat the attack most likely started on July 29, 2026, and affected at least eight warehouses across Europe. CEVA Logistics is a global logistics and supply-chain company and a wholly owned subsidiary of CMA CGM, a French shipping giant. It provides freight forwarding, contract logistics, warehousing and transportation services to thousands of customers, including major companies in the consumer and retail, automotive, industrial and aerospace sectors. The company operates in more than 170 countries around the world and last year it generated $18.3 billion in gross revenue, so it is a major player and a key target for attackers. The details about the incident itself are scarce right now. We don't know how the crooks broke in (via a successful social engineering attack, or by abusing a software vulnerability, for example), how much data they stole, or if they demanded a ransom payment in exchange for deleting the stolen goods. From one of the victims, though, we have learned that some data was most likely compromised. When the effects of a cyberattack spill into the physical realm (as is the case here with eight affected warehouses) we can speculate the attack was eitherransomware, or disruptivemalware. Companies shut down parts of their IT infrastructure only when there is no other way to clear an infection or remove malicious outsiders. In the meantime, a small number of CEVA's customers confirmed suffering an attack and losing sensitive data. Among them is Bol, a Dutch online retail company, which said the incident affected two systems used for processing orders from one of its fulfillment "No bol systems were affected," it said. "However, data of customers whose orders were processed via this location may have been viewed or copied." Bol also said restoring operations at one of CEVA's locations was taking longer than anticipated. As a result, the assortment stored at the affected location was taken offline, and the products were unavailable for sale. Also, Bol is currently unable to receive goods from suppliers and sales partners at that location. A similar announcement was given by De Bijenkorf, another Dutch luxury retailer, who said that order processing, returns, and refunds, might take longer, but stressed that its stores remained open. It also said that some customer data may have been compromised, including names, contact details, online orders data and, in some cases, VAT numbers. Payment information, bank account numbers (IBANs), credit card information, usernames, or passwords, were not compromised, it was confirmed. Retail giants aside, PC gaming powerhouse Valve also notified its customers about the incident. It said CEVA ships Steam hardware to its European customers and as such, receives specific delivery-related information from Steam. This information, which CEVA retains for up to 90 days after the order, was most likely compromised. It includes names, street addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, and the type and price of ordered products. Valve warned its customers to expect fake messages, either via email, SMS, or phone, that might mention recent hardware orders. "They may quote your address back to you to prove they're genuine. They may ask you to confirm a delivery, pay a small customs or redelivery fee, or sign in somewhere to "verify" your order. Treat all of them as fake," Valve warned. The company also stressed that customer accounts are safe and that users need not do anything to secure them. Other details are missing, not just for the general public, but for the affected CEVA clients, as well. Valve said it was "pressing" the company for the full scope of what was taken and how, and added that it is notifying the relevant authorities, as well. A spokesperson of the Dutch data protection authority, Mark Schenkel, toldTechCrunchthe agency so far received 10 incident reports. Given the size of CEVA, it's safe to assume there will be others.

headline: King Charles death announced live on air in huge blunder as staff member 'panicked and fled'
body of the article: A radio station has been found in breach of broadcasting standards after it mistakenly announced thatKing Charleshad died. Essex-based Radio Caroline accidentally broadcast three pre-recorded messages, as well as 16 minutes of silence and the national anthem, on 19 May onThe Barry Marsh Show, before apologising for the error. One of the messages at the time even said: "We have suspended our normal programmes until further notice as a mark of respect following the passing of His Majesty King Charles III." Radio Caroline accidentally broadcast that King Charles had passed away (Getty Images) On Monday, Ofcom revealed the radio station had breached two rules by wrongly announcing the death of the King, who is currently enjoying his summer holiday in Scotland withQueen Camilla. Media regulator Ofcom said the incident breached Rule 5.1, which requires "due accuracy" and Rule 5.2, which requires that significant mistakes be amended quickly. The code reads: "News, in whatever form, must be reported with due accuracy and presented with due impartiality." In a statement, Ofcom said: "We considered this to have been a very significant inaccuracy about an issue of particular public importance." Radio Caroline issued a correction (Getty) The correction and apology were broadcast 30 minutes later, with Ofcom stating that the staff member who accidentally played the files "panicked and fled the premises". The on-air presenter could be heard saying: "I've just been informed that we've played in error some information a little earlier. I didn't hear this myself, but it is incorrect, it's a technical issue, and of course we apologise." Ofcom added that the files had been played "out of curiosity" when the staff member was performing maintenance and accessed pre-recorded obituary files, intended for use in the event of King Charles's death. Radio Caroline said they were streaming the programme remotely, meaning the presenter was off air, and the announcements were played instead. The station director was on a call during the inaccurate broadcast, leading to the delayed realisation and response that something had gone wrong. King Charles is alive and enjoying his summer break with Queen Camilla (Getty Images) Radio Caroline later said it had "acted as soon as possible" and that Ofcom only received two complaints. The station is run entirely by volunteers, meaning it does not have the same resources as larger broadcasters. The staff member in question is said to have been reprimanded, while the files have been moved to a studio desktop instead to prevent a repeat incident. HELLO!has reached out to Radio Caroline for further comment.

headline: Future of southern Lebanon peacekeeping uncertain ahead of UNIFIL phase-out
body of the article: Beirut, Lebanon –As time runs out on the mandate for UNIFIL, the United Nations peacekeeping force in southern Lebanon, there is still strong international and domestic support for peacekeepers in the region, devastated by an Israeli war since 2023, in which thousands have been killed. Even if another peacekeeping force is created once the UNIFIL mandateexpires at the end of the year, it will likely have fewer troops and be part of a regional agreement. "This requires Lebanese state authority and monopoly over arms, Israeli withdrawal and respect for Lebanese sovereignty, and Iranian compliance with noninterference in Lebanese affairs," Lebanese political scientist Imad Salamey told Al Jazeera. "International forces can monitor and support peace, but they cannot substitute for domestic and regional agreement to uphold it." UNIFIL's mandate began in 1978, during the Lebanese civil war. It has often been accused by all sides of not successfully implementing UN Resolution 1701, adopted 20 years ago. The resolution calls for the withdrawal of Israeli troops behind the Blue Line – the de facto border between Israel, Lebanon, and the occupied Golan Heights – the deployment of the Lebanese Armed Forces to southern Lebanon, and the disarmament of Hezbollah south of the Litani River. But implementing 1701 – currently the topic of US-brokereddirect talksbetween Lebanon and Israel – was never part of UNIFIL's original mission. "UNIFIL was never established … with powers to forcibly impose Resolution 1701 on either side of the border. Its mandate has essentially depended on monitoring, reporting, coordination, and assisting the Lebanese Armed Forces," Salamey said. "Expecting UNIFIL to forcibly disarm Hezbollah or compel Israel to withdraw or cease violations goes beyond the enforcement authority it was actually given." Analysts point out that the decision to refuse to extend UNIFIL's mandate came after the US adopted the Israeli position to oppose the mission so the Israeli military could operate in Lebanon without a monitoring body present. As negotiations continue between Israel and Lebanon, UNIFIL has found its role limited to monitoring violations. Israel and Lebanon agreed to a"framework agreement"on June 26. The agreement aims to establish so-called "pilot zones", where Israel would pull out its occupying troops and the Lebanese Army would take control and oversee Hezbollah's disarmament. UNIFIL has no role in the pilot zones, reflecting what analysts say is Israeli and US pressure to exclude them. "Under the latest Lebanon ceasefire arrangement, the US and Israel have clearly sidelined UNIFIL, along with various other members of the international community," the International Crisis Group's senior Lebanon analyst, David Wood, told Al Jazeera. "UNIFIL does not play a key role on the ground in implementing the 'pilot zones' scheme, and – unlike under the previous truce deal – it no longer occupies a seat on the ceasefire monitoring mechanism." Wood said that the approach reflects "shared US and Israeli scepticism" about UNIFIL's mission to keep Hezbollah out of southern Lebanon. Still, he said, excluding UNIFIL from any peace process has its drawbacks. "In the past, UNIFIL had helped to de-conflict stand-offs between the Lebanese and Israeli militaries, such as theeruption of gunfire[during the] Zawtar al-Gharbiyeh pilot zone's implementation," Wood said. "UNIFIL could resume this on-the-ground mediation role, along with monitoring functions, as short-term measures to prevent the situation in southern Lebanon from spiralling further out of control." As UNIFIL's mandate draws down, various states have said they are willing to contribute peacekeepers to any future force. Two European diplomats told Al Jazeera their respective countries were discussing sending peacekeepers to whichever mission replaces UNIFIL. One proposal is that the UN Truce Supervision Organization (UNTSO) could step in. The UNTSO, however, would be a much smaller force than UNIFIL, which boasted about 15,000 personnel at its peak and had approximately 7,000 in June 2026. In June, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres put forward three options to the Security Council that would see troop numbers range between 900 and 3,000. Analysts are still uncertain about what form the next peacekeeping mission in southern Lebanon will take. "It is difficult to know how an international force could help promote stabilisation in southern Lebanon, until the overall security arrangement between Israel and Lebanon becomes clearer," Wood said. If the process is not sped up, there are concerns about a security gap. "If the Security Council allows a vacuum to emerge between the end of UNIFIL's mandate and the establishment of a new international force, it could become very difficult to ever fill that gap once more," Wood said. Political scientist Salamey believes that a peacekeeping force alone cannot solve the wider issue of Hezbollah's arms and Israel's ongoing occupation of southern Lebanon. "Replacing UNIFIL with UNTSO, a multinational or a European force will make little difference without a broader political settlement," Salamey said.

headline: 'UK's first community-owned vets' among island funds winners
body of the article: What is described as the UK's first community-owned vets has been awarded more than £300,000 from the Scottish government as part of an island funding project. The local communities of Coll and Tiree bought their only practice after the previous owners retired last summer and no successor could be found. Animal Care Tiree, which uses vets visiting from the mainland, has handled almost 800 appointmentssince opening in February. It is one of 13 island projects to receive a share of £3m from the 2026-27 Islands Programme Fund, with Grimsay Heritage Centre in North Uist and Achnacroish Affordable Homes in Argyll among the others securing funds. Five islands secure funds towards carbon neutral projects 'Slow tourism' plan aims to double tiny island population Animal Care Tiree, working with development trust Urras Thiriodh and Tiree Rural Development, will use the £302,949 award to convert a former cafe at Tiree's mart into a permanent base for the vets practice. Argyll and Bute Council nominated the project for the Scottish government support. Rhoda Meek, chair of Animal Care Tiree, said: "We are thrilled. "Securing the future of veterinary care in Tiree is not only about people and animals - it is about buildings too. "A permanent, fit-for-purpose practice matters enormously for the future of crofting, which underpins so much of the island's economy, and for the households whose pets are part of the decision to stay in, or move to, an island." The Isle of Rum, viewed from a beach on Eigg, has received an award of more than £355,000 [Getty Images] The other projects to receive money are: Achnacroish Affordable Homes, Lismore, £272,506 Bendoran Marine Enterprise Hub, Mull, £345,500 Canna Contractor Accommodation, Canna, £76,000 Eigg Camping Pods Expansion, Eigg, £87,602 Gaeltec Community Hub Phase One, Skye, £393,000 Kinloch Village Road and Track Improvement Programme, Rum, £355,112 Grimsay Together, Grimsay, £600,000 Orkney's Creative Catalyst, Mainland Orkney, £71,773 Repurposing of St Rognvald's House, Mainland Orkney, £203,133 Mid Yell Pier Amenity Building, Yell, £156,496 Speldiburn Community Hub Enhancement, Bressay, £77,150 UHI Shetland Hairdressing Training Salon, Mainland Shetland, £58,779 Highland Council has welcomed the funding for projects on Skye, Rum, Eigg and Canna. Councillor Kate Willis, chair of the local authority's Lochaber committee, said: "I am delighted to see these funds going right to the heart of the challenges our island communities are facing. "They will be used to provide much-needed accommodation for workers, to support sustainable community-led development and to enhance the basic infrastructure that island populations need to thrive and grow into the future." First Minister John Swinney announced the projects which had been successful in securing funding ahead of a visit to North Uist. He said: "Our island communities have so much potential, and this funding will help them pursue ambitions rooted in local priorities, strengthening their long-term resilience and prosperity."

headline: Two in court over teens' Thailand drug courier case
body of the article: Two people accused of trafficking teenagers to Thailand as part of an international drug ring have appeared in court. Tremaine Jeanne and Jessica Sani, both 28, are charged with drug offences and conspiring to arrange the travel of another with a view to exploitation. It is alleged they used two 17-year-olds as drug couriers after they were caught with 64kg (141lb) of cannabis in their suitcases while travelling back to the UK. Theteenagers from Cardiff, were arrested in Thailand in June and remain in custody. They are being supported by the Foreign and Commonwealth Office. Four other peopleappeared at Cardiff Magistrates' Court last Friday in connection with the case. A 23-year-old man from Keighley, West Yorkshire, who was also arrested on suspicion of improper importation of controlled drugs, has been bailed. Jeanne, from Llanrumney, and Sani, from Newport, are both charged with conspiring to fraudulently evade a prohibition on the importation of a class B drug and four counts of conspiring to arrange or facilitate the travel of another person with a view to exploitation. They appeared via videolink and spoke only to confirm their names, dates of birth and addresses. They were not asked to enter pleas. Jeanne and Sani were remanded in custody and will next appear with their co-accused at Cardiff Crown Court on 4 September. South Wales Police officers were told in June the teenagers has been arrested, and launched an investigation into the "circumstances" behind their trip. A spokesman for the force said: "The children remain in custody in Thailand where they are being supported by their families and the Foreign and Commonwealth Office. "The families have been updated regarding the arrests and charges." headline: Houthi missile strike on commercial ship in Bab el-Mandeb kills two Pakistanis, one Indonesian
body of the article: Bab el-Mandeb is located between Yemen and the Arabian Peninsula, connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean. Two Pakistanis and an Indonesian national were killed in a Houthi missile strike on a commercial ship in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the Saudi state-owned Al Hadath reported on Tuesday morning. Bab el-Mandeb is located between Yemen and the Arabian Peninsula, connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean. This is a developing story.

headline: Many people feared trapped under rubble after earthquake in Colombia
body of the article: The death toll in the Colombian earthquake has risen to 132, the Asocapitales association, an alliance of the country's largest cities, said on Tuesday. On Monday evening, newly sworn-in President Abelardo de la Espriella put the death toll at 111. Hundreds have been injured in the 7.4-magnitude quake, one of the strongest in decades. A state of emergency has been declared. In the affected region in western Colombia around the epicentre near San José del Palmar, the quake caused numerous buildings either to collapse completely or to sustain damage. People are still believed to be trapped under the rubble. In the city of Cali alone, which lies to the south, 188 people were reported missing, de la Espriella said at an evening press conference at the scene. "This is where all our efforts will now be focused," he said. In addition to Cali, the cities of Pereira and Manizales were also badly affected. Pereira alone had recorded 66 deaths according to the latest figures from the city administration, making it the city with the highest number of victims. Eleven more people were reported missing, while 53 were believed to be trapped under the rubble, according to a post on the platform X. Fifty-eight buildings had completely collapsed. De la Espriella put the death toll in Cali at 35, with around 700 people injured. Three hospitals and around 40 buildings had completely collapsed, he said.

headline: ​Lieutenant-Commander Jeremy Knapp, naval aviator involved in two daring rescue missions
body of the article: Lieutenant-Commander Jeremy Knapp, who has died aged 88, was twice commended for saving life. In Borneo on November 27 1964, Knapp, then a lieutenant with 845 Naval Air Squadron, volunteered for a mission normally flown only by day: carrying a critically ill topographer 150 miles from the settlement of Nanga Gaat in Sarawak to Sibu. He flew blind through monsoon cloud, down to 100 feet, hugging a black river he could barely see through the downpour, judging his height by the reflection of the aircraft's landing light in the surface of the river. He was awarded the Queen's Commendation for Brave Conduct. Recalling the episode in an interview for the Imperial War Museum in 2016, Knapp shrugged it off as merely "a rather long night"; but colleagues judged it one of the most remarkable feats of aviation during the Confrontation in Borneo. Earlier, as a cadet, he had plunged into Plymouth Sound in a gale to rescue a stoker who had gone over the side at night, earning the Royal Humane Society Silver Medal. Worn, unusually, on the right of his uniform, it made him, to his embarrassment, the one cadet whom the inspecting officer always stopped to question. Jeremy John Donnell Knapp was born on August 4 1937 at Oxshott in Surrey, a descendant of the Yorkshire aviation pioneer John Stringfellow, who in 1848 achieved the first ever powered, heavier-than-air flight on record, with an unmanned, steam-powered monoplane. A postwar sea passage with his father, Captain A M Knapp, from Plymouth to Portsmouth, sealed young Jeremy's ambitions. Educated at St Piran's prep school in Maidenhead, and then Blundell's, Tiverton, and better at sport than in class, he passed for Dartmouth at the second attempt in 1956. As a cadet he once helped to maroon the future First Sea Lord Lt William Staveley up a mast in a bosun's chair. Lieutenant-Commander Jeremy Knapp Knapp served in minesweepers based in Malta and Singapore and in Persian Gulf frigates before turning to flying, learning on the Chipmunk at RAF Linton-on-Ouse in 1961. Converting to helicopters at Redhill, he judged them the superior art, since "there was no cruising, autopilot or safe lapse in attention." After a spell as weapons instructor with 706 Naval Air Squadron at Culdrose, Knapp joined 845 Squadron aboard Bulwark, sailing for Borneo in 1964. Flying Wessex helicopters into jungle clearings from unreliable maps, near the end of the deployment he nursed a stricken aircraft through a heavy landing after engine failure, holding it hovering while a platform was built beneath the wheels so that he could set it down and shut off the engine safely. It earned him a commander-in-chief's commendation for, as he put it, probably the only crash landing ever to be commended. In 1966 he converted to the Wasp and joined the frigate Juno as flight commander. In another incident, launched at maximum weight off Portland before the ship had steadied on course, he lost height sharply, skimmed the wave tops, and clawed the aircraft back to land partly in the flight-deck netting. Promoted lieutenant-commander, in the 1970s Knapp was senior pilot with 829 and 845 NAS, commander of 846 NAS, then of 848 Squadron in Albion, and finally of 846 again. Capable, informal and well-liked, he left the Navy in 1977, having flown 14 types of aircraft, from Chipmunks to Wessex helicopters, and logged 2,967 hours. Civilian life took him to Shell and Aberdeenshire, restoring a near-derelict house between spells of gardening, shooting and fishing, and working fortnight-on, fortnight-off as an offshore installation manager. In 1981 Shell sent him back to Sarawak to pioneer the first offshore platform off Borneo's west coast, where villagers at Nanga Gaat still remembered him. In 1983 he became a health and safety consultant at Shell, and he retired in 1994. Later the Knapps lived in Gloucestershire and Clare, Suffolk, but he kept travelling, and despite severe illness, borne with humour, in his mobility scooter "Harley" he visited 12 countries by plane, train or boat. He met Caroline Thompson of the Foreign Office at a London party in 1967 and they married the following year. She survives him with their two children.
