headline: Ebola death toll in DR Congo outbreak rises to more than 2,000, officials say
body of the article: An Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has killed 2,011 people out of 4,381 confirmed cases of the virus, Congolese officials said on Tuesday. The latest toll puts it close behind the DRC's deadliest Ebola outbreak in 2018-2020 when nearly 2,300 people died out of 3,500 recorded cases. The Ebola outbreak, which has hit the DRC's conflict-plagued eastern and northeastern regions, was declared on 15 May but is thought to have already been spreading for several weeks. It is the DRC's 17th surge of the highly contagious disease and is already considered the largest in the country's history "and could well become the largest outbreak ever," Sania Nishtar, chief executive of the Gavi global vaccine alliance, said. The case fatality rate of the current outbreak is estimated by Congolese health authorities to be 45.9%. Aid workers say the outbreak continues to outpace response that's been expanding across the five eastern provinces affected. Health workers interact at the Evangelical Medical Centre in Bunia, 3 July, 2026 - AP Photo/Dirole Lotsima Dieudonne Many health workers have gone on strike to protest lack of payment for their work since the outbreak was declared. On Friday, World Health Organisation (WHO) vaccine experts recommended a full-scale human trial of the only existing approved Ebola vaccine to see if it offered cross-protection against the strain of Ebola currently spreading in the DRC against which no specific vaccine currently exists. The Ervebo vaccine has proved safe and efficacious against the more common Zaire strain of Ebola virus and WHO experts said that early data, notably from animal trials, showed it may also give some protection against the rare Bundibugyo strain exploding in the DRC. Two potential Bundibugyo vaccines are in the early stages of clinical trials on humans, while a third is being worked on to bring it to that stage. The WHO regional director for Africa, Doctor Mohamed Yakub Janabi, told a news conference that officials are "chasing the virus, the virus is ahead of us." Ebola is spread by contact with bodily fluids and causes a haemorrhagic fever. The first Ebola virus to be identified was in 1976 near the Ebola River in what is now Congo.

headline: French newspapers target Google over AI summaries
body of the article: A federation of nearly 300 French newspapers said Tuesday that it filed a complaint with the country's competition authority over Google's new AI-generated summaries of search results, fearing the feature will erode traffic to their own websites. It is the latest salvo by media companies against the US tech giant's use of their articles and other content as they grapple with ad revenue declines. Google launched its AI Overviews in France in late July, which appear above regular links to search results and compile information from a wide array of sources. But the APIG association of newspapers wants the country's competition regulator to ensure "Google's respect of commitments made in 2022" as part of a compensation deal with French media groups. Information "has considerable value", APIG president Marc Feuillee, also managing director of the centre-right Le Figaro newspaper, said in a statement. "The editors are not seeking to halt innovation. They are asking for this value to be shared, and for compensation of the use of their content," the association said in its statement. It said Google had sprung the new artificial intelligence summaries without their consent, an alleged violation of the 2022 deal. The competition authority had already fined Google 250 million euros ($290 million) in 2024 for not respecting parts of the agreement. Many media groups have seen their revenue dwindle over the past two decades as advertising moved increasingly online, where tech firms take a big share of the profits. Critics say AI summaries cause further harm by leading to a drop in internet traffic to newspapers' articles -- with many users no longer clicking through to read the original source of the information. Google contends they let people ask more complex questions and discover new content, and says it provides controls to help publishers manage their content. The EU announced in December 2025 that it was investigating whether Google breached competition rules by using content put online by media and other publishers to train and provide AI services without appropriate compensation. reb/vg/js/st

headline: An Elderly Driver Opened His Glove Box and Found a 5-Foot Surprise
body of the article: Glove boxes tend to collect owner's manuals, registration papers, forgotten receipts and other junk. However, one Queensland driver recently opened his glove box and found something much more frightening than an old parking ticket. The older man discovered a 1.5-meter coastal carpet python occupying the compartment. That works out to nearly five feet of snake packed into such a small space. Sunshine Coast Snake Catchers 24/7documented the unusual find. A catcher named Summer arrived to remove the unexpected passenger safely for everyone involved. Summer described it as a good-sized carpet python for such a cramped hiding place. She suspected it might have eventually moved farther behind the dashboard if it had been left alone. Embedded media follows. Please allow a moment for it to load. The original Facebook reel documents Summer slowly opening the compartment and finding the patterned python folded comfortably inside. The snake barely appears to fit. Its body fills the back of the compartment and continues into the surrounding dashboard area. Afollow-up videofrom the snake-catching service records the careful removal. Summer warned a nearby person to step back while she worked with the defensive reptile. Summer ultimately successfully removed the python from the vehicle. A glove compartment may look like an enclosed plastic bin, but it normally sits within a much larger dashboard cavity. In many vehicles, removing the compartment provides access to wiring, air ducts or the cabin air filter. That leaves more room behind the visible box than a passenger might expect. The snake-catching service did not explain how this particular python entered the vehicle or reached the dashboard, but snakes have been found in other parts of cars throughout Queensland.A Bundaberg Regional Council reportpreviously documented a coastal carpet python hiding above a vehicle's front-right tire. Engine compartments, wheel wells and underbody openings can provide temporary shelter. Drivers in snake country may want to look before placing their hands into a dark vehicle compartment that has been left open or unused. Carpet pythons are nonvenomous, but that does not make an encounter inside a car harmless. A frightened python can still defend itself by striking and biting.The Queensland governmentsays carpet pythons average about two meters in length, while some can exceed four meters. Carpet pythons are primarily active at night and eat mammals, birds, reptiles, and frogs. They are frequently found in trees, although their climbing ability can also lead them into roofs, buildings, and other elevated hiding places. According to theCity of Moreton Bay, carpet pythons rarely attack when given the chance to retreat. They can become defensive when cornered or provoked, which is another reason a glove box is a poor place for an amateur to attempt removal. Queensland officials advise anyone who encounters a snake to remain calm, move to a safe distance, and allow it an escape route when possible. Most bites occur when people attempt to capture, interfere with, or kill a snake. A snake inside a vehicle presents an additional distraction risk. Drivers should stop somewhere safe, move away from the animal, and contact a licensed snake catcher instead of assuming it will remain in one compartment. Children and pets should also be kept away while help is on the way.

headline: Migrant tunnel discovered in Latvia under border fence to Belarus
body of the article: Latvian authorities have discovered an underground tunnel through which migrants could enter the EU country from neighbouring Belarus, Interior Minister Jānis Dombrava reported in Riga on Tuesday. Dombrava said the secret passage was discovered by border guards, the military and police near the closed Silene border crossing. "It is the first tunnel of this kind in Latvia," Dombrava said, according to Latvian media reports. He ordered a search for additional underground passages using electronic equipment. In recent weeks, secret tunnels under the border between Belarus and Lithuania had already been discovered. The tunnel, located about 10 metres from the border fence, was discovered while authorities were trying to reconstruct the route taken by a group of migrants who had been detained after illegally crossing the border. According to the Latvian border guard service, 15 people were arrested. Until now, migrants had only attempted to enter the EU country by scaling the border fence. According to a border guard spokesman, they had used various tools for this, including metal cutters and makeshift ladders made from branches and sticks. Latvia, like Lithuania and Poland, has repeatedly accused authoritarian-ruled Belarus of deliberately and systematically bringing migrants from crisis regions to the EU's external border. In response, Latvia strengthened border security and built a border fence. The country, which is also a NATO member, has launched a new operation to secure its eastern border under which drones will be deployed more extensively to detect illegal crossings.

headline: Oman confirms oil spill from grounded tanker spreads across 400km²
body of the article: A crude oil spill from the grounded tankerCaroline Bezengihas spread across almost 400km2off Oman's coast, according to a statement by the Omani government. The vessel, carrying nearly one million barrels of Russian oil destined for Asia, encountered problems in June 2026 while sailing off the coast of Yemen, reportedReuters. Maritime security sources have indicated that initial inspections pointed to an onboard explosion, although no party has claimed responsibility for an attack. Oman's Environment Authority announced that the spill, estimated at about 390km2(150 square miles), is located near the Hallaniyat Islands. The authority relayed through the state news agency that there is currently no threat to local facilities, including desalination plants or tourism infrastructure. The slick, extending northeast from the islands, is within approximately 7km of the coastline. Hallaniyat Islands were declared a nature reserve last year by royal decree from Sultan Haitham bin Tarik. The protected area is home to wildlife such as Arabian Sea humpback whales and Socotra cormorants. The Omani government stated it is working to manage the environmental impact caused by the leak. Greenpeace, an environmental organisation, previously estimated the spill covered around 600km2, using satellite imagery analysis. According to data cited byReuters, theCaroline Bezengideparted from Russia's Black Sea port of Novorossiysk in April and transited the Suez Canal at the end of May. The vessel was reportedly operating as part of a fleet of older tankers that do not hold Western insurance and often use different national flags to conceal ownership. Shipping records identifyCaroline Bezengias flying the Cameroon flag, though it was one of 39 tankers recently removed from the Cameroonian registry. The ship is under sanctions imposed by the European Union, Ukraine, the UK, Canada, and Switzerland. LSEG data lists Rentoor Shipmanagement as the registered owner and Villar Shipmanagement as manager, with both firms believed to be based in China. "Oman confirms oil spill from grounded tanker spreads across 400km²" was originally created and published byOffshore Technology, a GlobalData owned brand.

headline: From 4 to 200: The “Cocaine Hippos” Colombia Can’t Control
body of the article: The postFrom 4 to 200: The "Cocaine Hippos" Colombia Can't Controlappeared first onA-Z Animals. A newbornhippopotamusfound by fishermen along a riverbank in northwestern Colombia has put the spotlight back on drug kingpin Pablo Escobar. The tiny hippo, found dehydrated and malnourished, is one of 200 or so wild hippos that live in Colombia. Now an entire country is trying to figure out what to do with the non-native species. Pablo Escobar, the head of the Medellín drug cartel, imported four hippos in the 1980s for his private zoo at Hacienda Nápoles, his sprawling estate near Puerto Triunfo, Antioquia, roughly halfway between Medellín and Bogotá. The hippos came from a U.S. zoo. In the 1980s, drug kingpin Pablo Escobar imported four hippopotamuses to his private zoo in Colombia. ©Otto Borik/Shutterstock.com When Escobar was killed in 1993, most of his exotic animals were confiscated and moved to zoos. However, the hippos were too big and dangerous to move, so they were left behind. With nobody caring for them or paying attention to their enclosure, the hippos eventually escaped and fled to the nearby Magdalena River, Colombia's longest and vitally important waterway. The warm, marshy habitat of the Magdalena was ideal for the roaming hippos. There was plenty of food and, more importantly, no natural predators likecrocodilesor lions. The hippo population grew rapidly and has continued growing ever since. The latest estimates from Colombia's Environment Ministry put the current figure at about 200 hippos. A study estimates that the overall population increasesnearly 10 percent each year. The Colombian hippo colony is thelargest outside Africaand is considered thelargest invasive animal species in the world. In 2022, Colombia's Ministry of Environment officially declared hippos aninvasive speciesthrough Resolution 346. They cite the animals' ecological impact, damage to plant life, water pollution, and adverse impact on fishermen's livelihoods. "Because they are such large animals, they consume considerable amounts of grassland and produce significant waste, which then poisons the rivers," Audrey Huse, an independent journalist in Colombia, toldCBS News. After Escobar's death, the hippos were abandoned and eventually escaped to a nearby river. ©1001slide/iStock via Getty Images According to Huse, the hippos also killfishand threaten native animals liketurtles,otters, andmanatees. The hippos' heavy bodies erode river banks and destroy nearby forests. They compete with river manatees for food sources. They are also territorial and aggressive.Reportsstate that at least two people have been injured since 2019. This contrasts with theIUCN Red List, which listshippos as vulnerablein their native Africa. This illustrates how a species can be threatened in its native habitat while being considered dangerously invasive elsewhere. The Colombian government has been trying to control the invasive hippo population since at least 2009. At that time, the government attempted a small cull of the hippo population. However, a leaked photo of a killed hippo named Pepe sparked public outcry, and the lethal control approach was shelved. The government then tried a mass sterilization effort in November 2023. Each procedure costs about $9,800. However, officials later determined sterilization alone was not enough to control population growth. The government then tried exporting hippos to sanctuaries in India, Mexico, the Philippines, and Ecuador. However, a lack of permits in the receiving countries stalled the program. Cost was also a factor; it was estimated that moving just 70 animals would cost about $3.5 million. Now, the government is once again considering culling the unwanted population. A proposal to cull around 80 hippos has been met with mixed reviews. One Colombian senator called it an extermination and massacre. Not all locals support the plan, as some earn income from hippo tourism and oppose any reduction in the wild population. The newborn hippo that reignited this controversy was in rough shape when a group of fishermen found it. The newborn had been separated from its mother and was hidden in bushes along the riverbank near the village of La Sierra in the municipality of Puerto Nare in Antioquia. To protect the fragile newborn, the fishermen temporarily took it to their home while notifying environmental authorities. The family attempted to feed the newborn, but their efforts were unsuccessful. Veterinarians treated the baby for "advanced dehydration and malnutrition," according to astatementissued by Javier Valencia, director of the regional environmental authority. The process included subcutaneous hydration, since the doctors could not access the newborn's veins. After the baby was stabilized, it was transferred to Hacienda Nápoles, Escobar's former estate which is now a hippo sanctuary and theme park. Once the baby hippo overcomes its critical condition and completes its recovery, it will stay at the park and become part of the exotic animal collection there. The postFrom 4 to 200: The "Cocaine Hippos" Colombia Can't Controlappeared first onA-Z Animals.

headline: Japanese authorities use new tool to identify initial torrent uploaders — anti-piracy group says it identif...
body of the article: When you buy through links on our articles, Future and its syndication partners may earn a commission. Credit: Getty Images Recently, the Kyoto Prefectural Policecaught one of the initial-seedersof the well-known Japanese torrent website Nyaa. Masakazu Ono, 56, from Sagamihara in the Kamigawa Prefecture, was arrested after a multi-year investigation. While this news is straightforward by itself, the interesting bit is that CODA, the Japanese anti-piracy entity that performed the initial cyber-investigation, identified Ono allegedly without joining or monitoring BitTorrent swarm traffic, with the help of theJapan Hacker Association(JHA). CODA's description of only having "[analyzed] how data moves through torrent sites, such as index sites and tracker sites" is vague and can be parsed in a number of ways. The distinction between indexer and tracker is relevant: while an indexer is a user-visible list of torrents (usually a website), the tracker is the background service that software like qBittorrent actually connects to, and it lists everyone who's currently active in that torrent, whether sharing, downloading, or both. Our hypothesis is that CODA kept close tabs on the Nyaa trackers to see which IP address (in this case, Ono's) consistently appeared as the first person to offer up a 100% complete set of data for a show, a theory that would fit with how long the operation took. JHA's founder,Takayuki Sugiura,was the first to decrypt the Winny P2P protocol in 2004 tofind original uploader sources,and the methods used weren't too different from the aforementioned theory. It's also possible that Ono wasn't using a VPN but was logged into Nyaa, or activity at another website's cookies or CDN logs was used to establish a link to his activity at Nyaa, and from thereon, to the tracker. An initial-seeder is someone who is the first to offer up data for others to download — in this case, shows and movies. The show that reportedly got Ono nailed wasMidnight Taxi, a 2026 Japanese drama produced by NHK and WOWOW. However, the police apparently had been tracking him for quite a while and claimed that he had uploaded close to a thousand NHK recordings over the investigation's span. The processstarted in 2021when CODA first launched its Cross-Border Enforcement Project, aiming to identify Nyaa's uploaders. During three years, with the help of JHA, CODA seemingly collected enough information to get the Kyoto police involved in 2024. Three "secondary uploaders" from "reach sites" were charged in 2025, likely meaning regular users participating in the torrents, who got there through link aggregator sites. Fast-forward to a couple of weeks ago, and Masakazu Ono was formally arrested with specific charges. The most common techniques used by law enforcement agencies are creating a tracker honeypot or participating in the torrent swarm themselves in a bid to identify who's sharing files. However, Nyaa's list of trackers is small and comprises well-known, trusted servers, so together with CODA's wording, it's unlikely this was the method used. Furthermore, Japanese law generally frowns on non-targeted data monitoring, meaning that techniques likeDeep Packet Inspection(DPI) and traffic volume monitoring likely weren't used, at least until such time as Ono was identified.

headline: DRC Ebola death toll passes 2,000 amid fastest-growing outbreak on record
body of the article: More than 2,000 people have died of Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) sinceits outbreakwas declared fewer than three months ago. At least 1,000 of the deaths have occurred in the last three weeks, according to official government data, as the virus continues to spread at an alarming rate. A total of 4,381 Ebola cases across five provinces of the DRC have been confirmed as of Tuesday, including 2,011 deaths. It is the fastest-growing outbreak on record in the Central African country and is second in size only to the West African outbreak from 2014 to 2016, during which 11,310 people died. The response to the outbreak has been complicated by several factors, includingstrikes by unpaid health workers, misinformation and cultural traditions. These have included intimate family burials of some of those killed by the virus, potentially increasing the risk of further transmission. There is currently no approved treatment orvaccinefor the rare Bundibugyo strain of Ebola responsible for the DRC's current outbreak. The World Health Organization (WHO) announced last week that vaccine trials were under way but that it would likely take months before the results were received. On Monday, the WHO said the virus first surfaced in the country in February, three months before an outbreak was officially declared in the country and neighbouring Uganda on May 15. Meanwhile, the Israeli Ministry of Health announced on Tuesday that it had been alerted to a potential case of Ebola within its borders after one of its citizens returned from the DRC. In a series of posts on X, the ministry said tests had been performed after the person developed a fever. The results are expected within the next 24 hours, and the person remains in isolation.

headline: Africa CDC reports more than 2,000 Ebola deaths in Congo
body of the article: The number of Ebola deaths in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has risen to 2,011, the government reported on Tuesday, just under three months after the outbreak was officially announced, with the virus killing 45.9% of those infected. A total of 4,381 people contracted Ebola during this period, with 704 currently being treated in isolation units. The virus is transmitted through physical contact and contact with bodily fluids and causes a highly infectious fever with diarrhoea and bleeding. Jean Kaseya, director of the African health agency Africa CDC, said recently that the number of cases and deaths during the first 12 weeks of the outbreak was respectively eight times and more than six times as high as during the same period in the worst outbreak in West Africa to date, from 2014 to 2016. For the Congo, the worst Ebola outbreak to date was from 2018 to 2020, when 3,400 contracted the virus, fewer than the more than 4,000 infected with Ebola in just 12 weeks. The current outbreak of the Bundibugyo strain is proving highly problematic, as there is neither a specific vaccine nor specific treatment. Clinical trials of two antiviral treatment methods have been ongoing since early July. Given the severity of the outbreak, authorities also want to determine whether the pathogen may have mutated. There is concern that 86% of new Ebola cases currently cannot be traced back to contacts of confirmed cases. "We believe that more and more cases are going unreported," Kaseya said. Successfully containing the outbreak requires tracing 95% of contacts, according to the World Health Organization (WHO). The outbreak is centred in regions where security is poor and internally displaced people are living in cramped conditions. Much of the region is controlled by rebels.

headline: Vietnam to build its biggest warship yet to counter China
body of the article: Vietnam will build a new submarine-hunting warship as it steps up its ability to challenge China. The new frigate–Hanoi's largest and most advanced domestically built warship to date–will be equipped with air-defence missiles, advanced anti-ship missiles and electronically scanned array (AESA) radar. This isVietnam's latest effort to boost its military capabilities as it looks to counterChina's growing threat, especially over disputed islands in the South China Sea. The majority of the weapons and technology on board will be domestically produced, by the state-owned Viettel Military Industry and Telecoms Group and factories controlled by the defence ministry. The new warship will be built at the Song Thu shipyard in the coastal city of Da Nang and is expected to be completed in three years. A model was displayed at an announcement on Tuesday, equipped with mock radar sensors, a helipad and a deck gun. Both Vietnam and China – as well as the Philippines, Taiwan, Malaysia and Brunei – claim many of the same features across the Paracels and Spratly island clusters. The Paracels are about equidistant from the coasts of Vietnam and China, while the Spratly Islands are further south and nearer to the Philippines. Hanoi lays claim to many of the same features as Beijing, and the two countries have repeatedly faced off over the years while trading allegations of wrongdoing. While some of the tensions have cooled – with China assisting in the rescue of a sunken Vietnamese cargo ship in late July – Hanoi remains on high alert. As in the Philippines, whichregularly clashes with Chinaover the waters, fishermen in Vietnam have accused China of ramming and even sinking their vessels. Vietnam has also accused China of deploying a number of patrols around islands under its control in the South China Sea, which it calls the East Sea. In October last year, three patrol ships left one of China's bases on Mischief Reef, in the Spratlys, and circled several nearby features, including some where Vietnam has built facilities. While China has beenbuilding artificial islandsin the South China Sea for more than a decade and is by far the biggest builder, Vietnam has also made its own dent. The new warship will be Vietnam's largest and most advanced to date According to the US-based Centre for Strategic and International Studies, Vietnam had constructed more than 2,200 acres of artificial land in the South China Sea as of March, compared to nearly 4,000 acres built by China. As of June, Vietnam had built 27 sites across at least 18 reefs in the Spratly Islands, according to Radio Free Asia. Based on satellite images, many of these sites appear to be militarised, hosting ports, runways and communication arrays to keep a closer eye on Chinese activity. Vietnam's largest outpost in the South China Sea, located in the southern part of the Spratlys, is Barque Canada Reef. It has a long runway, currently being extended to 13,000ft, and a newly installed navigation beacon. Vietnam has also been expanding its missile technology in recent years, seeking to decrease its dependence on Russia, which has historically been its leading arms supplier. In May, Hanoi signed a 60bn-rupee (£485m) deal with India to procure BrahMos supersonic cruise missiles and was reportedly finalising a similar deal with Indonesia. In December, Vietnam will host the Vietnam International Defence Expo for the third time, in another effort to diversify its sources of military technology. At the first expo in 2024, Vietnam revealed its first domestically produced anti-ship missile, known as the Truong Son, also developed by Viettel. Try full access to The Telegraph free today. headline: Zelensky says North Korean missiles used in deadly strikes overnight
body of the article: Aug. 11 (UPI) -- At least nine people were killed and 25 injured in Russian strikes targeting Zaporizhzhia, Dnipropetrovsk and Kyiv with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky saying that Zaporizhzhia, where six people were killed and 19 injured, was hit with North Korean-made missiles. In apost on Xon Tuesday morning, Zelensky said emergency response efforts were still in progress dealing with the aftermath of a "vicious" attack on the city of Zaporizhzhia that involved North Korean ballistic missiles, Zircon hypersonic missiles and guided aerial bombs. "It was a vicious attack, calculated to inflict maximum damage specifically on civilian infrastructure. Unfortunately, as of now, six people have been reported killed and nineteen wounded in the city. First responders are continuing to extinguish a fire at one of the impact sites," wrote Zelensky. He said a missile strike also damaged an infectious diseases hospital building and businesses in Kyiv and the Dnipropetrovsk, Mykolaiv and Donetsk regions also came under attack. The other fatalities were all in Dnipropetrovsk, where five districts were attacked with artillery and drones, with Gov. Oleksandr Ghanza reporting inan online updatethat a middle-aged man was killed in the Synelnyky area, east of Dnipro, a teenage boy was killed In Kryvyi Rih and one person was killed in Pavlohrad. The Russian Defense Ministry said it launched strikes againsthubs for transport and logisticsin Kyiv and Zaporizhzhia, as well as "defense industry" targets. Officials in Russia's southwestsaid a manwas killed and two were injured in a Ukrainian drone attack on the Voronezh Region with two warehouses belonging to e-commerce giant Wildberries set ablaze. Zelensky said more than 120 drones were sent into Ukraine as frontline regions continued to experience what he described as "drone terror" on an almost daily basis, with power outages in Kherson and Kharkiv after strikes overnight. "Every step Russia takes -- increasing ballistic missile production, bringing in North Korean equipment, preparing for mobilization -- all of this shows that Moscow is preparing not for peace, but for escalation. And the world needs to respond now, not wait. More sanctions pressure specifically on enterprises that fuel Russia's war, more air defense assistance for Ukraine -- all of this is needed to give peace a chance," said Zelensky. Tuesday's strikes came hours after Zelensky warned in a televised address Monday that North Korea wasgaining battlefield experienceand boosting its military capabilities through its support for Russia, posing a growing threat to U.S. allies and other countries in the Asia-Pacific region. Zelensky said North Korea had supplied the Russian military with additional ballistic missiles and was preparing to deploy tens of thousands of troops to Russia. On Sunday, Zelensky called for increased co-operation between Seoul and Kyiv, particularly on air defense systems, warning that North Korea was preparing to send an additional 30,000 to 50,000 personnel to Russia on top of the 15,000 it already provided.

headline: Lebanon abolishes death penalty in landmark parliament vote
body of the article: BEIRUT (AP) — Lebanon's parliament Tuesday abolished the death penalty, making it the first country in the Arab world to replace the sentencing with life imprisonment with aggravated hard labor. The tiny Mediterranean country has committed to an unofficial moratorium on executions since January 2004. However, dozens of death sentences since then have been issued, but later suspended or commuted. A majority ofLebanon's128-member parliament voted in favor of ending the death penalty, with the exception of the parliamentary bloc of Hezbollah. Justice Minister Adel Nassar, who was in Parliament, called it a "historic step" for the country. Rights groups that have called for formalizing the moratorium or ending the death penalty altogether have also celebrated the vote. Ramzi Kaiss, Lebanon Researcher at Human Rights Watch, says Lebanon is "marking a final break from a cruel sentence that should never be imposed." "Capital punishment is unique in its cruelty and finality and is plagued with arbitrariness, prejudice, and error," he said. It's unclear how aggravated hard labor would be enforced, as some legislators said the terms of the new punishment are not yet clear. Lebanon does have the punishment of hard labor written into law and court decisions, but even those have been rarely enforced in recent years due to cash-strapped Lebanon's lack of resources and capacity within its overcrowded prisons. Lebanon's abolition of the death penalty comes as parliament is debating a controversial general amnesty law, the largest since the end of its 15-year civil war in 1990, that could reduce sentences or even release convicted militants and drug dealers, with some exceptions. Family members of Lebanese soldiers and servicemen killed or attacked by Islamist militant groups haverepeatedly protested against the law, some saying they had hoped to see the perpetrators who killed their family members executed rather than be issued reduced prison sentences. Hezbollah did not immediately issue a comment about the landmark vote. Neither did Lebanon's diverse religious institutions, where the death penalty is considered legal in some their respective court systems.

headline: Congo Ebola death toll tops 2,000 in fastest spreading outbreak on record
body of the article: Bunia, Congo — At least 2,000 people have died among the confirmed cases in Congo's Ebola outbreak that is the fastest-spreading on record, according to the latest government data, as health authorities struggle to get help quickly to remote localities due to rebel conflict, bad roads and work stoppages over payment issues. Data published overnight into Tuesday showed the outbreak has recorded a total of 4,381 confirmed cases, including 2,011 deaths. The grim toll comes nearly three months since the outbreak was declared on May 15. While it took about nine weeks for the outbreakto record 1,000 deaths, it's taken just around three weeks to record the additional 1,000 deaths, showing how fast the health crisis is moving beyond the control of responders. It's already the second-largest outbreak in history, only behind the 2014-2016 West Africa outbreak that recorded more than 28,000 cases including over 11,000 deaths. The World Health Organization has declared the outbreak, which has also led to cases in neighboring Uganda, a public health emergency of international concern. Aid workers say the outbreak continues to outpace the response that's been expanding across the five provinces affected. Many health workers have gone on strike to protest not being paid for their work since the outbreak was declared. And most new cases are recorded outside of contacts that are being monitored. The Ebola outbreak is unlike most previous ones because the rare Bundibugyo virus responsible for it has no approved vaccines or treatments. Clinical trials for those have begun in Ituri, the epicenter of the outbreak. The WHO said on Monday that the outbreak likely started in February, long before authorities detected it in one of Congo's most remote and vulnerable areas. WHO said some cases early on were wrongly attributed to malaria and typhoid, and that early testing was conducted for the more common type of Ebola. The WHO regional director for Africa, Dr. Mohamed Yakub Janabi, told a news conference that officials are "chasing the virus, the virus is ahead of us." The first Ebola virus to be identified was in 1976 near the Ebola River in what is now Congo. The current outbreak is the 17th — and largest — the Central African nation has faced.

headline: Canada Man Challenges Police Officers to a Boxing Match, Bodycam Reveals What Really Happened
body of the article: A video that went viral of two police officers within the Peel Regional Police Department being asked to box by a suspect. Of course, the video doesn't detail the full extent of what actually happened at the time of the incident, so Cst. Bell-Morena posted a video to the police department's official Facebook page to give some additional context. If you haven't seen the original video, it essentially consists of a man recording and goading officers to fight with him. In that video, the man recording made it seem as though the officers were the ones who initiated the encounter. However, according to the footage posted to Facebook, that very much was not the case. In fact, judging by the way the man was behaving towards the officers, I would have immediately thought him to be suspicious. I mean, who would entertain anyone who is asking a police officer to put on boxing gloves and spar with him for three rounds in the open? A crazy person, that's who. Please give the following video just a moment to load up completely. In the video, Cst. Bell-Morena explains that the two officers had actually been on foot and were responding to reports of people loitering and drinking alcohol publicly near a liquor store in Brampton, Toronto on July 29 at about 7:03 p.m. After checking things out, the two officers returned to their patrol car when they heard someone call out to one of the officers. The man who called the officer over asks, "Can you box? I have two boxing gloves in the car." You can tell that the officer was a little confused at the request, because he continued to ask the man what he meant. Because of how odd the situation was and the fact that the officers were called to the area for people drinking in public, they asked the man for a breath sample. Fortunately, he passed the test, but this is likely why he was so angry in the initial viral video, in which he asked the two officers to box. In this situation, context definitely matters. Many commenters said the body-camera footage changed how they viewed the encounter, with several arguing that it showed why full police video can matter when shorter clips circulate online. One person wrote that body-worn cameras "set the record straight yet again," while another said the footage was a strong example of why officers need cameras when people may try to spin the narrative. Others focused on the strange nature of the interaction itself. One commenter said asking an officer about boxing was such an unusual request that they understood why police chose to assess whether the driver was fit to be behind the wheel, while another simply asked whether the man could actually box at all. Several people also defended the officers' professionalism and sense of humor. One commenter praised the response as a good way to present the facts without leaning into clickbait, while another said it was refreshing to see the department show the entire encounter instead of only the version shared by the original poster. A few commenters joked about how young the officers looked, asking whether it was "take your kid to work day." Others pushed back on that idea, noting that everyone looks young at the beginning of a career and that police officers can still face serious situations regardless of age. headline: Construction begins on $444m Sydney’s Fairfield Hospital redevelopment
body of the article: Construction has commenced on a new multi-storey car park as part of the A$630m ($444m) Fairfield Hospital Redevelopment in Sydney, Australia. The project marks a significant phase in the New South Wales (NSW) state government's efforts to upgrade hospital infrastructure in the region. Situated at the southern end of Fairfield Hospital, the new structure will offer more than 450 parking spaces and provide pedestrian access to both the existing hospital and nearby Braeside Hospital. Rooftop solar panels are planned as part of the design to promote sustainable operations, and the facade has been created to complement the hospital's existing buildings and surrounding natural environment. Hindmarsh Construction has been contracted to deliver the multi-storey car park following a competitive tender process and receipt of the necessary planning approvals. The expanded on-ground car park areas have already been completed and are in use to reduce parking disruption for patients, visitors and staff during construction. The new car park and associated works are expected to continue through 2026 and are scheduled for completion in 2027. This multi-storey car park is one component of the broader Fairfield Hospital Redevelopment. The project also features plans for a five-storey clinical services building. The new facility will connect to the existing hospital and feature a new main entrance with a dedicated drop-off area. Current planning and design activities envision expanded services, including a larger Emergency Department, an Intensive Care Unit, operating theatres, medical imaging and inpatient wards. As part of the redevelopment, some existing departments are expected to be relocated or refurbished, although the final building design has not yet been confirmed. NSW Minister for Health Ryan Park said: "We are getting on with the job and delivering the first major upgrade to Fairfield Hospital in decades. "The Fairfield Hospital Redevelopment is part of the A$3.8bn being invested by the Minns Labor Government in western Sydney hospitals over the next four years. "We are committed to delivering more staff and more health services for families across Sydney's south-west, rebuilding the system after more than a decade of neglect from the Coalition." The NSW Government has allocated A$550m for the redevelopment, supplemented by A$80m in Commonwealth funding to support an expansion of the hospital's emergency services. The lead design team, including architect Architectus and project manager Turner & Townsend, was confirmed in September 2024. "Construction begins on $444m Sydney's Fairfield Hospital redevelopment" was originally created and published byWorld Construction Network, a GlobalData owned brand.

headline: Ebola death toll in DR Congo outbreak rises to more than 2,000
body of the article: An Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has killed 2,011 people out of 4,381 confirmed cases of the virus, Congolese officials said on Tuesday. The latest toll puts it close behind the DRC's deadliest Ebola outbreak in 2018 to 2020 when nearly 2,300 people died out of 3,500 recorded cases. The Ebola outbreak, which has hit the DRC's conflict-plagued eastern and northeastern regions, was declared on May 15 but is thought to have already been spreading for several weeks. It is the DRC's 17th surge of the highly contagious disease and is already considered the largest in the country's history "and could well become the largest outbreak ever", Sania Nishtar, chief executive of the Gavi global vaccine alliance, has said. The case fatality rate of the current outbreak is estimated by Congolese health authorities to be 45.9 percent. On Friday, World Health Organization (WHO) vaccine experts recommended a full-scale human trial of the only existing approved Ebola vaccine to see if it offered cross-protection against the strain of Ebola currently spreading in the DRC against which no specific vaccine currently exists. The Ervebo vaccine has proved safe and efficacious against the more common Zaire strain of Ebola virus and WHO experts said that early data, notably from animal trials, showed it may also give some protection against the rare Bundibugyo strain exploding in the DRC. Two potential Bundibugyo vaccines are in the early stages of clinical trials on humans, while a third is being worked on to bring it to that stage. Ebola is spread by contact with bodily fluids and causes a haemorrhagic fever. clt/kjm/giv

headline: East Libya military intelligence chief killed in car bomb blast
body of the article: The head of military intelligence for eastern Libya's self-styled Libyan National Army (LNA) has been killed in a car bomb blast, according to eastern Libyan authorities. Major-General Fawzi al-Mansouri was killed after an improvised explosive device was detonated as he entered his car outside his home in Benghazi's Hawari district late on Monday, the Reuters news agency reported, citing two security sources. Prime Minister of the eastern Libyan government Osama Saad Hammad condemned the killing and pledged to "uncover the circumstances of the crime". "We condemn, in the strongest terms, this treacherous terrorist act," he said in a statement on Tuesday. "There is no place in Libya for anyone who raises arms against the state, and no cover for anyone who plans, executes, finances, or incites assassination and terrorism crimes," he added. Al-Mansouri was appointed as director of military intelligence in Benghazi, with the rank of major-general, in 2024. The killing highlights continuing security challenges in Libya, where rival administrations and armed groups ⁠have retained influence despite a ⁠2020 ceasefire that halted major warfare. Libya split in 2014 between rival eastern and western factions after a ⁠2011 NATO-backed uprising toppled longtime leader Muammar Gaddafi. The LNA, led by renegade military commander Khalifa Haftar, controls much of eastern and southern Libya. It is aligned with authorities based in the eastern city of Benghazi. Libya's internationally recognised Government of National Unity is based in the capital, Tripoli, and controls much of the west of the country.

headline: Zelenskyy says Russia using North Korean missiles in Ukraine
body of the article: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused Russia of using North Korean ballistic missiles in its attacks, asanother night of bombardmentkilled at least nine civilians and injured dozens of others. Zelenskyy said Russian forces used ballistic missiles supplied by North Korea in their attack on the southeastern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia, where local officials said six people were killed and 19 wounded. Three more people, including a 15-year-old boy, were killed by Russian drones and artillery in the central Dnipropetrovsk region, local authorities said. Russia has received additional ballistic missiles from Pyongyang and is preparing to deploy more North Korean troops, Zelenskyy said late Monday. Russian President Vladimir Putin and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un signed a strategic partnership agreement in 2024 that pledged mutual aid if either country faced aggression. Since then, various reports of Ukrainian troops skirmishing with North Korean counterparts have emerged. The Ukrainian president warned that North Korea's missile capabilities are being improved by the collaboration with Russia. "The more North Korean strikes there are here in Ukraine, in Europe, the more their missiles and soldiers are used, the more they correct their shortcomings and blind spots, the greater the danger will later be for Japan, the Republic of Korea, the Philippines, and other countries in the region," Zelenskyy said on social media. In December 2024, South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff estimated that there had already been more than 1,000 North Korean troops in the war. In January 2025, Ukraine announced it had, for the first time, captured two wounded North Korean soldiers. Ukraine says Russia is scaling up its production of ballistic missiles, aiming to exploit Kyiv's critical shortage of Patriot air defense interceptors that can stop them. Kyiv also claims Moscow is preparing an increase in recruitment for a new push on the front line that stretches 775 miles along eastern and southern Ukraine. "Every step Russia takes — increasing ballistic missile production, bringing in North Korean equipment, preparing for mobilization — all of this shows that Moscow is preparing not for peace, but for escalation," Zelenskyy said on social media.

headline: Mystery solved: story of Wehrmacht motorbike found in the Danube
body of the article: The water level in the Danube has never been this low. The low water level is exposing what lay hidden on the riverbed for decades, including a Wehrmacht motorcycle of the DKW NZ 350-1 type from the Second World War. DKW is short for "Dampfkraftwagen", a former German car and motorcycle brand from the Saxon motor city of Zschopau that was later taken over by Auto Union. Low water level: Wehrmacht motorcycle found in the mud of the Danube in the heart of Budapest. (c) Volksbund - Volksbund The motorcycle was found on the riverbed in the centre of Hungary's capital Budapest, level with the Hungarian Parliament building. For staff at the local Institute and Museum of Military History it is a realonce-in-a-century discovery. According to the institute, the vehicle is almost completely intact. It was effectively preserved in the Danube's mud. DKW racing motorcycles from 1939 and 1931, archive - Copyright 2007 AP. All rights reserved. The motorcycle found is a model developed specifically for wartime use and produced from 1944 onwards. It was powered by a single-cylinder two-stroke engine delivering 11.5 hp. Thanks to their robustness and reliability, these so-called Kräder, or military motorcycles, were popular with the troops. One of the key identifying features of the DKW 350-1 is the metal side pannier, also found on the machine recovered from the Danube. Around 12,000 units were built by the end of the war in 1945. The predecessor model, theDKW(source in German)NZ 350, reached a top speed of 105 km/h, according to the ADAC. In the Wehrmacht, motorcycles were usually used as dispatch, reconnaissance or courier machines, carrying orders, reports and information materials such as maps. The Wehrmacht in Liège, Belgium, May 1940 (c) AP - AP Photo The motorcycle was manufactured by Auto Union AG, a car and motorcycle producer founded in 1932 that was then the second-largest German manufacturer after Opel. Auto Union AG was created through the merger of several brands, including Audi. On earlier models from the company, the frame components were still bolted together; on the NZ series they were welded. Because welding required a high power supply, this work could only be carried out at night, when the electricity grid was not under strain from other uses. German Tellermine 35 anti-tank mines, remnants of hand grenades and artillery shells have also been found on the Danube riverbed. This stretch of the Danube may have been used as a "war debris dump", according to the Hungarian Institute of Military History. On 2 August the motorcycle was discovered on the Buda side of the Hungarian Parliament, next to the harbour at Batthyány Square. Volksbund - Volksbund From March 1944 German troops occupied Budapest. Between October 1944 and February 1945 the Battle of Budapest was fought between the Soviet Red Army and German and Hungarian forces. Around 30,000 German, more than 17,000 Hungarian and some 80,000 Soviet and Romanian soldiers were killed. On 13 February 1945 the remaining German units surrendered. After the war the DKW production facilities were dismantled and transferred to the Soviet Union as part of war reparations. In Moscow and other locations they were used to build, in large numbers until 1951, the largely identical ISCH-350. Human remains were found beneath the motorcycle. The Volksbund Deutsche Kriegsgräberfürsorge, the German War Graves Commission, took charge of the recovery and said the remains belong to two Wehrmacht soldiers. Were they the motorcycle's crew? Their identity tags are well preserved, so they should be able to be identified. The two dead men are to be buried at the German war cemetery in Budaörs, west of Budapest. More than 16,000 German soldiers are buried there. The Volksbund is a non-profit association which, on behalf of the German federal government, searches for, recovers and buries war dead abroad. In 2025 alone it dealt with more than 5,500 cases. This text was translated with the help of artificial intelligence. Report a problem : [feedback-articles-en@euronews.com].

headline: Man dies after medical emergency off coast
body of the article: A man has died after a medical emergency on a French fishing vessel about 14 miles (22km) off Guernsey's west coast. A distress call was received at about 18:10 BST on Monday and the St Peter Port Lifeboat was launched with two St John paramedics on board, according to the Guernsey Coastguard. The seven-crew Spirit of Guernsey lifeboat reached the 22m (72 ft) trawler around the same time as a French military helicopter which lowered paramedics on board to the boat. The man was airlifted by the helicopter to Cherbourg, France, where he was pronounced dead, Guernsey Coastguard said. The lifeboat stood by as safety cover while the winching operation was under way to evacuate the man from the boat to the helicopter. Search mission coordinator Simon Granger said the operation involved "an excellent collaboration" between the Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre at Joburg, Guernsey Coastguard, St Johns, the RNLI and the French military. headline: Zelensky: 7 dead in Russian attack that also used N Korean missile
body of the article: At least seven people have been killed in overnight Russian missile and bomb attacks on the south-eastern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhya, Ukrainian authorities said on Tuesday. "It was a brutal attack, calculated to inflict maximum damage on civilian infrastructure," President Volodymyr Zelensky wrote on Telegram, adding that 24 people had been injured in the strikes that also involved a North Korean ballistic missile. There were also Russian attacks on substations in the cities of Kherson and Kharkiv, leading to power outages, Zelensky said. "Every move Russia makes - ramping up ballistic missile production, bringing in North Korean equipment, preparing for mobilization - all this shows that Moscow is preparing not for peace, but for escalation," Zelensky wrote. The Russian Defence Ministry said its attack on Zaporizhzhya targeted the local steelworks. Ukraine's Metinvest steel company later confirmed the strikes on the plant, saying employees were killed and injured while trying to seek shelter. Operations at the plant have temporarily been suspended, according to Metinvest. The Russian ministry also said it attacked a sorting centre of the postal company Nova Post in Kiev, which Russia claimed had also been used to store and distribute drone components and electronic warfare systems. It also said a large warehouse of around 50,000 square metres in Kiev was attacked. The Russian Defence Ministry claimed it served as a drone depot. The Ukrainian authorities confirmed damage to warehouse buildings in Kiev and in the Bucha district west of Kiev. There was one injured person. The Ukrainian Air Force said the Russian military used Zircon anti-ship missiles, ballistic missiles and 120 drones. The attacks were mainly aimed at the Kiev area and Zaporizhzhya, it said. There were impacts in 21 places. Russian attacks with drones and artillery killed at least three people in the Dnipropetrovsk region, authorities said. Another five were injured, military governor Oleksandr Hanzha said on Telegram. The dead included a 15-year-old boy. There were more than 20 attacks on targets in a total of five districts, according to the information. Ukraine has been defending itself against the Russian invasion for more than four years. Ukraine has set fire to at least one oil refinery and warehouses belonging to Russia's largest online retailer Wildberries in new massive drone strikes on Russian territory, killing one person. Warehouse space covering tens of thousands of square metres was ablaze in the Voronezh region, Governor Aleksandr Gusev said on Tuesday morning. He said a 49-year-old man had been fatally injured in the attack and that two others had been wounded. Wildberries said in the morning that the facilities at the logistics centre had been evacuated. According to the governor, the attack took place overnight and Russian air defences shot down 15 drones. He did not say how many drones reached their target. An oil refinery caught fire after a drone attack in Orsk in the Orenburg region on the border with Kazakhstan, according to social media reports. Governor Yevgeny Solntsev confirmed only that a fire had broken out at an industrial facility following the attack. He did not say it was a refinery. There were no reports of casualties. Russia's state news agency TASS reported a further fire at an oil refinery in Komsomolsk-on-Amur in the far east of the country. No details were initially given on the cause of the fire or drone attacks in the region. Ukraine's strikes on Russian territory are aimed not only at damaging the Russian economy: Kiev's stated goal is to make the war so costly for Moscow that the Russian leadership agrees to negotiate an end to the fighting. No such talks are currently in sight.

headline: Syrian court sentences Bashar al-Assad in absentia to death
body of the article: A Syrian court on Tuesday sentenced ousted president Bashar al-Assad in absentia to death on charges of premeditated murder, torture, arbitrary detention and crimes against humanity. Al-Assad is currently in exile in Russia, which has so far not extradited him to Syria. The verdict against al-Assad from the fourth criminal court in the capital Damascus was read out live on Syrian state television. Alongside al-Assad, his cousin Atef Najib was also sentenced to death. Najib, who is in Syria, is one of the few key figures of the al-Assad government who will stand trial in the country. In 2011, he was the security chief in the southern city of Daraa, where the anti-government uprising began after teenagers sprayed graffiti on the walls of their school and were arrested. This started the nearly 14-year civil war. Najib is accused in the indictment of crimes against the Syrian people including "systematic mass murder" and arbitrary arrests. Bashar al-Assad's brother Maher al-Assad and other representatives of the ousted government were also sentenced to death in absentia. They were accused of premeditated and planned murder and torture resulting in death. Dozens of people gathered in front of the Palace of Justice in Damascus during the verdict announcement. After Najib's death sentence, cheers and shouts of joy erupted, according to a dpa reporter on the scene. Some people held up pictures of those Najib is accused of killing. Eyewitnesses also reported expressions of jubilation in Daraa. These trials are part of a series of proceedings against prominent representatives of the former Syrian regime. When the rebel alliance was on the verge of capturing Damascus in December 2024, al-Assad fled to Russia with his family. According to reports, his younger brother Maher, commonly dubbed a brutal "butcher," has also fled to Moscow. So far, it seems unlikely that the sentences will be carried out. Should they ever be apprehended or extradited, they will immediately face imprisonment in Damascus.

headline: Syria sentences Assad to death
body of the article: Bashar al-Assad, the former Syrian dictator, has been sentenced to death in absentia for crimes against humanity. A Syrian court handed down the sentence against the former president and Maher Assad, his younger brother, on Tuesday. Both fled to Russiaafter they were swept from power in December 2024. A death sentence was also given to Atef Najib, Assad's cousin, who was in court, for leading a bloody crackdown in the southern province of Daraa that provoked the uprising and civil war that started in 2011. The ensuing conflict left around half a million people dead. During the fighting,the Assad regime perpetrated numerous war crimes, including the repeated use of poison gas against civilians. Najib heard the judge read his sentence standing in a cage wearing a prisoner's uniform. Atef Najib was in court to hear his sentence - Syria's Ministry of Interior / AFP via Getty Images The former Syrian army brigadier general who was head of the Political Security Branch in Daraa is one of the highest-ranking regime officials to have gone on trial. The acts attributed to him were "crimes against humanity", the court said as it handed down "the harshest punishment against him, which is the death penalty". Assad has not been seen since ordering his men to fight on while flying to a Russian air base in the west of Syria and then to Moscow,where he was granted asylum. His regime relied heavily on Russian military support against the rebel factions that flooded into the country after Barack Obama, the former US president, failed to make good on his threat to punish Assad if he crossed the "red line" of using chemical weapons. People in Syria celebrated after the sentences were handed down - Ghaith Alsayed On Saturday it was reported that Hassan Luka, a former senior Syrian intelligence official accused of orchestrating torture and massacres, had been found living in Moscow. Known as "The Spider" for his extensive network of informants, Luka was one of the most feared men in Syria, and had control over the country'smost brutal detention centres. He was traced to suburban Moscowthrough a phone book discovered in his abandoned Damascus residence by rebel fighters. Syria is nowunder the control of Ahmed al-Sharaa, who led the Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham (HTS) rebel group in a lightning string of victories from the north towards Damascus. Mr Sharaa is a former al-Qaeda militant who spent time in US military detention in Iraq and allegedly had links to Islamic State. Syria is now under the control of Ahmed al-Sharaa, a former al-Qaeda militant who spent time in US military detention in Iraq and allegedly had links to Islamic State - Omar Sanadiki HTS has been designated a terrorist organisation but the presidenthas the strong support of Donald Trump, with whom he has a good rapport. The US president has lifted some financial sanctions against the devastated Arab state and tried to encourage inward investment. Mr Sharaa's regime is not internally strong, and there have been massacres of minority groups. It also faces acts of terrorism from Islamist factions loyal to Islamic State. headline: Who is Atef Najib, former Syrian official sentenced to death with al-Assad?
body of the article: Atef Najib, the former Syrian security official widely seen as the man who oversaw a regime of murder, torture and forced disappearances against Syrians during the country's brutal 14-year civil war, has beensentenced to deathby a court in Damascus. On Tuesday, Najib was sentenced alongside ousted Syrian leader Bashar al-Assad and his younger brother, Maher al-Assad, who also received the death penalty in absentia for crimes including premeditated murder. The Fourth Criminal Court found that crimes committed by al-Assad's government in Deraa province in 2011 amounted to crimes against humanity. Unlike al-Assad and members of his family who fled to Russia when the regime fell in December 2024, Najib has been in detention in Syria since January 2025. During his trial, he was charged with at least 10 crimes, including murder, torture and responsibility for massacres, as well as crimes against humanity linked to the2011 Deraa crackdownon protesters. We unpack who Najib is, what he is charged with and what we know about his trial and verdict. Najib, 66, is the first cousin of former President Bashar al-Assad and the former head of political security in southern Syria's Deraa province. Al-Assad wasoverthrownin early December 2024, when a coalition of armed opposition groups seized Damascus in a lightning advance and toppled his government. Since his ousting, al-Assad has lived in exile in Moscow under tight Russian supervision, far from any formal role in Syria's new transitional authorities. Al-Assad had been in power since 2000 until he fled. He took over after his father, Hafez al-Assad, who had been in power since 1970, died. In the early 1980s, Najib joined the Military Academy in Homs after graduating from school. After completing his training at the academy, he became the head of political security in Deraa. The exact date he officially assumed his role is not documented in public state archives. He remained in his role leading up to and during the initial outbreak of the Syrian uprising in March 2011. Accused of violently quashing this uprising, the al-Assad regime officially removed him from his post in April 2011. Najib oversaw political security in Deraa when teenagers who scrawled antigovernment graffiti on a school wall were arrested and tortured. The case became a catalyst for a broader uprising, which ultimately morphed into a bloody civil war. The Ministry of Interior's general security forces arrested Najib in January 2025 during a campaign targeting remnants of the former government in Latakia province. Najib had fled the country after al-Assad's ousting, but then returned to Syria, Al Jazeera's Obaida Hitto said, reporting from Damascus on Tuesday. Najib's arrest was considered one of the most significant detentions of former security officials because he held a sensitive security position in Deraa at the beginning of the Syrian uprising. Najib's sentence was issued by the Fourth Criminal Court in Damascus on Tuesday, which oversaw the final review of his case and judgement. Closing arguments and his final statement had already been heard in the eighth session. The proceedings began on April 26. Najib was sentenced to death, alongside al-Assad and his brother. According to the court ruling, Najib was involved in the torture of a large number of detainees, including of children, and was responsible for the deaths of many of them during their detention. This marks the first decision by a Syrian court against a senior al-Assad‑era figure under the current transitional authorities. "This is a historic moment, here in Syria. Atef Najib is the only one of the codefendants who is actually standing trial here physically inside the country. The other codefendants are all being sentenced in absentia," Al Jazeera's Hitto said. He was accused of overseeing a violent crackdown on antigovernment protesters in Deraa during the 2011 uprising, which led to the 14-year civil war. Overall, he was charged with at least 10 crimes, including murder, torture and responsibility for the 2011 massacre in Deraa, which the court ruled was a crime against humanity. According to an Al Jazeera Mubasher report, 75 plaintiffs filed cases against Najib and were understood to have provided testimony during the trial. This trial was a test case for Syria's transitional justice system and for the new government's ability to hold al-Assad regime officials to account for abuses under his rule. The government of interim President Ahmed al-Sharaa has faced criticism for delays in launching a promised transitional justice process following the war, in which an estimated half a million people were killed. According to a 2025 report by the Syrian Network for Human Rights, more than 181,000 people were forcibly disappeared or arbitrarily detained during the war, 90 percent of them by the al-Assad regime. "The legal issues that were discussed today are going to set the precedent for future legal actions taken against anyone that was involved in these crimes," Hitto said. The verdict is therefore being seen by many as a test of how far al-Sharaa's government will go to mete out justice for past crimes. "What is at stake in these proceedings is not confined to the question of whether Najib will be held to account for his actions … Rather, the true significance of this trial lies in the legal foundation of the judicial record that these proceedings will leave behind," Fadel Abdulghany, the founder and head of the Syrian Network for Human Rights, wrote in an opinion piece for The New Arab last month. Hitto reported that people had gathered around the court in Damascus when the verdict was announced, and they were "relieved that this is happening in this way". Syrians could be seen celebrating the verdicts in the streets outside. "The country has been trying to reconcile more than five decades of dictatorship led by the al-Assad family over the last 18 months or so," Hitto added.

headline: Sudan exodus threatens humanitarian catastrophe in Chad
body of the article: Trapped in a desert encampment in Chad, Abakar Adam, 70, dreams of returning to his small farm in neighbouring Sudan, nearby to the village where he was born. But Mr Adam can't go home. Hidden from sight, he watched soldiers set fire to his farmhouse and slaughter his livestock three years ago. One month later, after resettling in the city of El Geneina in West Darfur he heard 40mm grenades rain down on hospitals while patients fought for their lives inside and witnessed civilians executed in the street. Shortly after, a bullet from the rifle of a Rapid Support Force (RSF) soldier ripped through his gut, and he recalls how he struggled to pull his daughter from the blood-soaked sand after her eye was gouged out by a militiaman during their escape from Sudan. Now, sitting outside his rotting, wooden shelter in eastern Chad, just 20 miles from the border with Sudan, he tells The Telegraph that he can't forget the faces of the blind and disabled who he witnessed being thrown onto piles of hay and burnt alive. Adam's story is not unique and the refugee camp where he finds himself with tens of thousands of others is on the brink of collapse. Abakar Adam witnessed atrocities before he was forced to flee his village - Mirja Vogel Since the start of the Sudanese civil war in April 2023, more than 1.3 million have fled to eastern Chad, one of the poorest counties on earth, stretching already pitiful resources beyond breaking point. The camp's inhabitants, almost all of whom, like Mr Adam, have been scarred mentally or physically by the RSF's brand of ultra,often overtly theatrical violence, are now battling thirst, malnutrition and the withdrawal of international aid. "We are scared to die," said Mazanik Ahosh, 23, a camp inhabitant with two children. "There is nothing for us here, not even water." Most disturbing when the Telegraph visited the border town of Adre in Chad, where the refugees are gathered, were the accounts of violence perpetrated by the predominately Arab fighters of the RSF against members of ethnic African tribes. Survivors said they saw RSF soldiers execute newborn babies and their mothers, rape girls as young as 10, torture civilians to death, enslave young boys and fire machine gun rounds into convoys of refugees trying to escape. "We risked everything to leave Sudan. During our escape, one of my sons was shot dead just three miles from the border. We had no choice but to leave his body next to the others that had piled up on the road," said Zahra Khamis Ibrahim, a refugee in Adre. Thousands are now living in desert encampments in very poor conditions - Mirja Vogel The war between the RSF and the Sudanese army is now deep into its fourth year. It has becomeone of the bloodiest conflicts of the centuryand there is little sign of a resolution being reached. Every week, thousands escaping Sudan pour into Chad, where Adre serves as the principal border crossing point. Home to a pre-war population of around 40,000 people, the town's needs have swelled uncontrollably since the war began. Meanwhile, humanitarian funding has been slashed. Today,more than 280,000 Sudanese refugeeslive in dilapidated shelters in a brittle town bursting at its seams. Searing 42-degree heat makes the emergency all the more urgent. The few trees that still stand are naked and the rivers dry. In its rural outskirts, crops cannot grow in the arid dirt because rain is yet to fall. Food was recently so scarce that starving refugees broke down termite mounds to harvest the larva inside them. Carrying as many people and water containers as they can bear, a constant stream of emaciated donkeys and horses stagger through the city's dirt paths. Animals that succumb to exhaustion lie dead on the roadside, their carcasses picked apart by vultures. Along most streets, giant ovens built for firing bricks pump out clouds of toxic fumes, suffocating the dusty, orange air. At night, when the intermittent electricity clicks off, most of Adre is blanketed in an opaque darkness, only illuminated by a handful of battery powered spotlights in market stalls and the headlights of heavily armed Chadian military vehicles. Adre's largest state hospital is a makeshift assortment of open beds, broken mosquito nets and armed guards - Mirja Vogel At the border in Adre, just 50 metres from Sudan, one young man called Ahmed Hurum, 23, who arrived in April, stood completely still with his gaze fixed on the horizon. As he opened his mouth to speak, two skeletal horses raced past, flinging hot sand into his face, but he didn't blink. His glazed eyes, encased in high cheek bones and a furrowed brow, were vacant. "The attacks on my city in south Darfur were more violent than I could have ever imagined," he said, struggling to talk. "But here in Chad, I am alone with nothing." Two miles from the border, past winding dirt streets overflowing with rubbish, desperate patients seeking lifesaving care wait to be seen at the largest state hospital in Adre. It's a makeshift assortment of open beds, broken mosquito nets and armed guards. At the start of the conflict, six ambulances operated from the hospital. Today, there is only one functioning ambulance left and it is often too expensive to drive due to the soaring cost of fuel. "The most difficult problem we're facing is managing trauma injuries," said Dr A. Lucien, an emergency care doctor at the state hospital, moments after he had finished bandaging a deep soft tissue wound on a young woman's face. "At the start of July, there was a drone bombardment nearby in Sudan. People limped across the border and because we didn't have ambulances to take them for intensive care surgery, some of them died." Ahmed Hurum, centre, arrived at the camp in April - Mirja Vogel In the most isolated areas in eastern Chad, the daily fight for water and fuel is sparking new, inter-communal tensions with refugees and locals, which are increasingly turning violent. Standing by an empty water station in the Goudrane Camp in the neighbouring Wadi Fira province, next to a makeshift school with almost 5,000 students, a teacher told The Telegraph that "the lack of water makes it impossible for the children to stay healthy, let alone learn." The next day at 10.30am hundreds of women and children from the school dashed through the sand towards the water station. After five days without, water had finally been delivered and the taps were on. The crush of people clawed, scrambled and climbed over each other to reach the source. It was emptied in minutes and dozens left empty-handed. "People are really desperate when the water arrives," a worker for the NGO, Solidarites International, said. "We dig over 100-metres deep into the ground here and still we don't find enough water to pump into the camps for everyone." On four separate occasions in the Metche refugee camp, 20 miles from Adre, young women described being chased, threatened and beaten by members of local villages because they ventured outside the camp's boundaries to collect firewood, which they rely on for cooking and boiling dirty water. Samia Ali Kaukau, pictured with her younger brother - Mirja Vogel Sat next to her younger brother, who was tortured by the RSF in Sudan, Samia Ali Kaukau, 52, has taken up an unofficial role as a women's support leader there. "The threat to us is serious," she said. "Last month, a group of girls were captured when they left to collect wood. Men raped them for three days before they were allowed to come back." Another refugee reported hearing gunshots at night and described how his friend "was axed to death" by a local landowner in May, after he refused to pay him for weeks of manual labour on his farm. While the humanitarian catastrophe worsens in Chad, the weaponry used in Sudan is evolving. For most of the war, fighting was largely restricted to ground warfare. Now, the threat comes from the sky. Thanks to the influx of funding from foreign actors including the United Arab Emirates but also Egypt and Saudi Arabia, drones are now the preferred tool of destruction for both the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and the Sudanese Army. The humanitarian crisis in Chad is becoming a catastrophe - Mirja Vogel According to the United Nations, drone attacks accounted formore than 80 per cent of civilian deaths in Sudanthis year. Travelling over 1,000 miles along an indirect route to evade drone strikes, it took Soraya Anan, 41, three months to reach Adre from her home in Khartoum, Sudan's once-bustling capital which has been partially destroyed and is now littered with mass graves and unexploded ordnance. Exhausted after arriving just a few hours before, Anan described how she felt "lucky to be alive. "I had a heart attack during a particularly strong wave of drone strikes in Khartoum," she said. "By the time I recovered, we were being attacked every morning. It was too dangerous to stay another day longer." Among the refugees like Ms Anan who recently arrived in Chad, there is a growing fear that the war could spread across the border. Many belong to ethnic groups which have been deliberately targeted by the RSF in Sudan. They believe they would be the first to feel the flames of war again if the fighting spills over. According to Charles Bouëssel, Crisis Group's Senior Analyst for Central Africa, "the longer the war continues, the further Chad is likely to be dragged in. "The security crisis is also fuelled by an increase in drone strikes along the border and by increasing violent incursions of RSF fighters into Chad," he said. It took Soraya Anan three months to reach Adre from her home in Khartoum - Mirja Vogel On 21 February, RSF soldiers attacked Chadian army stations in Tine, a border town 150 miles north of Adre. Five soldiers and three civilians were killed. Less than one month later, a drone attack on the same town that was attributed to the RSF killed 20 civilians who were attending a funeral. Last week, more than5,000 people were displacedfrom 10 villages in Sudan's West Darfur state, near the border with Chad, following violent clashes between the Sudanese army and the RSF. Most fled to Chad. The United Nations is now warning of an impending large-scale atrocity in the city of El Obeid in central Sudan, home to over 500,000 people. As border clashes intensify and both armies prepare to fight over another major city in Sudan, the consequences of another massive, destabilising wave of refugees fleeing into Chad would be devastating. Adre's border also remains one of the most direct routes for the delivery of water, medicines, and other life-saving assistance to Sudan, but some humanitarian organisations have already started suspending operations due to the worsening security conditions. If the border collapses, thousands who survived the worst forms of physical and psychological suffering, could die in weeks as humanitarian support is cut off, shifting Africa's largest war into another, more deadly phase again.
