headline: Iraq’s semi-autonomous Kurdish region suffers as US-Iran war drags on
body of the article: Erbil, Iraq– For the last five months or so, Iraq's Kurdistan region has suffered the impact and ramifications of the ongoing United States-Israel war on Iran. Despite efforts by the government todistance itselfand not take sides or allow attacks on Iran from its territories, the repercussions were heavy on the semi-autonomous region and Iraq as a whole. Since the outbreak of the war in February, hundreds of missiles and drones have hit the Kurdish region. Masrour Barzani, prime minister of the Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG), told Al Jazeera the region has "paid a heavy price" in the war. "We have been targeted more than 1,000 times by missiles and drones directly from Iran or from inside Iraq by some of the militias. We think these are all unjustifiable attacks on Kurdistan. Unfortunately, we had casualties and we lost people. Many of our infrastructure have been hit badly," Barzani said during the Al Jazeera show, The Interview. "The regional conflict and the security repercussions led to a 70 percent decrease in trade across the Kurdish region," he added. According to KRG data, the attacks hit military and security sites, energy facilities, bases and headquarters of opposition Iranian Kurdish parties, in addition to civilian areas. A direct casualty of these attacks is the economy: The oil and gas sectors, and the movement of companies and investment. And it comes at a time when the Kurdish region is facing a chronic financial crisis amid ongoing disputes with the federal government in Baghdad over salary payments for state employees, oil sales, and revenues. "The scale of losses inflicted on the Kurdistan region as a result of the war, up to April, is estimated at one trillion and 500 billion Iraqi dinars ($1.14bn), and these figures were also handed over to the Iraqi government," Peshawa Hawramani, spokesman for the KRG, told Al Jazeera. "There is no convincing reason to strike the Kurdistan region. We were not a party to this war, nor will we be a party to it, and we have not worked to make the territory of the Kurdistan region a launching point for striking Iran," Hawramani said, adding that attacks were a "violation of the sanctity of Iraqi territory and Iraqi sovereignty". Kurdish authorities say they have named the perpetrators behind the attacks and provided them to the central government in Baghdad. "We have provided the names of these factions to the former and current Iraqi governments. These are factions that bear arms outside state institutions illegally, and yet, no measures have been taken so far by the Iraqi government towards these factions, whether the former or the current one," the spokesman said, adding that attacks were taking place even before the Iran war began. Within hours of the US-Israel attacks on Iran,US assets in Iraq's semi-autonomous Kurdishregion came under retaliatory attacks from Tehran-backed groups, dragging the country into the conflict that has since expanded across the Middle East and beyond. Since then, US assets in Iraq have come under multiple attacks from pro-Iran groups and Iran's powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). In response, the US has also carried out attacks against the Iraqi groups. The IRGC has also attacked Iranian Kurdish groups based in the Iraqi Kurdish region, after reports that Washington planned to arm them to fight Tehran. The leader of an Iranian Kurdish nationalist group based in the Kurdish regiontold Al Jazeerathat it is "highly likely" that Iranian Kurds will stage a cross-border ground operation into Iran. During the war,Iraq was also attacked. Drone and rocket attacks have hit Baghdad International Airport, which houses a military base and a US diplomatic facility, as well as oilfields and other facilities. For many in the Kurdish region, the Iran-backed armed groups are a cause of destabilisation and a source of concern. Jabbar Yawar, security expert and former secretary-general of the Ministry of Peshmerga in the KRG, said these groups do not adhere to the orders of the Iraqi government. "The continuous shelling by armed groups operating outside the law, which are known to everyone, and which do not abide by the decisions of the commander-in-chief of the Iraqi Armed Forces, creates security problems for the Kurdistan region," Yawar said. "There are five or six armed groups bombing Kurdistan, and they are known to everyone; among them are Iraqi Hezbollah, Sayyid al-Shuhada Battalions, Imam Ali Battalions, and the al-Nujaba Movement," Yawar explained. "Most of the bombing operations … come from the areas of the Nineveh Plains and the areas near the vicinity of Kirkuk and Salah al-Din," he said, adding that the KRG and the Iraqi government do not have comprehensive air defence systems. Buteconomic worriesare also weighing heavily not just on the Kurdish region but the whole of Iraq. Its Ministry of Oil announced a case of force majeure on all oilfields developed by foreign oil companies, citing disruptions to navigation through theStrait of Hormuzthat have halted most of the country's crude exports. Force majeure is an unforeseeable event that prevents a contract from being fulfilled. In this case, the Iraqi government has ordered a shutdown in oil production and no compensation to be paid to the foreign firms under their contracts. The crisis comes at a time when the government of Prime MinisterAli al-Zaidiwas proposing an economic programme based on implementing the "Development Road" project and expanding partnerships with the private sector and international companies, in an attempt to restructure the economy and reduce itsrelianceon oil. However, the closure of the Strait of Hormuz exposed the limits of Iraq's ability to face crises. The halt in oil exports led to a sharp decline in revenues, compounded by the stalling of projects to diversify export outlets through Turkiye, Syria, Jordan, and Saudi Arabia due to years-long political disputes, leaving the government facing an unprecedented financial strain. For Erbil, the continuation or expansion of the war could turn the security concerns into a deeper economic crisis, especially if the shutdown of oil and gas production is prolonged, or the attacks on energy facilities continue. Aland Kareem Salih, an economy researcher and vice president at the Vision Foundation for Strategic Studies, warns a total shutdown of oil exports could be disastrous for the Kurdish region. "If the war continued and became wider, it will inflict huge harm on the energy sector such as oil and gas and the damage then could be 100 percent," Salih warns, adding that the Iranian bombardment led to halted operations in Khor Mor gasfield and impacted electricity for the Kurdish region. "There is an agreement with the central government to export 200,000 barrels of oil daily. Now production has fallen to only 30,000. The figures are changing based on the security developments," he said. "The KRG was already witnessing a financial crisis for years and with this war, its non-oil revenues fell by around 70 percent, which cannot meet the basic needs of government departments. Even the real estate market witnessed a decline ranging between 15 percent and 20 percent of its prices as a result of the war," he says. Fears in the region's main cities – Erbil, Sulaymaniya and Duhok – are growing not only because of the attacks, but over the possibility of the region turning into a permanent arena for settling scores between Iran and its proxies versus the US and its allies.

headline: Fake chat screenshot misrepresented as Thai school shooter's message to mother
body of the article: Following a deadly school shooting on the outskirts of Bangkok on August 7, 2026, social media users shared a fake screenshot purportedly showing a conversation between the shooter and his mother on the LINE messaging app. But an analysis of the circulating image found garbled text and interface elements inconsistent with the messaging platform. A Thai police general told AFP the image was not authentic, saying the phone had been seized by investigators. "This is what caused the shooting, read this chat," says the Thai-language hashtag on aFacebook postshared on August 8. It circulated online one day after a deadlyschool shootingin Nonthaburi province, bordering Bangkok, where a 14-year-old assailant shot dead his grandparents at their home before killing six others at his school (archived link). The post includes a screenshot that purportedly shows a conversation between a son and mother, where he requests to be transferred to a different school to avoid being bullied. After being scolded, the son threatens to commit a mass shooting at his house and school. According to the screenshot, the mom responded: "If you're brave enough then do it, grandfather has a gun in the house." Superimposed Thai text above the screenshot, which was shared more than 250 times, reads: "This chat is depressing". Screenshot of the false Facebook post taken on August 10, 2026, with the red X added by AFP Similar claims have circulated elsewhere onReddit,Instagram,YouTubeand Facebook inThaiandBurmese, as social media users speculated on the shooter's motive. In vestigators have interviewed more than a dozen witnesses and were examining the boy's computer and phone to determine the "real cause of the shooting", Atthapol Anusit, a deputy police commander for the region surrounding the capital, told reporters on August 9. "We looked into his PC and found history that he watched violent videos on social media," Anusit said. Some commenters appeared to believe the image showed a real conversation between the shooter and his mother. "I pity the lad, he must have been under so much duress," one user wrote. Another said: "A mother must never speak like this, they shouldn't scold him for this." However, this is not a genuine screenshot taken from the shooter's phone. Anusittold AFP in a telephone interview on August 10 that the circulating claim was false, explaining that the shooter's phone had been seized by authorities (archived link). "This is not a genuine screenshot," he said. "His belongings, which include his phone, are currently being investigated by the Forensic Science Division." Areverse image searchon Google brought up other variations of the same purported conversation, but with differing timestamps. A close review of the text messages  identified typos and garbled Thai text, with inconsistencies seen in the same letters and words -- a characteristic of text fabricated by AI. Another visual anomaly is the LINE messenger app's user interface. In the circulating image, the number "99+" appears on the top left corner, which shows the user's unread messages from other chats. Screenshot comparison of the false Instagram post (L) and a genuine screenshot taken from LINE messenger, with highlights added by AFP This contradicts LINE's authentic user interface, where unread chat messages are instead displayed on a bottom tab as seen in examples shown in the app's previous redesignannouncementintroduced on December 8, 2020 (archived link).

headline: Colombia quake: Frantic search for survivors as over 2,700 reported missing
body of the article: Rescuers are searching through collapsed buildings in western Colombia for survivors after the country's strongest earthquake this century killed at least 224 people and caused widespread devastation, according to local media. Emergency teams in the worst affected cities, including Cali and Pereira, have been working through the night and into Tuesday, listening for signs of life and trying to reach people trapped beneath concrete and debris during the magnitude 7.4 earthquake. The Choco region west of Cali and Pereira has also been impacted, but the extent of the damage is still not clear. Authorities have warned that the death toll from Monday's quake could rise as search teams reach more affected areas in a big challenge for newly elected far-right President Abelardo de la Espriella. Here is what you need to know: Dozens of people were killed in Cali, located 280km (175 miles) southwest of the capital, Bogota. On Monday President De la Espriella said 35 people were killed in the city. Dozens of buildings were left leaning precariously or destroyed outright, forcing residents into ‌the streets in the city of about 2.2 million people. Local authorities farther north in the Risaralda region, where Pereira is located, said the death toll included at least 40 people killed there. Authorities also confirmed nine people killed in the Choco region, two in the Caldas region and a 73-year-old in the Antioquia region. At least 87 people were initially reported injured, but de la Espriella later reported 700 injured in Valle del Cauca alone. More than 2,700 people had been reported missing on citizen-run websites by Monday night although that figure does not necessarily represent the number of people confirmed missing. About 1,600 buildings have been damaged or destroyed, including the towers of a historic cathedral in the city of Manizales. Several of the top floors of one of Cali's hospitals – some dedicated to paediatric care – collapsed upon themselves, leaving some patients trapped and forcing about 600 others to be tended to on a street strewn with rubble, hospital director Irne Torres Castro told Caracol television. De la Espriella, who assumed power on Friday, said rescuing people trapped under rubble was the government's first priority, as he declared a state of emergeny. He traveled to Choco's capital, Quibdo, on Monday night and announced he had mobilised "the entire military and police apparatus" to respond, deploying engineers, rescue workers and search dogs. Cali and Pereira implemented curfews on Monday night. "Our ‌intention is to cooperate in any way necessary. Here, there are no distinctions or ideological divisions when it comes to defending our people or showing solidarity," the president told journalists. "Choco will never again be the 'land of the forgotten,'" he also said. Search and rescue operations continued into Tuesday with soldiers, emergency workers, firefighters, volunteers and relatives digging through collapsed buildings. In Cali, volunteers formed human chains to remove concrete, bricks and other debris by hand. Rescuers repeatedly stopped to listen for signs of life from people trapped beneath the rubble. Two women and two children were rescued from a collapsed building, firefighters said, while other teams continued searching for survivors. In Pereira, rescue workers said they were in contact with a boy trapped beneath a bakery while cranes were being used to remove dangerous sections of damaged buildings. Residents and rescue workers search through rubble after an earthquake struck Cali, Colombia, on August 10, 2026 [Santiago Saldarriaga/AP Photo] Authorities have also deployed engineers, rescue workers and search dogs to Choco, where the extent of the destruction remains unclear because the region is remote and difficult to access. De la Espriella said the government had mobilised the "entire military and police apparatus" for the response. The rescue effort faces particular challenges in the Choco region, more than 200km (125 miles) west of Cali and Pereira. The city of San Jose Del Palmar was the epicentre of the earthquake, the United States Geological Survey said. It is a community of 4,800 people about 400km (250 miles) west of Bogota. Much of Choco is reachable only by boat or plane, which may pose a problem for authorities in assessing the wider toll. Colombia's Geological Service said 21 aftershocks had been recorded by late Monday as authorities warned that further tremors were possible. (Al Jazeera) Camila Gomez, the deputy director of programmes for Colombia and Venezuela at the International Rescue Committee, warned that the powerful earthquake hit a region already in deep crisis. "This is the largest earthquake that Colombia has experienced in two decades," she told Al Jazeera. Gomez noted the damage in the areas hit was still being assessed. "From what we have seen already, there is a clear need, of course, for health services and education services because some of the education facilities – at least, I think, 50 of them – have been affected by this earthquake." The earthquake hit at 7:34 am local (12:34 GMT) on Monday, with rescuers most likely to find survivors within 48 and 72 hours of the disaster. Aside from extensive search and rescue efforts, Colombia declared a national state of emergency. De la Espriella visited Quibdo, the capital of the Choco region, and Cali and promised rental subsidies for people whose homes have been damaged. Authorities declared nighttime curfews in Cali, Armenia and Manizales. Cali also deployed additional police and military personnel amid concerns about looting. Hospitals in five cities were placed on red alert while authorities suspended operations at airports in Pereira, Manizales, Quibdo, Armenia, Cartago and Buenaventura to allow for structural inspections. Civilians have played a major role in the immediate response, bringing food and supplies and helping firefighters search for survivors. Carmen Yasmin Garcia, 43, a Cali resident volunteering with rescue teams, said on Monday afternoon that her group had freed seven people from a collapsed building but four others and a dog remained trapped. "A moment ago, there was scratching, but now we can't hear anything. We still have faith ⁠that the dog is alive and we can get these people out," Garcia said. "We need ⁠people with sticks and spades. The more people lending a hand the better." Authorities have also postponed the Petronio Alvarez Music Festival in Cali, an annual celebration of Pacific music that was due to start on Wednesday, as well as professional football matches. The US announced $15.5m in emergency assistance for shelters, food and other earthquake relief. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington was closely monitoring the situation and stood ready to support Colombia. The European Union said it mobilised the Copernicus satellite service to support rescue operations. Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele and Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum, whose countries were among the largest providers of aid to Venezuela after its twin earthquakes in June, said they were ready to assist Colombia. "From El Salvador, we are in communication and ready to provide immediate support with our rescue teams, medical personnel, paramedics, supplies or any other assistance that our Colombian brothers and sisters deem necessary," Bukele said. Colombian pop megastar Shakira also led calls for unity. "All my strength and love to my homeland. Let's hold each other tight," she said.

headline: Three Banksy artworks cost UK taxpayers almost £150,000 to remove
body of the article: ThreeBanksyartworks have cost the public purse almost £150,000 (€175,000) in removal, security and related costs. The single largest cost comes from a mural painted on theRoyal Courts of Justicein London in September 2025. Removal and security work there has so far cost more than £85,000 (€100,000), according to the BBC. The removal process is still ongoing and costs are expected to rise. The mural depicted a helpless protester lying on the ground holding a blood-spattered placard, while a judge loomed over him wielding a gavel. It was largely seen as a response to the UK government's crackdown on activist group Palestine Action. A freedom of information request revealed a breakdown of the costs. The Ministry of Justice told the BBC that £50,000 (€59,000) had gone on trying to strip the paint from the Grade II-listed building on Carey Street. A further £35,000 (€41,000) covered overtime and security. "The Royal Courts of Justice is a listed building and HMCTS are obliged to maintain its original character," the HM Courts and Tribunals Service said. Related Street artists from 21 countries transform Oslo into an open-air graffiti gallery Banksy's true identity revealed? New report claims to unmask world famous street artist A statue of a man holding a flag covering his face, and signed 'Banksy', which has appeared in Waterloo Place in London, Thursday, 30 April 2026. - Credit: AP Photo The anonymous Bristol-born street artist's work has also generated costs elsewhere in the capital. A further £60,000 (€70,000) was spent on security barriers, staff and administrative costs to protect aBanksy statuethat appeared in London in April. The work depicts a man walking off the end of a plinth. The figure is holding a flag pole, with the fabric covering his face. In August 2024, he also transformed aCity of London police sentry boxinto a giant piranha tank. The artwork was later removed at a cost of £2,200 (€2,500) and is due to go on permanent display at the London Museum later this year. The recent cases have renewed debate over the place of Banksy's work in public spaces and the extent to which public money should be spent protecting or removing it. Art critic Estelle Lovatt defends Banksy's work and highlights the benefits for tourism. "Some people visit Buckingham Palace and others visit Banksy's art," she told the BBC. "His work brings people together in a way that politics can divide us. He's like the Pied Piper or a town crier." But Shadow Justice Secretary Nick Timothy took a very different view, describing the use of taxpayers' money to deal with the artwork as "outrageous". "Our courts are a national symbol of justice and the rule of law," he said. "Banksy's vandalism should be stopped and he should foot the bill for the costs he imposes on others." In London, the debate centres on a work by one of the world's most famous artists. In Rome, the problem is far less glamorous as monuments, homes and newly restored buildings find themselves covered in anonymous tags. The Italian capital has become the unlikely workplace of 28-year-old architectural restorer Valerio Tuveri, who has built a following on Instagram and TikTok by travelling around the city removing tags and graffiti from its historic walls. Using a sandblaster and a camera phone, Tuveri has become known online as "the guy who cleans Rome". A wall outside Rome's historic Villa Sciarra daubed with graffiti before Tuveri's treatment - Credit: Giovanni Grezzi His latest project has been Villa Sciarra, a historic landmark in Rome, where fresh graffiti had appeared on newly restored walls. Wearing protective equipment and using a high-pressure sand blaster, he carefully removed the spray paint while preserving the stone underneath. "I decided to take this path, this 'battle', against graffiti because Rome is, in my opinion, the most beautiful city in the world, but at the same time the most vandalised city in Europe," he says. "There is meaningless writing everywhere: on monuments, private homes, cars and shutters." Tuveri believes there is a clear distinction between street art and the indiscriminate tags that cover many of the city's historic buildings. He says Italy should crack down harder on those responsible. He is calling for more surveillance cameras, stricter security checks and tougher financial penalties to discourage offenders.

headline: Australian TV host, social media users falsely claim Judaism removed from census
body of the article: Australia's census in August triggered a series of false claims on social media and network television that the government had "removed Judaism" as a religion option, playing into the Jewish community's fear and anger following the antisemitic Bondi Beach shooting. The Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) said the faith was not removed from the form, as it was not on the previous census -- and if residents do not see their religion, they can write it in under "Other". "This is a revolting slap in the face to the Jewish people of Australia... The religion, Judaism, has been completely removed from the written choices in the Census," says aFacebook postshared on July 31, 2026, in a group containing content critical of Prime Minister Anthony Albanese. The post includes a picture of what appears to be a question on the census asking "What is the person's religion?" and providing 10 options, as well as "Other" so residents could write in their answer. "The Jewish faith. REMOVED, ERASED. Are we still in Australia?" the Facebook post asks. Screenshot of a Facebook post captured on August 10, 2026, with a red X added by AFP The claim circulated ahead of the country'snationwide censuson August 11, which occurs every five years (archived link). It also comes months after a father-and-son duo opened fire at a Hanukkah celebration on Bondi Beach in December. Themass shooting, Australia's deadliest in 30 years, sparked national conversations about antisemitism and widespread anger over the failure to shield Jewish Australians from harm (archived link). Claims that Judaism was removed from the census also made their way to broadcaster News24, formerly Sky News Australia, where host Peta Credlin amplified them during an August 3 segment. "I am still appalled that as far as the ABS is concerned, Jews in Australia don't matter. And I say that because what other conclusion can you draw after the Australian Bureau of Statistics removed them from the form?" Credlin said in the clip, which circulated August 4 onFacebook. "In 2021, Judaism was on the official census form, and this year they are not". Screenshot of a Facebook post taken on August 11, 2026, with red crosses added by AFP Her segment has since been removed from News24'ssocial media pagesandaffiliated sites. Similar posts stillcirculatedelsewhere onFacebookandX, with some people also asking why Christianity was removed. "Why have they removed the category CHRISTIAN from the census?" says onepostin a Facebook group called "Made in Australia Movement". But both claims are false. The ABS said in an August 4statementthat the narrative "misrepresents the question on a person's religion and the way Judaism is captured and reported in Census data" (archived link). "The 2026 Census includes the same religious affiliation question wording and tick box options as the 2021 Census," the agency said. "Judaism has not been removed as an option from the Census form, as it has never been a pre-filled response option on the Census religion question." In its statement, the ABS included a link to the2021 Census form, which includes a question with identical options to the latest version (archived link). Screenshot of the religion question on Australia's 2021 census, taken on August 11, 2026 The agency said people who choose "Other" can specify their particular religion, and that "Judaism has been included as an example in the instructional text since examples were introduced in 2001". After the ABS published its statement, News24issued a correctionon August 5 (archived link). "The Credlin program published on 3 August 2026 stated that in 2021, Judaism was on the official census form, and this year, it is not. That was incorrect," the broadcaster said. "In both 2021 and 2026 the census forms provided Judaism as an example of 'other' religions to be specified by those completing the census in writing." The 2026 census, independently verified by AFP, lists Judaism as a write-in example alongside various denominations associated with Christianity, such as Catholic, Presbyterian and Baptist. Screenshots of the online form (L) and the paper census featuring the religion question from the 2026 census, with elements highlighted by AFP When asked how the ABS chooses which religion to include as an option, a spokesperson told AFP that "the selection and ordering of tick boxes... is usually based on the most common responses from the previous census". "When we use tick boxes, they must be mutually exclusive to avoid public confusion in responding and to produce accurate statistics. This means that including Christianity as a tick box would result in a loss of information on the specific Christian denominations, such as Catholic and Anglican," the spokesperson said in an August 11 email. "People can use the free text field if they want to respond with a religion not included in the tick boxes, including a response of 'Christian'." According to the 2021 census, fewer than 100,000 Australiansidentifyas Jewish -- about 0.4 percent of the country's population (archived link). The ABS explained its changes to the 2026 census in a listpublishedthe previous year (archived link). The agencydid the same thingbefore the 2021 census (archived link). The Australian Associated Pressand public broadcasterABCalso debunked claims that the government removed Judaism as a religion option on the 2026 census (archivedhereandhere).

headline: Syrian court sentences Bashar al-Assad in absentia to death
body of the article: A Syrian court on Tuesday sentenced ousted president Bashar al-Assad in absentia to death on charges of premeditated murder, torture, arbitrary detention and crimes against humanity. Al-Assad is currently in exile in Russia, which has so far not extradited him to Syria. The verdict against al-Assad from the fourth criminal court in the capital Damascus was read out live on Syrian state television. Alongside al-Assad, his cousin Atef Najib was also sentenced to death. Najib, who is in Syria, is one of the few key figures of the al-Assad government who will stand trial in the country. In 2011, he was the security chief in the southern city of Daraa, where the anti-government uprising began after teenagers sprayed graffiti on the walls of their school and were arrested. This started the nearly 14-year civil war. Najib is accused in the indictment of crimes against the Syrian people including "systematic mass murder" and arbitrary arrests. Bashar al-Assad's brother Maher al-Assad and other representatives of the ousted government were also sentenced to death in absentia. They were accused of premeditated and planned murder and torture resulting in death.

headline: Libyan authorities battle big blaze at major oil refinery
body of the article: Watch: Huge blaze after attack on petrol tank in Libya Libyan emergency services have been battling to contain a huge blaze at a major oil plant after it was targeted by unknown attackers. The Zawiya refinery, west of the capital Tripoli, was hit in a drone strike on Monday evening - the third such incident in two days. The National Oil Corporation (NOC) said a tank containing about 4.5m litres of fuel was directly hit, triggering a huge fire that caused it to collapse. It said it was considering suspending operations if the attacks continued. There were no "serious injuries" from the fire, with most patients treated for smoke inhalation, Libya's Ambulance and Emergency Service said on Tuesday. The Zawiya refinery is the largest operational facility in Libya, with an output of 120,000 barrels per day. The NOC condemned similar attacks in past days in Zawiya, including two drone strikes on a naphtha reservoir and a water desalination plant. It called on the authorities to investigate who was behind the violence. The attacks have highlighted continuing instability in Libya, which has been split in two since a civil war broke out after the ousting of former leader Muammar Gaddafi. Colonel Gaddafi seized power in 1969 and ruled autocratically for four decades until he was toppled and killed in 2011 in a rebellion assisted by Western military intervention Since his fall, rival power centres, one based in the east backed by military commander Khalifa Haftar, and one in the west in Tripoli, led by Prime Minister Abdulhamid Dbeibah, have been jostling for political and military dominance. Libyan prosecutors launch probe into killing of Gaddafi's son Libya's army chief killed in air crash in Turkey [BBC] Go toBBCAfrica.comfor more news from the African continent. Follow us on Twitter@BBCAfrica, on Facebook atBBC Africaor on Instagram atbbcafrica Focus on Africa This Is Africa

headline: Ethiopia's Tigray rebel authorities condemn army drone strikes
body of the article: Rebel authorities in Ethiopia's Tigray region on Tuesday accused the federal government of carrying out deadly drone strikes in the northern region, denouncing "a serious escalation" amid fears of a new war. Tensions have been growing for months, with federal and Tigrayan forces gathering on either side of the border of Ethiopia's northernmost regional state. Each side has accused the other of seeking to trigger a new conflict, less than four years after the end of a bloody war that killed hundreds of thousands of people. "There was a drone strike carried out by the Ethiopian government yesterday (Monday) in Merewa" in southern Tigray, near the border with the Amhara region, Amanuel Assefa, vice chairman of the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) told AFP. A medical source at a hospital in Alimata told AFP that four Tigrayan fighters -- a woman and three men -- had been wounded in the strikes. "Two of them have already undergone surgery," the source said, speaking on condition of anonymity. In a statement sent to AFP on Tuesday, the TPLF said the strikes targeted Tigrayan troops "causing human casualties", without providing further details. A spokesperson for the federal army has not yet responded to AFP's request for comment regarding the accusation. Amanuel also said that the strikes hit a high school, which AFP was unable to independently verify. On August 1, fighting broke out between federal forces and TPLF troops in northwestern Tigray, near the border with Sudan, according to the TPLF. The federal government has not commented on the incident. Tigray, home to around six million people, emerged in 2022 from a two-year war between TPLF forces and the federal army, supported by local militias and the Eritrean army. The conflict claimed at least 600,000 lives, according to an African Union (AU) estimate. A peace agreement signed in November 2022 put an end to the fighting, but several key points, such as the return of displaced people or the disarmament of the TPLF, have never been implemented. Direct clashes between Tigrayan forces and the federal army broke out again in late 2025, for the first time since the signing of the peace deal. Contacted by AFP about the TPLF drone strike claim, the AU, which mediated the peace deal and is based in the Ethiopian capital Addis Ababa, had yet to comment. - Rapprochement - For months, the federal authorities have accused the TPLF of growing closer to neighbouring Eritrea. Relations between Ethiopia and Eritrea have long been fraught, and the two Horn of Africa countries fought a 1998-2000 border war in which tens of thousands died. Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed initially sought rapprochement with Eritrea when he came to power, and the two governments cooperated against the Tigrayan rebels in the 2020-2022 conflict. However, they fell out over the peace accord, from which Eritrea was excluded, and which stipulated the withdrawal of foreign soldiers. Eritrea accuses landlocked Ethiopia of coveting its Red Sea port of Assab after years of Abiy insisting his country must have access to the sea through peaceful means. Amanuel told AFP that he wants to form alliances with anyone fighting the Ethiopian federal government, but gave no further details. According to statements gathered by Human Rights Watch and by AFP, rebel authorities in Tigray have for several months been carrying out a forced recruitment campaign. World Health Organization chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, who comes from the Tigray region, on Sunday on X urged "the federal government and all regional leaders to choose dialogue over guns, and to pursue real political solutions". The TPLF effectively ruled the whole of Ethiopia for nearly 30 years until Abiy rose to power in 2018. His government barred the TPLF from political activity last year, but it remains all-powerful in Tigray, with its own military. At the end of April, the group said it had reinstated a regional parliament, which had been deemed illegitimate. dyg/ayv/giv-kjm/st

headline: Nick Shirley says he was chased by man with knife covering Ceuta migrant crisis
body of the article: (NewsNation) — Independent journalistNick Shirleysaid he was chased by a man wielding a knife while reporting on a surge of migrants into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta. Shirley traveled toCeuta, Spain, at the end of July after a large number of migrants crossed into the territory from Morocco over a short span. He said he went to a local market to interview residents when a man began shouting in Spanish for him to stop filming. "They grab a bottle from the garbage, chucked it at us," Shirley toldNewsNation's Katie Pavlich. "Then he starts throwing rocks. And then he starts coming towards us, and he says, I'm going to stab both of you, and starts pulling out a knife." US spy felled by energy weapon deserves recognition, widow says Shirley said he and his crew ran and were eventually met by a police officer who escorted them back to their car, which had been parked near where the confrontation happened. "Actually, after I ran down to the bottom of the hill, we found a police officer, and they escorted us back up to our car," Shirley said. Shirley said the migrants he spoke with, most of whom he described as men in their 20s, told him theycrossed the borderwith the goal of eventually reachingmainland Europe. He said Moroccan authorities did not stop people from approaching the border, and he alleged Spanish border guards opened the gates to let the crowd through, saying there appeared to be coordination between officials on both sides. Marine One close call puts FAA staffing back in the spotlight "The gates were literally opened by the Spanish border patrol," Shirley said. "And the Moroccan authority let all those people come through as well." He also said he sawchildrenamong the migrants without adequate food, water or shade. Copyright 2026 Nexstar Media, Inc. headline: Old video from India misrepresented as sectarian violence in Nepal
body of the article: Footage of men climbing to the top of a mosque's minaret and attempting to hoist a saffron flag has been falsely shared in social media posts claiming it shows Hindus vandalising a mosque during religious violence in southern Nepal in late July 2026. The footage has circulated since February 2020, and in fact shows a mosque that was vandalised in Delhi's Ashok Nagar area during deadly sectarian clashes. "After Muslim jihadist extremists pelted stones at a Hindu procession, Hindus became furious and vandalised a mosque before setting it on fire," says part of the Hindi-language caption of aFacebook videoshared on August 1, 2026. The video shows men ripping off the muezzin's loudspeaker on top of the mosque's minaret and placing a Hindu religious flag and an Indian flag. Screenshot of the false post captured on August 5, 2026, with a red X added by AFP The clip also circulated in similarInstagramandX postsasviolencebetween Hindu and Muslim communities in several towns in southern Nepal left at least three people dead and dozens injured (archived link). The violence began late on July 26 in a village in the southern Sunsari district, which borders India, after an argument over loud music and the use of religious flags during a Hindu procession, according to officials. Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah,  who has kept a low profile since being elected in March, broke his silence to deliver his first address to the nation, calling on his countrymen to be "responsible citizens and remove the clouds of unrest". The circulating video, however, is several years old and in fact occurred in India's capital New Delhi. Areverse image searchon Google usingkeyframesfrom the falsely shared video led to thesame clipshared on X on February 25, 2020 (archived link). The video is captioned: "Update Ashok Nagar, Delhi 6.00pm: A mosque has been vandalized by Hindutva terror forces, as they brazenly revisit their demolition tactics." Screenshot comparison of the falsely shared video (L) and the X clip from February 2020 Similar visuals were also shared inmedia reportsabout sectarian violence that erupted inDelhiin February 2020 (archivedhereandhere). These clashes began on February 24, 2020 amidworsening religious tensionsfollowing a citizenship law that critics said was part of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Hindu nationalist agenda (archived link). Supporters and detractors of the citizenship law then descended into pitched battles between the mobs. The riots, among the worst communal violence in the capital in decades, left at least 27 people dead and more than 200 injured. Local fact-checking organisation BOOM Livereportedon February 27, 2020 that the mosque shown in the falsely shared clip was located in Delhi's Ashok Nagar area (archived link). AFP photos from the time also show the damaged mosque. A man speaks on his mobile phone as he walks past a burnt-out mosque and shops following clashes between people supporting and opposing a contentious amendment to India's citizenship law, in New Delhi on February 26, 2020. Sajjad HUSSAIN AFP AFP haspreviously debunkedother false claims aboutreligious violencein Nepal.

headline: South Korea arrests two Chinese nationals over military spying
body of the article: South Korean authorities have arrested two former Chinese military officers on suspicion of spying on fighter jets near an airbase, South Korea's official Yonhap news agency reported on Tuesday. One of the suspects, a Chinese national in his 60s, is suspected of "benefiting the enemy" and breaking a law on the protection of communications after making multiple visits to South Korea on a tourist visa, Yonhap reported. He is believed to have listened in to communications between fighter jets and air-traffic control towers from a hotel near an airport in the south-western city of Gunsan, according to the Gyeonggi Nambu Provincial Police. Both South Korean and US Air Force units are stationed at Gunsan Airport. The man's stays in South Korea are said to have coincided with joint air force exercises conducted by South Korea and the United States. According to Yonhap, the second suspect is a 45-year-old ethnic Korean who holds Chinese citizenship. He is alleged to have recruited a South Korean woman who worked at Camp Humphreys, a US military base in South Korea and the largest US military base outside the US. She is alleged to have obtained classified information about US-South Korean military exercises from there. The two could face life in prison if found guilty of "benefiting the enemy," Yonhap reported. The US has around 28,500 troops stationed in South Korea and conducts military exercises with the South Korean armed forces every year. The next joint exercise begins next week.

headline: Russia accelerates roll out of Starlink rival
body of the article: Russiais ramping up the deployment of a satellite internet system that rivals SpaceX'sStarlinknetwork, according to Ukrainian officials. The Rassvet network, which beams high-speed broadband to people on the ground, currently has 16 satellites in operation but is expected to grow to a constellation of nearly 300 satellites by next year. Starlink is banned in Russia but is widely used in Ukraine, where it has given Kyiv a major advantage in drone operations and battlefield communications. SpaceX bossElon Muskhas blocked efforts from Kyiv to use the Starlink service for drone strikes within Russia, claiming that it could lead to an escalation in the conflict. Russian forces had been using grey-market Starlink terminals in Ukraine until Kyiv successfully lobbied SpaceX to disable them earlier this year, one of several factors that shifted battlefield momentum in Ukraine's favour. In an interview with Ukrainian media outlet RBC-Ukraine, Major General Vadym Skibitskyi, who is the deputy chief of Ukraine's GUR military intelligence service, ⁠said Russia is building its Rassvet network much faster than previously thought. "They have already `begun launching it much faster than originally planned," said Major General Skibitskyi. "It will continue launching more in order to create a constellation of 292 satellites in 2027 and expand it to 924 satellites by 2035. "Once Russia deploys a full satellite constellation, the system will operate like Starlink. Discussions are already underway on how to counter it." Developed by Russian aerospace company Bureau 1440, the system can currently operate only ‌intermittently when one of the satellites passes ‌over Ukrainian territory, according to Ukrainian intelligence. SpaceX's Starlink network has more than 10,000 operational satellites in low-Earth orbit, with plans to expand it to quadruple its current size. Other commercial space internet ventures include Eutelsat's OneWeb and Amazon Leo, both of which have already launched several hundred satellites. Additional reporting from agencies

headline: Iranian-backed Houthis kill 6 in attack on vessel, and other developments in the Mideast
body of the article: Yemeni authorities say six people were killed by Iran-backed Houthi rebels attacking a vessel in the Bab el-Mandeb strait. Here's a look at the latest developments in theIran warand the wider Middle East. Full coverage can be foundhere. Six people were killed Tuesday byHouthisfiring missiles on a vessel in the Bab el-Mandeb strait, Yemeni authorities said. Yemen's coast guard said the dead included four crew members and two members of the government-allied National Resistance Forces. Houthis fired three ballistic missiles at the Yemeni commercial vessel, according to the Transportation Ministry of Yemen's internationally recognized government. They are the first known deaths from Houthi attacks on shipping off Yemen in thelatest bout of fightingin the Arab country. With the Strait of Hormuz effectively shut down by Iran, there has been a renewed focus on the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb strait at Yemen's southern tip, which is an alternate route for Saudi Arabia to ship its oil. The deadly vessel strike came amid Houthi attacks on the government-held port city of Mokha on the Red Sea and other areas of the country. Dozens of government troops and civilians have been killed in attacks since last week, according to the Yemeni military. The strikes are part of an escalation by the Houthis against government forces in Yemen and oil facilities in neighboring Saudi Arabia, which supports the Yemeni government, and the kingdom's shipping in the Red Sea. The Houthi attacks could reignite Yemen's civil war following a 2022 truce, and open a new front in the Middle East war. Mohammed Abdul-Salam, the Houthis' chief negotiator and spokesperson, accused Saudi Arabia in a social media post of exploiting the ceasefire to tighten an air and sea blockade it imposed in 2015. He said the Houthis are open for negotiations but any settlement must include lifting the blockade. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told reporters that the country had "astonished the whole world" in the war against the United States and Israel, proving "that it is a tough and invincible power." Iran has refused to back down on demands that the U.S. end its blockade of Iranian ports,lift sanctions on the Islamic Republicand fulfill other conditions before Tehran will consider reopening theStrait of Hormuz. Iran effectively closed the strait after Israel and the U.S. attacked the country on Feb. 28. Attacks on the key waterway — through which roughly one-fifth of the world's traded oil supplies passed before the war — and uncertainty around its future have kept energy prices a major focus of U.S. politics ahead of November's midterm elections. U.S. PresidentDonald Trumpsaid Monday in an Oval Office exchange with reporters that the U.S. Navy's blockade is preventing Iran from selling its oil on the international market, effectively choking the Iranian economy. "Yeah, they can make trouble," Trump said, "but they're broke." Pakistani Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi traveled Tuesday to Tehran for talks aimed at encouraging Iran to resume negotiations with the United States under an interim peace deal brokered by Pakistan in June, two officials said. The officials spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the media and they provided no further details. Pakistan's government had not publicly announced Naqvi's visit. It is his sixth trip to Iran as part of Pakistan's diplomatic efforts to ease tensions between Iran and the U.S. —Munir Ahmed in Islamabad In Syria, acourt sentencedformer President Bashar Assad along with his younger brother to death for crimes against humanity and war crimes during Syria's 14-year conflict that left about half a million people dead. Assad and his brother Maher, who fled to Russia after insurgents marched into Damascus in December 2024, were sentenced in absentia at the Fourth Criminal Court in the Syrian capital. ___ This story has been corrected to state that Bashar and Maher Assad fled to Russia in 2024, not 2014.

headline: Drone strike sparks massive blaze at Libya’s Zawiya refinery
body of the article: CAIRO (AP) — Firefighters in western Libya fought Tuesday to extinguish the remnants of a massive fire caused by a drone strike on an oil facility, and a car bomb killed a senior military officer in the country's east, in the latest attacks inthe chaos-stricken North African nation. The drone hit a gasoline tank at the Zawiya oil refinery in the Mediterranean town of Zawiya on Monday, about 47 kilometers (about 30 miles) west of capitalTripoli, the state-run National Oil Corporation said. The attack ignited a massive blaze at gasoline-storage tank that burned through the night and was still burning as of Tuesday afternoon, according to the Civil Defense, a first responders' agency. There were no reports of casualties, the health authorities said. No group has claimed responsibility for a series of attacks on oil facilities in Zawiya, or the car bomb in the eastern city of Benghazi on Monday. Footage aired by local media showed massive flames and fireballs erupting from the tank, with black and orange smoke rising in the sky as firefighters spray what appears to be foam or water in efforts to quench the intense fire. As they fought the flames, another drone hit close to a key oil tank nearby but did not cause casualties or damage, the company said. The company said the tank, which held 4.5 million liters of fuel when it was hit, collapsed, and declared a state of maximum emergency at the facility. Two drones hit the town's power plant, with one damaging its firefighting system while the second landed close to the facility's main fuel storage, local media reported. Monday's strikes were the latest in a series of drone attacks on oil infrastructure in Zawiya, which houses critical energy infrastructure including the country's largest oil refinery, an export terminal and a power plant. The drone strikes come as Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan is set to arrive in Libya for a visit. He is due to visit both Tripoli and Bengahzi. Over the weekend, the oil company said drone strikes had hit a fuel tank and a desalination plant linked to the oil facilities in Zawiya. It said the tank was damaged. The attacks come as tensions are rising between the government of western Libya and a warlord who controls the city of Zawiya. Much of western Libya is ruled by local militias loosely allied to Prime Minister Abdul-Hamid Dbeibah's government in Tripoli. Jalel Harchaoui, an analyst affiliated with the Royal United Services Institute in London, said warlord Mohamed Bahroun has been cornered by the government and his forces "are likely to resort to desperate measures." Separately, a senior military officer with the forces of powerful commander Khalifa Hifter was killed in a car bomb Monday evening in the eastern city of Benghazi, authorities said. Maj. Gen. Fawzy al-Mansouri, director of the military intelligence of Hifter's self-styled Libyan National Army, was killed when an explosive-laden vehicle exploded into his car in the Sayyida Aisha neighborhood in Benghazi after, the LNA said. The LNA is allied with one of Libya's two rival governments, which controls the country's eastern and southern parts. The attacks underscoredthe fragility of securityin the oil-rich country. Libya, a largely lawless Mediterranean country, has been plunged into chaos and division following the 2011 uprising-turned-civil war, which toppled and later killedlongtime dictator Moammar Gadhafi. Amid the chaos, militias grew in wealth and power, particularly in Tripoli and the western part of the country. The county has been divided for years between rival administrations in the east and west, each backed by armed groups and foreign governments. Currently, it is governed by Prime Minister Abdul-Hamid Dbeibah's government in the west and by the administration of Prime Minister Ossama Hammad in the east.

headline: Wildfire at Indonesia's Mount Bromo mostly contained as smoke forces school closures
body of the article: MOUNT BROMO, Indonesia (AP) — Indonesian firefighters have mostly containeda wildfirethat has scorched a large area of a national park on the main island of Java, though crews are battling several remaining hot spots in the popular tourist destination, authorities said. The fire, which began last week, impacted nearly 900 hectares (2,224 acres) across the Bromo Tengger Semeru National Park as of Tuesday, after large areas of dry grassland, vegetation and protected edelweiss flowers burned in 36 hot spots, said Rudijanta Tjahja Nugraha, head of the park located in East Java province. The volcanic landscape of Mount Bromo, one of Indonesia's best-known attractions, is in the impacted area and has been closed as firefighters work to prevent the blaze from spreading in the conservation zone. As of Tuesday, active hot spots remain in two locations within the park: Puncak 30, a popular viewpoint for tourists visiting the volcanic landscape of Mount Bromo, and Dengklek, an area where the volcano monitoring post is located, said Suharyanto, the head of National Disaster Management Agency, or BNPB. "We expect the two remaining hotspots to be extinguished by Friday," said Suharyanto, who like many Indonesians uses a single name, during a visit to Mount Bromo on Tuesday. "That would allow us to redeploy two of the three water-bombing helicopters to help fight forest fires that are also burning in other areas." Teams have been working to prevent flare-ups on the ground and with aerial operations, Nugraha said. "We are not only trying to put out the fire, but also ensuring it is completely extinguished and does not reemerge," he said. Indonesia faces a growing wildfire crisis during the dry season. The BNPB said nearly 48,900 hectares (121,000 acres) of peatland had burned across six fire-prone provinces as of Monday, with the largest affected area in West Kalimantan province on Borneo island. In the West Kalimantan provincial capital Pontianak, the city's Education and Cultural Office on Monday ordered schools to suspend in-person classes after air quality deteriorated to unhealthy levels and health officials reported a rise in respiratory illnesses. The Indonesian government has intensified firefighting efforts across Sumatra and Borneo islands, deploying more than 35 aircraft including water-bombing helicopters and patrol airplanes. "Aerial operations are supporting ground operations which are especially critical in peatland areas," said Suharyanto. "Because peat fires can continue smoldering underground long after surface flames disappear and can reignite if not fully extinguished." Peatland fires generate dense smoke that contributes to hazardous haze, worsening air quality and increasing health risks across affected areas, sometimes even in neighboring countries, he said. Forest and peat fires in Indonesia have strained relations with neighboring countries. Satellite imagery has shown a haze of wildfire smoke drifting from West Kalimantan into neighboring Malaysia on several days this month, according to BNPB. Haze has worsened in Malaysia's Sarawak state, which shares a border with Indonesia's Kalimantan province on Borneo. The air pollutant index of Malaysia's Department of the Environment showed the number of areas recording unhealthy air quality levels in Sarawak rising to 11 early Tuesday. Sarawak's government told schools in those areas to halt outdoor activities. Fires are often started illegally by plantation owners or traditional farmers to clear land for planting and those burns periodically blanket parts of Southeast Asia in hazardous haze, authorities said. ___ Associated Press writers Niniek Karmini in Jakarta, Indonesia, and Eileen Ng in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, contributed to this report.

headline: Former Syrian President Assad sentenced to death in absentia for war crimes
body of the article: DAMASCUS, Syria (AP) — A Syrian court on Tuesday sentenced ousted President Bashar Assad and his brother in absentia for murder, torture and crimes against humanity committed before and during the country's 14-year civil war that left about half a million people dead. The verdicts by a court in Damascus are the first against Assad or any members of hisinner circlesince his family'sfive decadesin power came to an end 20 months ago. They are mostly symbolic, however, because Assad and his brother Maher hadfled to Russia, where they received asylum after the Syrian government's stunning collapse in December 2024. Six other former officials were also sentenced to death in absentia. The only former official sentenced to death and in custody is Assad's maternal cousinAtef Najib, who oversaw a crackdown on dissent that led to an uprising that sparked the civil war. Najib stood inside a cage wearing a prisoner's uniform as the judge read his sentence aloud, and a crowd gathered outside the heavily guarded courthouse. Even though Assad is unlikely to ever face justice, the verdicts will be popular among many Syrians, especially those who have expressed frustration that the new government hasn't moved with enough speed or strength against Assad-era figures. Some human rights groups, though, expressed concerns that the trials were rushed, potentially unfair and, at the very least, exposed flaws in Syria's justice system. "Bashar Assad used state agencies to commit war crimes and crimes against humanity," said judge Fakhareddine al-Aryan during a court session that was aired live on state TV — a contrast with Assad-era trials, which were conducted in secret. The verdicts al-Aryan read aloud found Assad and the others guilty of premeditated murder, including against children, as well as other acts of brutality, including torture. Al-Aryan said Najib could appeal. "Today is the day of justice for all the wounded, martyrs, detainees and Syrians who were forced to leave their country," said attorney Adnan al-Masalmeh who represented families of Najib's victims. "Today marks a victory of right against injustice, a victory of the Syrian people against the ousted regime." Najib is one of the highest-ranking security officials to be put on trial. He is a former army brigadier general who was in charge of political security in Syria's southern Daraa province. During his tenure, more than a dozen teenagers who scrawled anti-government graffiti on a school wall were arrested and tortured. The case became a catalyst for mass protests against the repressive policies of Assad's security forces. The protests were met by a brutal government crackdown in 2011 that spiraled into the civil war that ended with Assad's ouster in a lightning rebel offensive. Some of Najib's victims were present at the courthouse, including two who were teenagers in 2011 and expressed their opinions to The Associated Press. "Today we reached a point where the blood was not wasted," said Mouawiya Sayasneh, about those who died in the crackdown. Fifteen years later, "there is happiness that Atef Najib was sentenced to death," he said. Another man, Nayef Abazeid, who was detained at the age of 13 in 2011, expressed his satisfaction with the sentence, adding that "our biggest happiness will be when Bashar Assad is executed." Maher Assad was a former commander of the Syrian military's 4th Armored Division — which opposition activists have accused of killings, torture, extortion and drug trafficking, in addition to running its own detention centers. "Today's scenes outside the courthouse reflect 15 years of pain and a justice long denied," said Hiba Zayadin, Syria researcher at Human Rights Watch. She said the rights group opposes the death penalty in all cases, including this one, because "it's cruel and irreversible, especially when a fair trial isn't guaranteed." She said the appeal process for Najib "needs to meet fair trial standards." Real accountability for Assad-era crimes depends on Syria building a justice system that lasts, she said. The Washington-based Syria Justice and Accountability Center described Tuesday's conviction of Najib as a "historical step in Syria's transitional period," but said it exposed major flaws in the justice system which likely jeopardized his right to a fair trial. It said that SJAC's trial monitoring team attended Najib's trial and documented multiple issues such as rushed proceedings and witness testimony that did not connect Atef to the crimes he was charged with. SJAC said Najib's lawyer "lacked the capacity and willingness to meaningfully engage with the case or mount an adequate defense." ___ Associated Press writers Kareem Chehayeb and Bassem Mroue contributed to this report from Beirut. ___ This story has been edited to correct that Bashar and Maher Assad fled to Russia following the collapse of their government in December 2024, not December 2014.

headline: Meta and TikTok agree to fact-check content on Spain border crossings after deadly rush
body of the article: BRUSSELS, Aug 11 (Reuters) - Social networks Meta and TikTok have agreed to fact-check content on border crossings into Spain following ‌the massive rush to enter the Spanish enclave of Ceuta from ‌Morocco, European Union tech chief Henna Virkkunen said. The purpose is to prevent criminal networks ​from enticing potential migrants to attempt to cross with false information, which has led to tragic deaths, she said in a post on X late on Monday. • More than 70,000 would-be migrants flooded into Ceuta on July ‌30 in a surge ⁠that left nearly 100 dead. • Would-be migrants were encouraged by a handful of viral videos, including some posted ⁠by a Spanish news outlet intended to highlight the burden of migration pressures. • Meta and TikTok agreed with the EU to set up an "ad-hoc escalation ​and cooperation ​mechanism with fact-checkers" as part of ​crisis protocols, according to the ‌post. • The platforms have also committed to prohibit content related to people smuggling, a Commission spokesperson added on Tuesday. • The spokesperson told reporters the platforms act to block or deprioritise content on a voluntary basis — the European Commission does not force them to remove any content, but ‌opens a dialogue with them so they ​act responsibly. • The Commission and pan-European police ​force Europol are discussing ​the situation with the two companies every day, Virkkunen's ‌post said. • Virkkunen also spoke to ​Oscar Lopez, the Spanish ​minister for digital economy, on how to prevent border crossings and the loss of lives. • Ceuta and Melilla have the EU's ​only land borders with ‌Africa and both cities periodically experience surges in attempted crossings ​by migrants seeking to reach Europe. (Reporting by Inti Landauro; Editing ​by Kevin Buckland and Alison Williams)

headline: Russian attacks kill 10 in Ukraine as Zelenskyy says Moscow is getting more North Korean missiles
body of the article: KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Russia attacked Ukrainian cities with missiles, drones and glide bombs Tuesday, killing at least 10 civilians, officials said, as President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Moscow is getting new military help from North Korea for its more than4-year-old invasion. Zelenskyy said Russian forces used ballistic missiles supplied by North Korea in an overnight attack on the southeastern city of Zaporizhzhia, where a company said seven workers at its steel plant were killed and 21 injured. Three more people, including a 15-year-old boy, were killed by Russian drones and artillery in the central Dnipropetrovsk region, authorities said. In addition to the ballistic missiles, North Korea is preparing to deploymore of its troopsto Russia, Zelenskyy said late Monday. Russian President Vladimir Putin and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un signed astrategic partnership agreementin 2024, pledging mutual aid if either country faces aggression. Kim has sent thousands of troops andhuge supplies of weaponsto support Putin's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Some experts say the engagement with Moscow is helping improve North Korea's military capabilities, and Zelenskyy said the battlefield experience would help Pyongyang menace other countries in its region. Ukraine says Russia is scaling up its production of ballistic missiles, aiming to exploit Kyiv'scritical shortageof Patriot air defense interceptors that can stop them, and claims Moscow is preparing to recruit more troops for a new push on the front line that stretches 1,250 kilometers (775 miles) along eastern and southern Ukraine. "Every step Russia takes — increasing ballistic missile production, bringing in North Korean equipment, preparing for mobilization — all of this shows that Moscow is preparing not for peace, but for escalation," Zelenskyy said on social media. In an unusual step, Ukraine's air force didn't say in its daily report how many missiles Russia launched overnight. It was not clear whether the omission was deliberate, and Kyiv officials made no immediate comment. U.S.-led diplomatic efforts to stop the war have fizzled as Washington grew frustrated with the lack of progress and its attention turned to theIran war. In an indication that Putin is determined to press on with the invasion, Russia's highest court on Monday ordered that Yabloko, the only political party opposing the war, to beexcluded from the ballotin the Sept. 18-20 parliamentary election. "The Kremlin will not enter serious negotiations or make meaningful compromises on its demands as long as Putin believes that he has a viable military path to achieving his full objectives," the Institute for the Study of War, a Washington-based think tank, said in an analysis Monday. "Ukraine's Patriot shortages offer Russia an opportunity to cause very serious damage to Ukraine over the coming winter and will therefore contribute to delaying meaningful negotiations and protracting the war," it said. Russian forces also struck parts of the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, overnight, according to officials. One strike hit the grounds of a children's hospital, leaving two craters and shattering windows, the State Emergency Service said. Children and medical workers were in bomb shelters and nobody was hurt, it added. At another location in Kyiv, a Russian strike started a fire in a warehouse that spread across about 1,200 square meters (nearly 13,000 square feet), according to emergency officials. The Russian Defense Ministry said its forces overnight struck "military industrial facilities and transport and logistics centers" in Kyiv and Zaporizhzhia with "ground-based precision weapons." It said in a statement that it hit civilian storage facilities housing drones in Kyiv and a metallurgical plant in Zaporizhzhia. Metinvest, a major Ukrainian mining and metals company with operations in Zaporizhzhia, said seven of its steel plant employees died as staff tried to reach shelters after a warning of an incoming ballistic missile. The company, which employs tens of thousands of people, said in a statement that the attack damaged its blast furnace and other equipment and forced the plant to shut down. Russia targeted Kyiv and Zaporizhzhia with Zircon anti-ship missiles and Iskander ballistic missiles, while launching 120 long-range strike drones across the country, Ukraine's air force said. Meanwhile, the Russian Defense Ministry said its air defenses overnight intercepted nearly 400 Ukrainian drones over 14 regions and Crimea, the peninsula that Moscow illegally annexed from Kyiv in 2014. Russia's biggest online retailer, Wildberries, said in a statement its logistical facilities in the Voronezh region on the border with Ukraine came under attack and caught fire. It added that the fire was extinguished and goods stored there were "largely undamaged." Ukraine has repeatedly struck Wildberries warehouses and has also bombarded Russian oil facilities in what it says is a strategy to compel Putin to negotiate an end to the invasion. Ukraine's General Staff said its forces struck an oil refinery in the city of Orsk in Russia's Orenburg region near the border with Kazakhstan, about 1,500 kilometers (930 miles) from Ukraine, causing a fire. The refinery, with an annual processing capacity of about 44 million barrels of crude oil, produces gasoline, diesel and aviation fuel, among other products. The extent of the damage was being assessed, the military said. ___ Follow the AP's coverage of the war in Ukraine athttps://apnews.com/hub/russia-ukraine

headline: Bashar al-Assad, Atef Najib sentenced to death in landmark Syria trial
body of the article: Syria's former President Bashar al-Assad, his brother Maher al-Assad and cousin Atef Najib have been sentenced to death after being convicted of crimes during the country's nearly 14-year war. The Fourth Criminal Court in Damascus on Tuesday found Bashar al-Assad, who was toppled in December 2024 and now lives in exile in Russia, guilty of premeditated murder, torture and crimes against humanity, and sentenced him to death in absentia. The court also sentenced his younger brother Maher al-Assad, also now living in Russia, to death in absentia for premeditated murder and torture. Najib, the former head of political security in southern Syria's Deraa province, who was arrested in January last year, was sentenced to death for "crimes against humanity". Najib, who launched a deadly crackdown on protesters in Deraa in 2011, which led to the uprising and later civil war, stood inside a cage wearing a prisoner's uniform as the judge read the sentence. His crimes include murder, "the intentional killing of children under 15" and "torture leading to death", according to the court. Judge Fakhr al-Din al-Aryan said Najib had denied the charges against him and showed "no remorse". Several other former military and security officials who fled Syria were sentenced to death in absentia, including al-Assad's Defence Minister Fahd al-Freij and his military intelligence chief in Deraa in 2011, Louay al-Ali. The ruling against al-Assad and his relatives is the first under the transitional authorities who began trying figures from the former government this year. Addressing the court, Judge al-Aryan said witness testimony established the former Syrian leader's role in the crimes as "the highest decision-maker" and that he had used state institutions to facilitate their commission. Al Jazeera's Obaida Hitto, reporting from the Syrian capital, Damascus, said the ruling "is going to bring a lot of relief to the Syrian people", contributing to their "healing process". "This is something they've waited for a long time," Hitto said. "They want to see these people that tortured their children, displaced them from their homes and destroyed their communities be held to account for these crimes." "This is a historic moment for Syria," he added. A crowd gathered outside the Damascus court after the sentencing, with some people holding up pictures of victims of torture and killings during the war. Hitto said the verdict would also set a strong legal precedent for others accused of crimes under al-Assad's rule. "People across Syrian towns are looking for justice, not just for al-Assad, but for the executioners," said Al Jazeera's Osama bin Javaid. Syria has repeatedlydemanded that Russia extradite al-Assad, a longtime ally of Moscow who reportedly now lives a life of luxury in the Russian capital. But despitenurturing ties with Syria's new government, Moscow has so far refused to extradite al-Assad, whom it hasgranted asylum. Hitto said Moscow is unlikely to reverse course on al-Assad, barring "a major political breakthrough between the two countries". However, he said other al-Assad-era officials residing elsewhere, such as in Lebanon, could potentially be returned. "The Syrian government has been working with Lebanese officials to identify individuals who are currently in Lebanon to bring them back to the country," said Hitto, adding that Damascus is calling on countries where wanted al-Assad-era officials "are either in hiding or being detained" to send them back to Syria.

headline: Nearly 28 million Australians to take part tonight in largest and most inclusive census ever
body of the article: Australianswill be asked theirgenderandsexual orientationfor the first time when they participate in the nationalcensuson Tuesday night, a count of nearly 28 million people that decides how the country spendsmoneyonhospitals,schools,andtransportfor the next five years. Every person in the country on census night, including visitors and temporary visa holders, is mandated by law to fill in the census form, with a fine of up to A$364 (£190) per day for those who do not. The last census in 2021 counted 25.4 million people in 10.8 million households. People aged 16 and above will answer separate questions on their sexual orientation, sex recorded at birth and gender. The 2026 form drops gendered wording from questions about household and family relationships. Liz Allen, a demographer at the Australian National University, described the change as the biggest since the census began asking about Indigenous status more than 50 years ago. "These questions mark a massive watershed forAustralia," she told InDaily. "This moment in time is monumental, not necessarily just for the data, but more so for the signal that it sends to individuals across Australia that we all count, we all matter." Census numbers determine how federal and state governments distribute money and plan services, from healthcare and education to transport. Campaigners have argued for years that the absence of data on LGBTQ+ Australians left their needs out of that calculation. People participate in the 47th Sydney Gay and Lesbian Mardi Gras Parade in Sydney (AFP/Getty) The change followed a complaint to the Australian Human Rights Commission in 2022 by the campaign group Equality Australia and April Long, a parent who found that the 2021 form asked where their son's mother and father were born when he had two mothers. The Australian Bureau of Statistics published a statement of regret the following year and set up an expert advisory committee. "When my son started school, I wanted him to be able to grow up and know that there are families like ours, and that we are part of the country's story," Ms Long told theGuardian, which reported that they became the target of abuse during the campaign. The government briefly ruled out asking about either sexual orientation or gender identity in August 2024, with deputy prime minister Richard Marles saying it did not want to open up divisive debates in the community. Facing mounting anger from LGBTQ+ groups and criticism from Labor backbenchers, prime ministerAnthony Albaneselater told ABC radio that a question on sexual orientation would be included.

headline: King Charles Was Falsely Declared Dead After an Extraordinary Radio Mistake
body of the article: U.K. radio station Radio Caroline reportedly wrongly announcedKing Charles'death reportin May. On August 10, U.K. media regulator The Office of Communications, or Ofcom, explained that the aforementioned radio station had breached two broadcast standards. Notably, King Charles III succeeded his mother, the late Queen Elizabeth II, as monarch in 2022. U.K. radio station Radio Caroline reportedly falsely declaredKing Charles' death, breaching crucial broadcast codes (viaPEOPLE). On May 19, Radio Caroline aired three pre-recorded statements stating that the current monarch, King Charles, had passed away. This announcement aired during The Barry Marsh Show. The Office of Communications, also known as Ofcom, shared that they received two complaints about the reports that interrupted regular music programming. In their third statement, Radio Caroline said "news media" had confirmed that Charles had died. As per Ofcom's report, the national anthem was then played before one of the statements was repeated. Next, a 16-minute-long silence followed the shocking announcement. Notably, after a brief period of silence, the radio station continued with its regular programming. However, 30 minutes after the statements aired, the host apologized to listeners. The host assured listeners that the previous statements were false and that the King was very much alive. The host explained that they didn't hear the statements themselves and attributed the grave error to a "technical issue." On August 10, three months after the incident, Ofcom declared that it considered the incident a breach of two rules under the Broadcasting Code. The first code states: "News, in whatever form, must be reported with due accuracy and presented with due impartiality." The second code explains: "Significant mistakes in news should normally be acknowledged and corrected on air quickly. Corrections should be appropriately scheduled…" In their defence, Radio Caroline explained that a staffer accessed the three files prepared for King Charles' death and played the statements out of curiosity. The radio station revealed that these files carry strict instructions for presenters and managers to follow before airing. The staffer also "apologized" and was "reprimanded" for their actions. Originally reported by Anwaya Mane onMandatory. The postKing Charles Was Falsely Declared Dead After an Extraordinary Radio Mistakeappeared first onReality Tea.
