headline: Russia fired North Korean missiles in attack that killed six in Zaporizhzhia, Zelenskyy says
body of the article: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Tuesday that Russia fired North Korean missiles in an overnight attack that killed six and wounded 19 in the southeastern city of Zaporizhzhia. "The city was struck with North Korean ballistic missiles, Zircons, and guided aerial bombs," he said, referring to Russia's hypersonic cruise missile system, Zircon. Zelenskyy hadwarned on Mondayevening that Russia was preparing to station more North Korean troops on its territory and had already received more ballistic missiles from Pyongyang. He has repeatedly sounded the alarm over deepening military ties between Moscow and Pyongyang, often while appealing for more Western air-defence supplies. "This is the first time they cannot wage war without supplements from North Korea," he said in his nightly address, referring to Russian forces. "They are now preparing to deploy an additional contingent of Koreans on their territory. They have received, just imagine, additional ballistic missiles from North Korea," he added. Only certain air defence systems, including US Patriots, are capable of intercepting ballistic missiles. A shortage of PAC-3 interceptors has worsened since the war launched by the United States and Israel against Iran in February. At the same time, Ukraine has been increasing its strikes against Russian cities far from the border. At the weekend, Zelenskyy said a decision had been taken for 30,000-50,000 North Koreans to be deployed on Russian soil. He did not explain how he obtained those figures. North Korea has become one of Russia's closest military partners since Russian President Vladimir Putin and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un signed a mutual defence pact in June 2024. Moscow used the North Korean troops in a counteroffensive later that year that pushed Ukrainian forces out of the border Kursk region. Firefighters work to put out a fire after a Russian air strike on Zaporizhzhia, 11 August, 2026 - @ZelenskyyUa The overnight Russian attacks spanned Kyiv, Zaporizhzhia and Dnipropetrovsk, regional authorities said. Russia's defence ministry said its forces "delivered a group strike with high-precision ground-based weapons, hitting military-industrial enterprises and transport-logistics centres in the cities of Kyiv and Zaporizhzhia." In Zaporizhzhia, Ivan Fedorov, head of the regional military administration, said Russian forces launched a "massive" attack using missiles and guided aerial bombs. "Six people were killed and 19 others wounded," Fedorov wrote on Telegram, updating an earlier toll of five dead. In the eastern Dnipropetrovsk region, Russian drone and artillery strikes on five districts killed three people and wounded five others, regional military administration head Oleksandr Ganzha said on Telegram. Related WHO warehouse in Ukraine destroyed after overnight strikes Russia preparing to station more North Korean troops on its territory, Zelenskyy says Journalists in Kyiv said they heard a series of explosions shortly after midnight after authorities issued a missile alert. Mayor Vitali Klitschko said on social media that the capital was "under ballistic missile attack." Ukraine's emergency service said a warehouse caught fire and one person was wounded. About 600 North Korean troops were killed fighting for Russia against Ukrainian forces, South Korea's spy agency told lawmakers last year. North Korea has suffered some 4,700 casualties, including injuries and deaths, the South Korean National Intelligence Service (NIS) told a parliamentary committee. About 2,000 injured soldiers were repatriated to North Korea by air or train between January and March, according to the NIS. Russian President Vladimir Putin speaks in Ulan-Ude, 10 August, 2026 - AP Photo The dead soldiers were cremated in Russia before their remains were sent back home, the intelligence agency said. The assessment came after Pyongyang confirmed for the first time that it had sent troops to help Russia recapture parts of the Kursk region, which Ukraine took control of in a surprise incursion. Meanwhile, North Korea's economy was showing signs of recovery as Pyongyang deepened trade and diplomatic ties with Russia and China, South Korea's unification ministry said in a report in April. Rigid socialist planning and high military spending undermined growth in North Korea for years, as have sweeping international sanctions aimed at scuppering its development of nuclear weapons. Soldiers march during the military parade marking the 80th anniversary of the founding of the ruling Worker's Party in Pyongyang, 10 October, 2025 - AP Photo China has long been the diplomatically isolated country's main economic backer, though Pyongyang has also drawn closer to Moscow since it launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Those relationships are now driving an improved economic outlook, with the North appearing to have "moved beyond a period of contraction" and "entered a phase of gradual recovery," according to the South Korean ministry. Analysts said the North was also receiving economic and military technology assistance from Russia in return for sending troops and ammunition to help it fight Ukraine.

headline: At least 14 artisanal miners killed in collapse at an illicit mine in South Africa
body of the article: JOHANNESBURG (AP) — At least 14 artisanal miners died and eight were injured when the walls of a minein South Africacaved in on them, police said Tuesday. North West provincial police commissioner Lt. Gen. Arthur Adams said a search was ongoing and it was not yet clear if there were more victims. Sniffer dogs and specialized equipment were deployed to search for any others trapped underground. Police said the cave-in happened Monday night while the miners were operating illicitly near the city of Rustenburg, a hub for platinum mining in South Africa about 130 kilometers (80 miles) northwest of Johannesburg. Tens of thousands ofartisanal miners work illegallyin South African gold and platinum mines that are no longer used by mining companies, or dig their own mines to search for deposits. They often operate without proper safety equipment and sometimes stay underground for weeks. South Africa has the largest platinum reserves in the world. Three of the miners injured in the collapse were released from a hospital and placed under arrest on suspicion of illegal mining. The five others who were hurt remained in the hospital under police guard, Adams said. Most of the miners who died appeared to be nationals of the neighboring country of Lesotho, police said in a separate statement. Illegal mining is a deep problem in South Africa and isconnected to criminal syndicates, according to authorities. The informal miners are renowned and known as zama zamas, which translates loosely as "chance takers." They often operate in gangs that fight violent battles with rivals and are accused of terrorizing local communities. South Africa's most recent major disaster involving illegal mining was in late 2024, when hundreds of minersbecame trapped undergroundat a gold mine that had been surrounded by police. The standoff lasted months and more than 80 miners died underground, according to authorities. South African President Cyril Ramaphosa took the unusual step earlier this year ofdeploying soldiers on the streetsin a yearlong operation to combat organized crime, with illegal mining one of the focuses of the operation. ___ AP Africa news:https://apnews.com/hub/africa

headline: Zelensky says Russia war is strengthening North Korea military
body of the article: SEOUL, Aug. 11 (UPI) -- Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky warned Monday that North Korea is gaining battlefield experience and improving its military capabilities through its support for Russia, posing a growing threat to U.S. allies and other countries in the Asia-Pacific region. Inan addressfrom the presidential office in Kyiv, Zelensky said North Korea was preparing to send a new contingent of troops to Russia and had supplied Moscow with additional ballistic missiles. "This is the first time in Russia's history that they no longer have a secure strategic rear," Zelensky said. "For the first time, they cannot wage war without reinforcements from North Korea." North Korea has sent munitions and roughly 15,000 troops to support Russian forces in the Kursk region, according to South Korea's National Intelligence Service, which estimates that about 2,000 of the deployed troops have been killed. On Sunday, Zelensky said North Korea was preparing to deploy an additional 30,000 to 50,000 personnel to Russia and called for closer cooperation between Seoul and Kyiv. "We would very much like to receive support from South Korea in an area where we have a shortage,"he wroteon X. "That is air defense systems. They have a legal restriction under their Constitution. We would like to have this cooperation and are counting on it. Our diplomats are in contact." Seoul has maintained a policy of providing humanitarian and nonlethal assistance to Ukraine while declining to directly supply lethal weapons. Zelensky said Monday that the battlefield experience North Korea was gaining in Russia posed a mounting threat to countries in the Asia-Pacific region. "The more [North Korean] missiles and soldiers are used, the more they correct their shortcomings and blind spots, the greater the danger will later be for Japan, the Republic of Korea, the Philippines, and other countries in the region," he said. Zelensky added that international support for Ukraine could help deter Pyongyang from using the conflict to test and improve its military capabilities. "We are also, in fact, speaking about taking away North Korea's appetite and any interest in coming here -- to our land and into our skies -- with its weapons in order to learn how to wage war," he said. The United States and South Korea are incorporating the threat posed by North Korea's battlefield experience into their upcoming major summerjoint military exercise, officials said Monday. "DPRK soldiers have deployed and fought in Ukraine and they've taken those lessons they learned there and brought them back to North Korea," U.S. Forces Korea spokesman Col. Ryan Donald said at a press briefing. "That changes the DPRK capability and our training accounts for that threat." The Democratic People's Republic of Korea is the official name of North Korea. Seoul's Foreign Ministry on Tuesday called for an immediate halt to North Korea-Russia military cooperation but declined to confirm Zelensky's estimate of the size of a potential new deployment. "Our government considers military cooperation between North Korea and Russia to be a matter directly linked to our security and an act that violates U.N. Security Council resolutions," ministry spokesman Park Doo-soon said. Park also declined to comment on diplomatic discussions over potential South Korean defense assistance to Ukraine, saying Seoul's provision of military equipment to other countries is conducted in accordance with domestic laws and policies. "We have provided support to Ukraine in various fields, including energy, infrastructure, health, medical care, and education, and we plan to continue reviewing measures for the restoration of peace and reconstruction in Ukraine," he said.

headline: Israel razes West Bank home nearly three weeks after deadly clash
body of the article: The Israeli army has demolished the home of a Palestinian involved in a deadly confrontation in the occupied West Bank nearly three weeks ago, video footage showed on Tuesday. The footage showed the three-storey building in the village of Tell, near Nablus, being brought down in a controlled explosion. The military initially made no comment. The owner of the house was killed last month during confrontations with Israeli settlers and soldiers. According to the Israeli army, he had seized a weapon from a security officer and opened fire on Israelis. An officer and a member of the civil defence force were killed. The Palestinian Health Ministry said a total of four Palestinians were shot dead by Israeli soldiers during the incident. The situation in the occupied West Bank has deteriorated further since the Hamas massacre in Israel on October 7, 2023, and the Gaza war it triggered. According to the Palestinian Health Ministry, more than 1,100 Palestinians have been killed in the West Bank since then in Israeli military operations, armed clashes and attacks of their own. Violence by radical Israeli settlers against Palestinians has also increased sharply. The Palestinian Foreign Ministry said the escalation of "settler terrorism" was a direct consequence of the protection, political backing and complete impunity granted by the Israeli government and army. Israel took control of the West Bank and East Jerusalem in the Six-Day War in 1967. Around 700,000 Israeli settlers now live there alongside 3 million Palestinians. The Palestinians claim the territories for a state of their own. Israel rejects this.

headline: The lonely Chinese men being conned by fake brides
body of the article: At 37, Wang Zhuang had almost given up hope of finding a wife, until he saw the glossy matchmaking adverts. They promised he wouldn't have to waste years on building a relationship that had no future. They offered to introduce him to a demure, devoted woman. "The matchmakers said that girls from Guizhou are frugal," Wang says. "They told me they are good at running a household, able to do housework, and their families are very poor, so after marrying into your family, they would settle down and live a life with you." So Wang travelled to Guiyang, a city in the southwestern province of Guizhou, in the hope of finding his soulmate. He thought he had, when he was matched with a woman who seemed to tick every box. They had only met a few times before they married. Then, almost as quickly as his new life had begun, it was over. "My whole family has been thrown into chaos," he says, shaking his head. He is still picking up the pieces more than a year after he discovered that everything he had been told by his wife was a lie. She was a former karaoke hostess who'd been married three times, had three children, a serious sexually transmitted disease and was deeply in debt. She had even lied about her age. He is fighting for a divorce and cannot return home to his old life - at least until he can recoup some of his life savings, which he says he paid to the agency within hours of being introduced to several potential matches. "My parents blame me. I have insomnia and anxiety. I can't focus on work." Chinese brides are in huge demand because of a steep gender imbalance [Getty Images] Wang's story is an extreme symptom of a demographic crisis that has long been in the making in China. For decades, China's Communist Party decreed that couples could have only one child. They reversed course in January 2016 but by then the "one-child" policy, coupled with a preference for boys, had produced a shrinking pool of women and a stark gender imbalance. There are now 30 million more men than women in China – that's more than the male population of the UK, or the entire population of Australia. This has left men like Wang, who are in their late 30s and who live in smaller cities or far-flung, rural areas, with few options. Women in these places can afford to be choosy as they know they are in demand. "The requirements for men are very high in my city. You need to have a car, a house and your family should preferably run a business," he says. Many families also demand a high "bride price", a longstanding Chinese custom where the groom's family gives money to the bride. In parts of China, where men far outnumber women, this has become a significant financial burden. Hence the appeal of matchmaking agencies like the ones in Guizhou, which are proposing a one-stop, quick solution - or "flash marriages". Matchmaking agencies are hardly new in China, but many seem to be finding vulnerable targets in men who are struggling to find partners as they grow older. So much so that state media recently reported that the industry had seen "rapid growth" which had "bred illegal practices and chaos". The "flash marriage" market is now on Beijing's radar [Getty Images] It's hard to determine the scale of such fraud across China but it has grown enough to draw the attention of Chinese officials. Between January 2024 and March 2025, prosecutors handled cases involving 1,546 individuals for crimes related to the matchmaking industry. This month, five separate authorities jointly launched a nationwide crackdown on the matchmaking industry after the issue generated "widespread public concern". In one case, a matchmaking agency reportedly used karaoke waitresses as bait to defraud 128 victims of more than 2.5 million yuan (£274,000, $371,000). "I think the government could introduce industry-specific regulations targeting flash marriage scams," Fan Binghe, from the Nanjing Office of the Beijing Jingshi law firm, told the BBC. Although Guiyang has become synonymous with this booming "flash marriage" market, there is little to suggest it is a romantic hub. The agency offices sit in a dense warren of buildings above a shopping precinct, where vendors sell local fruit and workers queue for takeaway sour soup rice noodles. Wang, however, was convinced he could trust them after the company told him they would do a full background check and that he would be entitled to compensation if he was the victim of fraud. So he paid up and the introductions began. Wang was drawn to Guiyang by the promise of a demure spouse [BBC] He met seven women in various "blind date" rooms over a few days while being carefully supervised by agency staff. He asked questions about where they came from, if they'd been married before and if they had any kids. He set his heart on the eighth woman he met. He was hoping to meet someone who hadn't been married before, with no children and who was just a little younger than him. "She also dressed very simply," he recalls. "She looked introverted and honest." They met four or five times for just eight to 10 minutes each time. He says they had been under strict instructions not to exchange phone numbers or any details on private messages, or they would be fined. After two or three days he decided she was the one and he agreed to pay her a substantial bride price. "I spent more than 300,000 yuan [$44,000]," he says, with a pile of well-thumbed legal papers in hand to prove it. "If you include the wedding banquet and everything else, I spent around 400,000 to 500,000 yuan." The whole process was documented by the matchmaking agency in a series of glossy photos, which they also use to advertise their services on Chinese social media. In the video the couple are holding hands on a red carpet and smiling while romantic music plays in the background. Wang with his ex-wife in a photo taken soon after their wedding [BBC] Just months into the marriage, debt collectors started calling, alleging she owed them money. Wang grew suspicious and wanted to know what else she had kept hidden. He checked her phone and found details of her former life, her birth certificate and former marriage documents. When he confronted her, she offered him a divorce, but refused to return a single penny of the bride price. He says he tried to hunt down the agency responsible for his marriage, but when he returned to their offices, they had packed up and disappeared. From his rented flat in Guiyang, just across from the main district which houses most of these agencies, Wang now spends his time making social media videos trying to warn other men about what can go wrong. In Guiyang, it is difficult to find an agency where the staff is willing to talk. One agency boss agreed to talk to us in their offices – although his business partner later asked us to leave. Inside there was a red carpet littered with fake petals ready for a proposal. He told us a couple had pledged to marry just hours before we arrived. "There's a huge market for flash marriages in China. It only really emerged over the last two or three years," he told us. The agencies claim families here did not strictly adhere to the one-child policy, which means the area has a larger pool of women. "Even if a family had two or three daughters, they would keep trying for a son," one of them told the BBC. They say they are now trying to match these women with men from central provinces – like Wang who lives in Hebei – who are relatively wealthy but have few women around them. "Our clients are free to choose whoever they like. The purpose of our business is to help people find someone they genuinely want to be with." One of the advertisements assures their prospective clients that "Three days with the right introduction can beat three years of dating". It was in a room like this where Wang met his bride [BBC] Wang now spends his time trying to help other victims of similar spiels. His rented flat is full of men who are either searching for the owners of the agency who scammed them, or are trying to recoup their losses from their wives who ran off after only a few weeks of marriage. On a fold-up bed by the window, 59-year-old Xu Rulin from Jiangxi province pulls his carefully collated evidence out of a red plastic shopping bag. He spent nearly 500,000 yuan trying to find his son a wife through a "flash marriage" agency. Together they travelled to Guiyang - more than 1,000km away - and his son wed just seven days after he first met his bride in a "blind date" room. Xu says after the marriage was registered, she demanded they buy her an iPhone and transfer around 20,000 yuan to help her with her business. She also asked for 120,000 yuan for a wedding dress and jewellery, he claims. "All I wanted was for her to genuinely settle down and live with us," he told us. "She said she wanted a house and I agreed to buy one for them. It was all agreed." But he says she ran away after living with them for less than two weeks. She has been detained by the police, and the couple have been able to get divorced. He says the owners of the matchmaking company were also arrested in January this year, but he is still in Guiyang trying to recover some of the losses. The bride Xu Rulin spent a fortune finding for his son ran away within two weeks [BBC] The agency manager the BBC spoke to admitted there were no formal background checks on their clients. "The women are introduced by local matchmakers who already know them very well. They know their family background because they're often from the same village. The male's matchmaker also usually knows the man very well." They would not say how much their services cost because that information was "confidential". He did say that if the information provided by either side is not truthful, then the client is entitled to get their money back. "I'd say more than 90% of what our clients tell us here is true," he claimed. "We have a saying here in China. One rotten mouse dropping spoils the whole pot of soup. That's exactly what it's like. We regularly attend meetings with the local police. If a matchmaking agency is found to be involved in marriage fraud, it will be held legally responsible." This matchmaker says most people in the industry are genuine [BBC] This brings little comfort for those who have lost whatever money they had saved. "I never imagined that with the agency charging such a high service fee, a local matchmaker in her hometown checking her background and the company offering so many guarantees, that the women's information would turn out to be completely fake," Wang says. He is almost resigned now to his losses. And he blames himself for falling for the scam: "Only women with problems would agree to these kind of flash marriages." He has kneeled at the police offices in Guiyang pleading for them to help him get his money back and he has even travelled to Beijing to urge the authorities to do more to combat this type of crime. These cases are difficult to prosecute, says Fan Binghe, the lawyer who has handled many. For one, Chinese law has no specific criminal offence which covers this kind of marriage fraud, and so to bring criminal charges, a victim has to establish that the aim of their spouse was always to take their money. "In cases I've handled, suspects often argue that they genuinely intended to marry and live a good life but realised they were incompatible, had conflicts, and decided to end the relationship," he says. "In situations like that, the line becomes blurred. Relationship issues are difficult to disprove." Wang's apartment has turned into a refuge for scammed men [BBC] Even harder is getting money back from sham matchmaking agencies which often shut up shop as soon as they have made enough cash. Wang has managed to get some money back, but not all. "After going through something like this, I don't even know if I can still get married. It was already hard for me to find someone. And now I've spent so much money. I won't consider it now." Wang's life, and the life of the men in the apartment, all appear to be in limbo. "It has taken almost two years, and even now I still don't know when I can divorce her," he says, surrounded by his legal paperwork. "I don't know when this will be resolved, so I can restart a normal life. It feels endless."

headline: France bans unsolicited telemarketing calls, with hefty fines for violators
body of the article: PARIS (AP) — France has banned unsolicited telemarketing calls under a new law aimed at protecting consumers from intrusive sales pitches and shielding vulnerable people from fraudulent commercial practices. The law backed by President Emmanuel Macron's government entered into force Tuesday. While several countries have tried opt-out systems, France is hoping more muscular obligatory opt-in rules will be more effective. Here's a look at the measure and its potential impact. Previously in France, people who wanted to avoid marketing calls had to register their number with a government-run service, but consumer groups said some call centers ignored the list. Now, "businesses are prohibited from contacting consumers without their prior consent," said Alice Vilcot, chief of staff at the Directorate-General for Competition, Consumer Affairs and Prevention of Fraud. "That consent can be withdrawn at any time." The government says the law is a response to years of consumer complaints. Authorities estimate that about three-quarters of people in France receive at least one unsolicited sales call every week, and many receive more. In 2024, 11 consumer organizations issued a joint call for a ban, denouncing "relentless harassment of consumers through countless unwanted telemarketing calls to both landlines and mobile phones — an intrusion that has become a regular part of their daily lives." Parliament approved the law last year. Individuals who make illegal calls can be fined up to 75,000 euros ($87,000) per call. Companies can face fines of up to 375,000 euros ($435,000) per call. There are exceptions. Consumers may consent to receive marketing calls, for example by checking a consent box on a form. Companies can contact customers with new commercial offers if they already have a contractual relationship. People can report unsolicited calls through a government website. Vilcot noted that an Ireland-based company was fined 6 million euros ($6.9 million) last year for violating France's previous telemarketing rules by calling people on the no-call list. France's new law has raised concerns in Morocco, where the minister of employment, Younes Sekkouri, told lawmakers up 50,000 jobs were at risk in the country's call centers. Sekkouri said the industry has attracted around $100 million in investment and generates more than $1 billion in annual revenue in the country. Low labor costs, a large French-speaking workforce and relatively weak unions have made Morocco an attractive outsourcing destination for international companies, particularly French firms seeking to reduce costs. Youssef Chraïbi, president of the Moroccan Federation for Outsourcing Services, told the local daily Le Matin that the French market has historically accounted for more than 80% of the industry's revenue. "Pure telemarketing now represents only 15% to 20% of total activity," Chraïbi said, adding that the sector has increasingly diversified beyond traditional call center services. Neighboring Germany has had a similar ban since 2009. The Netherlands tightened rules on telemarketing calls last month. The country had already banned unsolicited sales calls but now, companies are not allowed anymore to call their own customers with promotional offers without previous authorization. Many other countries rely on opt-out systems. In the United States, people can sign up for the national Do Not Callregistry, which cuts down on unwanted sales calls, Canada has its own Do Not Calllist, while the U.K. has the Telephone PreferenceService. In Britain, companies that call people who have opted out can be fined up to 500,000 pounds ($670,000) per call. ___ Associated Press writers Jill Lawless in London, Molly Quell in The Hague, Netherlands, and Akram Oubachir in Casablanca, Morocco, contributed to this report.

headline: Ukraine's drones torch oil refineries, giant warehouse deep in Russia
body of the article: Ukraine has set fire to at least one oil refinery and warehouses belonging to Russia's largest online retailer Wildberries in new massive drone strikes on Russian territory, killing one person. Warehouse space covering tens of thousands of square metres was ablaze in the Voronezh region, Governor Aleksandr Gusev said on Tuesday morning. He said a 49-year-old man had been fatally injured in the attack and that two others had been wounded. Wildberries said in the morning that the facilities at the logistics centre had been evacuated. According to the governor, the attack took place overnight and Russian air defences shot down 15 drones. He did not say how many drones reached their target. An oil refinery caught fire after a drone attack in Orsk in the Orenburg region on the border with Kazakhstan, according to social media reports. Governor Yevgeny Solntsev confirmed only that a fire had broken out at an industrial facility following the attack. He did not say it was a refinery. There were no reports of casualties. Russia's state news agency TASS reported a further fire at an oil refinery in Komsomolsk-on-Amur in the far east of the country. No details were initially given on the cause of the fire or drone attacks in the region. Ukraine's strikes on Russian territory are aimed not only at damaging the Russian economy: Kiev's stated goal is to make the war so costly for Moscow that the Russian leadership agrees to negotiate an end to the fighting. No such talks are currently in sight. Ukraine has been defending itself against Russia's full-scale invasion for more than four years.

headline: Mass grave with 25 bodies found in Sudan’s Kurmuk after army retakes town
body of the article: Sudanese armed forces have discovered at least 25 bodies in a mass grave in the southeastern Blue Nile State, with local officials accusing the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) of carrying out the killings. The grave was found in the town of Kurmuk, a month after the Sudanese army regained control of the area after weeks of heavy fighting. Abdel Aty Mohamed al-Faki, the commissioner of Kurmuk, announced the discovery on Sunday, according to The Sudan Tribune, saying the Sudanese armed forces found the grave during sweeping operations in the northeastern part of the town. The grave included the remains of children, women and hospital staff. Al-Faki said the victims had been executed near Jebel Fankat, a hilltop position the RSF had used to launch drone attacks during its assault on the area. There was no comment from RSF. The RSF, which has been fighting the Sudanese army since April 2023, has been accused of carrying out mass killings, including in the capital,Khartoum, the city ofel-Fasherand the centralGezeirastate. Al Jazeera's Almigdad al-Ruhaid, reporting from Khartoum, called the discovery in Kurmuk "significant and disturbing". "The local authorities have accused the Rapid Support Forces of executing them during its occupation of the town of Kurmuk," he said, adding that the discovery comes as RSF attacks also continue in Blue Nile State. "In the city of Kurmuk, the Rapid Support Forces have launched explosive drone attacks for the second consecutive day," al-Ruhaid said. "So while the map of control between both sides may be changing", fighting between the two sides continues, creating "mass displacement". Intense fighting also continues in West Darfur, the main stronghold for the RSF, with Sudanese armed forces reportedly repelling the paramilitary force's attacks in Bir Saliba, located about 40km from the city of el-Geneina, he added. Theconflict has killedan estimated 40,000 people, according to the World Health Organization, and forced more than 14 million people to flee their homes.

headline: Shakira, J Balvin and more call for support for Colombian earthquake victims
body of the article: A host of Colombian stars are calling for support amid the devastating earthquake on Monday morning local time.Some of the country's biggest stars, including J Balvin, Maluma, Shakira and more are using their platforms to call attention to the aid and recovery efforts. Colombia was hit by a 7.4-magnitude earthquake with the epicentre reportedly close to San José del Palmar in the Chocó department. The effects of the natural disaster were far-reaching, with reports of collapsed buildings, injuries and deaths in the cities of Cali, Armenia, Manizales, Pereira and Quibdó. The reported death toll is more than 100. Shakira shared a message about the situation in a post in Spanish on X. "Beloved Colombia, my heart is with everyone who felt this earthquake today and with the families who are going through moments of anguish. In times like these, we Colombians know how to come together and support one another. All my strength and love for my homeland. Let's embrace tightly and stay tuned to the instructions so we can help as soon as possible." On his Instagram stories, J Balvin wrote in his native Spanish, "Much strength with the situation of the earthquake in Colombia. Strength to all the people and families affected. We're going to move quickly to help with the situation." Maluma also shared a message of strength, writing, "It is heartbreaking, everything that is happening in Colombia. A hug from the heart to all the victims' families, and we're here to help." Balvin, Maluma, Karol G, Ryan Castro, Manuel Turizo and other artists have shared a link to donate to an organisation called Colombia Se Levanta, which is providing support to families affected by the quake.

headline: The 9 Countries With Some of the Strictest Internet Restrictions in the World
body of the article: Most people who scroll through social media, stream a show, or search for something online rarely think twice about whether they're allowed to do it. Yet for hundreds of millions of people, every click carries a different kind of weight. In several nations, going online means navigating a maze of blocked platforms, government surveillance, and laws that can turn a simple post into a criminal offense. North Korea: A Nation Almost Entirely Offline (Image Credits: Unsplash) North Korea remains in a category of its own when it comes to digital isolation. Only the regime's most trusted citizens can use the global internet, and the country scored 0 for internet freedom in recent rankings. The vast majority of the population instead uses a heavily monitored domestic intranet that offers none of the open access the rest of the world takes for granted. Even basic communication tools are treated as security threats. VPN use is banned and highly punishable in North Korea, since all internet access is government controlled. The result is a country where the outside digital world essentially does not exist for ordinary residents. China: The Architecture of the Great Firewall (Image Credits: Unsplash) China's approach to internet control is less about total blackout and more about total management. China's Great Firewall now blocks virtually all Western platforms including Google, Facebook, Twitter (X), Instagram, and YouTube. In their place, the government has cultivated homegrown alternatives that are far easier to monitor and moderate. Getting around these blocks is also legally risky. Only government licensed VPNs are allowed in China, and all others are considered illegal. Enforcement has grown more sophisticated too, with China's Great Firewall actively detecting and blocking unauthorized VPN traffic using advanced technology. Iran: Licensing Loopholes and Real Consequences (Image Credits: Unsplash) Iran controls its internet through a mix of legal requirements and technical filtering rather than a single blunt wall. VPN use is technically legal only if the service is government approved, and noncompliance may result in fines or arrest. This creates a system where the line between permitted and forbidden technology is often blurry and enforced unevenly. The penalties for stepping outside those lines are far from symbolic. Iran imposes up to one year in prison for unauthorized VPN use, while China terminates internet accounts for similar violations. Iran has also had this framework in place for over a decade, since Iran has restricted unauthorized VPNs since 2013, requiring both providers and users to obtain government permits. Turkmenistan: One Provider, One Voice (Image Credits: Unsplash) Turkmenistan often gets overlooked in conversations about internet censorship, but it may run one of the tightest systems on the planet. The country operates a total gagging of the internet through just one government-owned internet provider, a practice in place since 2001. That single point of control gives authorities near-complete power over what citizens can see and share online. Social media access reflects this same tight grip. Popular platforms like Twitter, Facebook, and Instagram are blocked throughout the country. Circumvention tools offer little relief either, since Turkmenistan is among the small group of nations where VPNs are not just restricted but flatly illegal. Myanmar: Restrictions Born From Political Upheaval (Image Credits: Unsplash) Myanmar's internet landscape shifted dramatically following its political turmoil in recent years, and the restrictions have only deepened since. Myanmar is now classified among the high repression jurisdictions alongside mainland China, Russia, Iran, and Belarus. Access to independent information has become increasingly difficult for ordinary citizens caught in that environment. Circumvention tools are treated as a direct threat by authorities there. Myanmar is one of seven countries with a full ban or block on VPN use, alongside China, Iran, Iraq, North Korea, Turkmenistan, and Russia. This puts the country firmly among the small handful of nations willing to criminalize the very tools people use to reach the open internet. Russia: Escalating Controls Since 2022 (Image Credits: Unsplash) Russia's internet policy has tightened sharply in recent years, moving from selective blocking toward a more systemic clampdown. In March 2024, the country enacted a law prohibiting websites from sharing information about VPNs or promoting their use, and shortly after, thirty web pages offering guidance on accessing banned platforms were blocked, with penalties for VPN use also intensified. These moves signal a government less interested in loopholes and more focused on closing them entirely. The pressure on circumvention tools has continued into the following year as well. In 2024, Russia ordered nearly 100 VPN apps to be removed from app stores for allowing access to content considered illegal in the country. Officially, the legal status of VPNs remains murky, since authorities have not banned VPNs outright, but they do block specific providers that do not follow local censorship laws. Belarus: A Quiet but Firm Digital Lockdown (Image Credits: Unsplash) Belarus rarely makes international headlines for its internet policy, yet it sits comfortably among the world's most restrictive regimes. VPNs are illegal in Belarus, alongside North Korea, Oman, Turkmenistan, and Myanmar. This places the country in a small, exclusive group willing to criminalize the technology outright rather than merely regulate it. Circumvention options are limited even beyond VPNs. Belarus blocks both VPNs and Tor, cutting off two of the most common tools people use elsewhere to bypass government filtering. For residents, that leaves very few legal paths around state-approved content. Saudi Arabia: Filtering Layered With Legal Risk (Image Credits: Pixabay) Saudi Arabia's internet restrictions extend across nearly every category tracked by researchers who study digital freedom. The country scored just 12 in a recent internet freedom ranking, a poor showing across all measured categories, alongside Yemen, the UAE, Syria, and Egypt. That low score reflects heavy content filtering combined with limited legal protection for what users say online. VPN use in the Gulf region carries financial risk that can be severe. The UAE, a neighboring Gulf state with similarly strict policies, fines VPN users up to 540,000 dollars. Saudi Arabia's regulatory posture follows a comparable logic, treating unsanctioned circumvention tools as a legal liability rather than a gray area. Vietnam: Following a Familiar Regional Playbook (Image Credits: Pexels) Vietnam has increasingly modeled its internet governance on its northern neighbor, and the resemblance is intentional. Vietnam has been taking cues from its close ally China, which asserts internet control via the Great Firewall, a collection of gateways that filters all internet traffic entering and leaving the country. That influence shows up in how Vietnamese authorities manage both platform access and the flow of politically sensitive content. The country consistently appears alongside other tightly controlled states in independent assessments. Vietnam is named among nations that consistently appear at the restrictive end of global censorship rankings, alongside China, North Korea, Iran, Myanmar, Turkmenistan, Saudi Arabia, Russia, Cuba, and Eritrea. While Vietnam's economy has opened considerably in other respects, its approach to online speech has not followed the same trajectory. Why I'm putting the majority of my spending on 1 card in 2026 (Featured Image) These nine countries do not share identical systems, but they do share a common instinct: treating information as something to be managed rather than freely exchanged. The global decline in internet freedom has continued for fourteen consecutive years, with around 80 percent of global internet users now living in countries that exercise some form of online censorship or surveillance. That statistic is a reminder that restricted access is not a fringe issue affecting a handful of outliers, but a condition shaping how a large share of the world actually experiences the internet.

headline: AI-altered image used to push claims India behind Pakistan-administered Kashmir protests
body of the article: As protesters and security personnel engaged in deadly clashes in Pakistan-administered Kashmir ahead of regional polls, an AI-doctored image was falsely shared in posts claiming it showed India was pulling the strings of the protest movement. The image was altered to make it appear as if an Indian official was at a demonstration in the UK drawing attention to the unrest, but a review of footage of the rally shows the official's face had been superimposed over that of another man in the crowd. "We've been saying from day one that India's Hindutva Modi government is backing the Indian Action Committee," says part of the Urdu-language caption of aFacebook imageshared on August 4, 2026. The "Indian Action Committee" is a mocking moniker for the Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC), a protest movement in Pakistan-administered Kashmir. The Muslim-majority region is claimed in full by both India and Pakistan, but has been divided between the two countries since their independence from British rule in 1947. Opponents of the JAAC -- which the Pakistan government banned under anti-terrorism laws in June, sparking a wave of demonstrations and clashes that killed dozens with hundreds arrested -- allege the group is backed by India. The shared image appears to show a man taking part in a protest on a British street, with some demonstrators carrying the flag of Azad Kashmir, the Pakistan-administered territory of Kashmir. Superimposed in the bottom-left corner is a photo supposedly showing the same individual, next to a screenshot indicating his name is Shri Ram Prakash and that he works at the Indian High Commission in London. "The participation of the Indian High Commission in the Indian Action Committee's rally in London has proven this to be true," the caption concludes. Screenshot of the false post captured on August 6, 2026, with a red X and AI label added by AFP The same image was also shared in similarInstagramandX postsafter protesters and security personnel in Pakistan-administered Kashmir engaged indeadly clashesas the sensitive Himalayan region goes to the polls (archived link). The JAAC has been calling for the abolition of 12 seats in the local legislature reserved for people who migrated from Indian-administered Kashmir. Supporters of the movement, who urged residents to boycott the vote, argue that major Pakistani political parties use these seats to influence the composition of the local parliament in their favour with those who mostly reside outside the region. Polling in two districts was postponed because of security concerns, the election commission said on August 7, days before the third phase of elections was scheduled. Overseas Kashmiris have organised demonstrations in the United Kingdom to raise awareness about the situation, but the circulating image does not show an Indian official attending one of these rallies -- it was manipulated with AI. Areverse image searchon Google led to correspondingfootage sharedby Pakistani news outlet Geo News' UK Bureau Chief Murtaza Ali Shah on X on August 2 (archived link). "British Kashmiris marched through Luton to express concern over the ongoing situation in AJK," reads its caption, using the initials for Pakistan-administered Azad Jammu and Kashmir. The X video, however, shows a different man to the person highlighted in the false posts. Screenshot comparison of the individual in the falsely shared image (L) and the person shown in Murtaza Ali Shah's X video, highlighted by AFP The same person shown in Shah's video can be seen elsewhere in the footage he shared, as well as inother footageof theLuton demonstration(archivedhereandhere). Screenshots showing the individual shown in Murtaza Ali Shah's video appearing elsewhere in footage of the Luton demonstration An analysis of the falsely shared image using Open AI'simage verification sitedetected aSynthID watermarkand concluded it was "generated using Open AI tools" (archivedhereandhere). Screenshot of the OpenAI tool's results The person named in the false posts, Shri Ram Prakash, islistedon the Indian High Commission in London website as the Principal Private Secretary (Second Secretary) to the Deputy High Commissioner (archived link). But the individual whose face was used in the false posts isHarsh Kumar Jain, the Indian ambassador to the Philippines (archived link). The picture used in the bottom-left corner of the falsely shared image was lifted from aphotographof Jain taken during a meeting with Ukraine's then first deputy minister of foreign affairs, Andrii Sybiha, in April 2024 (archived link). At the time, Jain was India's ambassador to Ukraine. headline: Rescuers search rubble in Cali as Colombia’s strongest quake in decades hits
body of the article: In Cali, Colombia's third‑most populous city after Bogotá and Medellín, residents and rescue workers picked their way through shattered concrete and twisted steel on Monday 10 August 2026, searching for survivors as ambulances crowded the streets around collapsed buildings. The footage shows people clearing rubble by hand and passing debris along human chains, while injured survivors are led away from the wreckage. A six-month-old baby and her mother were among those pulled from beneath a five-storey building, while patients were evacuated from a hospital after part of the structure collapsed. A 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck western Colombia, killing at least 132 people and injuring 570, according to an evening update from the Colombian Association of Capital Cities, with the toll expected to rise. The US Geological Survey placed the epicentre near San Jose del Palmar in Choco province, 400 kilometres west of Bogota, at a depth of 107 kilometres. Pereira alone reported 60 deaths, and 86 buildings collapsed nationwide. Newly inaugurated President Abelardo de la Espriella declared a national disaster, with more than 1,600 buildings damaged. With at least 188 people still missing, Cali Mayor Alejandro Eder appealed to Bogotá and Medellín for urgent assistance. The quake was Colombia's strongest in the 21st century.

headline: China missile test deepens Pacific divide over growing militarisation
body of the article: (Corrects dateline to Aug 11) By Lucy Craymer SUVA, Fiji, Aug 11 (Reuters) - China's test of a nuclear-capable missile last month has exposed the limits of Pacific leaders' ambition to make the region an "Ocean of Peace", free from the crossfire of major-power rivalry. The July launch, China's first known ballistic-missile test into the Pacific ‌since September 2024, was fired into the Pacific just hours after Fiji and Australia signed a major defence treaty, marking Fiji's first ever alliance. More than a month ‌after the test, Pacific Islands foreign ministers were unable to agree on a collective statement condemning Beijing's missile test, despite individual leaders expressing alarm, publicly and privately, about militarisation of the region. The test was "totally inappropriate", Papua New Guinea ​Foreign Minister Justin Tkatchenko told Reuters on the sidelines of the foreign ministers' meeting in Suva last week. "China is a very close friend and ally to Papua New Guinea, but we feel this doesn't help at all," he said, adding that Beijing had given PNG advance notice of the launch but no details on where the missile would land. At the time of the launch, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said it was conducted "safely", adding: "We hope relevant countries will not over-interpret the matter." The missile launch capped a year of more visible military activity across the Pacific, which is ‌fiercely contested between the U.S. and China for influence. That ⁠has included Chinese naval deployments and live-fire drills in the Tasman Sea, U.S.-allied exercises around Guam and Hawaii, and a steady flow of warship visits linked to expanding security partnerships. The United States, meanwhile, retains a substantial military presence across the region, including in Hawaii, Guam and the Marshall ⁠Islands. Tuvalu permanent foreign secretary Pasuna Tuaga, who was speaking in a personal capacity, was concerned about growing militarisation, not only because of the missile test but also security arrangements such as the AUKUS partnership between Australia, Britain and the United States. UNITED, BUT DIVIDED In September 2025, Pacific Leaders endorsed the Ocean of Peace Declaration, which committed to safeguard the region, recognised the right of the people to peace, and resolved ​to ​contribute to and strengthen international peace and security. David Peebles of the Australian National University's Pacific Security College ​said Pacific countries had long resisted having peace and security defined by ‌outside powers and their competing Indo-Pacific strategies. The Ocean of Peace initiative was an attempt to reclaim that agenda, he said. The regional declaration inspired the defence pact signed between Australia and Fiji last month, known as the Ocean of Peace Alliance. Australia's Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade did not immediately respond to a request for comment on concerns that the growing number of regional security pacts could further militarise the Pacific. For many governments, security partnerships bring benefits: surveillance against illegal fishing, disaster response, policing support and access to equipment and training. But critics fear a proliferation of bilateral arrangements could leave Pacific countries with little say over how their territory, waters and infrastructure are used. Solomon Islands Foreign Minister Rick Houenipwela, who chaired the talks ‌in Suva, said the region's agenda must remain "conceived by the Pacific, shaped by the Pacific and only ​by the Pacific." Yet by the end of the one-day meeting, no unified statement in response to the missile ​test had emerged. Kiribati and Nauru, which have deepened ties with Beijing since switching diplomatic ​recognition from Taiwan in 2019 and 2024 respectively, did not support the statement's wording, according to an official familiar with the discussions. New Zealand Foreign ‌Minister Winston Peters blamed foreign influence for the failure to reach consensus, ​without naming a country. The impasse illustrates the central ​challenge facing these small island nations which have different economic, political and security interests. In the northern Pacific, where the U.S. has maintained a military presence for decades, some governments want deeper security engagement with the U.S. while others remain wary. Fiji Foreign Minister Sakiasi Ditoka said Pacific governments faced an unavoidable tension. Countries wanted "to be free of ​all these war-making paraphernalia," he said, but also recognised that some ‌security capabilities helped keep them safe. "I believe it's maintaining that balance." Fiji for the first time participated last month in U.S.-led war games in the Pacific known ​as RIMPAC. Pacific leaders will meet in Palau in three weeks for the Pacific Islands Forum leaders meeting, where the missile test and regional unity are expected ​to return to the agenda. (Reporting by Lucy Craymer; Editing by Praveen Menon and Sonali Paul)

headline: IDF locates three Israelis who crossed border into Syria, transfers them to police for questioning
body of the article: The military condemned the civilians' behavior, explaining that such incidents disturb IDF activity in the area. Three Israeli civilians who crossed into Syria from the Mount Hermon area overnight were returned to Israel by theIDF, the military announced in a Tuesday morning statement. It noted that upon return, all three were transferred to Israel Police for questioning. The military condemned the civilians' behavior, explaining that such incidents not only disturb IDF activity in the area, but are also considered to be criminal offenses. The incident follows a rising trend of Israeli civilians and activists breaching the Israel-Syria border over the past few weeks. In late July, theIDF detained two Israelis who had crossed the border,while Syrian media separately reported that troops had arrested a Syrian citizen during an overnight raid in the Quneitra area. View of the Israeli border area with Syria, as seen from the northern Golan Heights, April 11, 2026. (credit: MICHAEL GILADI/FLASH90) According to the military, troops dispatched to Mount Hermon located the two, returned them to Israeli territory, and transferred them to police. Two days later, theIDF said it had detained three Israeli settler activistsfrom the "HaBashan Pioneers" settler movement after they breached the Syrian border in the Mount Hermon area. However, an earlier report from Army Radio said the activists were only inSyrianterritory for several hours on Wednesday morning before being located by the IDF. The activists were returned to Israeli territory and handed over to police, the IDF said, noting that the military "strongly condemns" such incidents as they disrupt operations and create a dangerous situation for all involved. Sarah Ben-Nun and Jerusalem Post Staff contributed to this report.

headline: Yemen’s Houthis launch ballistic missile attacks on al-Makha and Marib
body of the article: The armed forces of Yemen's internationally recognised government have accused the Houthis of launching another round of ballistic missile attacks on the Red Sea port city of al-Makha and on residential areas in the central city of Marib. Yemeni forces did not state whether the attacks on Monday caused any casualties. The attacks came a day after Houthi missiles killedat least seven peopleand wounded 30 others in al-Makha, which is also known as Mocha. The strikes caused extensive damage at the city's port area. Elsewhere in Yemen on Monday, a Houthi drone strike killed two Yemeni government soldiers and wounded seven others in the south-central province of Shabwa, according to local media reports. Yemeni forces, in a series of posts on X, said they targeted Houthi rebels and their sites in eastern al-Jawf province, northwestern Saada province and the al-Tibas area of central Marib province. The tit-for-tat attacks are thedeadliestin years in Yemen's civil war and mark a major escalation in the conflict, which has been reignited by the war launched by the United States and Israel against Iran on February 28. The Iran-backed Houthis captured Yemen's capital, Sanaa, in September 2014, with a Saudi-led coalition intervening in March 2015 on the side of the government. The conflict, which has killed hundreds of thousands of people, deteriorated into a deadlock, and the warring parties reached a truce in April 2022 that ended major fighting across the country. But the violence reignited on July 13 with a Saudi air strike on the runway of Sanaa airport, preventing the landing of an Iranian flight carrying a high-ranking Houthi delegation. Following the strike, the Houthis attacked the Abha airport in southwestern Saudi Arabia and announced a blockade on Saudi shipping in the Red Sea. They have also attacked Saudi vessels as well as oil facilities in the kingdom, adding further disruption to the global economy. The Saudi-led coalition in turn has struck Houthi-controlled Hodeidah and Kamaran, Yemen's largest island in the Red Sea. It has also reinforced Yemeni troops along the front lines in Yemen to launch a ground offensive on Houthis. Meanwhile, the United Nations has called for restraint. "Yemen today faces a greater risk of renewed large-scale conflict than at any point since the UN-brokered truce of April 2022," UN envoy Hans Grundberg warned on Friday. The escalation, he said, risks "jeopardising the gains of the 2022 truce … while also drawing the country into a broader regional confrontation, with devastating consequences for its people".

headline: Charity races to raise millions to buy historic English estate
body of the article: For sale: thousands of hectares of "rare beauty" owned by an English lord, which could become one of Britain's biggest sanctuaries of biodiversity. A leading UK conservation charity is in a crowdfunding race against time in an ambitious bid to buy a swathe of rolling moorlands and woodlands, in the largest land sale in England in three decades. The Wildlife Trusts organisation needs to raise £30 million ($40 million) to acquire the whole 3,800-hectares Rothbury Estate in northern Northumberland. It has launched a major donations campaign and so far collected £20.6 million in just under two years. But that leaves a little less than £10 million to find by the end of September. "This is a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity and we can't let this go," Peter Batchelor, who is managing the acquisition plan for the Wildlife Trusts, told AFP. More than 20,000 people have contributed to date, "some giving £5 and others £5 million", he said. The Wildlife Trusts bought part of the estate -- including the famous Simonside Hills -- in late 2024. Its sale has surprised many given the Percy family -- the Dukes of Northumberland -- have owned it for almost eight centuries, using the land until 2022 for grouse shooting. The current duke's son, Max Percy, has said it is too difficult to manage from his home in southern England, and has agreed to give the charity two years to raise the funds to buy the remainder. - 'Nature-depleted' - Carpeted with purple heather and green ferns, conservation specialist Duncan Hutt can already imagine what the entire estate -- an area as big as central London -- might look like if acquired. It could feature "new scrub, trees, woodland", restored peatlands and cattle pastures, he said, gazing out over the site some 30 miles (50 kilometres) north of Newcastle. If the fundraising effort falls short, the charities fear the estate will be carved up and sold to different owners, who could exploit the lands for commercial purposes. "We were very concerned about who would buy it and what they would do with it," said Katy Nickolls, secretary of Rothbury's Women Institute who has lived locally for 30 years. Famed UK naturalist David Attenborough has even voiced his support in a video, triggering a surge in donations -- £1 million in a single week. Bordered by several nature reserves and restoration project areas, the Wildlife Trusts and owners of those sites dream of one day creating a 65-kilometre-long biodiversity corridor stretching inland from the estate by the North Sea. It would provide a much-needed sanctuary for wildlife in the densely-populated, nature-ravaged UK. According to the State of Nature 2023 report -- compiled by dozens of conservation organisations and research institutes -- it is "now one of the most nature-depleted countries on Earth". The report blamed "intensive management of agricultural land" as "the most significant factor driving species' population change". - 'Big' patch - Katy Barke, head of nature recovery at Northumberland Wildlife Trust which is a member of the Wildlife Trusts network, watched through binoculars as skylarks flew over a flower-filled meadow. Other species include red squirrels, cuckoos, hares and butterflies. Pine martens and golden eagles, which already inhabit the region, could potentially return. The potential introduction of beavers would create pools teeming with insects and invertebrates, and strengthen resilience to floods, which have become more frequent due to the impacts of climate change. Meanwhile, the lands also harbour archaeological treasures, including prized Neolithic rock carvings. Barke noted the size and "integrity" of the Rothbury Estate set it apart. "In terms of England, it's about as big a patch of land that you (can) get ... so that's really special," she told AFP. The sale has caused "some nervousness" among local people about the change of ownership, admitted Sophie Bulgin, estate project manager. There have been rumours of the possible reintroduction of wild animals such as bison. But the coalition has said any such move would be put to public consultation. The Wildlife Trusts want to encourage the dozen farmers, mainly keeping sheep, to adopt more environmentally friendly practices, using fewer pesticides and chemical fertilisers. The charity insists it wants to involve local communities in its efforts to promote nature and biodiversity. For recreation, the Trusts also plan to turn an old railway line running through the estate into a cycle path and hiking trail. cla/jj/jkb/rmb

headline: New food waste caddies being delivered to residents
body of the article: Residents will have to separate their food waste as part of an England-wide scheme to be more environmentally friendly. North Northamptonshire Council will start delivering two food caddies to households in Kettering and Wellingborough over the next few weeks ahead of collections starting in autumn. The UK produces about 6.4 million tonnes of food waste annually, according to the environmental action body Wrap. Most of that currently gets scraped into people's black bins along with general rubbish, meaning it is burned or sent to landfill - creating unwanted greenhouse gases. The council said there is set to be a smaller bin for inside the property and a larger bin to be placed out for collection. It is hoped the scheme will encourage people to reduce how much food they waste. Food waste recycled separately can be used to produce electricity, reducing the amount of waste rotting in landfills and releasing greenhouse gases. In February, West Northamptonshire Councilsaid itcollected about 187 tonnes of food waste a week — which equates to about 19,700 tonnes a year. The council said between April and 31 December 2025, the average household was throwing out six stone (39kg) of food. Reform UK councillor Ken Harrington, executive member for assets, waste and environmental services, said: "Residents in Kettering and Wellingborough areas have been keen to have food waste collections for some time, and we're nearly ready to roll out the service - keep an eye out for an exact start date. He continued: "In the meantime, keep your new caddies safe and take a look at the information about what can be placed in your new bins." Do you have a story suggestion for Northamptonshire? headline: Russian barrage on Ukraine kills 9, wounds dozens
body of the article: Russian attacks across Ukraine killed at least nine people overnight and wounded dozens, authorities said Tuesday, after Kyiv warned that Moscow had received more ballistic missiles from North Korea. Russia has stepped up ballistic missile strikes on Ukrainian cities in recent weeks, with Ukraine responding with strikes deep inside Russian territory. The overnight attacks spanned Kyiv, Zaporizhzhia and Dnipropetrovsk, regional authorities said. Russia's defence ministry said its forces "delivered a group strike with high-precision ground-based weapons, hitting military-industrial enterprises and transport-logistics centres in the cities of Kyiv and Zaporizhzhia". In Zaporizhzhia, Ivan Fedorov, head of the regional military administration, said Russian forces launched a "massive" attack using missiles and guided aerial bombs. "Six people were killed and 19 others wounded," Fedorov wrote on Telegram, updating an earlier toll of five dead. In the eastern Dnipropetrovsk region, Russian drone and artillery strikes on five districts killed three people and wounded five others, regional military administration head Oleksandr Ganzha said on Telegram. In Kyiv, AFP journalists heard a series of explosions shortly after midnight after authorities issued a missile alert. Mayor Vitali Klitschko said on social media that the capital was "under ballistic missile attack". Ukraine's emergency service said a warehouse caught fire and one person was wounded. President Volodymyr Zelensky had said earlier that Russia was preparing to deploy more North Korean troops and had received new ballistic missiles from Pyongyang. Only certain air defence systems, including US Patriots, are capable of intercepting ballistic missiles. A shortage of PAC-3 interceptors has worsened since the war launched by the United States and Israel against Iran in February. At the same time, Ukraine has been increasing its strikes against Russian cities far from the border. fv/phz/des/abs/giv

headline: Britain cannot afford to be complacent about the China threat
body of the article: Military technology is undergoing a revolution, and it is essential that Britain's Armed Forces do not get left behind as battlefields become increasingly saturated with AI and unmanned systems. But The Telegraph's revelations that cameras fitted to the Royal Navy's new K3 Scout surveillance drones hadsecretly transmitted data to Chinashould serve as a warning. The supply chains for advanced military equipment are enormously complex and internationalised. The cameras were apparently compliant with US National Defense Authorization Act rules that bar components from blacklisted Chinese manufacturers. Yet these cameras, fitted to vessels used by the Royal Marines and the Special Boat Service (SBS), were still able to transmit so-called "heartbeat" signals confirming they were online and functioning to an IP address in China. Both the MoD and Kraken Technology Group, the British defence contractor who sourced the components, have insisted that no sensitive data had been sent abroad. That is not entirely reassuring. China is not a friendly nation. It is anincreasingly antagonistic communist superpower, with designs to replace the US-led international order. Warnings have been raised about the vulnerabilities inherent in a swathe of Chinese-produced goods. The Telegraph previously reported that the SBS had banned Chinese-made electric cars from its headquarters over spying fears. We have been here before. Under US pressure, Britain in 2020 banned Huawei from its telecommunications infrastructure, with operators given a deadline of 2027 to strip all the company's hardware from their networks. The long period allowed to do this was surely a reflection of how difficult it is to disentangle systems from Beijing's potential influence. Fully securing military supply chains is similarly unlikely to be achievable overnight, not least because there may currently be no alternative suppliers for certain components. But they must be encouraged. The hope was that, by opening up to trade with the West, China would become a friendlier international partner. Instead, it seems to have decided to use its exports as a weapon in its great struggle. Britain cannot afford to be complacent about the threat. Try full access to The Telegraph free today.
