headline: Jackie, the famous California bald eagle, dies after weeks of intensive care
body of the article: Wildlife organisation describes Jackie's condition before her death Jackie, a bald eagle in California who became an online star, died on Monday after receiving weeks of veterinary treatment. Jackie was being cared for by Ojai Raptor Center, a wildlife rehabilitation organisation, after she was attacked by other eagles. The bird had underlying health issues that caused anaemia and weight loss. "Over the past several days, her condition continued to deteriorate despite intensive treatment and the combined efforts of our veterinary team and consulting specialists," Ojai Raptor Center said in a statement. A livestream featuring the Big Bear Valley nest of Jackie and her partner, Shadow, has hundreds of thousands of subscribers. The Big Bear Eagle Nest Cam, run by the nonprofit Friends of Big Bear Valley in California, amassed a loyal following and Jackie was frequently spotted in the area since she hatched in the spring of 2012. Jackie and Shadow had been mates since 2018, the Friends of Big Bear Valley website said. "Our team is heartbroken. It has been an extraordinary privilege to care for her," the Ojai Raptor Center said. "We know this news will be deeply felt by the many thousands of people around the world who have followed her journey, hoped alongside us, prayed for her, and supported the people caring for her. "We are working closely with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and the California Department of Fish and Wildlife and will provide a more comprehensive statement including additional information on her treatments and test results." Jackie's remains have been transferred to the California Department of Fish and Wildlife, the Ojai Raptor Center said.

headline: Return of displaced Syrian Kurds to hometown suspended after violence
body of the article: The return of displaced Syrian Kurds to their northeastern hometown of Ras al-Ain was suspended on Monday after a first group of returnees was attacked, prompting protests in other Kurdish-majority parts of Syria. Hundreds of people had gone back to the town on Monday, months after a January agreement with the Syrian government on merging Kurdish forces and civil institutions into the state that included provisions for the return of displaced Kurds. Jawan Isso, from a committee representing displaced people from Ras al-Ain, told AFP that a "first batch" of around 2,500 people were headed home but were later attacked by "armed groups". Mahmud Khalil Ali, deputy head of security forces in Syria's Hasakeh province where Ras al-Ain is located, said several of those involved in the attacks were arrested, but return trips were "temporarily suspended as a precautionary measure to ensure the safety of residents". "These trips will resume as soon as the situation stabilises and full protection is provided for the returnees." A second batch of Kurds was supposed to head to the town in the coming days, according to Isso. Tens of thousands of Kurds were uprooted when Turkey and allied Syrian fighters seized an Arab-majority strip of territory along the Turkish border, including Ras al-Ain, from Kurdish control in 2019 during Syria's civil war. The attacks on Monday sparked a demonstration in nearby Kurdish-majority Qamishli, where an AFP correspondent saw angry protesters try to break into the security forces' headquarters, with Syrian officers pushing them back. In Kobane, a Kurdish-majority town in the north, Syrian state television said people attacked government offices and took down the Syrian flag in front of the local security forces headquarters. Quoting a security source, state television then said authorities imposed a curfew on Kobane while looking for the perpetrators. "We condemn the assault to which the displaced Kurdish families were subjected during their return," Mazloum Abdi, leader of the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces who signed the January deal with Damascus, said on X. "We understand the angry reactions in the Kurdish street in response to this assault, and at the same time, we call on our people to exercise self-restraint, refrain from being drawn into any irresponsible acts, and preserve our civil and security institutions," he added. Ahmad al-Hilali, deputy governor of Hasakeh condemned both the attacks on returnees and on state institutions in other areas like the multiethnic Hasakeh city. "A number of rioters have already been arrested in several areas," he added, vowing that there will be "no leniency" towards those who threaten "civil peace". - 'Waiting for this moment' - Earlier in the day, an AFP correspondent saw dozens of trucks loaded with furniture and other belongings waiting to set off from near the city of Hasakeh, with men, women and children eager to depart. "I've been waiting for this moment... It's like a dream for a person to return to their home," said returnee Nora Khodor, 37. Isso said that around 100,000 people from the Ras al-Ain area had applied to return. Human rights groups say residents' homes and belongings there were seized or looted after the offensive. Some of the fighters subsequently settled in the area with their families, with some reportedly still living in the formerly ethnically mixed region, known as Sari Kani in Kurdish. Turkey launched successive cross-border offensives against Kurdish-led forces in the country's north before Syria's new Islamist-led authorities ousted longtime ruler Bashar al-Assad in December 2024. Since then, the authorities have been extending central government control across the country, including formerly Kurdish-held areas. "We are very happy about returning," said Rawda Mohammed, 39, before the violence erupted. "I asked about my home. They told me it is totally destroyed, but we did not get pessimistic because we're happy to return, and when we get there we'll see what we can do." Some 5.5 million people remain internally displaced in Syria following the more than 13-year civil war, according to the United Nations. str-lk/lg/nad/smw/phz

headline: Canadians made overnight drive to safety as fire spread
body of the article: After being ordered to evacuate their homes at 3:00 am because of a fast-spreading Canadian wildfire, Larry and Mora Goodman formed a convoy with their neighbors, driving as a group towards safety. "Many of our residents are elderly, and afraid to drive in the night," Mora Goodman told AFP in West Kelowna, British Columbia, one of the communities hosting those displaced by the Bald Range wildfire. The fire in the interior of the western Canadian province began on Friday and spread with terrifying speed over the weekend. More than 20,000 people have been forced from their homes and officials have warned that the situation could worsen due to drought-like conditions in the region more than 400 kilometers (250 miles) northwest of Vancouver. An 80-year-old woman died while fleeing her home and the provincial government has declared a state of emergency. The Goodmans live in Peachland, one of the communities under direct threat from the Bald Range Fire. Mora Goodman said that after ensuring everyone was properly packed, Larry put a light on the hood of his car to improve visibility as the convoy set out towards West Kelowna, about 20 kilometers away. "We all caravaned down the highway, in the middle of the night," she said. Larry Goodman said he considered himself among the "lucky ones," with no indication yet that his community had been destroyed. "We're eating far more food than we ever would at home," Mora added, citing the local restaurants and civil society groups around West Kelowna that have mobilized support. - 'Uncertain' - Canada is extremely vulnerable to intense, extensive wildfires and experts say emergency evacuations in the summer months are set to persist. Canada is home to about a quarter of Earth's boreal forest area and average annual temperatures in the country are increasing roughly twice as fast as the global average. There are also growing communities scattered across the vast country in areas highly susceptible to fires. Ottawa is trying to adapt, procuring more water bombers and backing proactive forest management strategies, but those tactics have limits. More than 4 million hectares (10 million acres) have burned so far this year, an area roughly the size of Switzerland. Tens of thousands of people have been forced from their homes and major population centers like Toronto endured some of the worst air quality in the world last month. In West Kelowna, Salvation Army officer Rob Henson said a wide range of people had been impacted by the Bald Range blaze. "There's migrant workers that we're supporting here that have had to come off the farm where they would normally work, and now they're here without any clothing or anything." "People are just uncertain," he added. "They want to go back to where they were, and that's tough." str-bs/sla

headline: Divers Discover Rare WWII German Torpedo Boat After Searching for More Than a Decade
body of the article: Divers say they discovered a rare World War II-era German military boat 315 feet beneath the Ionian Sea The AegeanTec team's search began in 2013 with information about a vessel lost while being towed by German forces The team says years of historical research eventually led divers to the wreck north of the Greek island of Lefkada For more than a decade, a team of divers and researchers searched for a German military boat that disappeared beneath the waters off Greece during World War II. Then, 315 feet below the surface of the Ionian Sea, its silhouette finally appeared. The team fromMarinos AegeanTecannounced that it had located the wreck north of the Greek island of Lefkada after a search that began with a single clue in 2013. "Some pursuits of hidden wrecks are measured in meters. Others are measured in years," the team wrote onFacebookwhile sharing images from the discovery. According to Marinos AegeanTec, German naval historian Peter Schenk first contacted team member Vasilis Mentogiannis with information about a small Kriegsmarine Leichte Schnellboote — or Light Fast Boat — that had been lost between Lefkada and Preveza while being towed by German forces. That message kicked off years of research. Working with historian and researcher Giorgos Karelas and information gathered by Dimitrios Giannoulatos, the team studied historical records and charts before narrowing down several possible locations for the wreck. The vessel has since been identified as LS 6, a rare German military boat that sank in the area during World War II, according toGreek Reporter. The outlet reports that the vessel went down in September 1943. More than a decade after the search began, divers finally descended approximately 96 m — or 315 feet — to the site north of Lefkada. "The moment the silhouette emerged from the depths reminded us exactly why we do what we do," Marinos AegeanTec wrote. The wreck's location wasn't the only remarkable part of the discovery. Greek Reporter reported that the vessel remains largely intact after more than eight decades underwater, with features helping researchers identify it as LS 6. For the team that spent years trying to find it, however, reaching the wreck meant finally seeing a piece of history they had previously known only through records and clues. "Few experiences compare to the privilege of being the first to dive, document and identify a forgotten piece of history," Marinos AegeanTec wrote. "This is more than a dive. It's a journey through time!" And researchers aren't finished with the wreck yet. Marinos AegeanTec said it plans to share more about the evidence behind the identification and what divers found at the site in a future update. Read the original article onPeople

headline: Desperate California dad goes on hunger strike after son was ‘abducted’ and taken to Kazakhstan
body of the article: A California dad launched a hunger strike Monday in a desperate bid to try to finally find his 4-year old autistic son, who he claims was abducted by his ex-wife and flown to a remote part of Kazakhstan. Guillaume Garreau, a 40-year-old tech worker, told the California Post that he started the drastic measure outside the prosecutor's office in Almatyin the central Asian countryin a last-ditch effort to force foot-dragging local authorities to uphold court orders to recover his young son, Maximilien. Guillaume Garreau launched a hunger strike in hopes of reuniting with his autistic son, Maxmilien, whom he claims was kidnapped by his ex-wife. Courtesy Guillaume Garreau "I am doing this not because I want to, but because I am a parent who has been left with no other way to make the authorities hear that my child is still missing and that every day without action is another day of suffering for me and for him," Garreau said in an email. The hunger strike is the latest chapter in a hellish 28-month saga for the Bay Area tech professional, who says he hasn't seen his son in two years after alenient judgeallowed his ex-wife, Sana Onayeva, to take the boy overseas even after she was found to be abusive.Onayeva had suspiciously wired $220,000 to her brother in Kazhakstan before the alleged abduction, but the San Francisco judge, former public defender Michelle Tong, allowed her to travel with the boy anyway, the dad said. The hunger strike is the latest chapter in a hellish 28-month saga for the Bay Area tech professional, who says he hasn't seen his son in two years. Courtesy Guillaume Garreau Onayeva and the toddler never returned. The heartbroken father says he will be stationed outside the government building in Almaty until he gets answers on the whereabouts of his son, whom he hasn't seen since March 2024. The heartbroken father says he will be stationed outside the government building in Almaty until he gets answers. Courtesy Guillaume Garreau Garreau takes a selfie with his young son. Courtesy Guillaume Garreau Garreau and Onayeva, 46, married in 2020 and welcomed Maximilien the next year, but the marriage soon unraveled. Garreau alleged that Onayeva, a former adjunct professor at the University of San Francisco, according to a social-media profile, became verbally and physically abusive toward him, and he filed for separation in February 2023. Judge Michelle Tong allowed Sona Onayeva to travel with 4-year-old Maximilien despite red flags, the dad says. ASSOCIATED PRESS Before Tong was assigned to the case, a family court found that Onayeva had committed domestic abuse, according to theSan Francisco Standard. Garreau's lawyers had argued that his ex shouldn't be allowed to travel home to Kazakhstan with the boy, particularly given the country's lack of a Hague Abduction Convention treaty that allows authorities to more easily recover missing children, but Tong sided with the mom. Sana Onayeva-Garreau with Maximilien. Facebook/Sana Onayeva-Garreau A felony kidnapping warrant was issued in 2024 for Sana Onayeva-Garreau. Facebook/Sana Onayeva-Garreau A felony warrant for kidnapping was eventually issued March 30, 2024, according to theNational Center for Missing and Exploited Children. The French-American dad has spent more than $250,000 trying to compel authorities in the US, France and Kazakhstan to help locate his son, who suffers from autism. The boy and his mother are believed to be in Almaty, Kazakhstan. Getty Images Authorities found the boy last month, Garreau claimed, but the 4-year-old suffered an "acute distress episode" requiring medical treatment, and he and his mother once again "disappeared." Kazakh courts have recognized the abduction and ordered Maximilien's return to California effective February 2025, the dad said. "The central issue is immediate: if authorities know where the child is, why has there been no swift, transparent action to secure his safety and enforce the law?" Garreau said."This is no longer just a custody dispute. It is a case raising urgent questions about child welfare, law enforcement credibility, and possible obstruction of a lawful process," Garreau said. "A vulnerable child has already shown visible signs of extreme distress in the middle of a chaotic and mishandled intervention. Every additional delay increases the risk to the child's physical and psychological well-being."

headline: Magnitude 7.4 quake rocks western Colombia, killing at least 111 people
body of the article: CALI, Colombia — A powerful 7.4 magnitude earthquake struck western Colombia on Monday, killing at least 111 people, damaging hundreds of buildings and leaving many trapped under debris while their loved ones and rescue workers searched through rubble. Search teams and civilians picked through the remains of destroyed buildings in the country's third-largest city, Cali, passing large pieces of concrete and other rubble down a long line of volunteers. "Our building has basically been left in ruins, and the building next to ours? Completely collapsed," said Álvaro López, who cradled his dog as he watched the search. The desperate scene recalled the searches still ongoing in neighboring Venezuela weeks after that country was devastated by two powerful earthquakes. Besides Cali, the quake ravaged cities across western Colombia, including Pereira, Quibdo and Manizales, and was felt in neighboring Ecuador and Panama. The epicenter was in San Jose del Palmar, a community of about 4,800 people in the Choco region about 250 miles west of Bogota, the U.S. Geological Survey said. Colombia's President Abelardo de la Espriella said at least 87 people were injured and around 1,600 buildings were damaged, including at least 61 that completely collapsed. He declared an emergency to expedite funding for the quake recovery. "We aren't going to leave people alone. They are in our hearts and we are going to tend to people with our full determination," he said. Colombia's Geological Service said Monday's quake was the country's strongest recorded "in the 21st century," and that it was followed by several aftershocks. Colombia's Pacific region around the epicenter lies along the "Ring of Fire," the line of seismic faults encircling the Pacific Ocean where most of the world's earthquakes occur. The Pacific, particularly the Choco region, is one of Colombia's poorest, nestled in dense jungle. Much of Choco is only reachable by boat or plane, which may pose difficulty in assessing the wider toll. Local authorities said the death toll included at least 40 people who were killed in the Risaralda region, where Pereira is located, and 27 people in the Valle del Cauca region, where Cali is located, including three children. Authorities also confirmed nine people killed in Choco, two in the Caldas region and a 73-year-old in the Antioquia region. It was not immediately clear where the other 32 people died. The earthquakes left many in the Andean nation unnerved after two back-to-back quakes devastated neighboring Venezuela in late June, destroying hundreds of buildings and killing more than 6,300 people. By Monday afternoon, people had begun reporting their loved ones missing on digital databases just as civilians did following Venezuela's earthquakes. One database had more than 2,000 people, mostly in Cali and Pereira, with the number steadily climbing. Photos of the missing included a young mother and her baby in Pereira; another showed an 80-year-old woman in Cali whose family was desperately looking for details after her building collapsed. Jorge Moncayo, a 64-year-old taxi driver in Cali, said he saw plumes of dust shoot up across the city as buildings collapsed. Residents and rescue workers were searching the rubble for survivors. The local government said that people remained trapped in a number of the city's 380 damaged buildings. "My entire house shook. I've never lived through such a powerful earthquake," he said. "We're thanking God we're alive." Little was known about the extent of the damage in Choco, a remote region where officials reported dozens of injured people and damaged buildings but few other details. Phone signals were out in many parts of the region's capital, Quibdo. The town closest to the earthquake's epicenter, San Jose del Palmar, has no airport, and is located on top of a mountain ridge along a highway linking the cities of Cali and Pereira. In Pereira, further south in the coffee-producing mountains of Colombia, photos and videos on local media showed pieces of the airport ceiling falling onto travelers taking shelter and screaming. People ran through rubble and plumes of dust, and residents said collapsed stores, residential buildings and homes lined the city. Pereira Mayor Mauricio Salazar told a local radio station there were at least 15 collapsed buildings where people were feared trapped. In nearby Manizales, one of the towers of the neo-Gothic cathedral collapsed and fell on the nave. Mayor Jorge Eduardo Rojas asked residents to stay outside in case of aftershocks. Authorities said flights were suspended at the airports in Manizales, Quibdo, Armenia, Cartago, Buenaventura and Pereira as they assessed damage. Small earthquakes, known as "temblores," are common in central and western Colombia, but those above 6.0 magnitude are rare. In 1999, a 6.2 magnitude quake near the city of Armenia killed more than 1,100 people. Response to the earthquake presents the first major challenge to de la Espriella, a Trump ally who was sworn in as president over the weekend. A divisive figure because of his pledge of an all-out crackdown on criminal groups, de la Espriella said he had personally taken charge of the government's response to the emergency. On Monday night, the U.S. State Department announced it would provide $15.5 million for emergency shelter, food and other earthquake response aid. Governments across Latin American also lined up to to help. El Salvador's President Nayib Bukele and Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum — whose countries were among the largest providers of aid to Venezuela following its recent crisis — said they were ready to assist Colombia. "From El Salvador, we are in communication and ready to provide immediate support with our rescue teams, medical personnel, paramedics, supplies, or any other assistance that our Colombian brothers and sisters deem necessary," Bukele said. Chilean President José Antonio Kast said Chile, one of the region's most earthquake-prone countries, "knows the pain and the challenge left by earthquakes" and pledged help.

headline: Mom Says Man Avoided Her Kids on Train Because of Their Race — ‘What the Hell Do People Want?’
body of the article: A parent is drawing attention online after posting a video of a man on a train who she claims avoided interacting with her children. X user @ImMeme0, who reshared the clip, claimed it was the mom recording the clip, which is captioned, "POV: Watching adults act completely paralyzed just because my kids exist in the same space with a different skin color." The caption suggests the mother believed the man was avoiding her children because they were sharing the same space on the train. Here's what can be seen from the video and how people are reacting to the parent's post. In the clip, the parent is recording her two kids sitting in a stroller. They're on the train, which is already moving, and over to the right of them near the door is a man standing. He is holding a shopping bag and looking at his phone. Since the space looks a bit confined, he looks as though he backed up into the corner where there's a small wall, and he's standing next to the doors, perhaps to leave space so passengers can walk back and forth to get on and off the train or to give the parent and her kids some space so he's not standing up on them. But according to the clip's caption, the parent interpreted the scene differently. She claimed the man was acting "paralyzed," as though he could not move closer because her children were nearby. But she takes it a step further and not only implies he doesn't want to be near her kids for the sake of them being kids, but also because of their skin color. The caption identifies the children as Black, while the man appears to be white. The X user called the mom out for suggesting the man was a "villain" simply because he didn't pay her kids any attention. And commenters, like the X user, seem to think the whole thing is wild. "Why the hell does he have to pay attention to your kids? That's your job. If he had she'd be screaming he's a pedophile. You can't win these days," one X commenter wrote. The X user also wrote in the comments, "If he had engaged with these kids, she probably would have recorded it and said that white people can't leave them alone." Another commenter similarly said the man was simply minding his own business, writing, "Looks like he's minding his own business. What the hell do people want? If we give attention were racist. If we ignore were racist. WTF?" The Daily Dotwas unable to independently verify the circumstances surrounding the encounter or the mother's interpretation of the man's behavior. The information in this article is based on the video shared on X, its accompanying caption and comments from users discussing the footage.

headline: Mina Chan’s Death And Perez Hilton’s Crisis Raise Questions About TikTok Live Safeguards
body of the article: Two unrelated mental health crises unfolding onTikTok Livewithin days of each other have placed renewed attention on the platform's ability to recognize imminent danger and respond before it is too late. K-pop influencerMina Chandied at age 26 after broadcasting a livestream from South Korea on August 5. One day earlier, celebrity bloggerPerez Hiltonappeared to harm himself during a separate TikTok broadcast from his Florida home. Concerned viewers contacted authorities, and he was transported to a hospital, where his family said he remained in "serious but stable" condition. The incidents had different outcomes and no known connection. Together, however, they raise the same difficult question: What happens when an online audience witnesses a mental health emergency in real time? As The Blast previously reported,Chan was a Japanese social media personality living in South Koreawho became well known within the ENHYPEN fandom under the username sweeter_nk. Police were alerted at approximately 5:33 a.m. on August 5 to a TikTok livestream involving a Japanese influencer in her 20s who appeared to be in immediate danger. The Yongsan Police Station in Seoul is reportedly examining the circumstances surrounding the incident. Shortly before her death, she became the target of widespread criticism following an incident at one of the group's concerts in the United States. She subsequently apologized to Sunoo, Ni-ki and their fans, admitting that her actions may have crossed appropriate boundaries. Meanwhile,Perez Hilton's crisis occurred on August 4and prompted several viewers to call authorities. Miami-Dade County deputies responded to his South Florida home and transported him to a hospital for treatment. According to an official update from his family,Hilton experienced "significant blood loss and … additional injuries that will require surgery." Janet Gough / AFF-USA.COM / MEGA TikTok's currentCommunity Guidelinesstate that the platform does not allow content that shows, promotes, or provides instructions for suicide or self-harm. The company says content initially passes through an automated review process. Material identified as a potential violation may be removed automatically or forwarded to human moderators for further examination. TikTok also relies on users to report broadcasts and posts that may violate its rules. Content receiving increased attention or multiple reports can be subjected to additional review. In situations involving what the company describes as a specific, credible and imminent threat to someone's life, TikTok says it may contact local emergency services. According toPEOPLE, TikTok said its automated system flagged Hilton's livestream but that a moderation error delayed its removal. His account was subsequently banned for violating the company's self-harm policy. That reported delay illustrates the central challenge facing TikTok and other livestreaming platforms: A safety system can identify prohibited content and still fail to intervene quickly enough during a rapidly developing emergency. Unlike prerecorded posts, TikTok Live allows creators and viewers to interact instantaneously. That immediacy is one of the feature's biggest attractions, but it also leaves moderators with significantly less time to make high-stakes decisions. A creator may begin a livestream normally before showing signs of distress. Automated systems must then determine whether the person is discussing a past experience, seeking support, or facing an immediate threat. TikTok permits users to share stories about overcoming suicidal thoughts or self-harm urges, provided they do not describe methods. It also allows prevention content and information directing people toward professional help. That means the platform cannot simply remove every video containing mental health language. Its systems must interpret the context surrounding the words and images appearing on screen. Users may also speak indirectly or use coded language, potentially making an urgent situation more difficult for automated technology to recognize. Once a threat is identified, the platform or concerned viewers still need enough information to locate the person and contact the appropriate authorities. Jeffrey Mayer/JTMPhotos, Int'l. / MEGA TikTok's responsibility does not necessarily end when the original broadcast is removed. Screen recordings can be uploaded to X, Instagram, YouTube and other platforms within minutes. In Hilton's case, clips continued circulating on X after TikTok removed the original video. Reuploads can expose additional users to the footage without warning and prolong the trauma for the creator's loved ones. They can also transform a private person's worst moment into viral material circulated for shock value, commentary, or engagement. KWKC/MEGA Both Chan's family and Hilton's relatives have asked for privacy and compassion. The two cases do not prove that self-harm broadcasts are becoming more common. They do, however, expose the enormous stakes involved when a platform built around instant interaction must distinguish between content moderation and an emergency unfolding in real time. If you or someone you know is experiencing emotional distress or considering suicide, call or text the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988. headline: 108 Years Ago, A Reluctant Tennessee Soldier Captured 132 Germans In WWI
body of the article: Roughly 108 years ago today (October 8, 1918, precisely) in the tangled hills of France's Argonne Forest, a 30-year-old American soldier named Alvin Cullum York found himself in the middle of one of the most extraordinary small-unit actions of World War I. York was a corporal in the U.S. Army's 82nd Division serving with the 328th Infantry Regiment during the Meuse-Argonne Offensive. This was the massive American campaign to break German defenses and help end the war. The offensive was already littered with horrific casualties, and the terrain was unforgiving: steep ridges, dense woods, machine-gun positions, and deeply entrenched German troops made every advance costly. York's platoon, advancing on orders to move through the area near the German-held Decauville Railroad and seize a commanding position, came under intense machine-gun fire. Several Americans were killed or wounded, including the platoon's officers. With his superior officers down, York suddenly found himself responsible for a small group of soldiers, and with little time to debate what their next move. So, the Americans moved toward the German positions in a desperate attempt to suppress the guns that had pinned them down. EVA HAMBACH / Getty Images York and 16 other Americans pushed through the German defenses. The group encountered a German machine-gun position and succeeded in capturing several enemy soldiers. An already precarious situation turned even more dire when German troops began firing on the Americans from multiple positions. Amid the intense firefight, York took up a position from which he could fire on the German soldiers operating the machine guns. He engaged the enemy positions at close range with just his rifle and pistol. Meanwhile, the American patrol's numbers dwindled significantly as the platoon continued its advance. With six American soldiers killed and three others wounded, York and the few men left were effectively cut off from the rest of their unit. At that point, German troops attempted to overwhelm the Americans, but York kept firing, targeting soldiers who tried to bring their weapons against his position. According to the later Army account of the action, York's marksmanship became remarkably decisive. Every mark and every spent bullet were critical. York's decisive resistance was so effective that, at one point, a German officer reportedly attempted to organize an attack for just him. York caught the movement and shot the officer's horse, causing the officer to fall, and then confronted him. The German officer eventually surrendered. Paul Thompson/FPG / Getty Images The astonishing part of York's story was that the battle did not end with the capture of the German position. Instead, York persuaded the German officer and the remaining soldiers to surrender. The resulting group of prisoners was enormous compared with the handful of Americans escorting them. Remarkably, York and his surviving men marched 132 German prisoners back toward American lines. The official account credited York's small group with killing approximately 25 German soldiers, of which York himself took down more than 20 during the engagement. Later historical accounts have debated some of the precise numbers because battlefield records and eyewitness recollections did not always align perfectly. In any case, what wasn't up for debate was the extraordinary outcome of York's valor. A small American patrol had been sent on a mission that took them into a dangerous German position that cost several American lives, yet the survivors returned with more than a hundred prisoners. Though historians note some discrepancies in the exact numbers, the records give us a fairly clear picture of how many men were involved. York was part of a group of 17 men (including himself) tasked with pushing through the German defenses during the Meuse-Argonne Offensive. Archive Photos / Getty Images Out of those 17, six were killed and three wounded, which means York was among just a handful of survivors that were cut off from the rest of their unit. Still, the battered men managed to march 132 German soldiers about ten miles back to American positions at Varennes after the firefight near Chatel-Chehery, France. It's worth noting that, after days of shelling and rain, the rugged and muddy Argonne Forest and the surrounding valleys made for a particularly dangerous march. The surviving eight had to escort a massive column of prisoners while managing wounded comrades. They risked counterattacks or artillery fire, effectively thrusting York's leadership to critical levels. There are reports that the German soldiers thought York's group was much larger. In any case, the prisoner march from Chatel-Chehery to Varennes alone symbolized York's ability not only to fight but also to control and protect under extreme pressure. York's actions would make him a legend throughout the American Army. He was promoted from corporal to sergeant and eventually received the Medal of Honor, the United States' highest military decoration, for his conduct during the battle. Interestingly, the man behind the legend was uncomfortable with the attention. York had grown up in rural Tennessee and had once been deeply opposed to taking human life for religious reasons. Yet on that October morning, surrounded by machine guns and enemy soldiers, he had made a series of decisions that transformed him from an obscure Army corporal into one of America's most celebrated soldiers of World War I. While the Meuse-Argonne Offensive continued for weeks after York's action, October 8 stood out as one of its most famous individual chapters. That day is remembered because a handful of soldiers, led by a reluctant Tennessee farm boy, managed to change the outcome of a deadly fight. headline: State of emergency declared as 111 confirmed dead in major earthquake in Colombia
body of the article: At least 111 people were killed and hundreds of buildings damaged after a powerful 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck Colombia, the country's President Abelardo de la Espriella said on Monday. De la Espriella said that at least 87 people had been injured and that he had declared a state of emergency. "You are not alone. The state is present and taking action," he said. The quake trapped residents under debris, leaving more injured and forcing people to evacuate their homes as far as the capital of Bogotá. The epicentre was in San Jose Del Palmar, a community of about 4,800 people in the Choco region about 250 miles west of Bogotá, theUS Geological Surveyand Colombia's counterpart reported. Colombia's President Abelardo de la Espriella, left, and Vice President Jose Manuel Restrepo lead an earthquake response meeting in Bogotá, 10 August, 2026 - AP Photo The USGS said it struck at a depth of 107 kilometers and was also was felt in neighbouring Ecuador and Panama, though minimal damage was reported there. The quake left cities across the west of the country ravaged. A mix of residents and search teams picked through the rubble of collapsed buildings amid concerns by authorities of aftershocks. Colombia's interior minister said more than 20 municipalities across the country had been hit. Jorge Moncayo, a 64-year-old taxi driver in Cali, said he saw plumes of dust shoot up across the city from his home in hills of the city as buildings collapsed. Residents in the city and rescue workers were searching the rubble for survivors. "My entire house shook," he said. "I've never lived through such a powerful earthquake." Residents and rescue workers search through the rubble of a collapsed building after an earthquake struck Cali, 10 August, 2026 - AP Photo Colombia's Geological Service said on Monday that it had been "the highest magnitude earthquake registered in Colombia in the last decade" and that it had been followed by two 2.8 and 4.8 magnitude aftershocks. Authorities also reported that flights were suspended in the airports of Manizales, Quibdo, Armenia, Cartago y Buenaventura and Pereira. The earthquakes left many in the Andean nation unnerved after two back-to-back quakes devastated neighbouring Venezuela in late June, destroyed hundreds of buildings and killed more than 5,000 people. At the same time the quake brought down buildings in Colombia, desperate families in Venezuela continued to search the ruins for the bodies of their loved ones. People stand outside their homes after a quake was felt in Bogotá, 10 August, 2026 - AP Photo In Pereira, photos and videos published by local media showed pieces of the airport ceiling falling down on travellers taking shelter and screaming, and people running through rubble in a panic. Pereira's mayor, Mauricio Salazar, told a local radio station that at least 18 people had died and that many more were trapped under "a massive quantity of collapsed buildings." In nearby Manizales, a city nestled in the coffee-producing mountains of Colombia, one of the towers of the neo-Gothic cathedral collapsed and fell on the nave. Jorge Eduardo Rojas, the mayor of Manizales said two people had died in the city "because of the quake" and asked residents to stay outside in case of aftershocks. Authorities in the rural state of Choco, the epicentre of the quake, reported injured people and damaged buildings in the capital, but provided few details. In Cali, a city 2 million people, Mayor Alejandro Eder said that residents were trapped in at least 19 buildings that had collapsed. Small earthquakes, known as "temblores," are common in central and western Colombia, but those above 6.0 magnitude are rare. In 1999, a 6.2 magnitude quake near the city of Armenia, killed more than 1,100 people. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said on Monday the bloc was "ready to provide more support" after a powerful earthquake struck Colombia. "Tonight, Europe's heart is with the people of Colombia after the terrible earthquake in the Choco region. We have already mobilised Copernicus, our satellite service, to help with rescue operations," von der Leyen said in a post on X.

headline: California man trapped in Colombia reveals his terror as massive earthquake struck
body of the article: A Northern California man visiting family in Colombia found himself in a fight for his life whena monster 7.4-magnitude earthquake struckon Monday. Andres Martinez, from Roseville, was enjoying a quiet morning in Manizales— about 100 miles from the epicenter—when the ground started violently shaking. He told KCRA: "We were just sitting down to have breakfast. I was having my coffee and it started shaking. It just kept shaking and shaking and shaking. A Northern California man visiting family in Colombia found himself in a fight for his life when a monster 7.4-magnitude earthquake ripped through the region. AP Photo/Miguel Angel Lopez "And finally, like 10 seconds, I'm like, 'I got to get out.' Everybody got out and it just got stronger and stronger." The survivor, who is partly handicapped and endured the infamous 1989 Loma Prieta quake in the Bay Area, said this latest jolt was a different beast that just wouldn't quit. He told the outlet that as the walls groaned around him he was nearly trapped inside the crumbling structure until a relative intervened. Roseville resident Andres Martinez was enjoying a quiet morning in Manizales—a coffee-growing region about 100 miles from the epicenter in San Jose del Palmar—when the world began to tear apart for 30 terrifying seconds. Colombia's President Abelardo de la Espriella said at least 87 people were injured and declared an emergency to expedite funding for the quake recovery while saying he would visit the disaster zone. REUTERS While neighbors huddled in the streets, Martinez witnessed terrified schoolchildren in uniform, weeping as the earth continued to heave. The earthquake haskilled at least 111 people. Colombia's President Abelardo de la Espriella said at least 87 people were injured and declared an emergency to expedite funding for the quake recovery while saying he would visit the disaster zone. Most of the dead were in the city of Pereira, where 18 people were killed, and others were trapped under the rubble. At least 30 buildings collapsed in Cali, where video shows people searching through the debris as emergency crews assessed the damage. "We aren't going to leave people alone. They are in our hearts and we are going to tend to people with our full determination," he said.

headline: A 3-Year-Old Girl Was Attacked by a Bear While in Her Yard. Authorities Shot and Wounded the Bear But Have Yet to Recover It
body of the article: A 3-year-old girl is in the hospital after being attacked by anadult black bear in British Columbia. The attack happened Sunday morning at a home in Maple Ridge while the little girl was playing on the back deck. A parent chased the bear away, but officers who responded witnessed the animal's aggression. "The bear returned to the residence and the immediate area multiple times, showing a high degree of interest in the location," according to the Maple Ridge Royal Canadian Mounted Policein a releaseposted late Sunday. "Officers made the decision to discharge a firearm in an effort to protect public safety in the immediate area. The bear was struck but continued to flee into a wooded area." Anecropsyof another bear killed in the area confirmed the offending bear is still at large. Neighbors are advised to stay indoors while officers continue to look for the wounded bear. The 3-year-old victim was airlifted to the hospital with what police describe as non-life-altering injuries. Black bear sightings are common in Maple Ridge due to the city's proximity to forested habitat. The city, with a population of about 100,000 people, is situated less than an hour from Vancouver and has its own Wildlife and Vector Control Bylaw. Thebylawmandates many bear-proofing strategies including garbage cans that must not be out before 5 a.m., fruit trees that must be harvested as soon as they're ripe, and beehives that must be inaccessible to bears. Fines for bylaw violations range from $100 to $500 daily. "Due to the abundance of food available to black bears, the population has exploded," reads the city'swebsite. "The grizzly bear population has shrunk in our area due to high human occupation, but grizzlies have been sighted." TheVancouver Sunreports a British Columbia Conservation Officer Service predator attack team has joined the search for the wounded bear in Maple Ridge. Another predator attack team also investigated a different bear attack Sunday. This one happened near Pemberton, about three hours from Maple Ridge. It involved a male hiker and a grizzly bear.  The man has non-life-threatening injuries and investigators determined it was a surprise encounter so that bear won't be tracked down. "Officers have confirmed there is no ongoing threat to other backcountry users," BCCOSsaid in a statement. "Warning signage is being installed in the area." B.C. is home to 120,000 to 160,000 black bears, about one quarter of Canada's black bears. That's considered the current population estimate, but it's based on 2001 statistics. Organizations and tribes have called on the Canadian government for updatedresearchsince development cutting into old-growth forests may be reducing  the black bear population more than suspected. Read Next:72-Year-Old Hiker Is Hospitalized After Grizzly Attack. Authorities Are Not Attempting to Capture the Bear The government does keep an annuallogof known black bear deaths. It tallied a 15-year-low for British Columbia with 240 black bears killed or euthanized (does not include hunting) in 2025. Of those, 178 were killed by conservation officers for public safety reasons. By comparison, officials have killed 73 black bears for the same reason in the first half of 2026.

headline: K-Pop Influencer Dies During TikTok Live Days After Perez Hilton’s Disturbing Incident
body of the article: K-pop influencerMina Chanhas died at age 26 following an intense wave of online criticism from members of the ENHYPEN fandom. The Japanese social media personality, who lived in South Korea and posted under the username sweeter_nk, died by suicide on August 5. Police reportedly responded after receiving a call concerning a livestream involving a Japanese influencer in her 20s. Chan's death was confirmed the following day in a statement posted by an account said to belong to her younger sister. Chan had built a following through her popular ENHYPEN fan account and became a familiar face within the boy band's international fandom. She regularly attended the group's concerts and fan-signing events and was especially vocal about her support for Ni-ki, ENHYPEN's Japanese member. In the days preceding her death, however, Chan faced mounting criticism over an interaction at a United States concert in late July. Chan reportedly attempted to have fellow ENHYPEN member Sunoo deliver flowers to Ni-ki. Some fans accused her of overstepping boundaries and attempting to draw attention away from the event. The criticism continued online, prompting Chan to publish a lengthy apology on X. Chan expressed regret over the flower incident and acknowledged that her actions may have placed Sunoo in an uncomfortable position. "I feel like my actions ended up taking advantage of Sunoo's kindness," she wrote. "I'm truly sorry. I feel so apologetic toward Sunoo and all the Sunoo fans." Chan also reflected on the number of ENHYPEN events she had attended and admitted that the repeated interactions had affected the way she viewed her relationship with the performers. "By attending ENHYPEN's fansigns multiple times, I had deluded myself into thinking I was closer to the members than I actually was," she continued. The influencer went on to apologize for how she conducted herself during the American concert. "I deeply regret the rude behavior I exhibited in America. I ruined the atmosphere of the venue by prioritizing my own desire to meet Ni-ki over the precious time Ni-ki, who loves America so much, deserved. I'm truly sorry." She concluded the message by addressing the people who had followed her fan account. "To everyone who has supported me as sweeter_nk until now, thank you so much." According to South Korean news agencyYonhap, police received a report at approximately 5:33 a.m. on August 5 about a Japanese influencer in her 20s who was attempting suicide during a TikTok livestream. Seoul's Yongsan Police Station is reportedly investigating the circumstances surrounding Chan's death. An account believed to belong to Chan's younger sister confirmed the loss through an Instagram Story on August 6. "My beloved older sister, who was always kind and warm to everyone she met, has passed away," the statement read. The family member said she would not disclose additional details about Chan's passing and requested compassion as the family grieves. "I kindly ask that you keep my sister in your thoughts and prayers," she concluded. No further statement from Chan's family was included in the available reporting. ZUMAPRESS.com / MEGA News of Chan's death comes as another disturbing livestream involving celebrity bloggerPerez Hiltonhas raised concerns about self-harm content appearing on social media. The two incidents are unrelated. Hilton recently broadcast a TikTok livestream in which he appearedto engage in acts of self-harm.The video was later removed from the platform, but clips continued circulating elsewhere on social media. The distressing broadcast prompted multiple calls to authorities, and Miami-Dade County deputies responded to Hilton's South Florida home that night. Hilton was subsequently transported to a local hospital for medical treatment. MBS/MEGA According to an official update from his family, he remains in "serious but stable" condition after experiencing "significant blood loss and … additional injuries that will require surgery." Hilton's family has requested privacy while he receives treatment and begins what they described asa lengthy recovery process. Chan's family has similarly asked the public to remember her while allowing those closest to her to grieve privately. If you or someone you know is experiencing emotional distress or considering suicide, call or text the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988. headline: Chinese rocket explodes less than 90 seconds after liftoff (photos)
body of the article: When you buy through links on our articles, Future and its syndication partners may earn a commission. A Long March 7A rocket carrying the ChinaSat 4B satellite explodes shortly after launching from the Wenchang Spacecraft Launch Site on Aug. 10, 2026. | Credit: Meng Zhongde/VCG via Getty Images China's latest rocket launch ended in failure this morning, lighting up the skies with some unwanted fireworks. The state-owned China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation (CASC) launched a Long March 7A rocket today (Aug. 10) from the Wenchang Space Launch Site, in the country's Hainan province, just after 8:00 a.m. EDT (1200 GMT; 8:02 p.m. local time). Around 85 seconds into the launch, the rocket exploded, generating a massive fireball and a cloud of smoke and debris while still soaring throughEarth's atmosphere. CASC had not yet released a statement about the incident by the time of this story's publication, butvideo reposted to social mediacaptured the shock of onlookers the moment that the rocket burst into flames. Based on such views, the mission will almost certainly be deemed a complete failure, with total loss of vehicle and payload. Today's launch was the18th Long March 7A missionsince the rocket's debut in 2020, which, subsequently, also ended with thevehicle's explosion. China traced that mishap to an engine malfunction that occurredshortly after first-stage separation. This morning's launch, however, didn't get that far. The Long March 7A's four side boosters and core stage detach as a full cluster during first stage separation, which typically occurs just under three minutes after liftoff. As today's incident occurred just 85 seconds into flight, the rocket was still engaged in the main stage's initial engine burn to escape Earth's atmosphere. The 7A — a variant of China's Long March 7 rocket family — stands just over 197 feet (60 meters) tall and combines the first two Long March 7 stages with a hydrolox (liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen)-powered third stage capable of launching up to 7 tons to geostationary transfer orbit (GTO). A Long March 7A rocket carrying the ChinaSat 4B satellite launches from the Wenchang Spacecraft Launch Site on Aug. 10, 2026. The launch was not successful. | Credit: Meng Zhongde/VCG via Getty Images According to China National Radio, today's launch carried China's Zhongxing-4B spacecraft,, a communicationssatellitepresumably bound for GTO. China'sZhongxing satellitesprovide telecommunications and broadband internet services and are also thought to provide services for China's military. It is unclear what repercussions today's explosion may have on upcoming launches, including a Chinese Zhuque-3 rocket liftoff scheduled for Monday evening. That mission is scheduled to fly from China's Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center, more than 1,500 miles (2,415 kilometers) from Wenchang, at 7:45 p.m. EDT (2345 GMT; 7:45 a.m. local time), and is expected to feature a first-stage landing attempt. CASC uses the standard Long March 7 rocket, which shares its core stage with the 7A, as its launch vehicle for delivering cargo to theTiangong space stationinlow Earth orbitabout every eight months. The most recent of those missionslaunched in May, putting the next resupply launch sometime around January 2027. Depending on the cause of this morning's explosion, that mission and others could face delays as China investigates the incident. Editor's note:This story was updated at 4:20 p.m. ET on Aug. 10 with new photos of the launch.

headline: Jordan to celebrate 2,000 years since Jesus’ baptism
body of the article: (NewsNation) — Christians around the world are looking forward to a series of major 2,000-year milestones culminating in 2033, marking Christ's Resurrection, and Jordan is preparing for the first of them: the 2030 anniversary of Jesus' baptism at Bethany Beyond the Jordan. Bethany Beyond the Jordan, also known as Al-Maghtas, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site on the east bank of the Jordan River. It has been venerated as the authentic location where Jesus of Nazareth was baptized by John the Baptist since the Byzantine era, according to UNESCO, and has been visited by three popes - Popes John Paul II, Benedict XVI and Francis. Inside the Vatican: Perspective on the first 'American' pope According to media reports, Jordan is raising $100 million to build a first-century Palestinian village as part of the commemoration. Jordan's prime minister, Jafar Hassan August, chaired the first meeting of a national committee to prepare for the events, according to Vatican News. The site was inaccessible to pilgrims and visitors after the 1967 Six-Day War, and archeologists didn't begin proper excavation until 1994, following a peace treaty between Jordan and Israel.  The UNESCO-protected area covers over 1,300 acres, including five separate archaeological sites from the Roman and Byzantine periods. Eastern Christians commemorate Epiphany or Theophany on 19th January each year. Pilgrims from Orthodox Churches attend the Al-Maghtas, known to be the spot on the River Jordan where the baptism of Jesus took place. headline: Tehran appoints key senior military leaders, including IRGC chief
body of the article: Iran has replaced six senior military figures, according to decrees published on Monday evening on a Telegram channel that disseminates news from Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei. Iranian media also reported the appointments and published images of a ceremony in which Khamenei, however, was not visible. Given that US-Israeli airstrikes had specifically targeted and killed military leaders in the country, the new appointments could bring a degree of order to the leadership. Furthermore, the appointments could signal that Tehran is moving away from a state of acute crisis towards the formalization and consolidation of the power structure. Ahmad Vahidi was promoted to the rank of general and formally appointed commander-in-chief of the powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). He had already been serving in the role since the killing of his predecessor. Hossein Taeb, a long-serving intelligence officer, was appointed as the new head of the paramilitary Basij militias. Brigadier Generals Ali Abdollahi and Ali Asmai were appointed chief of staff of the armed forces and commander of the IRGC's naval forces, respectively. Two further appointments concerned deputy positions. It comes after Khamenei appointed former IRGC commander Mohsen Rezaee as the new chairman of Iran's National Security Council on Sunday. In comments to the New York Times, Iran expert Hamidreza Azizi described the appointment as a move to counterbalance the influence of Parliament Speaker Mohammed Bagher Ghalibaf, who most recently acted as chief negotiator in talks with the US.

headline: Police in India use tear gas, water cannons on demonstrators
body of the article: Aug. 10 (UPI) -- Police in Jharkhand, India used tear gas and water cannons on demonstrators who were demanding investigations into recruitment for government jobs on Monday. Thousands of protesters were met withpolice wielding batonsas they marched to the state legislature building. Protesters pushed past some police barricades and there were injuries on both sides. The protest was sparked by allegations of irregularities in recruitment drives for government jobs. Protesters called for India's Central Bureau of Investigations to probe the allegations. Young adults in Jharkhand, the poorest state in India, have taken to the streets in an outcry over allegations that they are not being given a fair chance to compete for highly coveted government roles. Demonstrators say there have been gradingerrors and financial irregularitiesin recruitment exams. They have also called for the cancellation of three recruitment exams, which the Jharkhand government agreed to on Sunday. The Jharkhand Mukti Morcha, a political party in the state, also agreed to speed up the investigations that demonstrators asked for. Government jobs are highly sought after in India. Recruitment for job listings can result in hundreds of thousands of applications for 500 to around 2,000 openings. One recruitment push for 2,025 jobs received about 640,000 applications. Another drive for 510 jobs received 322,000 applications. In May, India scrapped the results of its medical college-entrance exam, a test that requires students to spend years studying. The exam was scrapped after its question papers were leaked, which has happened multiple times throughout the country. In July, protests erupted in the capital city New Delhi with demonstrators marching on Parliament and calling for the resignation of India's top education chief. Law enforcement activity heightened as a result, leading to allegations of police brutality.

headline: What to Know About the Earthquake in Colombia
body of the article: A 7.4-magnitudeearthquakerattled western Colombia on Monday, causing widespread destruction and leaving more than 100 people dead. Colombian President Abelardo De La Espriella, who was sworn into office just days before the disaster struck the nation, said in apost on Xon Monday morning that he had "directly assumed leadership of the emergency response." Inanother postthat morning, he said that he was traveling to the nation's capital, Bogotá, "to focus on addressing the emergency facing our country." "To the Colombians who are going through difficult times today, I want to say: you are not alone," he said. "You have a President who cares deeply for his people and who will do everything necessary to protect you, support you, and move forward together in rebuilding the affected regions." The Colombian President declared an emergency later that day,The Associated Pressreported. Here's what to know about the earthquake. The earthquake hit Colombia at 7:34 a.m. local time, according to theU.S. Geological Survey(USGS). The epicenter of the earthquake was near San José del Palmar, a community west of the country's capital with apopulation of 5,000. Other cities nearby, including Pereira, Manizales, and Cali, were impacted, too. Neighboring countries, including Venezuela, Ecuador, and Panama, also felt the quake. The damage sustained by the Manizales Cathedral are pictured after the earthquake in Manizales, Colombia, on Aug. 10, 2026. —Andres Valencia—AFP/Getty Images USGS reported that the earthquake that struck Colombia had a 7.4 magnitude. "Magnitude" indicates the size of a quake—one with a 5.3 magnitude, for instance, is a "moderate" quake, whereas one with a 6.3 is considered "strong," according toUSGS. Theback-to-back quakesthat shook Venezuela in June and leftmore than 6,000 people deadeach had a magnitude above 7. The Colombian Geological Servicereportedthat the quake had a depth of about 103 km, in addition to its 7.4 magnitude, andsaidit was the largest seismic event recorded in the country in this century According topreliminary informationfrom the Colombian Association of Capital Cities (Asocapitales), at least 132 people have died, and at least 570 people were injured in the quake as of Monday evening. But the death toll is still expected to rise, as local officials said that they had received reports of many people trapped under buildings that had collapsed. A police officer walks amid the debris of a damaged commercial store after the earthquake in Manizales, Colombia, on Aug. 10, 2026. —Jonh Bonilla—AFP/Getty Images De La Espriella said on Monday that the quake damaged more than 1,500 homes—adding that it completely destroyed some of them. More than a dozen health centers and even more schools were also damaged in the disaster, theNew YorkTimesreported. Asocapitales added that 86 buildings have collapsed, seven airports suspended operations, and five cities—Pereira, Cali, Quibdó, Manizales, and Armenia—are "experiencing the most severe impacts." The International Rescue Committee (IRC) said that its teams are monitoring the situation. "Our teams near the epicenter in Chocó are reporting damages to infrastructure, including to hospitals and clinics," Nicole Kast, IRC's Country Director for Colombia, Venezuela and Ecuador, said in a statement. "Impacted communities were already facing armed conflict and high levels of poverty before the ground began to shake. The IRC is monitoring the situation and stands ready to scale up its response as the full extent of the destruction becomes clear." Colombia's civil aviation authority said in apost on Xon Monday morning that it had received reports of damage at airports in Pereira, Manizales, Quibdó, Armenia, Cartago, and Buenaventura, and that operations there were being suspended "for safety reasons" until the damage had been assessed. An elderly woman is carried on furniture near a collapsed building after an earthquake in Cali, Colombia, on Aug. 10, 2026. —Joaquin Sarmiento—AFP/Getty Images While earthquakes can sometimes trigger tsunamis, the U.S. Tsunami Warning Systemsaidon Monday that there was no warning, advisory, watch, or threat for a tsunami after the earthquake in Colombia. Governments across Latin America offered assistance. Venezuela, which is still recovering from quakes that shook it in June,offeredColombia the deployment of rescue workers and humanitarian aid: its foreign minister Félix Plasencia said in astatementthat Caracas "expresses its deepest solidarity and fraternity" with the people of Colombia. El Salvador's President Nayib Bukelesaidthey are communicating with Colombia and are "ready to provide immediate support with our rescue teams, medical personnel, paramedics, supplies, or any other assistance." Mexico's President Claudia Sheinbaum alsooffered assistanceshould Bogotá require it. The U.S. State Departmentannouncedit would provide $15.5 million for emergency shelter, food, and other earthquake response aid. Ursula von der Leyen of the European Commissionsaid on social mediathat the European Union has already mobilized its satellite service to assist in rescue operations and is ready to provide additional support. —Chad de Guzman contributed reporting.

headline: 'Dreams disappear' as Gaza students await evacuation to Italy
body of the article: Dozens of Gaza students who won scholarships to universities in Italy are still waiting to be evacuated due to bureaucratic red tape, leaving qualified students in a deadly conflict zone, AFP has found. Although more than 200 Palestinian students have been successfully enrolled in Italian colleges through a government university corridor project started in 2025, others have been left behind. About 50 students are still awaiting clearance to leave the Israeli-occupied territory where most higher education institutions have been destroyed -- despite having met the same requirements of previous Gazan students now in Italy, non-governmental organisations say. Between September 2025 and June, 246 scholarship recipients from Gaza were flown to Italy and San Marino in a series of evacuations through Italy's "IUPALS" program for Palestinian students, according to the foreign ministry. But there have been no evacuations since June 1, said Anna Giada Altomare, founder of the Fiori dai Cannoni charity that helps the accepted students, who cited conflicting rules and a lack of transparency within the program. One male student still waiting in Gaza -- who requested that his name not be used -- described to AFP a "long waiting period, the uncertainty about the travel date, and the fear of losing an educational opportunity obtained after great effort". "The Italian government could resolve this situation very quickly," Altomare said, adding: "It is the state that should accelerate the process." Neither the foreign ministry nor the ministry for universities and research responded to a question from AFP about the evacuation delays. Contacted by AFP, the Israeli foreign ministry also did not immediately respond for comment. - Universities destroyed - Nada Abunada and Mohamed Arafat are among the lucky ones. They began their studies in economics at Rome's Sapienza University in November 2025, having graduated high school in Gaza with scores above 99 percent. "I couldn't enrol in university (in Gaza) because the war started. Everything that I had been planning for disappeared," Abunada told AFP in Rome, adding that "most universities were destroyed". Arafat was studying business administration at Gaza's Al-Azhar University before the war forced him to stop. "We were focused on surviving," he said. They were alerted to their evacuation just the day before by Italy's consulate in Jerusalem. "I didn't tell anyone until the very last day because I wasn't sure it would happen... I didn't have much time to say goodbye," said Arafat. Students left behind say they are facing bureaucratic problems, including confusing evacuation criteria. The young man still in Gaza -- who was awarded a scholarship to study computer engineering in October 2025 -- wonders whether his score on an Italian proficiency exam may have played a role in delaying his evacuation. "I tried to answer as much as I could since I had been learning Italian despite all the difficult circumstances, including internet outages, fear, and the pressure of daily life during the war," he said. In July, Italy's university and research ministry called for greater flexibility in applying the language requirement to students from conflict zones. But that hasn't helped the students still waiting in Gaza. - Disappearing dreams - Other Palestinian students hoping to study in Turkey, the Netherlands, Germany and Belgium face similar unexplained delays, the student said. A pre-med graduate, who also asked not to be named, told AFP she was accepted to an Italian master's program in June 2025 without asking for a scholarship. She was later told by the Italian consulate that those without scholarships would not be evacuated. Altomare said students with private Italian sponsors are also not being evacuated, questioning the rationale for rejecting such applicants. Beyond administrative hurdles, students face difficult personal choices, such as family separation and mothers unable to evacuate with their children. "I find it absurd that a woman should be forced to choose between continuing her education and leaving her child behind in Gaza," said Altomare. Student Arafat worries whether his family will be forced to leave their home, where they hear nightly strikes from nearby Israeli forces. He is trying to help his younger brothers study in Italy, but said they face even greater challenges than he did. They have been asked to provide an equivalency assessment of their grades -- one they cannot possibly meet because, he said, "there are no functioning ministries or institutions" in Gaza. Back in Gaza, the computer engineering student expressed the frustration felt by many. "We are not just files or numbers," he told AFP. "All we ask is to be given the opportunity we have already earned, and not to let our dreams disappear while we wait." str-ams/giv/st

headline: British teenager dies after boat ‘explodes’ during family holiday
body of the article: A teenage cheerleading coach died when a boat "exploded" on a family holiday in the Dominican Republic. Abbie Lainton, 16, was on a tourist boat when the vessel burst into flames on July 27. Abbie's family, from Swindon, were on the boat with about 30 others during the incident. She was badly burnt and taken to intensive care, where she died three days later. Her two siblings, Carley and Bradley, were injured and remain in hospital, according to The Sun. The boat was taking tourists from a trip to Saona Island, part of the Cotubanamá National Park, to the port of Bayahibe. Authorities said 24 people were injured, with 11 taken to hospital for treatment for burns. They have not yet revealed the cause of the fire, but have launched an investigation. The boat had been taking tourists from a trip to Saona Island, part of the Cotubanamá National Park, to the port of Bayahibe An official in the Dominican Republic said: "It was an accident at sea and was very tragic. The young lady and her injured siblings were moved immediately to the hospital in the city of La Romana, but sadly she did not survive. "Despite the best efforts of medical staff, she did not make it. Her injured siblings are continuing to be looked after in the hospital." Navin Torres, 35, who was on the boat and suffered first degree burns, told The Sun passengers heard a "pop" when it suddenly accelerated before it "exploded". Mr Torres said: "The front of the boat exploded. It took me a couple of seconds to analyse what was going on, and the fire started spreading towards me and my wife." His wife Gisell Segovia said: " All I remember was hearing a pop noise. And then the people sitting on the left side of the boat, they flew off their seats, including the benches that they were sitting on. "Everything started flying and boat pieces that were on fire started flying everywhere. My husband, he got cut and burned on the side of his forehead with one of the pieces." She said she remembered Abbie "because of her eyes", adding that they were "beautiful". A GoFundMe page set up to help Abbie's family has received more than £17,500 in donations. The page says: "Abbie had her whole life ahead of her. She should have been enjoying the summer with her friends and looking forward to receiving her GCSE results. She was so loved by her family, friends and everyone who knew her." Swindon Lightning Cheerleading club, which Abbie attended, told Metro: "There are simply no words that feel enough. Abbie was a much-loved member of our Swindon Lightning family. "Her kindness, infectious smile, unwavering encouragement and love for cheerleading touched the lives of so many athletes, coaches and families over the years." Tanwood School for Performing Arts, Abbie's former school, also paid tribute to her. A spokesman said: "Abbie always performed with a huge smile, and those beautiful feet. "We are all in complete shock at this heartbreaking news, and send so much love and support to her family and friends at this unimaginable time. You will always be in our hearts." A spokesman for the Foreign Office said it was in contact with local authorities and providing consular support to Abbie's family, as well as assisting other British nationals and their families affected by the incident.
