headline: Lebanon ‘files new lawsuit against’ ex-central bank chief Riad Salameh
body of the article: Lebanon has indicted ⁠former central bank Governor Riad Salameh and a former commercial banker over accusations of financial crimes, including embezzlement and illicit enrichment. A judge accusedSalamehand Samir Hanna, the former head of Lebanon's Bank Audi, of embezzling tens of millions in funds ‌from the Banque du Liban or Lebanese central bank, the Reuters and AFP news agencies reported on Monday, citing judicial sources. Salameh, who headed the central bank for three decades, has already been indicted and arrested in Lebanon over other alleged financial crimes committed during his tenure. He has denied any wrongdoing, insisting he is being made a "scapegoat" for the country's economic crisis. This is the first time a commercial banker has beenindicted in a financial crimescase related to Salameh, showing that Lebanese investigations into the former governor are expanding to the private sector, the source told Reuters. The source added that the file includes accusations that Hanna bribed Salameh while he was central bank governor. Salameh, 76, headed the central bank from 1993 to July 2023. He was placed in custody last month after missing a hearing over the case, ⁠but is currently under medical supervision at a government hospital outside Lebanon's capital, Beirut. Hanna, 88, paid a $1m bail and is not in custody as financial investigations continue, according to the reports. In January, Lebanon's current central ⁠bank governor Karim Souaid told reporters that the central bank had filed a criminal complaint against an unnamed former official of the central bank, ⁠a former banker and a lawyer over alleged illicit enrichment ⁠through misuse of public funds. He said the operations were carried out through four offshore shell companies in the Cayman Islands that he did not name. Salameh was detained for about 13 months over alleged ‌financial crimes ‌committed during his tenure, but was released in September after paying a record bail of more than $14m. He also faces investigations abroad, including in France, Switzerland and Germany.

headline: Iran hierarchy consolidation as IRGC veteran tapped for key security role
body of the article: Tehran, Iran –The office of Iran's ⁠⁠Supreme ⁠⁠Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has announced a series of new appointments in key positions, including the naming of a former wartime commander and longtime political insider to helm the country's top security body. Mohsen Rezaee, who was commander-in-chief of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) for 16 years, including during years of war with Iraq in the 1980s, was named secretary of the Supreme National Security Council (SNSC) and Khamenei's representative in the top decision-making body on Sunday. Six new military positions were also officially filled on Monday, with Ali Abdollahi, head of Iran's joint war command, appointed as the new chief of staff of the armed forces and Ali Ozmaei named as the head of the IRGC Navy. Brigadier General Ahmad Vahidi was also confirmed as commander-in-chief of the IRGC "with the rank of major general", officially succeeding Mohammad Pakpour, who was killed during the opening salvo of the US-Israel war on Iran in late Feburary. Sina Azodi, assistant professor of Middle East Politics at the George Washington University, said the appointments signalled no softening in negotiations with the United States. "There is little question that Khamenei, Vahidi and the IRGC leadership all share the view that continued resistance to the US is strategically necessary," Azodi told Al Jazeera. He said Rezaee brings deep institutional experience and considerable authority among both senior IRGC commanders and the rank-and-file. "His appointment therefore appears intended to strengthen internal cohesion, reinforce the leadership's control over the organisation, and draw on the experience of a figure who helped shape the IRGC into the military and political institution it is today," added Azodi. Rezaee used to be the secretary of the Expediency Council, another top state arbitration body, as he increasingly turned to politics and macroeconomics after the end of the grinding Iraq war that left hundreds of thousands killed. The 71-year-old also helped develop a long-term national development plan and was given high-level economic coordination authorities during the Ebrahim Raisi presidency between 2021 and 2024. But he has never held elected office, having run for president unsuccessfully four times. Rezaee made a comeback in military uniform during the ongoing conflict, becoming military adviser to the supreme leader just over a week after Mojtaba Khamenei replaced his assassinated father, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, on the first day of the war. Since then, he has projected a message of defiance and resilience to the US, Israel and regional actors during interviews with media and posts online. Rezaee also expressed opposition to the memorandum of understanding (MoU) signed with the US in June, which temporarily lifted a naval blockade and suspended oil sanctions to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. He argued that his position was closer to that of Mojtaba Khamenei, who ended up approving the MoU despite stated reservations. "I ask friends who are against negotiations to wait, the Americans will destroy it themselves and won't let it lead to any results," he said in early July, shortly before the agreement ended up being suspended following the resumption of attacks. Last week, he said the US must change its behaviour, or face serious risks and casualties to its forces. Iran "will never permit the opening of a second corridor in the Strait of Hormuz", he said. State-linked outlets said 12 out of 13 voting members of Iran's Supreme National Security Council were in favour of the MoU, with ultraconservative Saeed Jalili standing as the only opposing member. But a number of hardline MPs, media and supporters of the Islamic Republic blasted the agreement as they believe the strait should not have been allowed to reopen until the US gives more concessions. The SNSC brings together Iran's presidency, foreign ministry, armed forces and security and intelligence organisations, and also coordinates communication with the office of the supreme leader, which has to give final approval on decisions. Local media had reported in recent days that Rezaee might soon be assuming the top security position, with some saying President Masoud Pezeshkian was resisting the appointment by initially rejecting a resignation from former security chief Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr. Zolghadr – himself among the IRGC old guard and a relatively hardline but pragmatic figure, although with less seniority and political connections compared to Rezaee – was eventually replaced. But he was immediately appointed as political adviser to Khamenei, who has himself not been seen or heard from publicly since the start of the war. An official with the IRGC's Basij paramilitary organisation said this week that state media will soon release new pictures from the supreme leader taken after the war to disprove claims by the US and Israel that he may have been badly wounded in the same February 28 strikes that killed his father and other top commanders. The state-linked Mehr news service this week recirculated old and undated video from Khamenei, showing him speaking to a handful of clerics and followers during a meeting. Pezeshkian also said on Monday that he recently had a seven-hour meeting with Khamenei when the supreme leader emphasised "unity". According to an editorial by Nournews, an outlet affiliated with the national security council, Rezaee's appointment signalled the beginning of a broader "strategic restructuring" suited to Iran's new wartime circumstances. It rejected the notion that Zolghadr was removed for failure or dissatisfaction or that the government opposed the appointment, adding that Rezaee could better integrate military, diplomatic, economic and energy policy to overcome "siloed management". "The central issue is not one secretary's departure and another's arrival, but how consequential the steps taken by the SNSC secretariat in this new phase will be," Nournews said. Analysts have noted that Zolghadr was close to Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Iran's parliament speaker and chief negotiator in talks with the US, so his replacement could also be an attempt to tame Ghalibaf's growing influence. But Ghalibaf was among senior officials who released congratulatory messages on Monday for Rezaee – as did Vahidi and newly reappointed judiciary chief Gholam-Hossein Mohseni-Ejei. Vahidi, among the most powerful people in Iran at the moment, said Rezaee's presence in the council can "advance a strategic coordination between the field of battle and diplomacy, as well as economic and political security with an approach of resistance and hope-inducing governance". The Ministry of Foreign Affairs also congratulated Rezaee but said it was important to note the significance of institutions in the Islamic Republic. "The whole world has clearly seen over the past year-and-a-half that our country is a country of institutions, not individuals. This was exactly the secret of the longevity and victory of the Islamic Republic in these challenging conditions," spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei told reporters during a news conference on Monday. Israel reacted harshly to the appointment, pointing out that Rezaee – along with Vahidi – is subject to an Interpol Red Notice for his alleged role in the 1994 bombing of a Jewish centre in Argentina's capital, Buenos Aires, which killed 85 people. "The Iranian regime worships terror, rewards its architects and promotes them to the highest levels of power," Israel's Ministry of Foreign Affairs said. After the appointment, some Iranian users online remembered a number of Rezaee's controversial comments that made headlines over the years. In one such comment in July 2015, months before Iran signed a landmark accord with world powers that lifted sanctions in exchange for nuclear curbs, Rezaee suggested readiness for a US ground assault on Iranian soil. "If the Americans want to look at Iran with ill intent or think about a military attack, they can be sure that in the very first week we will capture at least 1,000 Americans as prisoners," he told state television. "Then, to free each of them, they will have to pay a few billion dollars, which could resolve many of our economic problems." Shortly after the announcement of the appointment, state television aired a historical segment accompanied with footage from Rezaee during the Iraq war, which described him as a commander with a "strong military logic". A number of hardliners in Tehran also appeared pleased with the change at the security council as a hardline figure, unafraid of military confrontation, was taking charge, with some using it to attack Pezeshkian's pro-deal government. "After it emerged that the supreme leader selected Mohsen Rezaee as his representative in the council, the other thing that became clear was that Pezeshkian had for long been standing up to the leader on changing Zolghadr with Rezaee," said hardline MP Amirhossein Sabeti, affiliated with Jalili's Paydari Front.

headline: Video shows moment magnitude 7.4 earthquake strikes Colombia
body of the article: Dozens of people were killed after apowerful magnitude 7.4 earthquake rockedwestern Colombia early on Monday, Aug. 10. The earthquake brought down buildings across several cities in the country and left people trapped in the rubble, local authorities said,according to Reuters. The epicenter of the devastating earthquake was near San Jose del Palmar, in Choco, a sparsely populated province on Colombia's Pacific Coast. Choco Governor Nubia Carolina Cordoba-Curi said there were injuries and significant damage in Quibdo, the provincial capital, and warned residents about potential aftershocks. Colombia'sdisaster agency saidthe shake, which happened at around 7:30 a.m. local time, was felt in nine departments and all 32 departmental capitals. The country's geological service measured the magnitude at 7.4 and said it struck at a depth of 60 miles. The Aug. 10 earthquake in Colombia comes more than a month after apair of devastating earthquakesstruck Venezuela in late June, causingmore than 5,000 deathsand leaving more than 16,000 people injured. The two earthquakes hit less than a minute apart on June 24 just after 6 p.m. local time. The quakes had magnitudes of 7.2 and 7.5, and were centered about 14 miles southeast of Yumare, Venezuela, some 173 miles west of the capital of Caracas. The quakes sent buildings tumbling, damaged infrastructure and left nearly 18,000 displaced from their homes. USA TODAY's Jeanine Santucci and Reuters contributed to this report. headline: Cuba expands solar power with growing support from China
body of the article: Aug. 10 (UPI) -- Cuba expanded incentives for importing renewable energy equipment, as China delivered another 5,000 photovoltaic systems to the island -- part of the country's efforts to increase solar power generation amid a prolonged electricity crisis. A Ministry of Finance and Prices resolution signed Wednesday replaces regulations approved in February and consolidates into a single document tax benefits for individuals and companies that adopt renewable energy technologies. The resolution eliminates tariffs on imports of photovoltaic solar systems and their main components. The benefit also covers solar water heaters, photovoltaic pumps, small wind turbines, biodigesters, solar lighting and air conditioning systems powered by renewable energy sources. The measure seeks to make these technologies more accessible to the state sector, private companies and individuals as Cuba tries to increase renewable power generation and ease pressure on its deteriorating electrical system. The electricity crisis continues to affect much of the island. The Electric Union said Monday that blackouts persisted throughout Sunday and into early Monday. For Monday's peak demand period, the company projected that only 1,100 megawatts would be available against demand of 3,300 megawatts, enough to cover approximately one-third of the country's needs. The blackouts are also affecting other basic services. The state-run Aqueduct and Sewerage Co. said in July that about 225,000 people were having difficulty receiving water, largely because power outages prevented pumping systems from operating. The Chinese government delivered a second donation of 5,000 photovoltaic systems Friday for rural areas and essential services in the country's 169 municipalities, Granma reported. President Miguel Díaz-Canel thanked China for the assistance Sunday and said it adds to Cuba's efforts to "change its energy mix." "We deeply appreciate this gesture by the Chinese people and government, which adds to the efforts Cuba is making to change its energy mix, amid the genocidal blockade," Díaz-Canel wrote on X. "We continue alongside our brothers in building the Community with a Shared Future." Foreign Trade and Foreign Investment Minister Oscar Pérez-Oliva said the equipment will benefit rural areas, healthcare centers, day care centers and bank branches, El Economista reported. China had already donated another 5,000 photovoltaic systems whose installation began before the latest delivery. The Electric Union said in March that 2,671 of those systems were intended for essential services and another 2,329 for isolated homes. The expansion of solar energy goes beyond those donations. At least 41 medium-sized solar parks and 18 smaller ones were built over the past two years, according to RenewAtlas data cited by La Tercera. The government also announced plans to build 92 medium-sized solar parks by 2028. The new projects could provide about 1,000 megawatts when operating at full capacity, compared with typical peak demand of about 3,200 megawatts. The Cuban government says solar power currently covers about 10% of the country's electricity needs, up from 3% at the beginning of 2025. China has become the main supplier of equipment for that expansion. It shipped $117 million worth of solar equipment to Cuba in 2025, up from $3 million in 2023, according to customs data compiled by Ember and cited by El Periódico de la Energía. However, the solar expansion has yet to resolve the electricity crisis. Cuba relies on aging thermoelectric power plants that suffer frequent breakdowns and faces fuel shortages, while insufficient storage capacity limits the use of electricity generated by solar parks after sunlight is no longer available.

headline: At Least 82 Dead After 7.4 Magnitude Earthquake Strikes Colombia, Causing Buildings to Collapse
body of the article: At least 82 people have died after a 7.4 magnitude earthquake struck western Colombia Colombian President Abelardo De La Espriella said on social media that he "will do whatever is necessary to protect" the people of his country after the natural disaster The mayor of Cali, the country's third largest city, said that at least 20 buildings had collapsed with people trapped inside At least 82 people have died after an earthquake struck western Colombia. On Monday, Aug. 10, a 7.4 magnitude earthquake struck the South American country around 7:34 a.m. local time, causing the collapse of dozens of buildings in its third largest city, Cali, and surrounding areas, according toReuters,CNNandThe New York Times. People gather in the streets after a powerful earthquake struck ColombiaCredit: Alexis Munera/Anadolu via Getty Local officials confirmed toThe Associated Pressthat at least 40 people were killed in the Risaralda region, which includes the city of Pereira. People look for survivors amid the rubble of a collapsed building after an earthquake in Cali, ColombiaCredit: Joaquin SARMIENTO/AFP via Getty While the epicenter of the quake was located in San Jose del Palmar, approximately 174 miles west of Bogotá, the powerful earthquake was felt in nine departments and all 32 departmental capitals, after which it triggered mass evacuations, according to Reuters. It was also felt in neighboring Ecuador and Panama. Alejandro Eder, the mayor of Cali, said that at least 20 buildings had collapsed in the urban city with people trapped inside. headline: Over 100 killed after Colombia struck by powerful earthquake
body of the article: More than 100 people have died after western Colombia was hit by a severe magnitude 7.4-earthquake, reducing buildings to rubble in a number of cities, officials reported on Monday. At least 111 people have been killed and 87 have been injured, President Abelardo de la Espriella said during a crisis meeting on Monday afternoon. More than 1,500 residential buildings were damaged and 61 buildings have collapsed, he said, amid fears that the death toll would continue to rise. The powerful quake struck at around 7:34 am (1234 GMT) in the Chocó department, with tremors felt in major cities including Bogotá, Medellín, Cali, Pereira, Popayán, Armenia and Manizales. Videos circulating on social media showed destroyed buildings and people rushing into the streets in panic. The earthquake was also felt in the neighbouring countries of Venezuela, Ecuador and Panama. At least 47 deaths were reported in Pereira, police chief Óscar Leonel Ochoa told Radio Caracol. Another 27 have died in the department of Valle del Cauca, including three children, according to Governor Dilian Francisca Toro. In the department of Chocó, at least four people were killed and 69 injured, the regional government reported. Three people have died in the city of Manizales, where 10 to 12 buildings collapsed entirely, while other houses sustained severe damage, according to Mayor Jorge Rojas. A tower of the cathedral in Manizales was also damaged. Power supplies, telephone services and other communication links have been disrupted. President de la Espriella said commercial traffic has been suspended at six of the country's airports due to damage sustained in the quake. In Cali, the mayor reported more than 20 collapsed buildings, with people believed to be trapped inside. In Quibdó, the capital of the Chocó department, panic broke out following the earthquake and several aftershocks. Governor Nubia Carolina Córdoba reported injuries and severe damage to buildings. The quake's epicentre was located near the town of San José del Palmar in the Chocó department, some 240 kilometres west of Bogotá, at a depth of 96 kilometres, the Colombian Geological Service (SGC) said on X, describing the tremor as the most severe to hit the country in at least 10 years. The United States Geological Survey (USGS) put the depth at 107 kilometres. President de la Espriella, who was sworn on Friday, ordered the establishment of a crisis task force in San José del Palmar to coordinate aid for those affected. Numerous countries have offered assistance. "Brazil remains at Colombia's disposal to provide the necessary support," President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva said. De la Espriella announced that he would travel to Pereira in person. Shortly after the main earthquake, the SGC recorded an aftershock measuring 4.6 in Nóvita, which is also located in the department of Chocó. The quake comes after twin earthquakes hit neighbouring Venezuela in late June, killing more than 6,000 people. Rescue workers arrive at the scene after a 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck Colombia. headline: Oman trying to contain extensive oil spill from stricken tanker
body of the article: Oman says it is working to contain an oil spill off its southern coast that covers almost 400 square kilometres (150 square miles) from a stricken tanker stranded for more than a month inside a protected marine area. The Oman Environment Authority said on Monday that the ongoing spill was within an estimated 7km (4.4 miles) of the coast, according to its most recent analysis. Environmental group Greenpeace last week estimated the slick at around 600 square kilometres (230 square miles), citing analysis of satellite imagery. The Caroline Bezengi loaded at Russia's Black Sea port of Novorossiysk in April and passed through the Suez Canal at the end of May, ship-tracking data shows. An investigation by the AFP news agency found that the tanker had been stranded since early June near Oman's al-Qibliyyah Island after it was rocked by an explosion, causing water to enter several sections of the vessel. The slick was concentrated around Oman's Hallaniyat archipelago, where Sultan Haitham bin Tariq Al Said established a marine reserve last year to protect sensitive ecosystems home to diverse marine life, including rare sea turtles. The country's environment authority said rapid action was needed to protect the area's biodiversity, including "coral reefs, turtle nesting areas, marine habitats and coastal areas of ecological importance". A report in the state-backed Oman News Agency quoted an official with the Transport Ministry as saying authorities were conducting aerial surveillance and had deployed divers. The official said authorities were in the early stages of developing a plan to transfer the vessel's oil cargo "to reduce the risks arising from the incident, ensure navigational safety and protect the marine environment". Omani authorities have not yet identified the cause of the spill. Greenpeace and Dutch peace organisation PAX told AFP that the spill was on the verge of causing an "environmental disaster", saying the tanker was carrying around one million barrels of crude bound for Asia. The ship is believed to be part ofRussia's "shadow fleet", which Moscow uses to circumvent Western sanctions on its oil exports, with ships sailing under the flags of various nations to obscure their true ownership. The fleet includes ageing vessels that have faced criticism over maintenance, insurance and safety standards. The Caroline Bezengi is subject to sanctions imposed by the European Union, Ukraine, the United Kingdom, Canada and Switzerland. Tankers have been frequently targeted in the Gulf region since theUS-Israel war on Iranbegan at the end of February.

headline: Ceuta leader wants migrant detention centre after mass influx from Morocco
body of the article: The leader of Ceuta demanded on Monday the detention and expulsion of the thousands of migrants wandering the Spanish north African territory's streets after last month's mass influx from Morocco. Some 72,000 migrants breached the border in an unprecedented and deadly rush between 30-31 July, with 70,000 having since returned to Morocco, according to Spanish government figures. But the thousands who remain, including hundreds of unaccompanied children who cannot be summarily deported, struggle to access food, water, shelter and sanitation while the tiny enclave's resources are overwhelmed. Their future has sparked a political battle between Spain's leftist central government and regions governed by the main conservative Popular Party (PP) and far-right Vox, which resist taking in unaccompanied children under existing legal provisions. "A space that acts as an internment centre for foreigners must be set up, where these people can be held and remain confined," Ceuta's PP leader Juan Jesús Vivas told reporters. Migrants who crossed into Spain from Morocco gather on a beach in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, 2 August, 2026 - AP Photo He said the measure "must be achieved urgently" so that the migrants "are not in our streets and that expulsion proceedings can be handled with greater speed and ease." Vivas called the situation "unsustainable", estimating that between 8,000-11,000 migrants were left in Ceuta, well above the government's figure of around 2,500. Thousands of residents of the territory of 84,000 inhabitants gathered to protest on Sunday at the handling of a crisis that they say has left Ceuta insecure and abandoned. The Spanish government minister responsible for relations with the regions, Ángel Víctor Torres, assured Ceuta's population that police and troop numbers had been ramped up, including 40% more Civil Guards. Reuniting the children with their families was "the priority," he added, without mentioning the possibility of expulsions. Migrants who crossed into Spain from Morocco sleep on a beach in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, 3 August, 2026 - AP Photo Ceuta is still trying to return to normal and authorities are preparing for the possibility of another attempted mass crossing. For several days, a call to cross the border from Morocco on 15 August has been circulating on social media, authorities to step up preventive measures. Concerns about a possible repeat of what happened on 30 July have also led to extraordinary measures to ensure staff availability. The Civil Guard has temporarily suspended the granting of new leave, holidays and licences for officers stationed in Ceuta and Melilla, although the measure does not affect those that had already been authorised. Related Frontex chief Hans Leijtens vows to change organisation's culture within three years European Union set to reform Frontex again in 2026 In parallel, the Ceuta Garrison has cancelled leave for military personnel stationed in the autonomous city from 13 August until further notice, except in exceptional cases. The measures reflect the level of alert that remains in place at the border less than two weeks after an unprecedented influx. The authorities are now trying to prevent a new episode of migratory pressure from once again pushing the autonomous city's services and resources to the limit.

headline: We are chasing Ebola virus - it is ahead of us, WHO warns
body of the article: The latest Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo began at least three months before it was officially declared - meaning the health authorities are still playing catch-up, the World Health Organization (WHO) has warned. More than 1,900 people have died from the virus since that declaration on 15 May, making this the second-worst Ebola outbreak ever. Infection rates are still high, adding to the concern that the authorities are struggling to get to grips with the spread of the disease. The epicentre of this outbreak of the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, is in the east of DR Congo where insecurity has hampered control efforts. There is also no approved vaccine or any recognised therapeutic drugs, making treating Bundibugyo harder. "We are chasing the virus, the virus is ahead of us," WHO Africa director Dr Mohamed Janabi said at a news conference in the city of Bunia, which is at the heart of this outbreak. He cited research showing that the virus started spreading in February and was initially misdiagnosed as malaria or typhoid. Janabi also said that, in part because of insecurity, health workers are only reaching about 30% of the cases with the rest dying at home. Traditional burial practices – where mourners touch the deceased's body - and a suspicion of health authorities in some communities have also made things difficult. But there are now several dedicated treatment centres in the east of DR Congo and people are getting diagnosed much more quickly. So far there have been 4,294 confirmed cases and 1,960 deaths, DR Congo's health ministry has said. The largest recorded outbreak was in West Africa between 2014 and 2016 when 11,325 people died. headline: Ukrainian drone attack on Russia's Tatarstan kills 13, authorities say
body of the article: A massive Ukrainian drone attack on the city of Nizhnekamsk in Russia's Tatarstan has killed at least 13 people, the authorities said on Monday. The head of the Tatarstan Republic, Rustam Minnikhanov, declared a period of mourning following the attack. Another 78 people required medical attention, with 25 hospitalized, according to his government, which is based in the major city of Kazan. Nine people were killed in a workers' hostel that was severely damaged in the attack, state news agency TASS reported, citing local authorities. Among the victims were citizens of Uzbekistan and Tajikistan, it said. The mayor of Nizhnekamsk, Radmir Belyayev, reported a major attack by Ukrainian drones on industrial facilities and civilian targets. Ukrainian media reported that one of the largest oil refineries in the area was targeted. The General Staff in Kiev later confirmed the attack on the Taneko refinery in Nizhnekamsk. Ukrainian drones also targeted the Western Siberian region of Tyumen. Regional Governor Alexander Moor said a fire broke out after "several drones" had crashed on the premises of an industrial plant. He did not provide any details regarding the plant's location. However, videos circulating on social media showed flames at a refinery in Tobolsk, according to media reports. The industrial city is located more than 2,000 kilometres from Ukraine. The General Staff in Kiev later confirmed an attack on a petrochemical plant in Tobolsk. It said that the plant produces raw materials of military importance. In its defensive struggle against Moscow's invasion, Kiev is targeting facilities belonging to the Russian oil industry. The aim is to deprive the Russian war machine of vital revenue, such as that derived from energy exports. Recently, an increasing number of civilians have been killed in Ukrainian counter-attacks. Ukraine also reported injuries on Monday, with 13 wounded in a Russian airstrike on the south-eastern city of Zaporizhzhya. The region's military governor, Ivan Fedorov, said a glide bomb was dropped on the industrial city, causing damage to residential buildings and cars. The city is under almost constant air-raid alarms, with the front line just 20 kilometres away.

headline: Ukrainian drone strikes deep inside Russia kill at least 13, authorities say
body of the article: At least 13 people were killed, including a child, and 78 others were injured in a Ukrainian drone attack in the Russian republic of Tatarstan, authorities in the region said. It was one of the highest civilian death tolls in the country in recent months. The head of Tatarstan, Rustam Minnikhanov, said the city of Nizhnekamsk, which is roughly 750 miles east of the Ukrainian border, came under a "massive" drone attack targeting industrial and civilian facilities on Monday morning. Russian media reported that the attacks hit a major oil refinery. Ukrainian officials confirmed their military had struck the oil facility "as part of efforts to reduce the Russian aggressor's military capabilities." Ukraine has targeted Russian oil facilities with long-range drones almost daily in recent months in an attempt to reduce Russian oil refining capacity to put further pressure on the country's fuel supply and economy. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says it is a campaign to try to force Russian President Vladimir Putin to the negotiating table and stop his more thanfour-year-old invasion. "We do deliver entirely justified responses, and every Russian strike will be met with our response. Russia's war will be felt more and more at their own home – in Russia," Zelenskyy said late Sunday on social media. "The only reason this is still continuing is Russia's unwillingness to end this war." Russia has also regularly battered Ukraine from the air using missiles, powerful glide bombs and drones, hitting civilian areas and causing thousands of civilian casualties, according to the United Nations. The World Health Organization's European office said Monday that one of its warehouses in the central Dnipro region of Ukraine had been struck twice in less than 24 hours. The attacks destroyed emergency supplies worth an estimated $500,000 that were intended for front-line health facilities, it said in a statement.

headline: Missing Mom Who Vanished on Vacation Most Likely Drowned After Swimming Off Island, Husband Says
body of the article: Elizabeth "Liz" Waddell, a 44-year-old mom from North Carolina, vanished while on her Grenada vacation on July 22 In a recent update, Waddell's husband, Cailen, said that he thinks his wife probably drowned He also said that he is still waiting for information on his wife's status The husband of Elizabeth "Liz" Waddell, the 44-year-old North Carolina mom who disappeared while on vacation in Grenada, said in a new update that he believes she likely drowned. Waddell was last seen on July 22 swimming near Grand Anse Beach in St. George's. Afinal video footageof her taken around noon local time showed her departing an Airbnb she was staying at with a friend and swimming out of frame. However, witnesses reported seeing Liz "far from shore" around 5:30 p.m., Cailen Waddell, her husband, said in aJuly 29 updateon a website that was launched to help find her. Now in aThursday, Aug. 6, update, Cailen addressed some questions "for all of y'all who know and love Liz." He wrote that Liz wasn't really a good swimmer, and that she felt most comfortable being in the water with a flotation device. "She took 4 with her to Grenada in her suitcase," he explained, "and for sure used 2 of them earlier in the trip but didn't have one as far as we know on that day." In response to jet skiers who may have witnessed Liz in the water that late afternoon, Cailen said he believed their account. "According to their report, they spoke with her for 5 or 10 minutes trying to convince her to ride in with them on a Jet Ski and not stay in the ocean," Cailen wrote. "Reportedly she said 'I'm a good swimmer' and gave them a thumbs up. I'll comment that I've never heard Liz describe her swimming as good, but the rest of the conversation and their description of her was consistent with it being Liz." Liz WaddellCredit: LizWaddellDPT/Facebook Cailen said in the update that Liz may have been floating and treading water in Grand Anse Bay "probably 1/3 mile from shore and a 1/3 mile northeast from quarantine point," which is about 17 feet deep based on chart information he found. "My commentary is I just can't believe that Liz made this swim," he added. "It is completely out of character for her, and seems far beyond my understanding of her swimming abilities." Cailen added they don't know if Liz drowned but it is the "most likely scenario" based on "everything we know." "I do not believe she swam for 5.5 hours (from when she was seen at 12:04 on camera)," he said. "Also she wasn't swimming towards where she ended up. Could she have been on the beach along Grand Anse? Absolutely, but we are not aware of any other sightings of her, or security camera footage from the numerous hotels showing her in this area." He believes that Liz might have been on a boat or is somewhere on land, but questions remain about why she is still missing and why she hasn't made an attempt to reach out to someone. "Liz is a free spirit," he wrote, "I can see her making friends and hanging out with people for an afternoon and showing up late in the day sunburnt and having had a great time. I can't see her disappearing for 2 weeks. It makes this scenario feel unlikely, but in the realm of possibility." Never miss a story — sign up forPEOPLE's free daily newsletterto stay up-to-date on the best of what PEOPLE has to offer, from celebrity news to compelling human interest stories. Meanwhile, Cailen acknowledged that the experience has been surreal to him, but he also expressed gratitude to those who have checked on him since Liz's vanishing. He then thanked an official with the U.S. Embassy in Grenada as he is still awaiting more information in the case. "As one of Liz's very wise friends put it — I am grieving her absence and the loss of her in my daily life right now, understanding that it is incredibly likely she is gone and hoping that the investigation will offer more clarity as to what happened," Cailen wrote. PEOPLE has reached out to the Royal Grenada Police Force on Monday, Aug. 10, but did not receive an immediate response. I In a July 28press conference, authorities said Liz arrived on the Caribbean island with her friend on July 11. They then went to the Airbnb on the southern part of the island on July 21. "The Royal Grenada Police Forcehas not reached or announced any final conclusionregarding the circumstances surrounding Ms. Waddell's missing person's status," Commissioner of Police Randy Connaught said. "At this time, the matter continues to be treated as a missing person investigation." Read the original article onPeople

headline: Colombia building collapses on camera as earthquake brings death, destruction
body of the article: A harrowing video captured the moment a building collapsed as a magnitude 7.4 earthquake struck western Colombia early Monday, killing at least 111 people and injuring 87 others. The video shows the building shaking and crumbling as onlookers scream before the structure ultimately gives way. Colombian President Abelardo De La Espriella declared a state of emergency as rescue crews searched collapsed buildings across several cities, according to Reuters. "The ​national government has all of its capabilities deployed to protect lives, assist affected communities and ⁠deliver aid wherever it is needed," De La Espriella said. "The first priority is rescuing the people trapped under the rubble." Exclusive: Franklin Graham Visits Emergency Hospital Treating Venezuela Earthquake Victims The U.S. Geological Survey said the earthquake struck near San Jose del Palmar in Choco at a depth of about 107 kilometers, or 66 miles. The U.S.tsunamiwarning system said there was no tsunami threat. Read On The Fox News App The quake struck just days into De La Espriella's presidency, presenting his new administration with its first major crisis. "The Trump Administration is closely monitoring the large earthquake that struck Colombia and stands ready to support the people of Colombia and President @ABDELAESPRIELLA's Administration,"Secretary of StateMarco Rubio wrote on X. Rubio urged Americans in Colombia to enroll in the State Department's Smart Traveler Enrollment Program and follow the U.S. Embassy in Bogota for updates. Multiple Deaths Reported, Dozens Of Buildings Damaged Following Magnitude 7.4 Earthquake In Western Colombia WATCH: COLOMBIA EARTHQUAKE VICTIMS FLEE IN TERROR AS DEBRIS FALLS FROM BUILDING: Some of the heaviest losses were reported in western Colombia. At least 40 people were killed in Risaralda, home to hard-hit Pereira, while 27 were killed in Valle del Cauca, where Cali is located, The Associated Press reported, citing authorities. Nine deaths were confirmed in Choco, two in Caldas and one in Antioquia, according to the outlet. Cali, one of Colombia's largest cities, suffered extensive damage. Mayor Alejandro Eder said more than two dozen structures had collapsed and people remained trapped, prompting the city to request additionaldisaster-response teamsfrom Bogota and Medellin. "At this point, two people have already been rescued alive, one elderly woman and one young girl. There are more people trapped," Eder told Blu Radio. "We have at least 12 critical points and 25 collapsed structures that we are responding to." The quake's epicenter was near San Jose del Palmar, in Choco, a sparsely populated province on Colombia's Pacific coast. Choco Governor Nubia Carolina Cordoba-Curi said there were injuries and significant damage in Quibdo, the provincial capital, andwarned residents about aftershocks. Colombia's civil aviation authority said flights were suspended at airports in Pereira, Manizales, Quibdo, Armenia, Cartago and Buenaventura while inspectors checked for structural damage. The country's disaster agency said the quake, which occurred at 7:34 a.m. local time (8:34 a.m. ET), was felt across much of Colombia, triggering evacuations and reports of damage. Venezuela was hit bydevastating twin earthquakes in June, which killed more than 6,000 people, mostly on the coast near the capital, Caracas. headline: Italian businessman is mastermind behind journalist bomb attack, police say
body of the article: A businessman who had ties to former Italian premier Silvio Berlusconi is the alleged mastermind behind anOctober bomb attackagainst one of the country's leading investigative journalists, police said on Monday. Rome'sCarabinieri policesaid they arrested Valter Lavitola for allegedly ordering the attack outside journalist Sigfrido Ranucci's house last year. The two men are said to be friends. The blast in a residential neighborhood of Pomezia, about 12 miles south of Rome, destroyed two cars belonging to Ranucci, known for investigations into corruption and the mafia. Ranucci had just returned home at the time, and his daughter had walked by a half-hour before, his employer said at the time. Video shot by Ranucci, who has been under police protection since 2021 because of his hard-hitting investigations, showed the mangled remains of the cars and the gate. Lavitola is accused of instructing a second man, Tavares Gomes Clesio, to recruit four men to place the bomb in front of Ranucci's home, police said. The four men werearrested near Naples in Junefor carrying out the attack. Police are still looking for Gomes. According to police, Lavitola and Gomes took part in an "initial exploratory inspection" outside of Ranucci's home in September. Lavitola thought the bombing would raise Ranucci's profile ahead of a possible career in politics, authorities wrote in the arrest warrant, according to local media. Ranucci, the popular star of the weekly investigative show "Report" on state broadcaster Rai, is not accused of any wrongdoing and detectives believe he was unaware of Lavitola's plans. Ranucci has taken on sensitive topics such as Italy's mafia and political corruption in past investigations, and has lived under police protection for years. He told the ANSA news agency the day after the attack that he had received "an endless list of threats." The journalist, who once described Lavitola as a "true friend," was not injured in the attack. Lavitola, a former journalist and import-export businessman who owns a restaurant in Rome, is well known in Italy, having been close to Berlusconi, who died in 2023. In 2015, a lower court convicted the former prime minister of having bribed a senator, handing him a three-year sentence. The same sentence was given to Lavitola, whom prosecutors accused of having handed the cash to the lawmaker. The explosion targeting Ranucci occurred on the eighth anniversary of the car bomb slaying of Maltese investigative journalistDaphne Caruana Galizia, who wrote extensively about suspected corruption in political and business circles.

headline: British couple held in Iran end hunger strike
body of the article: A British couple jailed in Iran after being accused of espionage have ended their hunger strikes after 93 and 84 days respectively. Craig and Lindsay Foreman were arrested in January 2025 while passing through Iran on a motorcycle journey from Europe to Australia. They were both sentenced to 10 years in jail in February, but Craig Foreman's family said his punishmenthad been extendedby two years after speaking to the media. The couple from East Sussex, who both deny espionage, went on hunger strike in May whenprison authorities prevented them from calling their families. The family of the couple said they had been protesting against how they and other prisoners were being treated. A spokesperson for the family said the couple agreed with prison guards to end their strike to be able to speak directly to their loved ones again. However, the family said contact was yet to be re-established, as of Monday afternoon. The family had also previously called for the coupleto end their hunger strike. Five people outside the prison joined the pair on their hunger strike for the final five days from Tuesday to Saturday as an act of solidarity, the family added. Lindsay Foreman's son Joe Bennett and four unnamed others took part in the UK, as well as other prisoners inside Tehran's Evin jail, the family said. "My mum and Craig have spent months on hunger strike, and even at the point of bringing it to an end they wanted to make it about something bigger than themselves," Bennett, from Folkestone in Kent, said. "Those final five days became about people standing together around values that should be universal: Truth, justice, kindness, peace and unity." By the end of the protest, Craig Foreman had been on hunger strike for 93 days, and Lindsay Foreman for 84 days, the family added. Although they said they were unaware of the condition of the pair, who had consumed just milk and either honey or salt in water during their strikes. Bennett said the couplealso went on a separate hunger striker back in Novemberas a "cry out for help". Bennett joined the latest hunger strike for the final five days [BBC] The family of the couple said the final five days of the latest protest aimed to "transform the last stage of the couple's hunger strike from protest into something constructive and collective". The couple's family recently met the UK's first envoy for complex consular cases, Alistair Burt, and the new minister for the Middle East, Stephen Doughty. Bennett said meetings had been "positive and constructive". "Now it is time for them to put their warm words into action and reach out to other states for support, reach out to Iran for discussions and name this as the arbitrary detention that it is," he added. "Sunday was the first time in three months my mum and Craig sat down to eat," Bennett said. "I will not rest until they can do it at home with us." The Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO) said the pair's incarceration was "unjustified and appalling". It said Doughty had met Craig and Lindsay Foreman's family to outline the action the government was taking to try to secure their release. "Craig and Lindsay's health and welfare is our priority," a FCDO spokesperson said. "Since their arrest last year, Britain's ambassador to Tehran, diplomats and officials in London have been working to provide consular assistance. "This includes the ambassador visiting them in prison and facilitating calls with their family back in the UK." Follow BBC Sussex onFacebook,X, andInstagramand listen to BBC Radio Sussex onSounds. headline: Jerusalem cafe becomes flashpoint in growing haredi protests over Shabbat
body of the article: Israeli police were out in full force after demonstrators broke through the barricades last weekend. By mid-morning on Saturday, the alleys surrounding Cafe Basimta were filled with haredi Orthodox demonstrators protesting the cafe's decision to open on Shabbat. It was the sixth consecutive Shabbat that the small cafe offAgrippas Streethad faced demonstrations, with no sign of change. Israeli police were out in full force after demonstrators broke through the barricades last weekend. Close to 100 restaurants, bars and coffee shops inJerusalemopen on Shabbat, according to Laura Wharton, a Jerusalem city council member from the Democrats party who founded Shabus, a cooperative that runs buses on Shabbat. Only one, Basimta, has drawn a crowd. Basimta, which opened at the end of May, is new, Wharton said, whereas the others have been open for decades. The cafe sits near what she called the undeclared border between the city's haredi neighborhoods and the rest of the city. Ultra-Orthodox protesters outside of the Basimta cafe on Saturday, July 4, 2026. (credit: Screenshot/X/@afdirohak) Agrippas Street runs along the Mahane Yehuda market, where almost every business closes for Shabbat. The cafe also opened its doors during the period when haredi yeshivas are on break, so teenagers who make up the bulk of the protestors have more free time to demonstrate. "There have been weeks when the average age was probably about 16 there," Wharton said.. The cafe is not only a flashpoint in the long-running fight between secular and religious Israelis over the character of the holy city. It has become the most visible front in a hot summer of protests and riots across Jerusalem, over a light rail line and extending forced army conscription to yeshiva students, both opposed by the Haredi community. For six years, hardline haredi demonstrators who say the light rail was planned without accounting for the community's sensibilities have fought construction through Bar-Ilan Street, a haredi thoroughfare, breaking into work sites and pulling down fencing. The vandalism and delays have cost an estimated 400 million shekels. The light rail project is going ahead despite years of obstruction, Wharton said, and Saturday is the one day there is no work at the site to disrupt, freeing up protesters to target the cafe. Nationally, 44% of Israeli Jews identify as secular and 16% as haredi, according to figures provided to the Jewish Telegraphic Agency by the Jerusalem Institute for Policy Research. That breakdown is vastly different in Jerusalem, where among the city's Jewish residents, 46% identify as haredi and 25% as religious-Zionist, while 13% identify as secular, according to the institute. That arithmetic, which speaks to the struggle over the city's identity, is what non-haredi Jerusalemites say is really at stake in an alley off Agrippas Street. Avi Dabush, a rabbi who directs Rabbis for Human Rights and is running for the Knesset as part of the left-wing Democrats party, said the cafe was symbolic of the larger national issue. "It's kind of an example for the battle that we are doing about the identity of Israel right now," said Dabush, who was raised in the religious-Zionist school system. He was there on Saturday along with Yair Golan, who leads the Democrats party, for whom the cafe has become an issue ahead of the Oct. 27 election. "We are in the midst of elections," Dabush said. "So it's part of it." Outside Cafe Basimta Saturday, demonstrators took turns screaming at each other in the alleys. The haredi teens, dressed in their black Shabbat best, yelled "One who desecrates the Sabbath, his sentence is death," a verse from Exodus. They also shouted "stop destroying Jerusalem," while at other times they gathered in circles to sing Shabbat hymns. Secular Israelis shot back with a slew of chants, of which "enlist!" appeared to be the most popular. They also shouted, "Only cowards send children," and carried signs reading "Haredim for our coffee," a play on a Hebrew word that means both ultra-Orthodox and devoted. Haredi children followed and tried to defend older members of the community during altercations. Lior Leon, a Jerusalem tour guide, blamed the adults. "The problem is not the kids; they push them," he said. The confrontations have grown more aggressive since the protests began in early July. Before dawn on July 25, someone threw a bag of feces at the entrance, and on Thursday, Israel Police announced the arrest of a 15-year-old boy. On Saturday, the JTA reporter at the scene was spat on by a demonstrator, as were other journalists, and Orthodox residents of the buildings lining the alley threw bags of water down at counter-demonstrators until police shouted a warning that they would be arrested. Israel Policesaid in a written statement to JTA that officers acted where they identified people "attempting to instigate violence or disrupt public order." Cafes and restaurants are granted an exemption from the city's prohibition on businesses opening on the Shabbat. Yohanan Weitzman, a Jerusalem city council member from the haredi Agudat Yisrael faction, told JTA that there was an unwritten status quo governing which businesses and cafes open in the city, which Basimta had violated. It "is not the desire of either party, but it is a necessary compromise to prevent conflicts," Weitzman said. There has been widespread violation of those agreements and a failure to enforce municipal bylaws, he said. Opening the cafe was "the straw that broke the camel's back." The protests are organized by the Committee for the Sanctity of Jerusalem, which acts for the Edah HaChareidis, the anti-Zionist body that includes some of the city's most militant Hasidic groups. Demonstrators are summoned by pashkevilim, the broadsheet notices pasted on walls in haredi neighborhoods with the time and place of each week's protest. Haredi groups who are more involved in Israeli society have been unsettled by the protests. "I am strongly opposed to any kind of violence," Eliezer Rauchberger, the deputy mayor who heads Jerusalem'sDegel HaTorahfaction, the Lithuanian stream that sits in Mayor Moshe Lion's coalition, said in a written statement. Asked which haredi groups were organizing the protests and which rabbis stood behind them, he declined to answer. One haredi demonstrator, who asked to be identified only by his first name, Avraham, told JTA the protests would not stop until the cafe closes. "We want it gone," he said. "It is desecrating our Sabbath." Wharton said a Supreme Court ruling exempts entertainment, food service and sports from the city's Shabbat closures, which is why three of Jerusalem's four cinemas and its municipal swimming pools operate on Saturday. Basimta, she said, is running legally. The cafe's ownership by a sect of Jews who have embraced Christian beliefs has also stirred some opposition. Or LeAchim, an anti-missionary organization, told JTA it is pursuing municipal channels to have Basimta shut, arguing it lacks a valid business license. Wharton said the only substantive complaint concerned tables and chairs placed outside without a permit, and that the furniture has since been brought inside. Yoel Ben David, who runs the cafe, told JTA in July that the municipality and police had been "incredibly supportive," and that city officials asked him to bring the tables in as a compromise, which he accepted. Wharton said the effort to shut the cafe had backfired. Basimta has been doing record business, boasting lines of customers from the moment it opens until it closes. Ben David is a member of the Jews for Jesus community, which owns and operates the cafe, as JTA reported last month. The revelation cost him support from some Israeli institutions, but it has not thinned the crowds, and demonstrators told JTA it is not what they care about. For Liora Bamberger, who lives in one of the high-rise buildings encircling the Basimta courtyard, the fight has taken away the one quiet morning of her week. "The only day in the week that we have a little bit of quiet," she said, before pausing. "Not anymore." Bamberger, who observes Shabbat, said the cafe should be allowed to open and that she did not expect this to end well. "When you have extremism, it's not gonna end," she said. "It's gonna be a boom." Asked whether she found common ground with the demonstrators, she said she found it with everyone. "This is the problem."

headline: Paris Just Made the High-Vis Vest Your Cheapest Scooter Accessory
body of the article: Seventy-nine peopledied in French e-scooter crashes last year. That's up from 45 the year before, according toBBC reportingciting French road-safety officials. In Paris alone, roughly 1,100 riders were injured — a33% spikeyear over year. Those numbers don't leave much room for half-measures. So Paris didn't offer any. Every e-scooter rider on public roads must now wear an approved helmet and high-visibility or retro-reflective gear. Skip the helmet:€135 fine. Forget the vest: another€35. The fines are specific, the scope is broad, and your pedal-assist e-bike gets a pass. Riding your scooter through the 11th arrondissement without a vest now costs more than the vest itself. The mandate covers not just e-scooters but hoverboards and Segways too — essentially anything classified as amotorized personal mobility deviceunder French law, per the Paris Préfecture de Police. Standard pedal-assist e-bikes remain under bicycle regulations and aren't affected. The geographic reach extends beyond Paris proper into the inner-ring departments of Hauts-de-Seine, Seine-Saint-Denis, and Val-de-Marne. €135 finefor no approved helmet; €35 for missing high-vis or reflective gear Applies to e-scooters, Segways, and hoverboards — pedal-assist e-bikes are exempt Covers Paris and the three surrounding inner-ring departments Existing rules alreadyban sidewalk riding, cap speedat 25 km/h, require riders to be at least 14, and prohibit passengers Excessive speed carries a separate€1,500 penaltyunder current French law Paris has moved from suggesting riders behave to demanding they dress for survival. The policy shift — from basic usage limits to mandatory protective equipment — reads like a city that tried the gentle approach and watched the casualty numbers climb anyway. When the reminders stopped working, consequences arrived. The harder question lingers. High-vis vests make riders more visible, but a vest catches headlights — it does not add a protected lane. Without betterbike gadgetsand infrastructure, lower car speeds, and smarter intersection design, the most vulnerable road users are being asked to solve a problem they didn't create alone. The rule has clear logic. Whether it addresses the root cause is a different conversation entirely. Compliance is cheap — and this rule is almost certainly a preview of what's coming elsewhere. If you ride anywhere in the Paris region, pack acompliant helmetand reflective gear before every trip. No exceptions, no gambles on enforcement gaps. A decent vest costs under€10. Other European cities watching their own injury stats climb are already paying close attention to what Paris does next — and how well it works. Gear up now, before your city decides to follow suit. headline: Stolen trailer investigation leads police to nearly $800K in cargo and vehicles
body of the article: Peel Regional Policerecovered nearly $800,000 in stolen computer equipment and commercial vehicles during their Brampton, Ontario investigation. July 22, detectives went near Heart Lake Road, close to Countryside Drive, for a missing-trailer follow-up. The search led officers beyond that original case. Inside nearby trailers, they found cargo from two unrelated thefts. Investigators located four stolen commercial assets nearby. Two separate computer shipments carried an estimated value of $681,083.68. Police connected those loads with incidents occurring July 17 and three days later. Both findings came from one follow-up effort in Brampton. While examining recovered trailers, detectives discovered computer equipment. That vehicle inquiry did not originally involve either shipment. Investigators believe stolen loads entered those units after each theft. The release describes one trailer investigation alongside two unrelated cargo incidents. Police identified recovered equipment only as computers. The release omitted manufacturer, owner, shipper and intended recipient names. Officials provided no pickup locations, destinations, carrier identities, recovery timeline or shipment details. Authorities continue examining this matter. Two Utility Manufacturing trailers, from 2016 and 2021, appeared among recovered assets. One 2015 Volvo VNL tractor joined 1998 Stoughton equipment, completing four-vehicle list. Police calculated their combined value at roughly $105,000. Together, those items brought the official total to $786,083.68. Peel Regional Police have not identified any suspects connected with these incidents. The Commercial Auto Crime Bureau continues handling the investigation. Authorities asked anyone with information to call 905-453-2121, extension 3313. The department did not respond to FreightWaves' additional questions before publication. Computer equipment remains attractive cargo because high values often concentrate within only several pallets. One trailer inquiry exposed losses tied to separate incidents here. Peel did not explain how criminals obtained either shipment, so prevention claims would go beyond available facts. headline: India police fire tear gas at protesters seeking exam reforms
body of the article: Police in India have fired tear gas shells on protesters demanding reforms to recruitment exams in the eastern state of Jharkhand. Thousands of students, job seekers and volunteers have been trying to reach the state's assembly in the capital city of Ranchi to register their protest. The BBC has seen some people who have sustained injuries, though the official number of injured is unclear. The protesters have been demonstrating for over two weeks now, demanding an overhaul of Jharkhand's government exam system. On Monday, many attempted to breach police barricades, causing police to use water cannons, batons and tear gas to try and disperse crowds, officials say. Ranchi City Superintendent of Police Paras Rana told ANI news agency that most protesters had been peaceful, but accused a smaller group of breaking through barricades and throwing stones at officers. He said three policemen had been injured. "About 90% of the students are peaceful, but there are some who are not listening even to their own representatives," he said. Rana said police had shown restraint and used "minimal force for a very short time" because the protesters were students. He appealed to them to remain peaceful, saying their demands were reaching the government. The protest comes weeks after thousands of young Indians attempted to march to the national parliament in Delhi, amid the massive "cockroach" protests over exam paper leaks. Students and job aspirants have been protesting to demand action against alleged examination irregularities in Jharkhand state [Getty Images] India's Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) - which is not a political party - called off its five-week-long protest on 25 July after education minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned. The CJP had attracted support from students based in different states of the country. Meanwhile in Ranchi, visuals from the state capital show thousands of protesters, police as well as media personnel on the streets, amid tightened security arrangements. Despite police efforts to disperse them, large crowds remain at the site. Protesters in Jharkhand have beengathered at a stadiumin Ranchi since 25 July - some have been sleeping in the open and several have gone on hunger strike. Even after multiple rounds of talks and the government accepting several demands, protesters say the agitation will continue until all their demands are met. The immediate cause of the anger is a preliminary civil service exam held by the Jharkhand Public Service Commission (JPSC) in April. After the results were announced in July, candidates alleged that leaked answer sheets shared on social media showed some successful applicants had answered far fewer questions than expected. This fuelled suspicions that the results had been manipulated. The state government has assured students that they will get justice. The allegations around the exam are being investigated by Jharkhand's Criminal Investigation Department (CID). More than a dozen people have been arrested. Investigators are also examining the role of a private company that conducted parts of the exam process after candidates raised questions about how it was selected. After talks with protesters on Sunday, the government agreed to cancel the exam in question, along with two others. Three JPSC members also reportedly resigned. This came after JPSC chairman L Khiangte stepped down on 22 July. He was questioned in the investigation and arrested on Monday. But protesters say several demands remain unmet, chief among them an investigation into the irregularities by the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI), India's premier federal investigative agency. The protesters are demanding an overhaul of the state's examination system [ANI] Unlike the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) protests, which emerged outside party politics, the Ranchi agitation has drawn strong political backing. The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) , which is in opposition in Jharkhand, has backed the protesters, staged demonstrations, raised the issue in the state assembly and demanded a federal investigation. Congress, a partner in the state government but the BJP's national rival, has also expressed support for the students. On Sunday, Jharkhand Chief Minister Hemant Soren, who is the head of the regional Jharkhand Mukti Morcha (JMM) party, alleged that vested interests were trying to disrupt democracy in the state. He warned that the protesters' agitation should not be politicised and also reiterated his promise to take action to deliver justice.

headline: Spain cancels all leave for soldiers tackling Ceuta migrant crisis
body of the article: Spain has cancelled all leave for military personnel in Ceuta amid the threat of a fresh incursion into the North African exclave. At least 72,000 people poured from Morocco intothe tiny Spanish territoryon July 30, with at least 80 dying in theattempt to illegally cross Europe's only land borderwith Africa. Amid reports of online chat groups plotting a new onslaught on Aug 15, all leave has been cancelled for the troops who were rushed to the Spanish territoryto deal with the crisis. Cadena Ser, a Spanish radio station, reported it had seen a directive sent from the defence ministry to the Ceuta general command on Sunday, entitled "cancellation of leave". It said all leave and time off for military personnel had been cancelled until further notice, except in "exceptional duly justified cases". The reason given was the "service requirements necessitating an increase in the activities deployed in Ceuta" in light of the"migration crisis". A spokesman for the Spanish defence ministry confirmed to The Telegraph that all leave had been cancelled for troops in Ceuta. Meanwhile, Spain and Italy failed to find a deal to end theirbitter immigration rowduring weekend talks with the European Commission. The diplomatic spat, considered an ideological battle between Pedro Sánchez's Left-wing Spanish government and Giorgia Meloni's Right-wing Italian government, threatens to undermine the EU's Schengen free-movement zone at the height of the summer tourism season. Late on Friday, Madrid retaliated against controls introduced by Rome because of the Ceuta crisis by imposing passport checks on arrivals at Spanish ports and airports from Italy. Thousands of migrants attempted to swim from Morocco to Ceuta at the end of July - Anadolu/Getty Images Magnus Brunner, the European migration commissioner, sought to cool tensions between the two countries over the weekend but failed to find a compromise. Antonio Tajani, the Italian foreign minister, suggested Rome would not consider dropping its border checks on arrivals fromSpainuntil Aug 15 at the earliest. Ms Meloni put out a joint Instagram post with Mette Frederiksen of Denmark on Monday, which called for the construction of "return hubs in third countries" through which failed asylum seekers would be repatriated. The Italian leader championed the idea after building two facilities in Albania. However, their use has been repeatedly stymied by court challenges. The two leaders said they were proud of "Europe's Christian cultural heritage" and said migrants must "not try to impose a way of life upon us that we do not want". They added that they did not "accept uncontrolled immigration to Europe" and accused illegal migrants of being responsible for "growing crime rates", including drug trafficking and sexual violence. Foreigners who committed crimes should be expelled from Europe, they said. Spanish soldiers escort a group of migrants to the border - Jon Nazca/REUTERS The EU is targeting online networks used by people traffickers to prevent a repeat of the migrant influx into Ceuta, Politico reported on Monday, citing three unnamed officials. Henna Virkkunen, the EU tech sovereignty commissioner, summoned Meta and TikTok for meetings last week. They will continue discussions on Monday to work out how to combat the online channels the platforms say smugglers used to encourage many of those who crossed into Ceuta. "Platforms identified a combination of smugglers offering services with various illegal routes or fake documents," said an EU official who took part in the meetings.. A spokesman for Meta, which owns WhatsApp, Facebook and Instagram, said it had a team monitoring the situation in Ceuta to remove "content that offers to provide, facilitate or seek human smuggling services", Politico reported. TikTok said it had established a taskforce and was using advanced technology to tackle exploitative schemes. Try full access to The Telegraph free today.
