headline: London Police Seize Ferrari SP2 Monza, Lamborghini Revuelto Among 90 Cars Worth $10 Million
body of the article: London's Metropolitan Police saidit seized a total of 90 cars over this past weekendduring an operation related to the department's ongoing crackdown against what officials have deemed as "antisocial driving behavior." The event marks the single highest number of cars, as well as the highest valued vehicles, that the operation has involved since it started some five years ago. Metropolitan Police confirmed on Monday that the department had seized more than seven dozen vehicles in some of London's most affluent neighborhoods, including Hyde Park, Kensington, and Chelsea, between August 7th and 9th. The cars, which included a 1-of-499Ferrari Monza SP2valued at around $4.7 million, reportedly totaled some $10 million worth of sheetmetal. According to the Met cops, the Monza had only been in the country for a few hours at the time of the seizure; he owner had been driving the car without proper insurance, and was on a provisional license. In the U.K., among other offenses, antisocial driving habits are said to include causing excessive noise pollution, street racing and cruising in a convoy, according toCBS News. Others had their vehicles seized as a result of other crimes, including one individual who was arrested on suspicion of possession with intent to supply Class A, B and C drugs. The operation involved 120 officers from the Met, including some 95 from the Special Constabulary and Vehicle Enforcement Team. The officers were supported in their efforts by agents from the Motor Insurers' Bureau. London Metropolitan Police "We regularly hear from local people who are fed up with people driving cars dangerously in the area, or with modifications which make them a nuisance to those who live nearby," special chief inspector Geoff Tatman said in a statement. "Through operations like this we're arresting these drivers and seizing their cars so we can keep our roads safe and send [a] clear message that we won't put up with their reckless and dangerous behavior." London Metropolitan Police Given the amount of success that was achieved with this particular sting, I wouldn't be surprised to see more enforcement actions like this in the future, and I doubt we'll have to wait long for this particular vehicle seizure total to be surpassed. That said, I doubt the Met will end up with another Monza in their possession. You Might Also Like If You Can Only Own One Car, Make It One of These These Are the Most Popular Cars by State

headline: Criminal gangs have diversified across Latin America, making them more resilient – but not untouchable
body of the article: Latin America's most powerful criminal groups have expanded beyond the drug trade – and have become more resilient as a result. That's what my colleagues and I discovered while researching for anew studyon the structural transformation of organized crime across Latin America and the Caribbean. Criminal networks now draw revenue from illicit and legal sources alike. Many of them police neighborhoods and influence local politics. Others invest in legitimate businesses and exploit global transport and financial systems, using shell companies and digital payment platforms to conceal the origins of their money. Their businesses extend into ostensibly legitimate sectors ranging from mining to fuel. This diversification shields criminal groups from "enforcement shocks," such as crackdowns on drug smuggling. It can also help thembuy protectionfrom compromised officials and allow organizations to embed themselves more deeply in local economies. The struggle is increasingly over who sets the rules and who can enforce them. Brazil is one place where these trends are on display. On Aug. 28, 2025, more than 1,400 Brazilian law enforcement agents fanned out across eight states in what officialscalled the largest operationagainst organized crime in the country's history. Their targets included more than a thousand gas stations, four ethanol plants, a trucking fleet, a port terminal, investment funds and offices on Avenida Faria Lima, the center of São Paulo's financial district. The investigation, known asOperation Hidden Carbon, exposed an alleged money laundering system tied to Brazil's most powerful criminal organization, First Capital Command, or PCC. Investigatorsallege that the networkused gas stations and other fuel businesses to launder illicit proceeds, channeling them through payment companies and investment vehicles that obscured their origins and ultimate ownership. The scheme reportedly movedbillions of dollarsthrough the motor-fuel sector and a web of payment companies and investment vehicles, with some fintechs allegedly functioning as unlicensed banks. Authorities initially seized about R$1.2 billion, or roughly US$220 million, in assets. Brazilian police launched a major operation on Aug. 28, 2025, against a vast money-laundering network involving organized crime and the financial sector.Miguel Schincarol/AFP via Getty Images Operation Hidden Carbon illustrates a broader shift in organized crime across the Americas. Several of the region's largest organizations now combine drug trafficking withillegal gold mining,fuel theft, migrant smuggling and the manipulation of digital payment systems. Others have also moved into logistics, finance, real estate and municipal services. Many alsoassume functionstypically associated with government, from enforcing local rules to delivering basic services. A 2025 survey across 18 countries found that 13% of respondents — equivalent to nearly 80 million people —said that local criminal groupsprovided order or reduced crime in their communities. Criminal diversification did not happen all at once. Latin American groups built international trafficking alliances in the 1980s and 1990s, but the shift toward multi-market networks became more pronounced in the mid-2010s. As drug trafficking grew riskier, groups moved into migrant smuggling and illegal mining. Cybercrimeopened new revenue streams, while cryptocurrencies made it easier to conceal proceeds. The pandemicaccelerated the trendby weakening state institutions and expanding informal economies. Diversification boosts profits and spreads risk, reducing dependence on any single commodity or corridor. Cocaine remains highly lucrative, so few organizations abandon it. Instead, they add new illegal activities to territories and logistical systems they already control. The same infrastructure and intermediaries can support several criminal markets at once. The organizational structures have changed too. Rigid hierarchies have given way to looser networks of transporters and financial specialists operating through front companies. Money and personnel can move between activities as enforcement pressure and market conditions change. Real estate and commercial businesses conceal proceeds, while digital assets make transfers easier. That wealth can then be converted into political influence. This adaptability complicates enforcement. Police and regulatory agencies are generally organized by crime type and national jurisdiction, while the networks they are attempting to shut down operate across markets and borders. Pressure on drug trafficking may push a group toward gold or extortion without destroying its finances. Raids may temporarily remove leaders but leave corrupt relationships and financial machinery intact, allowing the organization to regenerate. As my new study argues, political leaders across much of Latin America and the Caribbean are still judged primarily by how visibly they confront crime. People living with daily extortion and victimizationwant reliefquickly. Soldiers on street corners and prisoners paraded before cameras offer immediate proof that a government is acting. Financial investigations and judicial reform, by contrast, produce slower results and offer fewer immediate political rewards. These political incentives help explain the enduring appeal of "mano dura," or iron-fist security. El Salvador's state of exception became the regional reference point after the official homicide rate fell from roughly 105 per 100,000 in 2015 to 1.3 by 2025. By June 2026, more than92,000 peoplewere imprisoned. But the crackdown also suspended constitutional protections, leading to mass detention without due process andhundreds of deaths in custody. An alleged gang member is arrested by police in El Salvador.Yuti Cortez/AFP via Getty Images Since El Salvador imposed its state of exception in 2022, governments in Argentina, Belize, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, the Dominican Republic, Ecuador, Guatemala, Haiti, Honduras, Jamaica, Mexico, Panama, Paraguay and Trinidad and Tobago haveadopted hard-linesecurity measures inspired by or resembling mano dura. Peru's newly inaugurated president, Keiko Fujimori, haspromised a tougher security strategy, including a greater role for the armed forces in areas under states of emergency. Crackdowns that neglect financial and corruption investigations may suppress some forms of violence without dismantling the economic structures or political protection that sustain criminal power. Ecuador shows how quickly those gains can unravel. After declaring an internal armed conflict in January 2024, the governmentsent troopsinto prisons and violent cities. Homicides initially fell before surging past9,000 in 2025, the highest level in the country's modern history. The gangs survived because their power extended far beyond the streets. They retained control over prison networks and access to the ports that move cocaine through Guayaquil. Their relationships with corrupt officials also endured. Military pressuredisrupted the gangs, but it also caused fragmentation and intensified rivalry between the resulting factions. Across Latin America, right-leaning political candidates havegained groundby putting public order at the center of their campaigns. The resulting turn toward more punitive security policies makes slower institutional reform harder to sustain. Washington is reinforcing this trend. The United States hasexpanded its useof foreign terrorism designations against criminal organizations. In May 2026, the State Departmentannounced terrorism designationsfor the PCC and the Red Command, or CV, another major Brazilian faction, as foreign terrorist organizations. The designations took effect on June 5. By July 2026, U.S. forces had carried outat least 67 strikesagainst suspected drug trafficking vessels in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific, killing more than 220 people. Yet the campaign appears to havedone littleto constrain cocaine supply. Traffickers have shifted routes in response to the strikes, andavailable evidencesuggests no clear tightening of the U.S. market. In August, Washingtonannounced plansfor a $1 billion security package for Colombia, as the country's new government prepares to pursue a more militarized campaign against drug traffickers. Military pressure, however, addresses only part of what makes criminal groups resilient. Their stayingpower depends on relationshipswith public officials and access to financial systems. Control of legitimate companies allows them to conceal ownership and launder criminal proceeds. American financial intelligence and asset-recovery tools could helpdismantle that infrastructure, depriving these organizations of the resources they use to expand. Brazil's Operation Hidden Carbon points toward a more effective response. Investigators traced proceeds from gas stations through fintechs and investment funds, exposing the corporate structures and intermediaries behind them. They treated organized crime as a system embedded in the economy rather than solely as an armed threat on the street. Such work lacks the immediate public impact of an armed raid, but its effects can be far greater. Asset freezes can deprive criminal groups of the capital they use to buy political protection and expand into legal and illegal markets alike. That is why investigators must go after the money and companies, not just the gunmen. It was written by:Robert Muggah,Instituto Igarapé;Princeton University Read more: Bird flu decimated South America's marine mammals. What can Australia do differently? He also advises governments, private companies and international organizations the United Nations, the IMF and the World Bank.

headline: 'Not afraid to stay': The Canadians who want to change how wildfires are fought
body of the article: When a wildfire broke out near his First Nation community in northern Ontario, Hubert Wigwas decided to stay put. He put sprinklers on his roof to extinguish falling embers. He checked on elders in his community who also stayed behind, and he fuelled up four boats down on the lake in case they needed a quick escape. "This is everything I've built in my 58 years," Wigwas, a councillor from Gull Bay First Nation, told the BBC. "I'm just not going to run away and let it burn." Canada has seen some of its worst fire seasons in recent years, and experienced its most destructive on record in 2023, when blazes tore through forest land roughly the size of Syria. As of this August, more than 750 wildfires are actively burning across the country. The impact has been felt as far as the US Midwest, where smoke had choked the air in cities. Even President Donald Trump has taken note, threatening to further tariff Canada for allowing "filthy, polluted" air to waft south of the border. The intensifying wildfires have sparked a national conversation: Are there enough firefighters to battle these more challenging fire seasons? What happens when resources are stretched too thin? And how can remote communities, often closest to danger because of their proximity to Canada's vast boreal forest, learn to live with this new reality? Wigwas asked himself these questions when he decided to stay, even as he faces a fine of around C$800 ($570; £425) for defying evacuation orders. Leaders of Gull Bay First Nation, also known as Kiashke Zaaging Anishinaabek, have been urging residents to stay away since mid-July as more than 150 wildfires burn across Ontario's northwest. Its chief penned a letter on 29 July pleading with those who have remained to leave immediately, saying that Ontario firefighters cannot do their jobs safely with people still in their homes. It is the same message officials across the country have been conveying in British Columbia, where around 115 fires are currently burning. But with a wildfire 24km outside his community, Wigwas, speaking in late July, said he had yet to see fire personnel from out of town there to help fireproof properties or keep an eye out on the elders who remained. He said it made him realise that his First Nation would benefit from setting up its own wildfire emergency response and teaching residents how to protect their own homes. "Everybody talks about climate change, but nobody is doing something to unite the (First Nations) reserves and have a system like that set up," Wigwas said. Dave Bradley, a spokesperson for Ontario's ministry of natural resources, did not address Wigwas' claim directly, but said the province has been in "constant contact" with First Nations leaders. He added that fire fighting resources are directed based on "fire behaviour, weather conditions and risks to communities." 'Total incinerated destruction': Canada wildfire evacuees wonder if they still have homes In the west-coast province of British Columbia - long the front line of Canada's wildfire response - people are doing just what Wigwas is envisioning for his First Nation, with efforts underway to train residents of rural and remote communities how to safely respond to wildfires before out-of-town crews can arrive. Sonja Leverkus, a wildfire researcher and specialist, said she has helped train more than 400 people in and around her community of Fort Nelson over the last three years through a firefighting group she helped start called the Northeast BC Rural Incident Management Team. She told the BBC that her efforts are inspired by a realisation that Canada needs to change how it fights wildfires as climate change increases their frequency and intensity. "There are not enough human beings in Canada," she said, with the appropriate training, "to fight the fires that we have currently, especially over the last five years". Remote communities, where the nearest town might be hundreds of kilometres away, can sometimes be bumped down the priority list for BC firefighting crews if there are blazes threatening more populated areas, she said. Her crew, who are primarily indigenous, have carried out prescribed burns, also known as a hazard reduction burns – a practice of setting planned, controlled blazes to remove fuels that could contribute to wildfires. How Australia combines modern tech and Indigenous knowledge to fight wildfires They have also helped put out smaller fires before they grow out of control using fire wagons that they purchased through fundraising and grants, sometimes arriving ahead of provincial firecrews and then working in tandem with them, Leverkus said. When a major wildfire tore through Fort Nelson in 2024, she said she and 40 of her team members stayed behind and were hired by the province to clear flammables and support fire suppression activities. Leverkus also organised a structural protection training course for locals to learn how to shield buildings from embers that can quickly spur fires that engulf entire towns. "We have mechanics, we have carpenters, we have real good problem solvers," Leverkus said. "We're all not afraid to stay." Cam Allen, a 70-year-old former helicopter pilot in Fort Nelson who has previously fought fires from the air, said he recently took Leverkus' course to learn about ground fire suppression techniques, and, more broadly, how to help if a blaze reaches his town. He mentioned John Carr,a California man who went viral last yearfor staying behind and warding off flames with a garden hose during the Palisades fire, ultimately saving his home even when others around it burned down. "It makes you wonder, if 100 people had stayed or 1,000 people had stayed behind and actually did what he did, how much more could have been saved?" Allen asked. But not all were as fortunate as Carr during the Los Angeles fires, which killed a total of 29 people – a few of whom had, too, defied evacuation orders in order to protect their homes, even as officials urged thousands in the area to leave. Leverkus' group is not officially recognised by BC's government, and what it is trying to achieve highlights simmering tensions in fire-prone regions between those who enforce evacuation orders and those who defy them. Last week, wildfire crews in BC were forced to rescue a man when his home in the Village of Clinton was surrounded by flames, after he had refused to evacuate. In a wildfire update on Tuesday, BC's minister responsible for emergency management reiterated that all those who are under evacuation orders should leave. "We may not be able to get back to you if an emergency happens," warned Minister Kelly Greene, adding that evacuation orders are made as "a last resort to keep people and communities safe". Paul Kovacs, a researcher at the University of Western Ontario and director of its Catastrophic Loss Reduction Institute, said that Canada has had a lower fatality rate from wildfires despite their frequency in part because of its evacuation approach. The stay and defend mindset, he said, "is aggressively opposed" by the academic community in Canada, as opposed to other fire-prone countries like Australia. "In the hierarchy of what is it that you do to manage a wildfire, preservation of life is first," Kovacs said. Rural and remote communities can and should play an outsized role in informing officials of how best to protect their town, he said, and can do a lot of work to fire proof homes and structures. But that work, he argued, should not be done "while the fire is burning." A spokesperson for BC's Ministry of Forests told the BBC that self-organised groups in rural areas can be hired temporarily by the province during an active wildfire, but only when there are no more available provincial firefighters in the area. The ministry added that BC Wildfire's full-time staff has increased by 56% in recent years to respond to the growing frequency of fires, in addition to seasonal staff. Leverkus said she has been exploring ways to have her programme recognised by BC officials so that those trained through it can also help without being penalised for staying behind. She added that safety precautions are engrained in her courses, including training on how to predict fire behaviour and mapping out at least two safe escape routes. Not all of those who are trained want to stay back, she said, but those that do receive orders from trained crew commanders, including on when it's time to leave. "If people want to stay and defend, they need to understand what that means for themselves, what that means for their family," Leverkus said. Her goal is for the programme to one day become a blueprint that can be adopted by rural and remote communities across Canada, creating teams that can be relied on across the country. As for Wigwas, he will be fighting his evacuation fine in court. "If the chief and council want to charge me for saving my house, and I end up with nowhere to live, I might as well be in jail," he said. headline: 11 Charged, Including Teenagers, After Torture of 17-Year-Old Left Bound in Australian Bushland
body of the article: A teenager was found in bushland outside Townsville, wrapped in plastic, zip-tied at the legs, and unable to move for what police believe was more than five hours before someone stumbled on him. He was 17. What started as one horrifying discovery has turned into a case with 11 people charged, ranging from a 13-year-old boy to a 40-year-old woman, and the details that have come out in court since are somehow both clearer and murkier than the first headlines suggested. Here's what's actually known so far, and why the number "11" is doing a lot of heavy lifting in a story that still has major gaps. Police say the boy was discovered off Cape Pallarenda Road, restrained so heavily he physically could not move. He was found around 6:35 a.m. on July 18 near Pallarenda, wrapped in what investigators described as a substantial amount of plastic. Officers believe he had been left there for over five hours before a member of the public found him. He was taken to Townsville University Hospital in stable condition, but the injuries described in court later painted a much darker picture. Prosecutors laid out a list that included a broken nose, a spinal fracture, a fractured tibia, friction burns, and lacerations. He needed several surgeries. Police allege the assault didn't happen where he was found either; it started at a house in Heatley before he was moved. Investigators have been clear that the people involved weren't strangers acting on impulse; they had connections to the teenager. Detective Senior Sergeant Dave Miles called the level of violence deeply concerning andnoted that torture, as a charge, isn'tsomething police in the areadeal with often. That word choice alone tells you how seriously this is being treated. Some of the accused reportedly knew the teenager well, while others allegedly did not, which is part of what makes untangling this case so complicated. Prosecutors told the court that people weresocializing at the Heatley residencewhen two relatives of the teenager made allegations concerning him. What those allegations actually were has not been made public. That single missing detail sits at the center of the case, because it's presented as the spark, but nobody outside the courtroom knows what it actually was. Prosecutors allege the boy was kicked and hit with a horse whip, and that more people joined in as things escalated. A bat and another metal object were also allegedly used against him. From there, he was allegedly wrapped in industrial plastic, had his legs bound with zip ties, and was placed in the trunk of a car before being driven to the bushland wherehe was eventually found. A vehicle tied to the caselater drew police attentionafter allegedly being driven erratically along The Strand and crashing. Items recovered from that vehicle reportedly helped move the investigation along, though police haven't said publicly what those items were. The operation investigatingall of this has an official name, Operation Yankee Shadowmark, and it's still active. Image Credit: sisnenkiy/123rf Having 11 defendants doesn't mean there are 11 identical stories, and police haven't laid out who did what. The charges rolled in over a matter of weeks. A 13-year-old boy was charged on July 24 with deprivation of liberty, grievous bodily harm, and torture. A 35-year-old woman was charged days after that, followed by a 14-year-old girl. By early August, the count had grown to 11 total, including five more adults aged 24, 30, 32, 36, and 40, plus three separate 15-year-old boys. Most face a similar set of charges: deprivation of liberty, assault while armed or in company,grievous bodily harm, and torture. One defense lawyer has already pushed back publicly, arguing the case against a juvenile client is circumstantial and that the teen was more of a bystander than an active participant. Adults in the case are moving through Townsville Magistrates Court, while the juveniles are being handled separately in Children's Court. Police prosecutor Harriet Hearn described the alleged offenses as among the most serious the court sees, even accounting for cases involving young people. A magistrate went even further, calling the allegations against one 15-year-old "outrageous." Strong language like that reflects how seriously the court is treating this. It doesn't decide anything about guilt, though, and every person named still has their own case to answer. That distinction matters more here than in most stories, because right now the public knows the group narrative far better than any individual one. Cases like this tend to get flattened into one big shocking headline: eleven people, one victim, a horrifying scene in the bush. What actually happens next is slower and far less dramatic than that first wave of coverage. It's going to come down to evidence, testimony, and courtrooms working out exactly what each of these eleven people is responsible for, which is a much harder story to tell than the one that made headlines in July. What stands out most to you about this case: the number of people involved, the ages of some of the accused, or the fact that the motive still hasn't been made public? 21-Year-Old U.S. Marine Daniel Montano Killed in Wilmington Stabbing as Suspect's Long Criminal History Comes Under Scrutiny 17 parenting lessons that may do more harm than good Body Found in Queens School Chimney After Foul Odor Leads Exterminator to Grim Discovery Both Parents Face Felony Charges After Durham Teen Allegedly Took Abortion Pills at 31 Weeks The post11 Charged, Including Teenagers, After Torture of 17-Year-Old Left Bound in Australian Bushlandappeared first onFODMAP Everyday.

headline: Polish hunters spot large puma-like cat north of Warsaw
body of the article: Hunters in Poland have spotted a large cat prowling in an area around the village of Osiek-Wólka, about 75 kilometres north of Warsaw, the Fakt tabloid reported on Monday. The animal, which was seen at night through binoculars, looked similar to a puma, according to the report, which cited the local crisis centre. Tracks were later found in the area. "It wasn't a little kitten but a large cat," the crisis centre spokesman said, noting that a puma could travel up to 35 kilometres a day, meaning it could since have vanished from the area. People in the region were urged to avoid forests and wooded areas and not to let children play outside unsupervised. They were also told not to approach the animal. Forestry officials are patrolling the area, and wildlife cameras have also been installed. Pumas are native to North and South America. So far, Polish authorities haven't received any reports that a puma has escaped from a local zoo or a licensed breeding facility.

headline: ‘They need each other’: What’s behind the new Syria-Russia accord?
body of the article: Syria and Russia have spent the past 18 months negotiating the fate of Moscow's military presence in Syria following the fall of the Bashar al-Assad regime in December 2024. On Sunday, at least part of that question seemed to be settled after the post-Assad government in Damascusannounced a memorandum of understandingregarding Moscow's Hmeimim airbase and Tartus naval base. Russia was a major Assad ally during Syria's near 14-year civil war which began with Arab Spring protests in 2011 and ended when the current President, Ahmed al-Sharaa, led a lightning strike on Damascus and toppled the regime. Assad fled to Russia where he and his family were granted asylum. Under the new accord, Syria will take control of civilian facilities at the Hmeimim airbase and the commercial section of Tartus port. The military facilities will be transformed into joint Russian-Syrian training and qualification centres, with the transition expected to be completed within three months. Moscow has yet to comment on the deal. It marks a significant shift from the role both bases once played in service of al-Assad during the civil war which killed hundreds of thousands of Syrians and displaced millions. However, analysts say it could represent something more pragmatic, with Damascus reclaiming greater sovereignty over strategically important facilities while Moscow preserves a foothold and avoids being pushed entirely out of a country in which it has invested heavily for decades. "The agreement between Russia and the Syrian government indicates that both countries need each other," Alexey Muraviev, senior research fellow in defence and strategic studies at Edith Cowan University in Western Australia, told Al Jazeera, adding that Damascus is likely "not interested in terminating its prolonged relationship with Russia". Moscow was a key Assad ally during Syria's civil war, helping to keep the former leader in power by providing vital military support. The Russian military intervention in 2015 helped to turn the tide of the war in favour of the al-Assad-led government. Hmeimim became the centre of Russian air operations, while Tartus provided Moscow with its principal naval foothold in the Mediterranean. However, Russia did not interfere during the major advance towards Damascus that led to al-Assad's overthrow in December 2024. Following Assad's ousting, Russian troops still in Syria gradually left the country except for those stationed at the two bases. The Syrian foreign ministry said in a statement that the new arrangements for the bases represent a "reorganising of the Russian presence" along Syria's coast. "This move marks the most significant development since negotiations began approximately a year and a half ago, paving the way for a new phase in Syrian-Russian relations," the statement read. According to political analyst Ruslan Trad, a non-resident fellow at the Atlantic Council, Damascus has already moved on from Russia's role in the war. "Syrian President Ahmed Al-Sharaa's government fought al-Assad's Russian-backed forces for years, yet within weeks of taking power, it began quiet negotiations to keep Moscow present rather than expel it," Trad told Al Jazeera. "This confirms the classic realist maxim that in politics there are no permanent enemies, only permanent interests." In the same vein in which al-Sharaa has gone in efforts to strike cordial relations with Western powers such as the US – which bestowed him with the status of Specially Designated Global Terrorist in May 2013 during the civil war – Trad said the post-al-Assad government has likely calculated that punishing Russia for its wartime role would cost more than it was worth. "Moscow controls Bashar al-Assad's asylum, holds Syrian debt and reconstruction contracts, supplies subsidised oil and grain and remains a veto-wielding Security Council power that shielded Sharaa's own past terrorism designation," he added. Aron Lund, a fellow at Century International, said there is "lots of military and civilian technology" in Syria that comes from Russia and the former Soviet Union. "There is an old legacy of military, administrative and technical cooperation between Damascus and Moscow. It would be very painful for Syria to break that relationship completely," he told Al Jazeera. "It's transactional pragmatism on both sides," he told Al Jazeera. "Al-Sharaa's government, chronically cash-strapped and needing wheat, energy and technical support, has visited Putin twice in Moscow since taking power." "The leaders of both Syria and Russia have proven themselves to be very flexible and pragmatic." Lund said. That is reflected in the fact that the two sides began meeting and negotiating even before the toppling of the al-Assad regime was complete, he added. "They began to meet only some weeks after Assad's ouster. In practice, they were meeting and negotiating just weeks after Russian jets bombed al-Sharaa's fighters. In fact, the first agreements were made even before Assad fell, during the offensive that toppled his regime," he said. To this end, Al-Sharaa's government, "chronically cash-strapped and needing wheat, energy and technical support", says Trad, has visited Putin twice in Moscow since taking power. The Syrian president has taken pains to publicly acknowledge Russia's role "in stabilising the situation, not only in Syria but also in the region". Putin has welcomed al-Sharaa and signalled support for Syria's territorial integrity. Moscow, Trad said, needed to preserve its "only Mediterranean military platform for projecting power into Africa and the eastern Mediterranean", while offering "debt relief, economic cooperation and UN cover on terrorism designations in exchange". "So yes, both sides still need each other, just on renegotiated terms that reflect Syria's new leverage as sovereign gatekeeper rather than as Moscow's client," he added. Since the fall of al-Assad, Western and regional actors have sought to use Syria's political transition to curb Russian influence, said Muraviev. "Clearly, there was an attempt by the US and, to some extent, perhaps, the Israelis to push the new Syrian regime to terminate Russia's presence in Syria," he said. "But … an agreement means that the Syrian government has retained an interest, and withstood the pressure from other parties, because they clearly see the dividends of maintaining the relationship with Russia." The prolonged negotiations between Damascus and Moscow were themselves telling, he said. "The fact that those negotiations were held for about a year and a half meant that both sides were interested in not seeing these negotiations collapse," he added. Nevertheless, Muraviev stressed that keeping Russia in the picture does not mean Syria will close off avenues to other powers: "The new government would be open to develop strategic links with the US, Turkey, even working with Israel," he said. "But they would probably want to keep a multi-vectoral engagement … and having Russia in the equation will help them to use it as perhaps even a bargaining chip in their power game with other major powers." Lund noted that negotiations have been "very discreet", perhaps because Russia and Syria appear to have been concerned that "talking too much about the bases" could trigger US and European demands for their closure. "Al-Assad's fall was a major blow to Russia, but that has already happened. This agreement is about the post-Assad future, and it could be positive or negative for Russia. We shall see whether the new arrangement will constrain Russia even more, or, to the contrary, whether this deal will formalise and reactivate Russia's military presence."

headline: Rishon Lezion deputy mayor released after five days in custody in sex offense probe
body of the article: The Rishon Lezion Magistrate's Court ordered the official to two days of house arrest, barred him from the municipality for 30 days, and prohibited him from contacting the complainant. A Rishon Lezion deputy mayor suspected of committingsexual offensesagainst a municipal employee was released on Monday after five days in police custody, as the investigation into the allegations continues. TheRishon LezionMagistrate's Court ordered the official to two days of house arrest, barred him from the municipality for 30 days, and prohibited him from contacting the complainant or others involved in the case. The deputy mayor was arrested last week following an investigation that had been conducted covertly for roughly two months. The investigation was opened following a complaint by a municipal employee. Investigators held a confrontation between the deputy mayor and the complainant on Sunday as part of theinvestigation. At the center of the case is a dispute over whether sexual contact between the two was consensual. The complainant has maintained that it was not, while the deputy mayor has denied committing a sexual offense and said any sexual contact was consensual. Closeup of arrested hands with handcuffs. (credit: SHUTTERSTOCK) His defense has also argued that the complaint was retaliatory and connected to disputes within the municipality. Police did not seek to keep thedeputy mayorin custody beyond the five-day remand period, and the investigation remains ongoing.

headline: How an All-Female Patrol Is Protecting One of Nigeria’s Last Rainforests
body of the article: The postHow an All-Female Patrol Is Protecting One of Nigeria's Last Rainforestsappeared first onA-Z Animals. Deep within southeastern Nigeria's Cross River State, the 39-square-mile (100-square-kilometer)Afi Mountain Wildlife Sanctuaryshelters one of the country's last surviving rainforests. This rich ecosystem provides a crucial haven for rare species, including Nigeria-Cameroon chimpanzees, gray-necked rockfowl, drills, and blue duikers. In fact, the broader Afi landscape protects roughly a third of the world's remaining critically endangeredCross River gorillas, while its surrounding grasslands host one of Africa's largest seasonal roosts for European barn swallows. Despite its global ecological importance, the sanctuary has suffered years of relentless pressure from illegal logging, river pollution, poaching, and agricultural expansion — threats made worse by weak government enforcement. Refusing to wait any longer for official action, a group of women from the village of Ulom took matters into their own hands in 2023. Led by 42-year-old Mary Ofre, they formed the Ulom Women's Conservation Collective. Today, this self-funded, female-led patrol actively combats environmental crime in the sanctuary, inspiring neighboring communities to step up and defend their shared environment. Despite receiving official protection in 2000, Afi Mountain has endured years of severe neglect and lax law enforcement. Illegal hunting and snares have decimated wildlife, while logging, agricultural expansion, and seasonal bushfires steadily erode critical habitats. In some cases, fishers dumped toxic chemicals directly into the Afi River. This poisoned aquatic life and contaminated drinking water for neighboring communities and wildlife alike. Afi Mountain Wildlife Sanctuary was established in 2000. © Dotun55, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons –Original/License Traditional, male-dominated leadership proved ineffective against the destruction. Local leaders routinely struggled to hold offenders accountable — particularly when the perpetrators were friends or family — and secret deals with outside logging companies further undermined conservation efforts. Watching their vital natural resources slip away, many of the local women realized they could no longer afford to stand by while the forest disappeared around them. The movement sparked unexpectedly during a burial ceremony in nearby Bamba, where local women gathered to tackle the toxic river poisoning and destructive fishing practices in their community. Those conversations quickly led to a larger realization: protecting the rivers was impossible without also protecting the surrounding forest. Driven by this realization,Mary Ofrefounded the Ulom Women's Conservation Collective. What started as an effort to restore the waterways quickly grew into a full-scale campaign against illegal logging, poaching, and habitat destruction. Afi Mountain Wildlife Sanctuary is located in Southern Nigeria's Cross River State in the Boki Local Government Area. ©Charles Emogor, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons –Original/License For the collective's members, the mission is deeply personal. Some joined after human-caused wildfires destroyed their farms. Others were driven by childhood memories of thriving forests they hope to preserve for future generations. Refusing to wait for outside intervention, the women stepped in to lead where traditional authorities had failed. The collective combines routine patrols with direct, nonviolent enforcement. Members gather twice a month to plan operations, conducting scheduled patrols and surprise off-hour inspections for chainsaws, gunfire, or smoke. When necessary, they collaborate with village elders, state forestry officers, local task forces, and conservation groups. At the heart of their mission is strict equality: every offender faces the same consequences, regardless of family ties or social status. Violators face steep fines, equipment confiscation, or even community exile. To curb river poisoning, the group imposed a 500,000-naira ($356) fine and actively rehabilitates waterways by building temporary dams and draining contaminated pools. Cross River gorillas are critically endangered and one of the rarest gorillas in the world. ©Kit Korzun/Shutterstock.com When formal channels fall short, the women leverage collective social pressure. Since 2023, they have disrupted secret logging deals between by setting up roadblocks to prevent timber from leaving the village. They also used a powerful cultural tactic — threatening nude protests against non-compliant leaders — which effectively forced officials to cancel the agreements and uphold conservation laws. Around the sanctuary, the collective's efforts are paying off with clear, visible results. River poisoning has dropped dramatically, and degraded forest patches are naturally regenerating. Signs of wildlife — from nesting sites and fresh tracks to the calls of endangered Nigeria-Cameroonchimpanzees— are also returning. This impact reaches far beyond the tree line. Through targeted community outreach, the women have persuaded families to stop consuming endangered bushmeat. They have also guided young people away from poaching and illegal logging. Traditional leaders who once turned a blind eye now openly praise the collective, recognizing the women as the sanctuary's most effective defenders. Nigeria-Cameroon chimpanzees are only found in a few fragmented forests. ©Martin Pelanek/Shutterstock.com What began in a single village is now reshaping conservation across the entire region. Over half of the 16 communities surrounding Afi Mountain Wildlife Sanctuary are formingtheir own women's conservation groups. Leaders from Ulom, Buanchor, and Katabang actively mentor neighboring villages by sharing patrolling tactics and organizing strategies — a model that has already helped new groups to halt illegal logging in their own areas. However, the movement continues to face steep challenges. Operating entirely without external funding, members frequently lack basic gear like boots, GPS devices, protective clothing, and reliable transport. Many also navigate domestic opposition from husbands or families, forcing some women to step back. Despite these heavy personal and financial tolls, the collective remains steadfast in its mission to protect the sanctuary for generations to come. The Ulom Women's Conservation Collective demonstrates that effective conservation doesn't need to start with governments or large international organizations. Through relentless patrols, consistent enforcement, community outreach, and nonviolent resistance, these women have reversed years of environmental destruction and restored their community's commitment to the land. Blue duikers are a tiny antelope species that weigh less than 20 pounds. ©Roger de la Harpe/Shutterstock.com As neighboring villages adopt their approach, the collective offers a powerful blueprint forcommunity-led conservationacross West Africa. Their success underscores a fundamental truth: when women are empowered to protect their homeland, forests can recover, wildlife can return, and entire communities can transform into stewards of their natural heritage. The postHow an All-Female Patrol Is Protecting One of Nigeria's Last Rainforestsappeared first onA-Z Animals.

headline: Former Thai MP allegedly kills official and confesses on YouTube
body of the article: A former Thai MP allegedly shot dead a local official near Bangkok, then dialled into a YouTube livestream to inform the host - a political pundit - of what he had done. Former Nonthaburi MP Chalong Reawraeng told the shocked host, Anchalee Paireerak, that he had shot Thongchai Yenprasert, a former police official, outside Thongchai's office on the northern outskirts of the capital. Thongchai, who was hit in the neck, died in hospital. His driver was shot in the arm and hand. Chalong was arrested but then allowed to hold a press conference at a police station where he attempted to explain what had happened while smoking a cigarette. Police say they granted the unusual request so that Chalong could apologise to the victim's family - but once behind the microphone he described his actions in detail for over six minutes. He told reporters that Thongchai was "angry" at him, but did not explain why. He also said he did not intend to shoot Thongchai, whom he described as a "good friend". Chalong said he told Thongchai that he wanted to talk to him. According to local media reports, the two were involved in a personal dispute. "He [Thongchai] then pushed me, saying 'I don't want to talk, I don't want to talk.'" Chalong said he then followed Thongchai towards his car. "When I pulled the gun out, I didn't intend to shoot him. But then [Thongchai's driver] pulled his gun out and pointed it at me, so I fired." Thongchai, a retired police colonel, was president of the Nonthaburi Provincial Administrative Organisation or PAO, a local government body. [Reuters] Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul said on Monday afternoon said the treatment of Chalong, who is a former member of his party, by police was shocking. "The wrongdoer didn't have to wear the handcuffs, had a press conference and acted like it was a normal situation... this is not right." "No matter who he is, he is now a murderer," Anutin said, adding that authorities will pursue "full legal action" against Chalong. The Nonthaburi provincial governor denied Chalong had received any privileges and said the former lawmaker was allowed to smoke while he addressed media because he was stressed and his hands were shaking. Earlier, Chalong had called political commentator Anchalee Paireerak, who was livestreaming on YouTube at the time, to confess to the incident. Anchalee was filmed picking up a call midway through her programme. "I'll call you back... Oh, something big [happened]? Go ahead, what's that?" she said. Viewers could not hear what the caller said next, but Anchalee was seen reacting in shock. "Did he die? Did he die? You shot him in the head? You need to wait there for the cops," she said on the video, which was seen by the BBC. "Don't go anywhere." Monday's shooting came three daysafter a 14-year-old boy shot dead eight people at his home and school, then killed himself, in Thailand's worst mass shooting since 2022. The two attacks are not related. The latest shooting will further spur debate about gun control in Thailand, which has the highest rate of gun ownership in South East Asia by a wide margin. After Friday's school shooting, Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul ordered tougher enforcement of gun laws and said police would set up checkpoints as part of a crackdown. Other measures would include tightening controls on the possession, carrying and use of firearms.

headline: IDF urges Gaza residents to exchange old banknotes, prevent Hamas's financial exploitation
body of the article: "Most of the old-issue banknotes have already been replaced with new ones some time ago. If any of you still possess those old banknotes, you face a serious financial risk," Waweya wrote. The IDF urged residents of theGaza Stripto protect themselves from financial exploitation by Hamas and to replace old-issue banknotes with current ones on Monday, warning that soon the old notes could lose all value. "Most of the old-issue banknotes have already been replaced with new ones some time ago. If any of you still possess those old banknotes, you face a serious financial risk. In the very near future, these banknotes will be worth nothing, and you will be left with nothing,"IDFArabic Spokesperson Lt.-Col. Ella Waweya wrote on X/Twitter. Hamas is trying to exploit the situation through offloading banknotes that will soon be worthless onto the Gazan people and even their own operatives, according to Waweya. Maj. Ella Waweya, the new Arabic language spokesperson, pictured on July 7, 2024. (credit: MARC ISRAEL SELLEM/THE JERUSALEM POST) "While some movement elements receive their salaries in old banknotes, the leaders hold onto the new ones. The leaders care only about themselves, leaving their field operatives and the residents of theStripto bear the losses alone," Waweya wrote. Gazan residents are recommended not to accept salaries or payment in old banknotes. "Do not allow the terroristHamasleadership to burden you with the consequences of its losses," Waweya wrote.

headline: At least 132 dead as earthquake rocks Colombia
body of the article: Credit: X/@VickyDavilaH More than 130 people have died after an earthquake struck the west ofColombia. The 7.4-magnitude quake rocked the Choco region for four minutes on Monday morning, and was felt as far away as Panama, Ecuador and Venezuela. It was the country's most powerful earthquake in a decade, prompting the government to declare a national emergency. Buildings in cities including Manizales, Pereira, Cali and Armenia collapsed. At least seven airports were damaged and flights were suspended. The tremor, which was followed by two 2.8- and 4.8-magnitude aftershocks, trapped residents under debris, leaving more injured and forcing people to evacuate their homes as far as Bogotá, the capital. Residents and search teams picked through the rubble of collapsed buildings despite concerns of aftershocks. The death toll stood at 132 as of 7pm Monday local time (1am Tuesday UK time) and at least 483 people were being treated for injuries, the Colombian Association of Capital Cities announced. Colombia's interior minister said more than 20 municipalities across the country had been hit. At least 86 buildings had collapsed and five cities were on red alert, the capital cities association said. Credit: Social Media Local officials confirmed that at least 60 people were killed in the region of Risaralda, where the hard-hit city of Pereira is located, and 27 people in the Valle del Cauca region, which contains Cali, Colombia's third-biggest city. Two people also died in the city of Manizales. At least three of those killed in Valle del Cauca were children, Dilian Francisca Toro, the state governor, said. "I am in the University Hospital and we are overwhelmed," said Ms Toro. "There are five patients we haven't been able to evacuate who are under the rubble." In Manizales, footage shared on social media showed a steeple collapsing on the city's Cathedral Basilica of Our Lady of Rosary. Alejandro Eder, the mayor of Cali, said at least 20 buildings had collapsed in the city of two million, with many trapped under the rubble. Power cuts were reported, and interruptions to water and gas supplies. The well-known Hotel La Luna collapsed along with a water park, bakery and supermarket. Mr Eder added that the city had requested disaster teams from the capital and Medellín to help with rescue efforts. Residents and rescue workers search the rubble of a collapsed building after an earthquake struck Cali - Santiago Saldarriaga/AP "I ask the public to remain calm. Check your buildings for any apparent structural damage. If you don't feel safe, if you see very large cracks, please leave the building," the mayor added on social media. Joan Osorio, who lives in Cundinamarca near Bogotá, told The Telegraph he was awoken by the shaking of his apartment. He said: "The evacuation alarms went off and with my family, we dressed and left the house to head to the estate's meeting point. There were lots of frightened and nervous people still in their pyjamas; some were barely wearing any clothes. "It felt like we were there for ages, watching the structures and trees move from one side to the other." Jorge Moncayo, a 64-year-old taxi driver in Cali, said he saw plumes of dust shoot up across the city from his home in the hills of the city as buildings collapsed. "My entire house shook," he said. "I've never lived through such a powerful earthquake." Colombian Red Cross workers were seen carrying a survivor on a stretcher from one collapsed building in Cali. Patients are evacuated from a hospital in Cali after the quake - Santiago Saldarriaga/AP "The building completely collapsed. It sounded like a bomb. It was horrible," Juan Carlos Osorio told Caracol Television as he helped remove debris from a collapsed structure in Cali. "All of us neighbours are working together, forming human chains. We need heavy equipment. There are many people trapped." In Pereira, videos published by local media showed pieces of the airport ceiling collapsing on travellers taking shelter and screaming, and people running through the rubble in a panic. Mauricio Salazar, mayor of Pereira, told a local radio station that at least 18 people had died and that many more were trapped under "a massive quantity of collapsed buildings". The quake's epicentre was 3 miles south of San José del Palmar, in Chocó, a sparsely populated province on Colombia's Pacific coast, according to the US Geological Survey. "Significant casualties and damage are likely and the disaster is potentially widespread," the agency warned. Nubia Carolina Córdoba, the governor of Chocó, said there had been injuries and significant damage in Quibdó, the provincial capital, and warned residents about aftershocks. Jaime Velasquez, the secretary of the government of Novita in Chocó, said it had been the strongest earthquake in modern Colombian history and that the health centre had collapsed. Small earthquakes, known as "temblores", are common in central and western Colombia, but those above 6.0 magnitude are rare. In 1999, a 6.2 magnitude quake near the city of Armenia killed more than 1,100 people. Residents and rescue workers search through the rubble of a collapsed building in Cali - Santiago Saldarriaga/AP Abelardo de la Espriella, who was inaugurated as the president of Colombia last week, said he would personally supervise recovery efforts and install an emergency centre in San Jose del Palmar. He added that he would travel to Pereira, which appeared to be the hardest-hit city, to support survivors. "You are not alone. The state is present and taking action," he said. Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, said the Trump administration was "closely monitoring" the earthquake and stood "ready to support the people of Colombia" and Mr de la Espriella. The US state department then pledged $15.5 million to help provide shelter, food and protection for earthquake victims. A man leaves an apartment building after an earthquake struck Cali - Santiago Saldarriaga/AP Bernie Moreno, a US Republican ally of Mr de la Espriella, praised his response. "Excellent leadership...The US is ready to help our great ally," he said on social media. Carlos Fernando Galan, the mayor of Bogota, sent 100 rescue workers to affected areas as no severe damage had been reported in his city. The quake came two months after a pair of 7.2 and 7.5 magnitudeearthquakes devastated parts of neighbouring Venezuela. The quakes in June left more than 5,000 dead, with thousands trapped under rubble for days, and hundreds of buildings and homes destroyed. Try full access to The Telegraph free today. headline: Nestlé, Danone under scrutiny in Austria over infant-formula recall
body of the article: Nestlé and Danone are facing investigations by Austrian prosecutors over the infant-formula recall tied to cereulide contamination. The Vienna Public Prosecutor has opened a probe into Nestlé, while the Innsbruck Public Prosecutor is investigating Danone, according to the Foodwatch advocacy group. In a statement sent toJust Food, a Nestlé spokesperson said the company is treating the issue "very seriously". "Ensuring the safety and quality of our products is our highest priority. We continue to cooperate fully with the competent authorities. Based on the information available to date, no causal link has been established between the infant formula and the reported symptoms." The spokesperson added: "As investigations and legal proceedings are ongoing, we do not comment further on the details of the case." Meanwhile, Danone toldJust Foodit could not comment on ongoing legal proceedings but did supply a statement via a spokesperson. "Food safety is our highest priority, and we never compromise on this when it comes to our products," the company said. "We have further strengthened our ingredient and production controls and follow all guidance set by relevant food safety authorities. This includes the new guidance that was introduced in relation to cereulide levels earlier this year." The Austrian probe follows a criminal complaint filed by Foodwatch against the Swiss food giant Nestlé and France's Danone in March. In Dornbirn, a family has brought a lawsuit against Nestlé after their toddler allegedly developed symptoms of vomiting, breathing problems and weight loss late last year in connection with the recalled formula. According to Foodwatch, many parents have reported the same symptoms in recent months after using potentially contaminated milk powder. The civil case seeks damages from the manufacturer under the Product Liability Act, including compensation for pain and suffering and care costs, Foodwatch said. Nestlé and Danone have been central to a broader recall of baby powders contaminated with cereulide, a toxin associated with Bacillus cereus that can trigger vomiting, abdominal cramps and diarrhoea. Cross-border reporting byRadio France, RTSandRTBFhas raised further questions over how the recall was handled. Those investigations said Nestlé was slow to alert European authorities about the affected products. They also reported that products were withdrawn quietly in Austria and Germany. The European Commission has said a "silent recall" is not provided for under EU legislation. The formula recallwent global in Januarywhen Danone, Lactalis and some smaller producers joined the product withdrawals. That month, French prosecutors launched investigations into the deaths of two children reported to have consumed formula recalled by Nestlé. However, in March, prosecutors in Bordeaux said that the death of one babywas not connectedto recalled infant formula made by Nestlé. In February, more than 20 families in Francesued the governmentover alleged failures in the recall investigation. The same month, the EUtightened checkson arachidonic acid oil imports from China, the ingredient source connected to the cereulide contamination scare. "Nestlé, Danone under scrutiny in Austria over infant-formula recall" was originally created and published byJust Food, a GlobalData owned brand.

headline: German ministry rejects criticism of 'outdated' defence strategy
body of the article: The German Defence Ministry on Monday dismissed criticism of its strategic focus on procuring more tanks and ships instead of investing in drones, artificial intelligence and robotics. Moritz Schularick, president of the Kiel Institute for the World Economy (IfW), has warned that instead of investing a €700 billion ($809 billion) fund earmarked for the German military in modern weapons systems, Defence Minister Boris Pistorius is spending a large share of the money on outdated technologies. The largely debt-financed programme, which if properly deployed could also stimulate economic growth, therefore risked largely fizzling out, he said in comments published by the Süddeutsche Zeitung newspaper on Sunday. "We have a lot of capital, a lot of industrial know-how and in some areas still highly advanced technologies," the IfW chief said, pointing to Germany's strengths. "What we do not have is hundreds of thousands of people who want to climb into tanks and drive to the front. That means: instead of more soldiers, more manned vehicles and more barracks, we must - wherever possible - rely on AI, robotics, drones and satellite technology." In response, the Defence Ministry said the debate was noted but missed the point. The Bundeswehr must be ready to defend against a possible attack by 2029, a spokesman said on Monday, adding that it was clear the latest innovations could not all be in place by then and can only be a second step.

headline: Smart Glasses Are Being Used to Secretly Film Women, and It's Worse Than You Think
body of the article: Smart glasses that look just like ordinary eyewear are being used to secretly film women in everyday places, according to a new study from the University of Sydney. Researchers say most people being filmed have no way of knowing it's happening. Researchers are calling this pattern "ambient capture," according to the study. That's when someone uses smart glasses to secretly film people in places like gyms, workplaces, retail settings and campuses, then shares the footage online, the research team said. Some men do this within pickup artist communities, according to research. They compete to get a stranger's phone number or Instagram handle on camera, then share it online for engagement and social proof, the study found. The research draws on analysis of 350 publicly available Instagram videos posted between 2023 and 2026, according to theGoverning Immersive Tech teamat the University of Sydney. The study found growing use of discreet, point-of-view recording that's difficult for bystanders to detect. Within a subset of these covert point-of-view videos, researchers classified around 60% of interactions as potential harassment, according to the findings. Manywomenshowed discomfort or tried to refuse, the study found, yet filming and interaction often continued anyway. Getting a phone number is easy to block. A handle isn't, according to Dr. Milica Stilinovic, a postdoctoral researcher on the project. Photo credit: Depositphotos. Dr. Stilinovic said pickup artists are often told to ask for a handle instead of a number because it seems less pushy, a tactic she attributed to manosphere figure Andrew Tate. Unlike a phone number, she said, a handle is global, and can lead strangers straight to someone's identity and location. "You've basically handed your GPS tracker to the world," Dr. Stilinovic said. According to the study, women in 43% of the videos analyzed faced further exposure to derogatory commentary online. Some were identified and doxxed, the researchers found. Dr. Stilinovic said this kind of filming happens in places many people consider private, including workplaces, apartment stairwells, streets, gyms and beaches. "You don't know if you're being filmed," she said. "That footage is then uploaded, exposing you to a wider web of harassment." According to the researchers, current laws and platform moderation systems aren't built to catch this kind of harm. Most systems are designed to flag visible violations, like explicit harassment, nudity or threats, the study noted. Chanel Contos, founder ofTeach Us Consent, said regulation hasn't kept pace with the technology. The research originates in Australia, where smart glasses are already available for under $100, according to the release. "At best, smart glasses normalise filming and sharing people without their consent, feeding algorithms designed to reward voyeuristic, rage-baiting content," Contos said. "At worst, they are used as a tool for the sexual exploitation of children, women and other vulnerable groups." According to the research team, they're calling for clearer consent standards, stronger platform accountability and new design requirements for wearable devices, so people know when recording is taking place.

headline: Russia forced to give up control of key Middle East bases
body of the article: Russiahas lost a strategic foothold in the Middle East after being forced to give up control of two military outposts in Syria. Hmeimim air base and Tartus naval base, both of which are on the Mediterranean coast, will be taken over bySyriaand become joint Syrian-Russian training centres over the next three months, according to the Syrian foreign ministry. The civilian Latakia airport, which is part of the air base, will be integrated into the country's civilian infrastructure as part of an agreement that took 18 months to negotiate. Damascus has described the deal as leading to a "reorganising of the Russian presence" in Syria and "paving the way for a new phase" in relations between the two countries. Russia was a crucial ally of Bashar al-Assad, the ousted Syrian dictator, during the country's 14-year civil war, which ended in December 2024 whenarmed rebels overthrew his regime. A Russian warship at the Tartus naval base on the Mediterranean coast of Syria - Alexander Zemlianichenko / AP Immediately after Assad's fall, Russia initiated a large-scalewithdrawal of its military forces, pulling back from the country, but not fully pulling out. Even a year after the collapse of the former government, The Telegraph saw Russian flags flying at these military outposts. With a new government in Damascus, Russia's continued ability to maintain a military presence – and the fate of its bases in Syria – hung in the balance. Just before Assad's fall, a 49-year lease had been agreed for the bases, followed by 25-year extensions. Russia was keen to keep its position along the Mediterranean, which bolstered itsstrategic interests in North Africa. But for the new Syria, it was important to minimise the Russian military presence. Still, Damascus was negotiating from a tough position. At the time, many Assad-era sanctions were still in place against Syria, forcing the latter to buy energy supplies from Russia. The new Syria was also reliant on Russia for expertise and equipment to sustain its military, as various contracts and supply chains centred around Russian involvement had been inherited from when Assad was still in power. Russia, too, had given asylum to Assad, whofled with his family to Moscow– via Hmeimim air base – as a Syrian rebel coalition closed in. Russia scaled back its military presence in Syria after the fall of Bashar al-Assad - Umit Bektas / Reuters Thus it remained important for Damascus to maintain a working relationship with Moscow, despite the new government, led byAhmed Al-Sharaa, the president,having spent years being pummelled by deadly Russian air strikes, made possible because of the latter's foothold on the Mediterranean. Mr Al-Sharaa has toed the line, maintaining diplomatic relations and visitingVladimir Putinin Moscow twice since becoming leader, with talks focused on the Russian military presence in Syria. Mr Al-Sharaa has previously called on Russia to "address past mistakes" and pay compensation for war damage. Russia has not yet commented on the agreement with Syria. headline: We Must Increase Numbers of Righteous Rescuing Jews
body of the article: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu lays a wreath marking Israel's national Holocaust Remembrance Day at Yad Vashem Holocaust museum, in Jerusalem, April 14, 2026. Israel came to a standstill on April 14, as tribute to the 6 million Jews murdered by the Nazis during World War II. (Oren Ben Hakoon/Pool/AFP via Getty Images) Throughout history there have been heroes who have stood and fought with and for Israel and the Jewish people. Traditionally, these people have been honored with the title "Righteous Gentile," or "Righteous Among the Nations." As hatred of Israel and Jews has risen, this writer calls these brave and outspoken heroes "Lovers of Israel." They stand strong. Not because they need Jewish approbation. Not because they enjoy being regaled for their bravery. Because they are men and women who hold fast to their convictions. Because they believe in the battle to combat injustice. Because they believe that one must fight for what is right, decent and moral. Throughout history, they have stood tall and proudly with Jews – especially in times of crisis. The term Righteous Among the Nations, while used throughout history in describing people, was made popular byYad VaShem, Israel's Holocaust Museum, located in Jerusalem. Yad VaShem, defined Righteous Gentiles as people who saved Jews during the Holocaust. There wasno profitfrom their deeds. People who not only committed to these acts of bravery knowing there would be no monetary compensation, knowing they were putting their own lives and the lives of their family at risk. Knowing they could never tell another living soul of the acts of selfless bravery. These acts of selflessness came to light onlyafterthe Holocaust, when those Jews whom they saved — often hidden in convents, factories, or barns, or attics — nominated them to Yad VaShem. Two famous examples include Oskar Schindler and Raoul Wallenberg. If awarded the honor, Yad VaShem would plant a tree with their name and country on it. Those trees still stand — and flourish. However, many who were nominated and awarded the honor never accepted it because in the decades since their heroism, they live in communities still hating Jews and these heroes were afraid of the backlash. During the Holocaust most everyone was simply a bystander trying to survive the German invasion in midst of world war. There were, of course, others who collaborated with the Nazis. And there were small groups of partisans, locals who fought against the Nazis. The very smallest group was those who tried to save Jews by hiding them to prevent them from being murdered. Through their brave actions, these Righteous Gentiles successfully saved thousands of Jews. The Talmud teaches that if you save a single life, it is as if you saved the world. So true. The exponential multiplication of that one person in 1942 could have, by 2026, saved nearly 1000 descendants. A miracle — an act of bravery. In fact, when a small ad appeared in a newspaper in Israel calling for a reunion of those living in Israel who had been saved by Oskar Schindler, thousands up thousands of saved relatives attended the event. The original expression used by the rabbis for today's Lovers of Israel, is people who observed the 7 Noachide laws. According to the rabbis, and clearly reiterated by Maimonides, is that these souls have a place in the world to come. MalkiTzedek, whose biblical story is found in Genesis 14, is considered a Righteous Gentile. So, too, is Cyrus the Great King of Persia from the sixth century BCE who permitted the Jews to return to Jerusalem and rebuild the Temple after it was destroyed by the Babylonians. Because of that, Cyrus is a popular traditional Jewish name just like Alexander, named after the Roman emperor who was also good to the Jews. In 2006, Evangelical Pastor John Hagee, leader of Cornerstone Church, a mega church in San Antonio, Texas, with over 25,000 members created Christians United For Israel (CUFI). In 2012 there were about 1 million CUFI members. Today there the over 10 million members are called Christian Zionists. CUFI is one of the most vocal and visible of the non-Jewish groups standing together with Israel and fighting Jew Hatred. Speaking out against the hatred, helping victims in Israel and in the Diaspora, building relationships, they effectively lobby political leaders, both local and national, to defend and protect Jews and Israel. They — like Sen. Sen. Henry Martin "Scoop" Jackson, of blessed memory, Sen. Lindsay Graham, R-S.C. - of blessed memory and Sen John Fetterman, D-Pa., may he be blessed with a long life — are heroes of our generation. These Lovers of Israel are not involved in order to engage in inter-religious dialogue. They are people who recognize the biblical statement from Genesis 12:3, where God tells Abraham, "I will bless those who bless you, and whoever curses you I will curse; and all peoples on earth will be blessed through you." Those who have read and remember Balaam's blessing from Numbers 24:9: "Blessed are those who bless you, and cursed are those who curse you." Whether called Righteous Among the Nations or Righteous Gentiles or Lovers of Israel, they are unsung heroes from then and now. Their bravery and their cause must be recognized and applauded. Our goal must be to increase their numbers and their deeds — not just for the love of Israel, but because it is the right thing to do. Remember Anne Frank was hidden by a Righteous Gentile. And then murdered after her secret hiding place was revealed by a hater of Jews. Micah D. Halpern is a columnist, social, political and foreign affairs commentator. headline: TikTok Livestream Shooting: César Gastélum Killed in Mexico

The Mexican influencer was shot and killed on Tuesday, August 4, while broadcasting live outside a fast-food restaurant in Culiacán, becoming the latest content creator whose death has unfolded in front of an online audience—and adding to a growing list of social media personalities killed as cartel violence continues to grip the region. According toThe New York Post, Gastélum, who amassed nearly 600,000 followers on TikTok with comedy and lifestyle videos, was livestreaming with friends when two helmeted people rode up on a motorcycle, local authorities said.
