headline: Colombia declares emergency after magnitude 7.4 earthquake kills 132
body of the article: At least 132 people have been killed and hundreds remain missing after a magnitude 7.4 earthquake struck Colombia, the most powerful to hit the country this century, according to the Colombian Geological Service. The earthquake on Monday ravaged cities across western Colombia, including Cali, Pereira, Quibdo and Manizales, and was felt in neighbouring Ecuador and Panama. The epicentre was in San Jose Del Palmar in the Choco region, about 400km (250 miles) west of the capital, Bogota, the US Geological Survey said. The quake struck at a depth of 107km (66 miles). At least 21 aftershocks followed within hours. In Cali, the country's third-largest city, search teams and civilians picked through the remains of destroyed buildings, passing large pieces of concrete and other rubble down a long line of volunteers. Local officials said at least 20 buildings crumbled, while 380 were damaged, trapping many people. Jorge Moncayo, a 64-year-old taxi driver in Cali, told The Associated Press news agency that he saw plumes of dust shoot up across the city as buildings collapsed. "My entire house shook. I've never lived through such a powerful earthquake," he said. "We're thanking God we're alive." Juan Carlos Osorio told Caracol Television that the collapse of one building "sounded like a bomb", as he helped remove debris from a collapsed structure in Cali. "All of us neighbours are working together, forming human chains. We ⁠need heavy equipment. There are many people trapped." The earthquake struck just days after Abelardo de la Espriella wassworn in as president, thrusting the new administration into its first major crisis, with memories still fresh of devastating twin earthquakes inneighbouring Venezuelain June. "The national government has all of its capabilities deployed to protect lives, ⁠assist affected communities and deliver aid wherever it is needed," he said in a national address at about 1pm local time (18:00 GMT), upon declaring a national state of emergency. "The first priority is rescuing the people trapped under the rubble." De la Espriella said preliminary reports indicated 111 dead and 87 injured, along with dozens of collapsed buildings and damaged homes. The Colombian Association of Capital Cities, a think tank, said at least 132 people were killed and 570 others injured. Local authorities said at least 40 people died in the Risaralda region, part of Colombia's coffee-growing area. Pereira, the region's capital, suffered extensive damage, with rescue workers continuing to search collapsed buildings for survivors. At least 27 people died in the Valle del Cauca region, where Cali is located, including three children. Reports from Choco, near the epicentre, were slowed by communications outages, with some areas still lacking mobile phone service hours after the earthquake. Governor Nubia Carolina Cordoba said 12 people had been killed and 84 injured in the largely rural area. Luis Gregorio Moreno, a community leader in the region's capital, Quibdo, told the AFP news agency that many people were missing. "We are all devastated," he said. "At this moment, there are reported deaths, dozens of wounded, but what there are most of are missing people." By Monday afternoon, people had begun reporting their loved ones missing on digital databases, one of which had more than 1,400 people, mostly in Cali and Pereira, with the number steadily climbing. In Pereira, photos and videos on local media showed pieces of the airport's ceiling falling on travellers, who were taking shelter and screaming. The footage also showed a four-storey building crumbling. Pereira's mayor, Mauricio Salazar, told a local radio station there were at least 15 collapsed buildings where people were feared trapped. In nearby Manizales, footage showed one of the side towers of the city's landmark neo-Gothic cathedral collapsing and scattering debris onto nearby streets. The civil aviation authority suspended operations at several ⁠airports in Colombia's west, including Pereira, Manizales, Quibdo, Armenia, Cartago and Buenaventura, while engineers carried out structural inspections. Low-intensity earthquakes, or tremors, are common in Colombia, which sits along the seismically active Pacific Ring of Fire, but those above magnitude 6 are rare. In 1999, a magnitude 6.2 earthquake near the city of Armenia killed more than 1,100 people. The Colombian Geological Service said Monday's earthquake was the country's strongest recorded "in the 21st century". Northwestern University seismologist Suzan van der Lee said the earthquake's magnitude, inland location and strike-slip motion may have amplified damage in populated valleys despite its considerable ‌depth. "This one was far below the crust, and in theory, it shouldn't cause as much shaking. At this magnitude, it did actually cause a lot of shaking," she told the Reuters news agency. On Monday night, the US Department of State announced it would provide $15.5m for emergency shelter, food and other earthquake response aid. Washington is "closely monitoring the large earthquake that struck Colombia and stands ready to support the people of Colombia", Secretary of State Marco Rubio wrote on X. Governments across Latin America also lined up to help. El Salvador's president, Nayib Bukele, and Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum – whose countries were among the largest providers of aid to Venezuela following its recent crisis – offered help to Colombia. "From El Salvador, we are in communication and ready to provide immediate support with our rescue teams, medical personnel, paramedics, supplies, or any other assistance that our Colombian brothers and sisters deem necessary," Bukele said. President Jose Antonio Kast said Chile, one of the region's most earthquake-prone countries, "knows the pain and the challenge left by earthquakes" and pledged help. Israel, Ecuador and France also offered assistance.

headline: Record 230 people cross Channel in one small boat
body of the article: A small boat has crossed the English Channel carrying 230 people, the largest number to make the journey in a single vessel. It breaks the previous record set in July,when 165 people made the crossing on a single vessel. The boat arrived in the UK in the early hours of Monday. A picture taken off the coast of northern France showed the inflatable boat was so full many passengers had to dangle their legs in the water as it entered the busy shipping route. A Home Office spokesperson said this latest incident demonstrated the "reckless and dangerous tactics employed by criminal gangs... who continue to put lives at risk by cramming ever greater numbers of people onto unseaworthy vessels". French rescuers said the 15m (49ft) boat was "buckling" in the water and could have led to a "tragedy". The boat was already carrying about 50 people when it was seen heading towards a beach to pick more passengers up, the crew in Berck-sur-Mer added. French maritime officials said 30 migrants were left stranded by the tide during a boarding attempt at Berck beach in northern France. They were brought to safety by maritime and land-based rescue services, the statement from France's Channel and North Sea Maritime Prefecture said. The boat carrying 232 people continued its journey, before two passengers requested assistance and were taken to Calais by a French Navy rescue ship, the statement added. The 230 people on one boat breaks the previous record from July when 165 people made the crossing on a single vessel [SNSM] There are signs smugglers have been putting increasing numbers of people into each boat. In 2018, there was an average of seven people per boat - but last year, that had risen to 62. Last Tuesday,173 migrants had to be rescued from a single boat,which caught fire. Some 258 migrants arrived in the UK in four boats on Saturday, according to Home Office figures, with 423 arriving in five boats on Sunday. However, the number of crossings overall is on course to be lower this year. The provisional total for the number who have made the crossing so far in 2026 is 15,242, which is down by 43%, while the number of boats that have successfully crossed is down by 49%. Last month, the Home Office recorded the lowest number of crossings in July since 2020. Officials think this is partly because they have managed to disrupt the supply of small boats and engines to the people smugglers, with 1,100 seized since Labour came to power. Officials claim that with the sophisticated surveillance and reconnaissance operation now operating over the Channel, "unintercepted" beach landings have ended. All boats that make it across the halfway point in the Channel are met at sea by Border Force, which then brings the migrants safely ashore for processing. There is still clear demand for the crossings as the number of people waiting in camps in northern France has not reduced. At the same time, weather conditions have not been significantly different this year. Officials believe this shows their work to disrupt the smuggling gangs is beginning to show results. Despite this, concerns persist about the numbers still able to make it to the UK. Click here to see the BBC interactive Ten people have been sentenced for endangering lives at sea since anew law designed to target people who pilot small boatscame into force in January. A spokesperson for the prime minister said: "We've seen today some appalling images... of young babies being put into these unseaworthy craft... shocking images, and they show the reality behind the ruthless smuggling gangs that are prepared to risk human lives for profit..." "As the prime minister has said, we're not complacent and we are bearing down on these crossings, and that's reflected in the joint action that's prevented 47,000 attempted crossings since the election." The inflatable float used during the crossing was pictured deflated on the quayside in Dover [PA Media] The English Channel is one of the most dangerous, and busiest, shipping lanes in the world. Many migrants come from some of the poorest and most chaotic parts of the world, and ask to claim asylum once they are picked up by the UK authorities. On a recent visit to Dover, the prime minister pledged his government would be "relentless" in curbing the number of small boat arrivals. Andy Burnham said enforcement officers tackling people-smuggling gangs had been doubled on both sides of the Channel, but "a system that offers safe routes for people" needed to be built as well. In April,the UK and France struck a £662m (773m euro) dealaiming to address the issue. The three-year agreement included plans to send riot-trained police to French beaches to tackle violence and "hostile crowds", as well as France deploying millions of pounds worth of drones and two helicopters as part of a system to intercept people smugglers and illegal migrants. On X, Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said: "At 2.30am this morning a boat carrying 230 people was taken into Dover. "This is a record number in a single vessel. "It's yet more proof that this illegal invasion is a national security emergency." Earlier on Monday, a Home Office spokesperson said: "We are making progress, with the number of small boat crossings down this year and the lowest number recorded for the month of July since 2020. "But we must go further, which is why we have signed a payment-by-results deal with the French to put 40% more boots on the ground on French beaches." headline: Buildings collapse following powerful earthquake in Colombia Monday morning
body of the article: At least 79 people have died and buildings have collapsed after a powerful earthquake rocked western Colombia on Monday morning, sending people rushing into the streets as aftershocks rattled the region. The magnitude 7.4 earthquake struck at 7:34 a.m. local time, with the epicenter located about 250 miles (400 km) west of the capital city ofBogota, according to theUSGS. Shaking was felt as far away as Ecuador, Venezuela and Panama, with the quake being followed up by a magnitude 5.0 aftershock. Some of the most significant damage was reported in western and central Colombia where multiple buildings collapsed and emergency crews searched through piles of debris for survivors. By late Monday night, at least 11 fatalities had been reported, according toThe Associated Press. The full scope of the damage remained unclear as rescue crews continued searching damaged buildings and officials assessed hard-hit communities. Monday's tremor was the 10th earthquake this year worldwide to register at least a magnitude 7.0 on the Richter scale. It was also the strongest earthquake to strike Colombia since a magnitude 8.0 earthquake was recorded on July 31, 1970. A magnitude 7.4 earthquake struck near San José del Palmar, Colombia, on Aug. 10, 2026, around 7:30 a.m. local time. Photos from across the region showed crowds gathered in the streets, many waiting nervously for updates and bracing for additional aftershocks. In some areas, rubble spilled onto roads from damaged buildings and storefronts. The weather through Wednesday could impact search and rescue efforts across the region. "The weather in Colombia for until midweek will feature chances for showers and a few thunderstorms, which does include Bogota," AccuWeather Meteorologist Peyton Simmers said. "The shower chances will decrease Wednesday, Thursday and Friday." Simmers added that temperatures in the lower terrain of western Colombia will be 85-96F (29-36C), while in Bogota, high temperatures are expected to stay between 67-69F (19-21C). The tremor came 47 days after apair of catastrophic earthquakesstruck Venezuela on June 24, which resulted in over 5,000 fatalities. This is a developing news story. headline: Injured Hiker Was Stranded on Cliff Face with First Responders Overnight Before Dramatic Mountain Rescue
body of the article: A hiker was stranded on a cliff face for hours after he became injured while climbing a mountain in eastern Australia on Aug. 8 Rescue teams scaled a vertical wall to reach him and had to stay overnight until a helicopter could reach them The next morning, the man in his 20s was transported to a hospital in stable condition An injured hiker was saved from near the top of an a 1,824-foot mountain in eastern Australia after he and rescuers had to spend the night on a cliff face. "[We were] tied in to the rope, three of us on the side of the mountain," Ben Walker, a firefighter with the Queensland Fire Department, told9 Newsof the daring rescue from Mount Beerwah in Queensland's Glass House Mountains over the weekend. On the afternoon of Saturday, Aug. 8, around 4:30 p.m., a man in his 20s fell about 65 feet down the mountain face and injured his ankle, 9 News, theBrisbane Timesand radio station91.1 Hot FMreported. Following the accident, the hiker was unable to descend the mountain located in the Sunshine Coast hinterland and called for help. "This young fella by all accounts was prepared. He had water and phone charge, he had warm clothes with him," firefighter Matt Ginns told 9 News. In response, rescue crew members "battled dangerous and cold conditions" to rescue the young man, the Queensland Fire Department said in astatement. (The agency did not immediately respond to PEOPLE's request for additional comment.) Using drones, the fire department located the hiker about 330 feet from the top of the mountain. First responders then climbed down the vertical rock face to reach him and provide water, food and first aid, the agency said. Walker told 9 News that they didn't find the stranded hiker until about 2 a.m. local time. By then, it was too dark for a helicopter to reach them safely, so they stayed with the injured man overnight, according to the outlets. Mount Beerwah in the Glass House Mountains National Park in Queensland, Australia.Credit: Getty Never miss a story — sign up forPEOPLE's free daily newsletterto stay up-to-date on the best of what PEOPLE has to offer, from celebrity news to compelling human interest stories. By the next morning, around 9:30 a.m., the rescue team transferred the hiker to a helicopter, and he was transported to an area hospital in stable condition, according to the reports. The experience was a new one for Walker. "That's the first time I've had to bunker down for the night," he told 9 News. Read the original article onPeople

headline: Germany to invest further €10 million in concentration camp memorials
body of the article: Memorial sites dedicated to the victims of the Nazi era and the East German dictatorship are to receive €10 million ($11.5 million) in additional funding next year, Germany's minister of state for culture, Wolfram Weimer, announced on Monday. Half of the money is to go towards project funding, while the other half is intended to strengthen memorials already supported by the government, covering higher personnel costs and increased security spending. According to Weimer, the beneficiaries will include the Buchenwald and Dachau concentration camp memorials, the Topography of Terror museum in Berlin and the Saxon Memorials Foundation. The announcement is subject to the draft budget for Weimer's portfolio passing through parliamentary budget negotiations unchanged. "Especially at a time when disinformation and the distortion of history are on the rise and the voices of contemporary witnesses are falling silent, our culture of remembrance needs strong places of memory," Weimer said. He added: "Those who deny historical facts or attack places of remembrance are relativizing our history and defaming the victims of violence and oppression. That is why we are strengthening the memorials not only in their educational and outreach work, but also supporting them in effectively protecting their staff, their visitors and the historical sites themselves."

headline: Japan’s Future Emperor Gives His First Official Speech at Age 19
body of the article: For the first time in his 19 years,Prince Hisahito of Japanhas carried out official duties entirely on his own. He delivered his first official public address at the 19th Nippon Scout Jamboree, the country's largest national camping and scouting event held every four years, in the prefecture of Hiroshima on Friday. Speaking to an audience of approximately 8,000 scouts and attendees from Japan and abroad, he opened with a solemn note, expressing condolences for victims ofthe Kumamoto earthquake on July 28before turning to the spirit of the gathering itself. "I believe this will be an opportunity to work together, take on challenges, deepen our understanding of various issues including disaster prevention, and move forward strongly towards a better future," hesaid in his speech. "I myself hope to learn many things by participating in your activities." That same day, Prince Hisahito laid flowers at the cenotaph for atomic bomb victims at Hiroshima Peace Memorial Park, one day after the 81st anniversary of the United States' atomic bombing of the city on August 6, 1945, one of the deadliest single attacks in human history. PerThe Japan Times, he also visited Honkawa Elementary School Peace Museum, where part of a school building destroyed by the bombing has been preserved. Prince Hisahito is the son of Crown Prince Akishino and Crown Princess Kiko, and the nephew ofEmperor Naruhito. He is currentlysecond in line to the Chrysanthemum Throne, behind his father, making him the most likely future emperor of Japan despite not being the current Emperor's son. He holds this position because Japan's Imperial House Law bars women from succeeding to the throne, meaningPrincess Aiko, the Emperor's only child, cannot succeed her father. The prince at the traditional coming-of-age ceremony in September 2025.Anadolu - Getty Images Japan'sparliament passed revisionsto the Imperial House Law in July to address a growing succession crisis, though the ban on female emperors remained in place. The new law,which takes effect on October 24, allows male descendants from former imperial family branches to be adopted into the royal family, potentially expanding the pool of future successors. However, under the revised rules, Prince Hisahito still remains the most direct male heir currently within the Japanese royal family. headline: At least 13 killed in Ukrainian drone strike deep into Russia
body of the article: At least 13 people have been killed in a Ukrainian drone strike on the Russian republic of Tatarstan, local officials have said. They confirmed one child was among those killed, with 75 more people injured as drones hit Nizhnekamsk, more than 1,100 kilometres (680m) from the Ukrainian border. Ukraine's Armed Forces said the city's Tanevo oil refinery had been hit. It is one of the deadliest single attacks on Russia since the start of Moscow's full-scale war in Ukraine in 2022. Kyiv has recently stepped up its long-range strikes on facilities it says contribute revenue and logistics to Russia's war on Ukraine. The strike on Nizhnekamsk lasted several hours overnight and into the morning, according to local sources. Verified images on social media show large plumes of smoke and flames rising into the sky in daytime, with air raid sirens howling in the background. The Uzkbek consulate in Tatarstan said seven of those killed were citizens of Uzbekistan. According to Russian news agency RIA, most of the victims had been staying in a hostel at the time of the attack, and Russia's Investigative Committee said that "civilian individuals who were not involved in any military operations were present" where the drones struck. The BBC has not independently verified this information. Moscow said that "all those involved in the attacks" would "face inevitable and severe punishment". Oil refineries in Nizhnekamsk had already been hit once - on 12 June. "The facilities Ukraine targets are used to carry out attacks against Ukraine, manufacture weapons, support Russia's war effort," said Andriy Kovalenko, head of the Ukraine's Centre for Countering Disinformation. [BBC] The head of Tatarstan, Rustam Minnikhanov, confirmed the strike and shared his condolences with the families of the deceased, while Nizhnekamsk Mayor Radmir Belayev said the deaths had been a "a tremendous pain for all of us". Ukraine's Kovalenko said "every civilian death in Russia is on [President Vladimir] Putin" and that "Russians should direct their grievances at Putin and at the decisions made within their own country". "Without Putin, there would have been no aggression. Without the aggression, these people would still be alive," he added. More than 450 Ukrainian drones were shot down by the Russian air defences overnight across Russia, Moscow said. Elsewhere in Russia, fires broke out when an industrial facility in Siberia's Tyumen region was hit by several falling drones, according to local authorities. Kyiv has become increasingly successful at carrying out long-range strikes on Russia, often targeting warehouses or energy infrastructure, with civilian casualties mounting. Moscow, meanwhile, continues to target Ukraine with regular large-scale aerial attacks on cities and residential centres. Last week, a combined drone and missile strike on Kyiv killed 21 people. headline: Moldova recalls ambassador from Russia after drone explosion
body of the article: Moldova has recalled its ambassador from Russia for consultations following the explosion of a drone in the south of the country. The Foreign Ministry in Chișinău said it "condemned in the strongest possible terms" the incident near the village of Crocmaz. The incident constitutes a violation of Moldova's sovereignty and jeopardizes the safety of Moldovan citizens, the ministry said. On Sunday, a suspected Russian drone crashed and exploded near Crocmaz on the Moldovan-Ukrainian border. There were no reports of damage or casualties. President Maia Sandu condemned the violation of Moldovan airspace on X and called for an end to the Russian war on Ukraine. Russia has been at war with its neighbour Ukraine since February 2022. Russian drones and missiles repeatedly fly into Moldovan areas close to the border and also crash within the country, which is situated between Ukraine and Romania.

headline: Five bodies recovered in eastern Nepal after November avalanche
body of the article: The bodies of five mountaineers who went missing in an avalanche in eastern Nepal in November have been recovered, Nepalese authorities announced on Monday. They included two Nepalese mountain guides and three foreigners - a German, an Italian and a Canadian - the deputy police chief of Dolakha district Manoj Kumar Lama told dpa. Lama corrected an earlier official statement that said five foreign mountaineers had gone missing. The accident occurred on the 5,630-meter-high Yalung Ri in eastern Nepal, near the border with Tibet. The bodies were found below the summit on Thursday. The recovery operation had to be postponed because of poor weather. According to police, four bodies were taken to Kathmandu on Monday. The body of a Nepalese mountain guide remained at a clinic in Dolakha so that it could be handed over to his family there. The five were part of a group of 15 mountaineers who were caught in an avalanche last November while attempting to climb Yalung Ri. At the time, the bodies of two Nepalese mountain guides were recovered, while eight other members of the group were rescued.

headline: $580 million undersea power cable rerouted to spare Dobby the house-elf’s beachside ‘grave’
body of the article: A multimillion-dollar power link between the United Kingdom and Ireland has been diverted after distraught "Harry Potter" fans pointed out that its planned route would cut through a beachmemorialdedicated to a beloved character from the series,Dobby the house-elf. The £430 million (around $580 million) Greenlink interconnector links the UK's National Grid power transmission network to Ireland via a 125-mile cable between Ireland's County Wexford on the southeast coast and Freshwater West, a beach in Wales' southwest, where the death of Dobby was filmed for the Potter movie franchise. Dobby in action in the 2010 movie Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows: Part 1. - Warner Bros/Everett Collection Originally, the undersea cable — whose purpose is to share excess renewable energy, boost security and double the electricity transfer capacity between the two nations — would have disturbed the symbolic grave where Potter fans leave handwritten tributes to the magical creature on pebbles. But after a BBC News interview about the operation troubled fans, a torrent of concerned calls caused Simon Ludlam, CEO of project manager Etchea Energy, to rethink the cable's route, Ludlam revealed to the Energy Revolution podcast last week. "We got hundreds of calls; I mean, hundreds of calls," he said. Ludlam admitted that the uproar initially puzzled him. A colleague told him that "apparently, we're going to go straight through Dobby's grave." This meant little to Ludlam, who found himself saying, "Dobby, who's Dobby? I don't know Dobby?" Even after his colleague explained, Ludlam remained confused. He told the podcast: "I said, 'He's a fictitious character in a fictitious book, the whole thing is fictitious, what are you talking about?'" It was only when his colleague said, "No, it's very, very serious," that Ludlam grasped the situation. His team then got to work rerouting the cable to avoid Dobby's grave entirely. "A lot of people were very happy about that, and the project is now going (ahead) and Dobby's happy," Ludlam joked. Jack Nicholas is one of those relieved that Ludlam has taken the matter seriously. Local to Pembrokeshire, the Welsh county that is home to Dobby's memorial, Nicholas, 20, is on a mission to highlight all the area has to offer through videos posted online. "Dobby's Grave brings tourists from all around the world down to one of Pembrokeshire's most impressive beaches," Nicholas told CNN. "The memorial has rocks from places such as Italy, Australia and South Africa, showing how far people travel to see Dobby's Grave." "Tourism is one of the most important industries in Pembrokeshire, and all of the visitors will contribute to the local businesses," he added. Tourism in Pembrokeshire contributes an estimated £604 million (roughly $815 million) to the local economy, with more than 6 million visitors supporting 23% of all local employment, according to Pembrokeshire County Council. Sophie Pearce is a Welsh travel blogger who has visited Egypt, India and New Zealand on a quest to see magical, historic and bookish destinations. During the pandemic, however, she discovered she didn't have to travel very far at all to find a touch of whimsy. "Freshwater West is a magical, remote beach," Pearce told CNN. "There are all sorts of painted rocks with sweet messages left for Dobby. I've been back many times since my first visit, and it never fails to fill me with wonder," she added. unknown content item - "Dobby's Grave is a bittersweet place to visit for Potterheads as it's where he spent his last heroic moments among friends," Pearce, whose blog is called Third Eye Traveller, explained. "It would be a shame to destroy it," she added. But the reposition is not without issue, Ludlam said, as the cable now comes "quite close" to Bronze Age remains. CNN has reached out to Greenlink Ireland and Etchea Energy for comment. This isn't the first time Potterheads have protected Dobby's grave, which first appeared after the theatrical release of "Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows: Part 1" in November 2010, the instalment in which Dobby dies. In 2022, the National Trust, the conservation charity that owns the land,agreed it could remain in place following a consultation but warned fans against leaving souvenirs. Pilgrims to the site were in the habit of leaving a sock to honor the house-elf who, like all house-elves, was bound by magic to serve a wizarding family forever, or at least until a master presents them with an article of clothing, granting the elf freedom. Visitors were urged to refrain from leaving socks because the beach was environmentally sensitive. (The "Harry Potter" movie franchise is owned by Warner Bros., a unit of CNN's parent company, Warner Bros. Discovery.) Zoe Sottile contributed to this report. headline: Water outage forces Chessington theme park to close
body of the article: Chessington World of Adventures has closed for the day after a burst water main cut supplies to parts of south-west London. Thames Water said a burst on Leatherhead Road had affected customers in the KT9 area and that its specialist team was on site carrying out repairs. A Thames Water spokesperson said: "We're sorry to customers in the Chessington area who are currently without water, and to anyone whose plans to visit have been affected following today's outage." The company said most customers should have had their supply back to normal by 13:20 BST with temporary measures put in place while a permanent repair is completed. Thames Water has been working to fix the burst [pA] Some customers might notice low pressure for a short time as the flow returns to normal, it added. A spokesperson for the resort said: "We are currently experiencing operational disruption due to a burst water main that is affecting the local area. "As a result, the attraction is closed today while our teams work closely with Thames Water and local partners to restore normal operations as quickly and safely as possible." Guests with tickets for Monday 10 August will have them revalidated for a future date, the resort said. Those unable to return on another day have been told to contact its help centre for a refund. The closure falls in the middle of the school summer holidays, one of the busiest periods for UK theme parks. The resort, in the Royal Borough of Kingston upon Thames, is owned by Merlin Entertainments. Listen to the best of BBC Radio London onSoundsand follow BBC London onFacebook,XandInstagram. headline: Homicide Investigation Called Off After ‘Body’ Found Stuffed in Suitcase Is Revealed to Be ‘Life-Like Doll’
body of the article: Police in Australia launched a homicide investigation after two men found a suitcase with what appeared to be human remains inside Forensic examinations revealed the body was actually a "life-like doll" with "clothing, hair, and a nose piercing" Police also said the doll had "markings that resembled bruises and grazes" A homicide investigation in Australia has been called off after the 'body' involved turned out to be a "life-like doll" with its own "clothing, with hair and a nose piercing." On Sunday, Aug. 9, New South Wales Police (NSW) officers were called to the small town of Oallen, around 134 miles south of Sydney, at 12:50 p.m. local time, following reports that members of the public had found human remains stuffed inside a suitcase, per arelease. Officers from the Hume Police District found the bag on the side of the road, with what appeared to be the remains of a female inside, the release added. Initial investigations were undertaken by forensic officers at the scene before the bag was sent for forensic examination at a laboratory, the statement continued. Shortly after, the local authorities announced a homicide investigation, only to later backtrack perNews.com.auand theBBC. The body turned out to be a life like dollCredit: 7News Australia/Youtube "Following forensic examinations, this morning, police confirmed the item located in the bag was a life-like doll, wearing clothing, with hair and a nose piercing," said the NSW police release, published on Monday, Aug. 10. It added that the doll also had "markings that resembled bruises and grazes." Superintendent Linda Bradbury told reporters on Monday that the doll was "very realistic in the terms of looking like human remains," but said authorities had later confirmed they were not, News.com.au reported. "We don't necessarily like to disturb any crime scenes because that's our links to making sure that offenders are brought before the court," she said, per Australia outlet7 News. Bradbury said she had "no regrets" about the handling of the case, per the BBC. "The idea is to not disturb crime scenes as much as possible, to maintain the integrity of our investigation," she said. Want to keep up with the latest crime coverage? Sign up forPEOPLE's free True Crime newsletterfor breaking crime news, ongoing trial coverage and details of intriguing unsolved cases. The doll was found "stuffed inside a suitcase," which was placed behind a pine tree in an area with "limited to no CCTV," per Australian TV showToday. Bradbury said two men came across the suitcase when they stopped for a driving break over the weekend,Todayreported, per the BBC. "They were affected yesterday and we will be in touch to let them know that it was not human remains," she added. Police have now closed their investigation into the discovery of the doll. However, they are looking into how long it had been abandoned and exploring the possibility of the doll being linked to a nearby dumped car, per 7 News. Read the original article onPeople

headline: Spanish minister: 80,000 migrants temporarily entered Ceuta
body of the article: Spanish authorities on Monday updated the estimated number of irregular migrants who entered the Northern African exclave of Ceuta at the end of July to 80,000 from the previous 72,000. Territorial Policy Minister Ángel Víctor Torres gave the new figure during a visit to Ceuta. The unprecedented surge occurred mainly on July 30. Most of the migrants returned to Morocco within 24 to 48 hours, Torres said. Previous estimates had differed considerably. Ceuta's regional president, Juan Jesús Vivas, at times spoke of as many as 80,000 people, while Morocco put the number at around 40,000. Dozens of people died while trying to reach the exclave, mostly by swimming. The official death toll now stands at 83, up from 82. The influx sparked a debate about increased protection of the external borders of the European Union and controversy between Spain and other EU members. Around 5,000 residents took to the streets in Ceuta on Sunday evening to demand greater government support and stronger border protection, according to police estimates.

headline: Share of German population aged 15 to 24 at just 10%
body of the article: Just 10% of the German population was between 15 and 24 years old at the end of last year, with the figure even lower in the country's eastern states, the Federal Statistical Office reported on Monday. In the eastern state of Brandenburg, which surrounds the city-state of Berlin, young people aged 15 to 24 made up 8.8% of the population. This was followed by Mecklenburg-Vorpommern and Saxony-Anhalt, both at 9.1%. The highest proportions of young people are found in the city states of Bremen on 11.1% and Hamburg on 10.5%. The western states of Baden-Württemberg and Hesse are marginally above 10%, as is Berlin. In the early 1980s, young people accounted for the largest share of the population. The proportion of young people in Germany was slightly below the EU average of 10.7%, the statistical office said, citing figures from early 2025 and the EU statistical agency Eurostat. Without immigrants and their descendants, the share of young people in Germany's total population would be even lower.

headline: Europe wary as gas stocks languish at lows while winter looms
body of the article: Four years after Russia's invasion of Ukraine set off an energy crisis, European countries face new questions about natural gas security as the war in the Middle East drags on. Surging prices due to Iran's closure of the Straits of Hormuz are keeping liquefied natural gas (LNG) stocks unusually low, with winter just months away. That raises the spectre of both supply difficulties and prices remaining well above pre-crisis levels, just as colder Continental weather drives up demand. - Stockpiles slump - Besides its use in heating and producing electricity, gas also powers many factories across Europe. Summer is traditionally when energy firms take advantage of lower prices to fill LNG storage tanks, preparing for higher winter demand. In a typical year, storage sites would be filled to "around 75 to 80 percent", said Anne-Sophie Corbeau, a researcher at the Columbia University's Center on Global Energy Policy. Currently the level is just 58 percent -- the lowest since 2021 -- according to Gas Infrastructure Europe, an industry association cited by the resources consulting firm Kpler. - Why? - "The European Union ended last winter with underground gas storage at only 28 percent, significantly lower than in previous years," said Ronald Pinto, an analyst at Kpler First. European imports were curtailed by the US and Israeli strikes against Iran, which led Tehran to effectively close the Strait of Hormuz to Gulf tanker traffic. That halted gas shipments from Qatar, a key European supplier, driving up prices of contracts for future delivery, the main way of buying LNG on global markets. "Italy, Poland, and Belgium, contracted buyers of Qatari LNG, have borne the direct losses, as they have been unable to import any Qatari LNG volumes since April 2 -- the date on which Italy received its last vessel loaded with Qatari LNG," Pinto said. - Pricing pain - European buyers had hoped prices would ease by summer, allowing them to fill storage tanks later for less. The Dutch TTF contract -- the benchmark for European gas -- for September delivery is currently trading around 55-58 euros per megawatt-hour. The cost was just 30 euros before the Middle East war, and as low as 15-20 euros before the war in Ukraine. An EU Commission spokesperson expressed confidence that filling storage tanks to 80 percent of capacity "is sufficient to secure winter supply and it is technically achievable". Europe has significantly ramped up its import capacity since the war in Ukraine, which prompted it to slash its Russian gas supplies. Russia still supplies around 12 percent of the bloc's gas imports, according to the European Council, but by the end of 2027 it will ban them completely. "It is also worth noting that EU gas demand has decreased by 17 percent compared to pre-crisis levels" before 2022, the spokesperson added. - Austerity in store? - Analysts are not so sanguine. "Supply risks to Europe remain elevated amid reduced LNG availability from the Middle East," Rystad Energy analyst Antonia Syn said in a recent market update. Gas infrastructure routinely experiences breakdowns or technical disruptions that halt flows. And severe cold in the United States -- now Europe's biggest single supplier -- could divert its supplies to domestic buyers. Asian countries that usually buy from Gulf suppliers could also turn to US or other sources, driving up prices to painful levels for European buyers. So the longer Europe waits to fill up storage sites, the bigger the risks. "We believe this wait-and-see approach has kept TTF prices from reflecting a scenario of extreme gas scarcity during the winter period," said Pinto at Kpler First. He expects average monthly prices to remain at 55 to 62 euros per MW/h through the rest of the year. "For now we're seeing LNG go more to Asia than to us, because prices are even higher there," Corbeau said. "If stocks are down, if the winter is rough and some other problem happens, we'll have to start thinking about conservation measures," she warned, as was the case across Europe in 2022. nal/ved/js/gv

headline: Seven Uzbek citizens killed in drone attack on Russia's Tatarstan region, consulate says
body of the article: TASHKENT, Aug 10 (Reuters) - Seven Uzbek citizens were killed in ‌a drone attack in Russia's ‌Tatarstan region on Monday, the Uzbek consulate ​in Kazan said. The consulate did not immediately provide further details about the victims. Earlier local authorities said ‌that at ⁠least 13 people were killed, including a child, and ⁠39 injured in a Ukrainian drone attack on industrial and ​civilian targets ​in the ​city of Nizhnekamsk ‌in Tatarstan region. Between two and three million citizens of Uzbekistan, Central Asia's most populous country, work in Russia, with the Uzbek economy ‌partly based on ​remittances from migrants. Uzbekistan ​has struck ​a diplomatic balance on ‌the war in Ukraine, ​maintaining close ​ties with Russia while also stressing support for Ukraine's territorial ​integrity. (Reporting ‌by Muhammadsharif MamatkulovWriting by Maxim ​Rodionov and Felix Light; Editing ​by Toby Chopra)

headline: Pilgrim’s workers vote for further strike action at UK meat plant
body of the article: Further strike action over pay at Pilgrim's meat plant in the UK town of Enniskillen is planned for next week. The Unite union said in a statement on Sunday (9 August) that 130 workers at Pilgrim's Europe site in County Fermanagh, Northern Ireland, had voted to strike on the "picket line" on Friday. Industrial action at the facility first kicked off on 4 August, lasting for five days through Saturday 8 August. Unite said in its weekend statement that the "workforce is seeking a cost of living pay increase and an end to the current unequal payment of breaks". The union added it had "served notice" on Pilgrim's Europe, part of the Pilgrim's Pride business majority owned by Brazilian meat giant JBS, for a further two weeks of strikes from 17 August. Just Foodasked Pilgrim's Europe for an update on the negotiations today and to confirm how many staff are employed at the Enniskillen factory and what products are made there. The company did not clarify those points but did provide a statement. "We have made a pay offer above inflation and remain committed to constructive discussions with the union," a company spokesperson said. "Our priority is ensuring all employees feel safe and respected throughout this period while we continue to focus on serving our customers and supporting our people." Unite claimed Pilgrim's Europe had failed to offer an "inflation-proof pay increase that addresses unequal pay for breaks", explaining that workers on morning shifts were getting a 15-minute paid break, while staff on evening and nights shifts were entitled to 30 minutes. Its general secretary Sharon Graham said: "Pilgrims is a very successful company making huge after-tax profits. It can well afford to pay its workers properly but our members in Enniskillen are paid less than colleagues on sites elsewhere in the UK and little above the bare legal minimum." Unite claimed Pilgrim's Europe "declared after-tax profits" of £128.4m [$173.3m] in its 2024 financial year. The company operates 40 facilities across the UK, Ireland, France and the Netherlands, employing 17,000 workers, according to its website. It manufactures private-label meat products but also owns brands such as Moy Park, Richmond and Fridge Raiders. JBS holds an 80% interest in Greeley, Colorado-based Pilgrim's Pride through its US subsidiary JBS USA. In 2021, the Brazilian meat major approached the company to take full control butpulled back its offerthe following year. The Brazil firm acquired a controlling 64% stake in Pilgrim's Pride in 2009 for $800m after the US company filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy the previous year. It then went on to gradually increase its holding to 80.2%. United had not responded toJust Food'srequest for confirmation of what wage increases are now being sought and the current status of talks at the time of writing. In Sunday's statement, Unite's regional officer Greg O'Kane said: "Our members are determined to secure an improved pay deal offering real protection from the cost-of-living crisis and ending the current inequality around paid breaks. "They are set to escalate their strike to two weeks - management needs to return to the table with an offer meeting our members' pay expectations to resolve this dispute." "Pilgrim's workers vote for further strike action at UK meat plant" was originally created and published byJust Food, a GlobalData owned brand.

headline: Russia rolling out Starlink-style network faster than expected, Kyiv says
body of the article: KYIV, Aug 10 (Reuters) - Russia is rolling out its own version of the Starlink satellite internet system faster than expected and plans ‌to have nearly 300 satellites in orbit by 2027, according to ‌a Ukrainian intelligence official. SpaceX's Starlink network, which operates in Ukraine but not Russia, has given Kyiv ​a major advantage in drone operations and battlefield communications. Russian forces had been using grey-market Starlink terminals in Ukraine until Kyiv successfully lobbied SpaceX to disable them earlier this year, one of several factors that shifted battlefield momentum in Ukraine's ‌favour. In an interview with Ukrainian ⁠media outlet RBC-Ukraine, Major General Vadym Skibitskyi said Russia currently has 16 satellites in its Rassvet system. "They have already begun ⁠launching it much faster than originally planned," said Skibitskyi, who is the deputy head of Ukraine's GUR military intelligence service. The system can currently operate only intermittently ​when one ​of the satellites passes over Ukrainian territory, ​he said. However, Russia plans ‌to create a constellation of 292 satellites by 2027 and 924 by 2035, he added. "Once Russia deploys a full satellite constellation, the system will operate like Starlink. Discussions are already underway on how to counter it," he said. INCREASED MISSILE CAPACITY Russia has been pounding Ukraine with an array of supersonic missiles as ‌Kyiv has depleted its stock of interceptor ​missiles. Skibitskyi said Moscow had already met its annual ​production targets for Zircon and ​Oniks missiles in the first seven months of the year ‌and was exceeding its 2026 missile ​production goals by ​10% to 20%. He said Ukraine's emerging ballistic missile industry, along with drone production facilities, had become a priority target for Russia's missile campaign. Skibitskyi added ​that Russia's stockpile of ‌Iskander-M ballistic missiles, the mainstay of its supersonic strikes, was estimated ​at around 130, with 65 new ones made in July. (Reporting by ​Max Hunder. Editing by Mark Potter)

headline: Ukraine destroys air defences guarding Putin’s holiday home
body of the article: Ukrainian drones struck a missile launch pad used to guard one ofVladimir Putin's lavish residences from long-range attacks. The S-400 "Triumph" anti-aircraft missile launch pad, located around 12 miles from the Russian president's Italianate palace complex near Gelendzhik, southern Russia, is designed to repel aircraft,dronesand cruise missiles. It was left "ablaze and sputtering for three hours" after being targeted by Ukrainian drones, according to Major Robert Brovdi, the commander of Ukraine's unmanned systems forces. The air defence system is used alongside electronic warfare systems and mobile fire groups to defend the palace, which isencircled by a 27-square-mile "buffer zone", according to reports. Security officials maintain a permanent no-fly zone above the complex. Major Brovdi said that the launch pad had been repurposed to fire munitions at Ukrainian cities, including six missiles on Aug 8. Analysts said Moscow had turned to these systems to intensify its missile attacks on Ukraine because of a critical shortage of the Patriot interceptors that form its sole defence against ballistic barrages. "While less accurate and lethal, they still represent a threat to civilian infrastructure, particularly when launched at densely populated areas," wrote Fabian Hoffmann, a missile expert at the University of Oslo. S-400 'Triumph' anti-aircraft missile launchers on display at a military parade in Moscow - Sefa Karacan/Getty Images The residence near Gelendzhik, known as "Putin's Palace", may have set the Russian president back as much as £1bn, according to an investigation by the Anti-Corruption Foundation led byAlexei Navalny, the late opposition leader, in 2021. Navalny died in a Siberian prison in 2024. Journalists claimed that the luxurious complex housed a casino, vineyard, spa, ice rink, theatre, pole-dancing room, hookah lounge, "aquatic disco", miniature railway room and more. In 2023, it was reported that a chapel had been added. An attack in the same region last week led to Ukrainian drone fragments falling on a beach, killing seven bathers. Putin is believed to visit the Black Sea refuge only rarely,fearing Ukrainian long-range drone strikesand increasingly favouring his highly fortified luxury dacha on Lake Valdai, 185 miles east of Moscow. That residence, which is understood to be home to Alina Kabaeva, his covert long-term partner, and their two sons, is protected by at least 27 towers mounted with Pantsir anti-aircraft systems, costing some £16m per unit. Ukraine's military intelligence said on Monday that Kyiv's drones had also struck two Russian S-400 Triumf air defence launchers, as well as an antenna it uses to control medium-altitude Orion drones in occupiedCrimea. Losses from the strike could amount to the equivalent of tens of millions of dollars, Ukraine's directorate of intelligence said. An oil refinery in Tatarstan was targeted by Ukrainian long-range drones on Monday - Reuters Russia has struggled to defend itself against Ukraine's large-scale drone attacks, which have become a near-nightly occurrence. Overnight on Monday, more than 450 long-range drones sailed on to Russian soil, hitting an oil refinery in Tatarstan. The attack killed at least 13 people, making it one of the deadliest single attacks on Russian soil since the war began. Drone fragments also reportedly fell in Tyumen, Siberia. Kyiv hopes to use these attacks to increase pressure on the Kremlin to come to the negotiating table, but on Monday a Russian official dismissed Ukraine's demands to freeze the front line and implement a ceasefire. "No 'freeze' is possible without addressing the root causes of this crisis," said Mikhail Galuzin, the Russian deputy foreign minister. Try full access to The Telegraph free today. headline: No end in sight for German spy trial as ex-spymaster takes stand again
body of the article: More than two and a half years into the trial of a German intelligence official suspected of spying for Russia, no end is in sight to proceedings. Bruno Kahl, the former head of the Federal Intelligence Service (BND), appeared as a witness again on Monday on the 168th day of proceedings. Kahl, 64, is now serving as Germany's ambassador to the Vatican in Rome. He was first heard as a witness at Berlin's Higher Regional Court more than two years ago. At the time, the central question was what damage the alleged Russian espionage had caused. Kahl described it then as a "catastrophe." The latest questioning, held initially in open court, focused primarily on when the former intelligence chief learned of the suspicion that information may have been passed on, what steps were then taken to establish who was behind it, and how the BND employee came under suspicion. Few details emerged, however: As much of the information involved is classified, the hearing was open to the public only at the outset. The main defendant is the BND employee, who has been in pre-trial detention since December 2022. The Federal Public Prosecutor's Office accuses Carsten L, 56, and his alleged accomplice of treason. In the middle of the Ukraine war, the two are alleged to have passed secret documents and information from the German foreign intelligence service to the Russian domestic intelligence service FSB in 2022. According to the indictment, they were paid "agent fees" of €450,000 ($520,000) and €400,000 respectively. In April 2023, Carsten L denied the charges through his defence lawyer, as well as the account given by his co-defendant. Arthur E had previously given a comprehensive and colourful account of the case before the court. The trial is running significantly longer than planned, with hearings now scheduled through to January 2027. The court had originally set dates only through to mid-December 2024. According to a court spokeswoman, 98 witnesses and 7 experts have been heard so far. Further witnesses have been summoned.

headline: Japan’s 2026 defense white paper highlights ‘new era of crisis’ in Indo-Pacific
body of the article: Japan releases defense white papers each year, but its 2026 edition marked important shifts in the country's approach to defense strategy, procurement and production. "The international community is facing its greatest trial since World War II and [is] entering a new era of crisis," the document warned. "It cannot be ruled out that a serious situation similar to Russia's aggression against Ukraine may occur in the Indo-Pacific region in the future, particularly in East Asia." China, Russia and North Korea are fingered as culprits. In fact, Japan's 2026 Defense White Paper noted China presents "the greatest strategic challenge," also citing Beijing's growing concordance with Moscow in joint exercises as an alarming trend. After studying Ukraine and developments in modern warfare, the document highlighted necessary solutions such as renewed focus on lower-cost systems; innovations in research, development and production; increased production; and stockpiling of materiel. Japan is acquiring a large number of low-cost, unmanned vehicles in the air, sea and underwater domains. These unmanned systems will help establish what it calls the Synchronized, Hybrid, Integrated and Enhanced Littoral Defense, or SHIELD, by Fiscal Year 2027. The paper highlighted how Japan's indigenous defense industry is increasingly important. However, some companies like Komatsu and Mitsui have already abandoned or downsized their involvement in the defense sector. Tokyo believes increased spending will help reinforce the military-industrial complex, but it wants industrial innovation to develop military equipment in response to rapid changes in combat. The industrial base also needs to be scalable to meet Japanese requirements, the paper says. Likewise, Japan is strengthening defense equipment cooperation internationally, with the most obvious fruit being Australia's decision to buy Upgraded Mogami-class frigates. The white paper reiterated that the Japan-U.S. alliance remains its "cornerstone" relationship. However, Grant Newsham, senior research fellow at the Japan Forum for Strategic Studies, highlighted Japan's "decades of pathological dependence on the Americans to take care of Japan's defense," and its "so-called pacifist mindset and contrived constitutional prohibitions on an effective defense force" as challenges needing to be overcome. Nonetheless, the paper asserted, by FY 2027, the country "will strengthen its defense capability to the point where Japan is able to take primary responsibility for dealing with invasions against its nation, and disrupt and defeat such threats with the support of its ally and others." Tokyo has already achieved 2% defense spending as a proportion of GDP, and it is seeking a record JPY8.9 trillion, or $56.1 billion USD, defense budget next year. This budget request, likely to rise further, will be submitted at the end of August. "Ukraine really spurred Japanese awareness — figuring that Taiwan was next, with everything that would portend for Japan's security," Newsham told Defense News. "This has not, however, translated into a Japan Self-Defense Force that's organized and capable of fighting a war."

headline: Former Thai MP admits shooting dead ‘good friend’
body of the article: A former Thai MP has been arrested after calling aYouTuberto confess to shooting dead a friend. Chalong Riewrang, 71, said he had killed Thongchai Yenprasert, a government official, in Nonthaburi province on the edge ofBangkokon Monday. He also claimed to have injured Mr Yenprasert's driver. It comes days after aboy, 14, killed eight peoplebefore shooting himself dead at his school on the outskirts of Bangkok, raising questions over gun control in Thailand. Mr Riewrang phoned Anchalee Paireerak, a social media broadcaster and political commentator, who was live-streaming at the time, to tell her what he had done. Rescue workers try to save Thongchai Yenprasert after the shooting on Monday - Reuters Ms Paireerak could be heard saying: "Brother Chalong Riewrang, wait up – I'll call you back, I'm on air. What's the big story? What? What did you say? Why did you shoot him? And where are you? "You shot him just now? And did he die? Did he die? You shot him in the head? Now where are you going? You need to wait there for the cops. Don't go anywhere." Later, Mr Riewrang was heard saying: "The cops are here." Ms Paireerak replied: "You're with the cops now? Put your gun down and don't shoot anyone else, OK?" Hours later, after being taken into custody, he was allowed to give a press conference at the police station, during which he was seen without handcuffs and smoking a cigarette. Mr Riewrang, a former member ofThailand's house of representatives for Nonthaburi province, told reporters he had tried to resolve a financial dispute with his "good friend". Forensic police officers inspect the scene of the shooting on the edge of Bangkok - Reuters He said: "I followed him to his car and hit his car's window, saying I want to talk. He said he would not talk, so I pulled my gun. We spoke and he did not listen to me. He did not talk. He did not acknowledge anything. I can't believe I'm in this position, sitting here. "Throughout my life, I had never come to a police station. I did not aim to shoot, but his driver pulled a gun and pointed it at me, so I fired. I didn't intend to do anything, because he's a good friend of mine, but he didn't want to talk to me." Police said he was not given any special privileges by being allowed to host his press conference. Anutin Charnvirakul, the prime minister of Thailand, said legal action would be taken against Mr Riewrang without exception, local media reported. Mr Riewrang was said to be facing financial difficulties and needed the money owed, a total of 11m baht (about £250,000), to cover medical expenses. He claimed to have previously helped Mr Yenprasert, 71, with payments on properties. Police outside the government building in Nonthaburi province where the shooting took place - Arnun Chonmahatrakool/Reuters Mr Yenprasert was a former police officer and prominent local leader in Nonthaburi province. He was serving as president of the Nonthaburi Provincial Administrative Organisation, having held the role for more than two decades. Sakon Sukprom, director of Phra Nang Klao hospital, said the victim "lost a lot of blood" and his driver was shot in the right arm but "successfully underwent surgery". Thailand has one of the highest rates of gun ownership, with an estimated 10 million guns in circulation. Officials have since promised stricter gun laws, but previous pledges have failed to prevent repeated shootings. Try full access to The Telegraph free today. headline: Yemen conflict risks reigniting following Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia
body of the article: The risk of the Yemen war fully reigniting is growing, following a series of strikes by the Iran-backed Houthis on targets inside the country and across the border in Saudi Arabia. The Houthis fired on the southern Saudi region of Najran last week and on Saudi Aramco'sJazan refineryon Sunday. Over the same period, they launched dozens of missiles and drones at what it said were military sites in the center and east of Yemen, and on the Red Sea port of Mokha. The Saudi-backed, internationally recognized government of Yemen saidit had retaliated. Dozens of peoplehave been killedin these strikes, and both sides risk falling into apattern of escalation. The 12-year-old war, largely frozen since 2022, is heating up. The situation in Yemen has its own dynamics independent of the US-Iran war, but the Houthis' close ties with Iran and attacks on ships are part of a widening, low-intensity conflict. —Dominic Dudley

headline: Norway's Princess Ingrid Alexandra begins studies in Oslo
body of the article: Norway's Princess Ingrid Alexandra began her first exchange semester at the University of Oslo on Monday after returning from Australia on account of her mother Mette-Marit's serious lung illness. Mette-Marit suffers from the incurable disease pulmonary fibrosis and received a lung transplant earlier this year. The uncertainty led Ingrid Alexandra, 22, to pause her studies at the University of Sydney to be with her mother. On her first day of studies in Oslo, the rector, the dean of the Faculty of Social Sciences and the head of the student parliament welcomed the princess. Ingrid Alexandra's younger brother, Prince Sverre Magnus, will also begin university studies in this year, the palace announced. The 20-year-old is to study Business Management at Forward College. He will spend his first academic year in the Portuguese capital, Lisbon, before continuing his studies in Paris and Berlin. The princess and her brother are expected to continue to carry out selected official duties for the royal family while studying.

headline: Five years of Taliban rule: has the world given up on Afghanistan?
body of the article: When you buy through links on our articles, Future and its syndication partners may earn a commission. Around 4.7 million Afghans are facing 'life-threatening malnutrition' and almost 19 million are 'in the grip of acute hunger or worse'. | Credit: Illustration by Stephen P. Kelly / Getty Images Taliban fighters entered Kabul on 15 August 2021 as the Afghan government collapsed and US troops scrambled to complete their withdrawal from the country. A year later, the group declared the date an annual national holiday. In the five years since, the Taliban's "increasingly draconian policies have made Afghanistan one of the world's gravest human rights crises, particularly for women and girls", saidHuman Rights Watch. Among United Nations members states, only Russia has announced it formallyrecognises the Taliban regime, but "international condemnation is not enough", said HRW. On "The Proud Day of August 15", as the day has become known, Afghans are likely to see parades of the Taliban's "suicide bomber squad on motorbikes and American equipment left by Nato forces", said Christina Lamb inThe Times. Yet the country remains "on the brink of famine". Around 4.7 million Afghans are facing "life-threatening malnutrition", and almost 19 million are "in the grip of acute hunger or worse", according to the World Food Programme. Afghanistan remains the only country in the world to ban girls and women from secondary school and university, while "morality police" patrol the streets seeking infringements of dress codes. The Taliban has even "banned women being seen at windows", and recently "scrapped the minimum age for child marriage". Five years into its rule, the Taliban continues to expose the "wishful thinking of Western political and military leaders who insisted the movement had changed", said theLowy Institutethink tank. The West has a "wilful blindness" towards the regime and is "quietly lowering the threshold of behaviour it is prepared to accept". "Tellingly", theUnited Nationsnow refers to the "relevant authorities" in Kabul rather than the "de facto authorities", in effect "narrowing the linguistic difference between the regime and a recognised government". Warnings of the widespread repression under the regime are still "accurate"; what has changed is the "willingness of the world to act on them". Britain's hesitation to evacuate eligible Afghans who worked with British officials in the country is "typical" of the UK's "attitude to its obligations to Afghans generally", said an editorial inThe Independent. According to an internal government review conducted in February, 7,000 people have been found to be eligible for resettlement and "still likely to be at risk from Taliban retribution", yet Britain has scrapped plans to evacuate them. Made worse by a "catastrophic data breach in 2022", "obfuscation and delay", Britain has been "dragging its feet in protecting those who served alongside our troops in Afghanistan". It, like other countries, must "discharge its obligations to our Afghan allies, promptly and in full", as a "matter of national honour". The US, in particular, "has a moral responsibility to not simply look away," said Mursal Rahim, who fled Afghanistan in 2021, inThe New York Times. Since leaving Kabul, the US has "increasingly disengaged from the country and its people", closing the embassy, withdrawing diplomats and leaving "sharply reduced assistance" for Afghans coming to America. The situation in Afghanistan no longer "commands America's attention as it once did", but to continue in this vein risks accepting that the "systematic erasure of Afghan women is no longer its concern". It may be unpopular, but "Afghanistan's future depends on greater international engagement" with whoever is in charge, said Tobias Ellwood, former chair of the Defence Select Committee, inThe Telegraph. But importantly, "engagement does not mean recognition". The goal is to ensure that Afghanistan, and its population of 40 million people, is "stable, secure and prosperous enough", but that "will not be achieved by shouting from afar. It begins by re-engaging with those who govern Afghanistan today." "Far too little" is being done to protect girls from child marriages, and promote education, said former PM Gordon Brown inThe Guardian. Other countries in the region have had some success.Pakistan's Sindh province has criminalised marriage under 18 and introduced "penalties for those who facilitate it". Bangladesh has also tightened its birth registration system to make it harder to conceal a girl's age. Changes to the UK government's new immigration and asylum bill are positive recognitions of the problem. "But we must go further." We must establish a fund in support of Afghan girls who are threatened with child marriage. It should offer them "bursaries to continue their education, if necessary outside their home country". This may only be a "small gesture" after five years of Taliban rule, but "it is our moral duty to help them".

headline: Ukrainian drone strike kills 13 inside Russia, authorities say, in deadliest attack in two years
body of the article: A Ukrainiandrone strikehas killed at least 13 people and injured75others in Nizhnekamsk, a city in the Tatarstan region deep inside Russia, local authorities said Monday, marking the deadliest attack to hit the country in more than two years. Nizhnekamsk lies more than 600 miles (1,000 kilometers) east of Moscow and is the site of the major, technologically advanced Taneco oil refinery, which Ukraine's armed forces said they had targeted. Videos circulating on social media, and geolocated by CNN, show a huge blaze raging and plumes of smoke rising from an area just outside the city, close to what appear to be the characteristic towers of an oil refinery. It isn't clear exactly what was struck in the attack. The strike comes as both Russia and Ukraine intensify their aerial attacks against one another, while the frontlines of the war largely stagnate. More drones and missiles are slipping through both sides' fraying air defenses, meaning that the civilian death toll has increased, and more critical infrastructure is being damaged. July was the deadliest month for Ukrainian civilians since April 2022. And 1,396 people have been killed and 7,978 injured in the first six months of the year, an increase from 2024 and 2025, the UN said recently. A child was among those killed in Nizhnekamsk, according to the Russian Investigative Committee, while 21 people have been hospitalized, the region's press service said. And another four people were killed over the last 24 hours in the Russian region of Belgorod, which borders Ukraine, the region's acting governor Alexandr Shuvayev said Monday. As Ukraine's long-range drone technology has improved in recent months, it has demonstrated a newfound ability to frequently strike infrastructure deep inside Russia, like oil refineries, tankers, power substations and broader energy infrastructure as well as warehouses belonging to Russia's largest online retailer, Wildberries. Smoke rises from an oil refinery following a Ukrainian drone attack in Moscow, Russia, on June 18. - Reuters Attacks on Wildberries' warehouses last month killed at least eight people in a single day which, up until Monday's strike on Nizhnekamsk, was the deadliest Ukrainian attack inside Russia. Russia's daily aerial assualts on Ukraine still vastly outnumber Kyiv's retaliatory attacks. In just one night earlier this month, Russian missiles killed at least 17 people and injured dozens of others in the Kyiv region. Such attacks are made even more deadly by Kyiv's shortage of ballistic-missile interceptors, as it desperately seeks help from allies to replenish its supply of US-made Patriot interceptor missiles. CNN's Anna Chernova and Lauren Kent contributed reporting. For more CNN news and newsletters create an account atCNN.com

headline: King Charles Admits ‘It Was A Close Thing’ As He Revisits Decades-Old Tragedy
body of the article: King Charlesdid not need many words to revisit one of the most traumatic experiences of his life. While meeting mountain rescuers in Scotland, the monarch briefly acknowledged the 1988 incident that nearly killed him and claimed the life of his close friend,Major Hugh Lindsay. His simple description of the incident carried the weight of a memory that has followed him for decades. More than 30 years later, King Charles' personal connection to mountain rescue gave his meeting with the team an added significance. ZUMAPRESS.com / MEGA The avalanche remains one of the most serious dangers King Charles has personally encountered. While speaking with members of the Assynt Mountain Rescue Team at the Castle of Mey, he discussed the risks associated with mountain rescue and reflected on his own experience. Ben Dyson, the team's leader, recalled that the monarch described his survival in remarkably understated terms. "He said 'it was a close thing'," Dyson toldThe Times. The comment came as the Assynt Mountain Rescue Team marked its 50th anniversary on August 1. King Charles was reportedly "very appreciative" of the rescuers' work, with Dyson suggesting that surviving an avalanche himself had given the 77-year-old an understanding of just how dangerous mountain environments could become. ZUMAPRESS.com / MEGA King Charles survived the 1988 avalanche, but the disaster claimed the life of someone close to him. The incident occurred on March 10, 1988, when Charles, then Prince of Wales, was skiing off-piste with his party above Klosters in Switzerland. An avalanche suddenly swept through the area, sending Major Hugh Lindsay, a former equerry to Queen Elizabeth, approximately 1,312 feet down the mountainside. Patti Palmer-Tomkinson was also caught in the avalanche and suffered serious injuries. Charles and other members of the party reached safety, but they later returned to the site with their guide and a Swiss police officer in an effort to help locate those buried beneath the snow. Lindsay and Palmer-Tomkinson were eventually taken by helicopter to hospital in Davos. Sadly, Lindsay was pronounced dead after arriving. Mirrorpix / MEGA King Charles has been a topic of discussion over the last few months, especially due to his health. However, the monarch appears to be doing just fine. During a meeting with 104-year-old World War II veteran James Fenton on the Isle of Man in July, Charles was on the receiving end of some heartfelt concern when Fenton admitted he was "always concerned" about the King's health. Rather than dwelling on the subject, King Charles responded with a joke about his advancing years. "It is terrible because bits keep dropping off!" he quipped perPEOPLE. The exchange took place at Heroes On The Water Isle of Man, a charity supporting veterans, emergency service personnel and other uniformed public servants through outdoor activities. MEGA While the public continues to worry about King Charles, his health appears to be moving in an encouraging direction, with doctors reportedly "very pleased with his progress" as he continues cancer treatment. A royal source toldWoman & Homethat the monarch has been "on really good form" this year, with his royal engagements now "pretty much back to his pre-cancer levels." Courtiers had previously kept Fridays free for Charles to rest after his treatment began in February 2024, but he has continued taking on a demanding schedule. He is still receiving treatment, reportedly thought to be immunotherapy, while doctors monitor his progress. Charles and Queen Camilla have now retreated to their Birkhall home in the Scottish Highlands for their summer break, where they will later welcome members of the wider royal family to Balmoral. MEGA King Charles' own experience with cancer has occasionally surfaced in his conversations with patients, and one exchange in May offered a rare glimpse into a side effect he appears to have experienced himself. During a visit to Guy's Cancer Center in London on May 11, the King met 69-year-old chemotherapy patient Raymond Burgess, who mentioned the unpleasant taste caused by his treatment. Charles immediately related to the experience, telling him, according toThe Telegraph,"It's an awful sort of metallic taste." He then added, "It doesn't exactly help with eating." He was visiting the center as part of Guy's Hospital's 300th anniversary celebrations, where he also met medical professionals and learned about the use of artificial intelligence and robotics in cancer treatment.
