headline: Inside the Italian prison where inmates find freedom through theatre
body of the article: For some prisoners in Italy, life behind bars has become an unlikely route towards freedom. At Volterra prison, one of Italy's oldest jails,professional theatre-makershave spent almost four decades working alongside inmates to create ambitious performances that challenge conventional ideas about punishment, rehabilitation and the role of art. The project, known as the "Compagnia della Fortezza", was founded by director Armando Punzo, who originally entered the prison looking for actors for a theatre company unlike any other. "I wanted to put theatre to the test in a situation where, even if naively, I thought, and I believe it was the case, that art and culture had absolutely nothing to do with it. And I found that extremely interesting and challenging," says Punzo. Related Italian con artist jailed for building 'world's oldest and largest amphitheatre' 20-years ago Historic Italian theatres vying for UNESCO's World Heritage status Instead of professional actors, he found a multicultural group of prisoners with little or no connection to theatre. "I encountered people who had never once reflected on themselves differently. They were deeply immersed, just as we all are, in their ordinary lives, their lives were vastly different from ours, yet driven by the exact same mechanism," he says. "Being immersed in one's ordinary life, a life that was evidently extremely difficult, both for themselves and for others. Yet, I also found people capable of reflecting on themselves. This tells us that art and culture can truly reach everyone; if they fail to do so, it is simply because the necessary work to make that happen has not been done," he adds. A new production is created each year, while previous performances are revisited and brought back to the stage as part of a continuous process of research and artistic development. Prisoners are involved in the creative process itself, working alongside professional theatre-makers across different aspects of the productions. For many, it has become an important part of their lives and an opportunity to engage with a form of expression they had never previously considered. Giacomo arrived in Volterra from another prison in 2024. He had requested a transfer to this facility specifically because he was aware of the theatre work being done here, and he was immediately integrated into the company. "Life on the outside leads you to lose yourself, and to lose all those aspects that, however silly it may sound to say, I am actually rediscovering in here. The metaphor, which I find incredibly important, is that by losing my freedom in here, within a state of total confinement, I am finding total openness," he shares. That same openness allows prisoners to work side-by-side with other theatre professionals every day to create the shows. "Theatre can transform any space. Doing so is inherent to the language of theatre, and therefore, this is theatre. When we do this, the prison steps aside, much like an actor who sets aside a part of himself when stepping onto the stage," says Viola Ferro, a young actress that chose to join the acting company. For prison director Valentina Bruno, the theatre project forms part of a widerapproach to rehabilitation, in which prisoners are treated as people rather than simply as inmates. "They (prisoners) feel that the staff cares for them in the best possible way. They feel valued as individuals, not merely as numbers or files. They feel that they matter, and that their family context matters too, given the frequent contact we maintain with their relatives", she says. "Above all, I believe what they strongly feel is hope: the hope of returning to society, whether upon completing their sentence or even sooner, as changed individuals capable of giving something back to the community," she adds. The work of the company is perhaps most striking when its performances open the prison to the outside world. The courtyard becomes a theatre, with the fortress walls forming the backdrop and members of the public entering the prison to watch the performances. Writer Maria Nadotti, who regularly attends the performances, says the company represents something increasingly unusual in contemporary theatre. "I have absolute admiration for the work of the "Compagnia della Fortezza" and for something that, in my view, is increasingly rare in theatre, and not just in Italy, a combination of imagination, joy, energy, and an absolute passion for wonder, wonder is the soul of the world, and it is all present here," she says.

headline: Greece contains new wind-driven fire near Athens
body of the article: A wind-driven wildfire that broke out Monday near the Greek capital of Athens has been brought under control, firefighters said. The fire, fed by winds of more than 70 kilometres an hour (43 miles per hour), began around 8:00 am local time (0500 GMT) in Kouvaras, 60 kilometres southeast of Athens. Authorities immediately deployed a major response of nearly 200 firefighters, around 40 vehicles supported by two water‑bombing planes and four helicopters. Three hours later, the flames had subsided and the situation appeared much better, an AFP photographer observed. Early in the afternoon, "the situation has greatly improved," the fire service press office reported. "There is no active front, but we are maintaining our presence in the area, where temperatures remain high with strong gusts of wind," the same source said. The warehouse of a livestock farm was destroyed by the flames, according to images from Ertnews, which showed firefighters battling the fire on a mountainside farm. Several residential areas had to be evacuated. The blaze Monday marks the second fire near Athens this summer. One that broke out 10 days ago northwest of the Greek capital destroyed more than 11,000 hectares of pine forests and farmland. A large part of the country faces a very high fire risk Monday due to summer heat, with temperatures of up to 37C in the Attica region combined with strong gusts. Like much of the Mediterranean, Greece has experienced increasingly frequent and intense wildfires that scientists link to climate change. Greece remains on maximum alert on Monday, with several regions classified as being at a very high fire risk -- level four on a five-point scale. Experts have warned about the increased severity of the fires affecting Attica, where Athens is located. From 2017 to 2026, 42 percent of the total forest area in the region burned because of 15 major fires. hec/hba/hmn/dej/st

headline: WHO says Congo's fast-moving Ebola outbreak started months before it was declared
body of the article: BUNIA, Congo (AP) — The fastest-growingEbolaoutbreak on record started in February, months before it was officially declared in mid-May, theWorld Health Organizationsaid Monday as responders in eastern Congo struggle to catch up. The WHO regional director for Africa, Dr. Mohamed Yakub Janabi, told a news conference that sequencing indicated the outbreak's start. He said some cases early on were wrongly attributed to other diseases, including malaria and typhoid. "So we are chasing the virus, the virus is ahead of us," Janabi said. Dr. Thierno Balde, WHO's incident manager for the Ebola response, said the genetic sequencing was conducted under the leadership of Dr. Steve Ahuka, head of the virology department at Congo's National Institute for Biomedical Research. Confirmed cases of Ebola in this outbreak have reached 4,200, including over 1,900 deaths, according to the latest government figures. WHO assesses the global risk of spread as low because Ebola does not travel through the air, making it much harder to spread than respiratory viruses.Cases detected outside the affected regionhave so far been quickly identified and contained without leading to sustained transmission, according to the agency. The outbreak declared on May 15 is unlike most previous ones for Ebola because therare Bundibugyo virusresponsible for it has no approved vaccines or treatments. Early testing was conducted for the more common type of Ebola, contributing to delays. The outbreak is unfolding in some of the most challenging conditions imaginable, with strikes by someunpaid health workers, threats by rebel groups, anger from long-traumatized communities and misinformation asserting that Ebola isn't real. Health teams travel remote, unpaved roads and have reported shortages of protective gear, while a vast population of displaced people struggles to find reliable water sources for washing hands. This Ebola outbreak has killed more people at a quicker rate than any other, including the 2014-2016 outbreak in West Africa that is considered the worst on record with over 11,000 deaths out of at least 28,000 cases. That one took about eight months to reach 1,000 deaths. Ebola is rare but highly contagious and can be contracted from bodily fluids such as vomit, blood or semen and with contaminated surfaces and materials such as bedding and clothing. The disease it causes is severe and often fatal. Last week, WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesu said Ebola is spreading faster than efforts to fight it. New cases are doubling in some hot spots, Tedros said on X after meeting with officials in the capital, Kinshasa. Health authorities have said between 60% and 70% of new cases are recorded outside of contacts being monitored, and that the outbreak is spreading at an "alarming" rate. Access to healthcare in the region already had beenchallenged by years of rebel conflictin one of Congo's most remote and vulnerable areas, near the borders of South Sudan, Uganda and Rwanda. Now somepregnant womenand others are avoiding health centers for fear of the virus, at risk to their lives. Several past Ebola outbreaks have also been declared weeks or months late, including the 2014-2016 West Africa outbreak. That outbreak was declared in March 2014, although the first human case later was found to have occurred in December 2013. ___ Banchereau reported from Dakar, Senegal. ___ This version corrects the second reference to the WHO director-general to Tedros.

headline: No end in sight for German spy trial as ex-spymaster takes stand again
body of the article: More than two and a half years into the trial of a German intelligence official suspected of spying for Russia, no end is in sight to proceedings. Bruno Kahl, the former head of the Federal Intelligence Service (BND), appeared as a witness again on Monday on the 168th day of proceedings. Kahl, 64, is now serving as Germany's ambassador to the Vatican in Rome. He was first heard as a witness at Berlin's Higher Regional Court more than two years ago. At the time, the central question was what damage the alleged Russian espionage had caused. Kahl described it then as a "catastrophe." The latest questioning, held initially in open court, focused primarily on when the former intelligence chief learned of the suspicion that information may have been passed on, what steps were then taken to establish who was behind it, and how the BND employee came under suspicion. Few details emerged, however: As much of the information involved is classified, the hearing was open to the public only at the outset. The main defendant is the BND employee, who has been in pre-trial detention since December 2022. The Federal Public Prosecutor's Office accuses Carsten L, 56, and his alleged accomplice of treason. In the middle of the Ukraine war, the two are alleged to have passed secret documents and information from the German foreign intelligence service to the Russian domestic intelligence service FSB in 2022.

headline: German police to expand drone defence unit after Leipzig incident
body of the article: Germany's Federal Police are to expand their drone defence unit in response to the discovery of an explosive-laden drone at Leipzig/Halle airport. Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt is to order the unit to grow to 300 personnel on Monday, a ministry spokeswoman said. Instead of four locations, eight sites are now planned "in order to be on the ground quickly and flexibly when needed," she said. In response to the heightened threat from drones - primarily from Russia - Dobrindt commissioned a new unit in December tasked with detecting, intercepting and, if necessary, shooting down unmanned aerial vehicles. The unit's personnel are stationed at airports, in the capital and at security-sensitive sites across Germany to enable rapid deployment. In December, it was announced that the new unit would initially consist of around 60 Federal Police officers and would rapidly grow to 130 specialist officers. It would deploy AI-assisted jamming systems and automatic interceptor drones, among other equipment. The unit was also to support state police forces in an auxiliary capacity where necessary and where capacity allowed. Several politicians recently raised the possibility of legislative changes to enable more effective defence against the drone threat. The federal government, for its part, points to changes already implemented, including amendments to aviation security legislation. Deputy government spokesman Sebastian Hille said the federal government considered itself well-positioned in legal terms when it came to drone defence. Late last Tuesday night, a drone fitted with explosives and a detonator was discovered near Ukrainian transport aircraft at Leipzig/Halle airport. An aircraft also collided with an unknown smaller flying object - possibly a second drone. The Federal Public Prosecutor's Office is investigating on suspicion of attempted detonation of an explosive device and dangerous interference with air traffic.

headline: Ill-equipped Alpine hikers to pay for Austrian helicopter rescue
body of the article: Austrian mountain rescue conducted a complex rescue operation involving helicopters to rescue 36 ill-equipped hikers from three families, including small children in prams, police in Tyrol state reported on Monday. The group got into difficulties at an altitude of more than 2,300 metres during a spontaneous hike after setting out from the Wildspitzbahn mountain station near Sölden. The group - which included adults, teenagers and several small children - had "virtually no" suitable equipment, a police spokesman told dpa. They were from Belgium, the United Kingdom, the United States and Austria. He said the group would be charged for the rescue operation. According to the spokesman, the families repeatedly found themselves in difficult and dangerous terrain and at times strayed from the marked trail. Eventually, two members of the group made an emergency call. Two helicopters rescued 14 people, four of them using a winch. Another 22 people were brought down to the valley on foot by mountain rescuers. No one was injured.

headline: London police seize record $10 million in supercars in one weekend
body of the article: London police said Monday they had seized a record $10 million worth of supercars between Friday and Sunday in an operation aimed at curbing antisocial driving. Officers from London's Metropolitan Police seized a total of 90 vehicles across popular affluent London neighborhoods such as Hyde Park, Kensington and Chelsea, marking the highest value and number of cars impounded since they launched an operation to crack down on antisocial driving five years ago. Authorities in England consider antisocial driving to include causing unnecessary noise pollution, street racing and cruising in a convoy, among other types of public nuisance. In the summer months, it is common for owners of expensive and exotic cars, domestic or otherwise, to descend on some of central London's affluent and popular neighborhoods, often meeting up in groups. It's not uncommon for some drivers to be heard unnecessarily revving their engines, prompting complaints from locals. "The disruption caused by these reckless drivers and boy racers is often worse during the summer months and, as well as putting people at risk, causes significant nuisance for residents and businesses," Caroline Sargent, a lawmaker at Westminster City Council, said. This year, police have been given the power to seize vehicles involved in antisocial behavior rather than giving motorists a warning, the Met Police said in a statement. One of the vehicles seized included a Ferrari Monza SP2, which was one of only 499 made and can be auctioned for nearly $5 million. The police said the car had only been in the U.K. for a day and had no insurance. The driver was also on a provisional driving license, which can only be used for learning how to drive. Special Chief Inspector Geoff Tatman, who led the operation, said, "We regularly hear from local people who are fed up with people driving cars dangerously in the area, or with modifications which make them a nuisance to those who live nearby. "Through operations like this, we're arresting these drivers and seizing their cars so we can keep our roads safe."

headline: UK radio broke rules in announcing king's death: watchdog
body of the article: A community radio station breached the rules after accidentally announcing the death of King Charles III in a May broadcast, a UK watchdog said on Monday. Radio Caroline, a former pirate radio that now mostly plays rock music, apologised in May after airing messages falsely announcing the monarch's death. One of the messages had said "we have suspended our normal programmes until further notice as a mark of respect following the passing of His Majesty King Charles III". The national anthem was then played, followed by around 16 minutes of silence before the regular programme resumed. The presenter apologised 30 minutes after the messages were initially triggered, Ofcom said. The regulator, which received two complaints about the broadcast, said the "very significant inaccuracy" and the "considerable length of time" taken to acknowledge the error breached two of its rules. One requires news reports to be accurate and impartial. The other requires significant mistakes to be acknowledged and corrected on air promptly. Radio Caroline told Ofcom the error occurred when a member of staff accessed sound files pre-recorded in the event of the monarch's death while carrying out maintenance on the studio computer, as the programme was being streamed remotely. The staff member played the files "out of curiosity", which stopped the stream from the presenter's remote location and broadcast the files on air. The person then reportedly "panicked and left the premises" after realising what had happened, according to the Ofcom statement. Radio Caroline said the remote presenter "would not realise that they had gone 'off air' unless they were monitoring their output via an internet monitor." The presenter, believing they were still on air, was not actively monitoring their phone and did not immediately respond to calls from people at the station who had noticed the error, the report said. The station said the person who played the files had been "reprimanded" and had "apologised". It added the pre-recorded files had now been removed from the studio computer. lmc/jkb/fg

headline: British national killed at protest in Kashmir
body of the article: A British man has been shot dead in Pakistan-administeredKashmirduring clashes between security forces and protesters. Mohammad Akhtar, 50, from Peterborough, was killed on June 9 after a bullet fired by Pakistani security forces struck him in the chest. Protesters had gathered to demand electoral reforms in the region that is also claimed by India, but Akhtar's family insisted he was not part of the demonstrations. "He wasn't taking part in protests but the demonstrations were happening close to his house," Mohammad Saad, Akhtar's cousin, told The Guardian,which revealed the death. "There was firing by the forces that day and he was hit by a stray bullet. There was a bullet wound on the side of his chest," Mr Saad said. Pakistani security forces patrol in Muzaffarabad in Kashmir during protests - AMIRUDDIN MUGHAL/EPA/Shutterstock The family could not get a police complaint registered in Kashmir and feared that they could be targeted. It has emerged that another Briton has been held in a prison in the region for more than two months despite his family's attempts to secure his release through theForeign Office(FCDO). A Foreign Office spokesman said: "The UK is deeply concerned by the situation in parts of Pakistan-administered Kashmir. "FCDO ministers and the UK high commissioner in Islamabad are in touch with their counterparts, and UK travel advice was updated on 7 August and continues to advise against all but essential travel to affected areas." People protest after talks between JAAC and the Pakistani government collapsed - REUTERS Kashmir is a disputed Himalayan region divided between India andPakistan,and both claim it in its entirety. The crackdown on protests began after talks between the Pakistani government and Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC), a grass-roots movement advocating improved economic and political rights for Kashmir's population, collapsed over demands for electoral reforms. The group wants the abolition of 12 assembly seats reserved for Kashmiri refugees living outside the territory, in cities across Pakistan. The JAAC says Islamabad-backed political parties are weaponising the seats to influence the formation of the regional government and no longer reflect the political reality of the region. After talks broke down in late May, the JAAC called for a region-wide strike on June 9, triggering demonstrations across the territory. On June 5, authorities declared the JAAC a terrorist organisation and imposed a communications blackout on the region. Security forces have flooded the streets and been accused of killing at least 30 people. Men try to get mobile phone signal from a hilltop after a communications shutdown - AFP The government says the measures were necessary to maintain public order and denies killing protesters. The JAAC said it represented ordinary Kashmiris and accused authorities of criminalising peaceful dissent. "Branding a grass-roots organisation as 'terrorist' on vague grounds, while simultaneously cutting the region off from the outside world, raises serious concerns regarding the Pakistani authorities' conduct and their disregard for human rights," said Isabelle Lassee, Amnesty International's deputy regional director for South Asia. "The proscription of JKJAAC under anti-terror laws is disproportionate, unlawful and a violation of the right to freedom of association." The protests have overshadowed the ongoing voting for the regional assembly, which began on July 27. The government denies killing protesters - AFP The third and last phase of voting was scheduled to conclude on Monday, but has been postponed until the end of the month in some areas. JAAC has denounced the poll as a "sham" being held "at gunpoint" and says many of its supporters have been detained. Among them is Waqas Arif, 38, a British national from Nottingham, who has been held in Mirpur prison since June 5. His family said he was arrested during raids on their home because two of his brothers had joined the protests, but had not taken part himself. "Waqas was not involved in any kind of protests," his sister, Sumera Arif, said. "There is no charge. He hasn't done anything. This is my brother, but I think there are thousands of other brothers like him from everywhere who they have put in [prison] so they can minimise the protest power... they have not even been taken to court," she said. In a video appeal, his wife Varisha Kampulvi said she had been unable to speak to her husband or his family because of the communications blackout imposed across the territory. "I'm here today not as a politician or an activist," she said. "I'm here simply as a wife to my husband, Waqas Arif." A poster shared by Varisha Kampulvi on social media. Her husband Waqas Arif has been held in Mirpur prison since June 5 She urged the Pakistani government to free her husband and restore communications across the region. "He's an innocent man, a loving husband, son and father to his two beautiful daughters," she said. "He was just visiting his family in Azad Kashmir and has been caught up in what's going on there. He is not a threat to anybody." Ms Kampulvi said she had sought help from her local MP and the British authorities but that their ability to intervene was limited because Mr Arif holds dual British and Pakistani nationality. "I do urge the Pakistani government to release my husband immediately and also open up those communications," she said. Ms Kampulvi said British officials had been unable to speak directly to him. In an email sent to Ms Kampulvi on June 26, the Foreign Office said consular staff had contacted prison authorities, who confirmed that Mr Arif was in good health, although they had not been granted direct access to him. headline: Magnitude 7.4 quake rocks western Colombia, killing at least 111 people
body of the article: CALI, Colombia (AP) — A powerful 7.4 magnitudeearthquakestruck westernColombiaon Monday, killing at least 111 people, damaging hundreds of buildings and leaving many trapped under debris while their loved ones and rescue workers searched through rubble. Search teams and civilians picked through the remains of destroyed buildings in the country's third-largest city, Cali, passing large pieces of concrete and other rubble down a long line of volunteers. "Our building has basically been left in ruins, and the building next to ours? Completely collapsed," said Álvaro López, who cradled his dog as he watched the search. The desperate scene recalled thesearches still ongoing in neighboring Venezuelaweeks after that country was devastated by two powerful earthquakes. Besides Cali, the quake ravaged cities across western Colombia, including Pereira, Quibdo and Manizales, and was felt in neighboring Ecuador and Panama. The epicenter was in San Jose del Palmar, a community of about 4,800 people in the Choco region about 250 miles (400 kilometers) west of Bogota, the U.S. Geological Survey said. Colombia's President Abelardo de la Espriella said at least 87 people were injured and around 1,600 buildings were damaged, including at least 61 that completely collapsed. He declared an emergency to expedite funding for the quake recovery. "We aren't going to leave people alone. They are in our hearts and we are going to tend to people with our full determination," he said. Colombia's Geological Service said Monday's quake was the country's strongest recorded "in the 21st century," and that it was followed by several aftershocks. Colombia's Pacific region around the epicenter lies along the"Ring of Fire,"the line of seismic faults encircling the Pacific Ocean where most of the world's earthquakes occur. The Pacific, particularly the Choco region, is one of Colombia's poorest, nestled in dense jungle. Much of Choco is only reachable by boat or plane, which may pose difficulty in assessing the wider toll. Local authorities said the death toll included at least 40 people who were killed in the Risaralda region, where Pereira is located, and 27 people in the Valle del Cauca region, where Cali is located, including three children. Authorities also confirmed nine people killed in Choco, two in the Caldas region and a 73-year-old in the Antioquia region. It was not immediately clear where the other 32 people died. The earthquakes left many in the Andean nation unnerved aftertwo back-to-back quakesdevastated neighboring Venezuela in late June, destroying hundreds of buildings andkilling more than 6,300 people. By Monday afternoon, people had begun reporting theirloved ones missingon digital databases just as civilians did following Venezuela's earthquakes. One database had more than 2,000 people, mostly in Cali and Pereira, with the number steadily climbing. Photos of the missing included a young mother and her baby in Pereira; another showed an 80-year-old woman in Cali whose family was desperately looking for details after her building collapsed. Jorge Moncayo, a 64-year-old taxi driver in Cali, said he saw plumes of dust shoot up across the city as buildings collapsed. Residents and rescue workers were searching the rubble for survivors. The local government said that people remained trapped in a number of the city's 380 damaged buildings. "My entire house shook. I've never lived through such a powerful earthquake," he said. "We're thanking God we're alive." Little was known about the extent of the damage in Choco, a remote region where officials reported dozens of injured people and damaged buildings but few other details. Phone signals were out in many parts of the region's capital, Quibdo. The town closest to the earthquake's epicenter, San Jose del Palmar, has no airport, and is located on top of a mountain ridge along a highway linking the cities of Cali and Pereira. In Pereira, further south in the coffee-producing mountains of Colombia, photos and videos on local media showed pieces of the airport ceiling falling onto travelers taking shelter and screaming. People ran through rubble and plumes of dust, and residents said collapsed stores, residential buildings and homes lined the city. Pereira Mayor Mauricio Salazar told a local radio station there were at least 15 collapsed buildings where people were feared trapped. In nearby Manizales, one of the towers of the neo-Gothic cathedral collapsed and fell on the nave. Mayor Jorge Eduardo Rojas asked residents to stay outside in case of aftershocks. Authorities said flights were suspended at the airports in Manizales, Quibdo, Armenia, Cartago, Buenaventura and Pereira as they assessed damage. Small earthquakes, known as "temblores," are common in central and western Colombia, but those above 6.0 magnitude are rare. In 1999, a 6.2 magnitude quake near the city of Armenia killed more than 1,100 people. Response to the earthquake presents the first major challenge for de la Espriella, a Trump ally who wassworn in as president overthe weekend. A divisive figure because of his pledge of an all-out crackdown on criminal groups, de la Espriella said he had personally taken charge of the government's response to the emergency. On Monday night, the U.S. State Department announced it would provide $15.5 million for emergency shelter, food and other earthquake response aid. Governments across Latin America also lined up to help. El Salvador's President Nayib Bukele and Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum — whose countries were among the largest providers of aid to Venezuela following its recent crisis — said they were ready to assist Colombia. "From El Salvador, we are in communication and ready to provide immediate support with our rescue teams, medical personnel, paramedics, supplies, or any other assistance that our Colombian brothers and sisters deem necessary," Bukele said. Chilean President José Antonio Kast said Chile, one of the region's most earthquake-prone countries, "knows the pain and the challenge left by earthquakes" and pledged help. ___ Suárez reported from Bogotá and Janetsky reported from Mexico City. Associated Press journalists Manuel Rueda in Bogotá, Edith M. Lederer at the United Nations and Matthew Lee in Washington contributed to this report.

headline: AI Jesus can hear your confession — but can it forgive your sins?
body of the article: Imagine walking into a Catholic church, entering a confessional and finding Jesus waiting for you on the other side of the screen. Not a priest. Not an actor. An artificial intelligence version of Jesus Christ, capable of listening to your questions and responding almost instantly. It sounds like something from science fiction, but a Catholic church in Switzerland actually tried it. The experimental installation, called "Deus in Machina," placed an AI-generated Jesus avatar inside a confessional atSt. Peter's Chapel in Lucerne. Visitors could sit down, speak to the digital Jesus and receive responses generated with the help of artificial intelligence. The project immediately raised a much bigger question. If AI can imitate a spiritual conversation convincingly enough, could it eventually take the place of a priest? For the Catholic Church, the answer is much more complicated than what technology can technically accomplish. Visitors were invited to pose questions to the AI Jesus, viewed on a monitor behind a latticework screen.Courtesy of the Catholic Church of the City of Lucerne,CC BY The two-month project was created in collaboration with researchers from the University of Lucerne and Lucerne University of Applied Sciences and Arts. Visitors encountered a digital representation of Jesus on a screen behind the traditional latticework of a confessional. The AI system had access to theological material and could converse with visitors in multiple languages. People were explicitly warned that they were talking to an avatar and were advised not to disclose personal information. Despite the confessional setting, however, the installation wasn't actually designed to hear sacramental confessions. That distinction is important. A person could tell AI Jesus what was troubling them. They could ask about faith, morality, suffering, relationships or the meaning of life. What the AI couldn't do was forgive their sins. To someone outside Catholicism, the difference might sound technical. If a person confesses wrongdoing, receives spiritual advice and walks away feeling comforted, does it really matter whether the listener was human? Within Catholic theology, it matters enormously. Confession isn't simply a private conversation in which someone admits what they've done wrong. It is one of the church's sacraments, formally known as the sacrament of penance and reconciliation. A Catholic priest isn't merely listening and offering advice. He is acting in a specific sacramental role when he grants absolution. An AI system can't be ordained. It therefore cannot administer the sacrament. That puts a hard theological limit on something technology otherwise seems increasingly capable of imitating. AI may be able to sound compassionate. It may quote Scripture. It may explain Catholic teaching. It may even provide an answer that feels deeply personal. But sounding like a spiritual adviser isn't the same thing as being one. The human element isn't an accidental feature of Catholic confession. It goes back to Christianity's earliest traditions. The New Testament repeatedly places confession and forgiveness within a human community. In the Gospel of John, Jesus gives his apostles authority connected with the forgiveness of sins. The Epistle of James similarly tells believers to confess their sins to one another. Early Christian confession could actually be much more public than it is today. Christians accused of serious sins might perform public acts of penance before being formally reconciled with the church. Over centuries, the practice evolved toward the private, one-on-one confession Catholics recognize today. By the Middle Ages, private confession to a priest had become increasingly formalized. In 1215, church rules required Catholics to confess at least once a year. The familiar wooden confessional arrived later. A 17th-century confessional at the Toulouse St. Stephen's Cathedral.Didier Descouens via Wikimedia Commons,CC BY-SA Following the Council of Trent in the 16th century, confessionals with physical barriers between priests and penitents became increasingly common, providing privacy and anonymity. Ironically, that screen may be part of what makes an AI confessional seem strangely plausible today. Catholics have spent centuries speaking about their most private failures to someone they may barely be able to see. Replace the priest behind the screen with a computer, however, and the theological meaning changes completely. None of this necessarily means artificial intelligence has no role in religious life. An AI trained on reliable theological sources could answer basic questions at any hour. It could explain Scripture, define unfamiliar religious terms or help someone understand what a church teaches about a particular issue. It might even provide a low-pressure way for people who are embarrassed, curious or disconnected from organized religion to begin asking questions they would otherwise keep to themselves. There is also something revealing about the appeal. Talking to another person can be uncomfortable, particularly when the subject involves guilt, shame or doubt. A machine doesn't look shocked. It doesn't interrupt. It doesn't gossip. It doesn't visibly judge you. For some people, that may make AI unusually easy to talk to. But that advantage also exposes the central problem. As artificial intelligence becomes more conversational, the question extends far beyond Catholic confession. People are already turning to AI for advice about relationships, grief, anxiety, morality and some of the most personal decisions of their lives. Religion may be one of the clearest tests yet of where society draws the line between simulated human understanding and actual human connection. A chatbot can generate words of reassurance without feeling compassion. It can discuss grief without having experienced loss. It can talk about mortality without facing death. And an AI Jesus can discuss forgiveness without possessing the religious authority Catholics believe is necessary to grant it. That doesn't necessarily make the conversation meaningless. Someone may still find insight, comfort or even inspiration in what an AI tells them. But within Catholicism, a sacrament is not simply an exchange of information. It requires another human being. AI will almost certainly become better at mimicking the kinds of conversations people once assumed required another person. Future religious chatbots could know enormous amounts of Scripture and theology, remember previous conversations and respond in ways tailored to an individual's spiritual concerns. They may become extraordinarily convincing. But Catholic teaching presents technology with an unusual boundary: There are some things a machine cannot accomplish simply by becoming more intelligent. AI Jesus might answer your questions. It might offer advice. It might even say exactly what you desperately needed to hear. But if you're looking for absolution, you'll still need a priest. headline: Venezuela: Two earthquakes that exposed institutional failure
body of the article: Aug. 10 (UPI) -- On June 24, two powerful earthquakes measuring magnitude 7.2 and 7.5 struck northern Venezuela. The toll was catastrophic: more than 6,000 people were reported dead, tens of thousands were injured and thousands remained missing. Beyond the loss of life and the enormous economic damage, the disaster exposed a deeper problem. Its scale cannot be explained solely by geology. Human decisions also played a role. Earthquakes are natural phenomena, but their consequences are shaped by society. The extent of the damage depends on the quality of construction and whether safety standards are enforced. It also depends on whether the state has the capacity to anticipate risk and respond effectively when disaster strikes. When buildings collapse on a massive scale, investigators must look beyond the earthquake itself. Weak supervision, informal housing and poor urban planning can turn a natural hazard into a human catastrophe. That raises a broader question for Latin America: How widespread are these vulnerabilities, and must another major disaster occur before governments act decisively? Venezuela has had earthquake-resistant construction standards for decades. Technical institutions in the country have repeatedly addressed seismic risk and structural vulnerability. The central problem is not simply whether regulations exist. It is whether they are enforced. Reports and technical assessments cited by Venezuelan institutions have pointed to recurring problems such as inadequate compliance with construction codes and weak supervision. International organizations, including the U.S. Geological Survey and U.N. agencies involved in disaster assessment, have also emphasized the importance of structural vulnerability in determining the human impact of earthquakes. The lesson is straightforward: The force of an earthquake matters, but so does the strength of the society that confronts it. In Venezuela, institutional weakness has become increasingly difficult to separate from the country's broader political and economic deterioration. Officials who fail to perform the duties entrusted to them weaken public institutions. When inspections are neglected or construction standards are ignored, the consequences may remain hidden for years. An earthquake can suddenly expose those failures. Corruption makes the problem worse. When permits are improperly granted or public contracts lack transparency, citizens are placed at risk. When substandard materials are accepted, corruption ceases to be an abstract political offense. It becomes embedded in the physical structures where people live and work. Negligence must also be distinguished from corruption. Not every institutional failure involves theft or personal enrichment. Some result from incompetence, lack of resources or the gradual erosion of professional standards. That distinction matters because accountability must rest on evidence. Investigators should determine which agencies were responsible for inspections, what standards applied and whether warnings were ignored. They should also examine the role of private contractors and public officials. Where corruption or deliberate disregard for safety can be demonstrated, sanctions should follow. Where failures resulted from weak institutions or inadequate technical capacity, reform is necessary. Accountability should not become a substitute for evidence, nor should it become an instrument of political revenge. Its purpose must be to establish responsibility and prevent the same failures from recurring. This is especially important in a country where public confidence has been severely weakened. Venezuela has experienced years of institutional deterioration, patronage and political polarization. Those conditions create fertile ground for impunity. They also make it easier for administrative failures to become normalized. The earthquake revealed the consequences of that normalization. The response now should go beyond emergency relief. An independent assessment of damaged and vulnerable structures should be carried out, with the findings made public. Schools and hospitals should receive immediate attention. Older residential buildings in high-risk areas should also be evaluated. Construction permits and major reconstruction contracts should be subject to transparent review. Engineers and inspectors must be able to report violations without political interference. Informal communities require special attention. Many families live in vulnerable areas because they have no realistic alternative. Strengthening those neighborhoods will require technical assistance and safer construction methods, rather than punishing residents. International organizations can contribute expertise and independent evaluation. Their role should be practical and measurable. Venezuela needs help strengthening institutions and reducing future risks, not just expressions of concern after a disaster has occurred. The responsibility for reform, however, ultimately belongs inside Venezuela. The country must determine where public officials failed and whether those failures involved corruption, negligence or institutional incapacity. Justice should follow where wrongdoing can be proven. Reform should follow wherever institutions have failed. The lesson extends beyond Venezuela. Across Latin America, rapid urban growth has often outpaced effective regulation. Informal housing has expanded while public institutions struggle to supervise construction and prepare for disasters. Earthquakes cannot be prevented. The collapse of vulnerable structures, however, is not always inevitable. The damage caused by a natural disaster reflects choices made long before the ground begins to move. Governments decide whether regulations will be enforced. Institutions decide whether warnings will be taken seriously. Venezuela's tragedy should therefore be understood as more than a seismic event. It is also a warning about what happens when institutional weakness becomes normal. If that warning is ignored, the next earthquake may expose the same failures all over again. Carlos Cantero is a Chilean academic at the International University of La Rioja in Spain and the author of "Digital Society: Reason and Emotion." An international lecturer, adviser and consultant, he focuses on ethics, social innovation and human development. The views and opinions expressed in this commentary are solely those of the author.

headline: Iran Won’t Reopen Strait of Hormuz Without US Concessions and Other Mideast Developments
body of the article: Iran is insisting that the U.S. meet its demands in negotiations before theStrait of Hormuzreopens. Yemen's Defense Ministry announced a new death toll in the latest attack byHouthi rebelson the Red Sea town of Mokha. And Israel's military declared the Christian-majority town of Taybeh in the occupied West Bank a closed military zone after repeated settler attacks. Here's a look at the latest developments in the Iran war and the wider Middle East on Monday. Full coverage can be foundhere. An Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson said Iran will not reopen the Strait of Hormuz until the United States met its conditions. "It is up to the U.S. side to stop and make amends for its illegal and destructive actions," Esmail Baghaei said Monday, noting the American blockade of Iranian ports. Iran wantsthe U.S. to lift the blockade, pay compensation for months of war damage, lift economic sanctions and release Iran's frozen assets. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz — a waterway that normally carries roughly one-fifth of the world's traded oil supplies — has become the war's most lasting consequence. The impasse has kept energy prices as a major focus of U.S. politics ahead of November's midterm elections. Iran is holding separate talks with Oman over transit through the strait, including potentially a temporary shipping corridor. But it has said any actual reopening is contingent on talks with the U.S. Israel's military said Monday it had declared aChristian-majority townin the occupied West Bank a closed military zone to keep out Israeli settlers and other non-residents. The new tactic is designed to keep Israelis out of Taybeh, which is surrounded by settlements to its east and west and has been subject to arson, vandalism and settlers coming onto private and village property. The order does not apply to Palestinian residents or journalists, who the army said would be allowed unless soldiers determine their presence poses a threat. The army said its troops would detain suspects and disperse gatherings to keep the peace. The designation comes after months of the army and police struggling to maintain order throughout the territory, where at least 87 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli settlers or soldiers in 2026, according to the Ramallah-based Palestinian Health Ministry. Parts of Taybeh lie in what's called "Area B" where Israel maintains security control, but residents have complained that the army and police are slow to respond to attacks by extremist settlers. Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels attacked a Red Sea port town controlled by government forces on Sunday, killing seven and injuring 30 people. Yemen's Defense Ministry — which operates under its internationally recognized government — said four military personnel and three civilians were killed. The attack on Mokha is the latest inone of the largest wavesof Houthi strikes on Yemeni military positions and areas held by the Saudi-backed government since a 2022 truce. It comes as threats to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz have renewed focus on the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb Strait at its southern tip. Some shipping has shifted toward that route with Hormuz largely off limits to traffic. More than two years of war in Gaza flattened most of the territory and destroyed sectors of the economy, but beekeepers are now beginning to rebuild their businesses. Before the start of the Israel-Hamas war, the sector was based in agricultural lands near the perimeter of the strip, which today remains under the control of Israel's military. But beekeepers have returned to areas near the Yellow Line that divides the territory and found enough hives to restart honey production. Producers in Gaza City and parts of Jabalia near the line are now maintaining hives to try and provide some income for themselves and their families. Yet they say their efforts are constrained by Israel's blockade on many items from entering the strip, including ones used for beekeeping. "The bee sector is an important sector for sustainability, ecological balance and farming," said Ibrahim al-Dabbeh, the head of the Cooperative Association of Beekeepers.

headline: What happens when global power goes unchecked?
body of the article: What happens when the world's most powerful actors stop facing accountability? That's the question at the heart of the Atlas and Impunity, an annual report from the Eurasia Group that measures how people experience the abuse of power in nearly 200 countries.Ian Bremmersat down with International Rescue Committee president and CEODavid Milibandon GZERO World to talk about why the levels of impunity in conflict states like Sudan and Syria are spiraling out of control, and what the data reveals about the state of democracy, human rights, and how power is wielded around the globe. As Miliband points out, impunity extends far beyond dictators and war crimes. It's about the everyday consequences of power exercised without accountability. Corporations can exploit workers and consumers. States can exploit property rights. Even the climate crisis is a form of impunity against future generations and the planet. But despite a disturbing lack of accountability around the world, he explains, there are some reasons for cautious optimism. "The greatest cause for hope is the assertion of democratic rights," Miliband says, "If you're looking for bright spots at the moment, you have to look deep into civil societies that are mobilizing and organizing to defend the most basic rights." headline: Car Drives Straight Into Open Lift Shaft in Horror CCTV Video As Driver Hospitalized
body of the article: CCTV footage circulating viaNewsXandThe Sunshows a whitehatchbackslowlydrivingacross a tiled parking area in Maharashtra, India,brakelights fully illuminated, before the frontwheelsdrop into an open elevator shaft and the entirevehicledisappears into the darkness below. The clip, timestamped to early August 2026, has the quality of something you'd watch through your fingers. Thecardoesn't lurch or skid – it just keeps going, steadily, as if the driver hadn't realized the floor was about to run out. The back wheels tip upward as the rear falls, and then it's gone. An on-screen text overlay confirms the driver was taken to hospital following the fall. PerAsianet Newsable, the incident took place in Mumbai on August 4, 2026, in which a driver missed a turn while attempting to park and the vehicle plunged roughly 25 feet into a shaft where a parking lift was under construction. A wooden barrier was supposed to block the opening, but the vehicle broke straight through it. Witnesses nearby reported hearing the impact when the vehicle hit the bottom.Emergencycrews pulled the driver out and transported him to a local hospital. "He is currently undergoing treatment, though the extent of his injuries has not yet been confirmed," perAsianet Newsable. Mumbai has a grim trackrecordwith car elevator shafts specifically. An earlier tragedy at Iqbal Heights, a 22-floor building located in Mumbai's Agripada area, claimed the lives of a teenage boy, aged 14, and afamilydriver when their car plunged two floors down a car elevator shaft, as reported by theDeccan Herald. In May 2025, a parking lift at a 21-story building in Borivali West collapsed into a seven-meter pit, trapping two men inside, per the same outlet. According to figures gathered byLiftInverter.comfrom documented elevator incidents spanning2022to 2026, unguarded shafts and fall-relatedaccidentsrepresent one of the deadliest recurring hazards in the data – responsible for five of the twenty incidents on record and linked to every one of the three child deaths captured in the dataset. Falls into unguarded or inadequately guarded shafts, combined with entrapment between liftcarsand doors, represent the majority of serious outcomes.

headline: 'Racist incitement': Israeli medical groups decry claims of soldier abuse by Rambam's Arab staff
body of the article: "The Israeli health system relies daily on the joint work of doctors, nurses, and medical staff, Jews and Arabs, doctors in every person regardless of religion, nationality, or political position." The Mersham organization of medical professionals in Israel came out against therecent allegations against Arab staffat the Rambam Health Care Campus on Monday, calling it "racist incitement." "The Israeli health system relies daily on the joint work of doctors, nurses, and medical staff, Jews and Arabs, doctors in every person regardless of religion, nationality, or political position," Mersham stated. "It is possible and necessary to examine what concerns medical treatment. But when they speak out, and public figures join the attack, the damage seeps into the entire system." The Chairman of the Israel Association of Public Health Physicians, Professor Hagai Levine, also rejected the public response to the allegations. "The plots againstRambam Hospitalare sabotaging the entire health system," he stated. View of the Rambam Health Care Campus in Haifa, August 9, 2026 (credit: CHAIM GOLDBERG/FLASH90) "Lies born on social media about treatment at Rambam are not just 'fake news' - they are a dangerous blood libel aimed at dismantling from within the only system that still functions as an island of sanity and equality in Israel. When politicians spread nonsense about 'medical death' or treating the enemy at the expense of civilians, they do not only harm Arab teams - they harm every patient, Jewish orArab, who enters the hospital door." On Saturday, the brother of one of four soldiers recently wounded in Lebanon claimed that the troops were severely mistreated by Rambam's staff during their overnight stay at the Haifa hospital. Rambam stated that, after an investigation, it rejected all claims of wrongdoing by its staff toward the wounded soldiers. Later, Defense Minister Israel Katzcalled for an IDF investigationinto allegations levied on Saturday against Arab hospital employees accused of mistreating the four soldiers. Batya Giladi contributed to this report.

headline: Putin’s Desperate Plot to Fix Humiliating Military Crisis Exposed
body of the article: Vladimir Putinis opting for increasingly desperate recruitment methods for hiswar in Ukraine, according to a new report. The Russian dictator is said to be eager to avoid an unpopular mass mobilization and is leaning on a system of bonuses, tricks, and abductions to drag the new recruits he desperately needs for his army's meat-grinder tactics on the front lines. In the city of Penza in the south of the country, men have been dragged from the streets and workshops by peoplein plain clothesand made to sign contracts to sign up, according to a new report from theFinancial Timesciting activists. "Year by year and month by month, it's harder for the Russian army to find people," exiled anti-war activist Grigroy Sverdlin, director of Get Lost, told the FT. His organization, run from Georgia, helps Russian troops desert the army and leave the country. "Putin is evidently putting off a new wave of mobilization, so the defense ministry has to put more pressure on all sorts of people to sign contracts," he added. "They replenish the losses with people who sign new contracts, and there haven't been enough people willing to sign up for quite some time—even for the huge sums offered in the contracts." The last mobilization push was in 2022 and saw hundreds of thousands of Russians flee the country to escape conscription. However, fears have spiked that another could be planned for after the State Duma elections in September. Connection e.V. is based in Germany and assists conscientious objectors. Its military law expert Artyom Klyga said that Putin is now "trying to squeeze as much as they can from every category of men." "There are traps for each group to trick them or pressure them into signing a contract," he said. The system of bonuses can see new recruits earn up to $56,000. But the FT reports they are also being offered to third-party individuals, who cold-call potential recruits for a finder's fee. There have also been reports of efforts to convince people in delicate positions, such as those serving suspended sentences or suspects in criminal investigations. The German Institute for International and Security Affairs's Russian expert Janis Kluge told the newspaper, "Local authorities are under enormous pressure to recruit enough soldiers each year. "They know who is in debt, who is under police investigation and who has recently lost their driving license, and they home in on these men." Sources told the newspaper that the Kremlin has stepped up pressure on local authorities to help it reach its 409,000 target, this year, giving them the power to summon people to have their military records verified. Some women, meanwhile, have been reported to have been contacted because their educations and backgrounds would be useful in a theater of war. Former pharmacology student Indira told the FT she and several of her other classmates had received draft notices. "The fact of receiving it is itself certainly very concerning, but there is no reason to worry just yet," she said. Russian cops have said raids on workplaces have not been connected to sending people to the front, and the Kremlin has dismissed the possibility of another mobilization. It comes as support for Putin's war flags, among mounting losses, reported by theCenter for Strategic and International Studiesto be approaching half a million dead. Meanwhile, Ukraine has brought the war to Russia with an extended drone blitz over the summer that has targeted key energy and logistics infrastructure in highly visible attacks. The under-pressure president, 73, is also reported to be leaningmore and more heavily on the FSBto keep control of the country. It has sparked unease among Russia's middle classes and elites, and has been coupled with a drift towards hardliners enjoying more influence with Putin, sources toldBloomberg.

headline: Has the army turned the page on control of western Sudan?
body of the article: Khartoum, Sudan– A Sudanese army-led counteroffensive in the western region of Darfur has led to a series of gains for government-aligned forces over theRapid Support Forces(RSF) paramilitary group in recent days. In early August, Sudan's military and allied groups repelled two successive attacks by the RSF in the strategically important Bir Saliba region. It lies about 30km (nearly 20 miles) north of el-Geneina, the capital of West Darfur state and the RSF's last stronghold in the region. Government-backed forces have tried to put pressure on RSF supply lines by seizing control of crossings and desert routes along the border with Chad. The strategy could signal a shift in fighting towards el-Geneina. Leading to el-Geneina, the Bir Saliba region is of strategic importance. It has a network of roads that link the state capital with areas in the northwest of the region, particularly Jebel Moon and Kulbus, according to General Bahr al-Din Adam Karama, the governor of West Darfur state. Darfur Regional Governor Minni Arko Minnawi announced that Major General Mahdi Adam, known as "Jebel Moon" and one of the RSF's most prominent field commanders, was killed in fighting in western Sudan. The RSF has not officially confirmed his death, but if true it would represent a significant loss for the paramilitary group and leave a leadership gap along this key western front. Minnawi said the Joint Force of the Armed Struggle Movements, a coalition of former Darfur rebel groups that signed the 2020 Juba Peace Agreement and now fights alongside the Sudanese army against the RSF, also thwarted an attempt by the RSF to encircle Bir Saliba. One RSF force advanced from north of Kulbus while another moved from the direction of Sileia in the Jebel Moon area before launching a large-scale attack on the Joint Force. "[The RSF] bet on the element of surprise to break through the Joint Force's defences, but they received another lesson," Minnawi said. Major Mutawakkil Ali Wakil Abu-Ja, the Joint Force's spokesman, told Al Jazeera that the Joint Force destroyed more than 38 combat vehicles and seized 27 others in the campaign. The commander of the attacking RSF force was also killed, he said, with fighters fleeing the battlefield and leaving their dead comrades behind. Abu-Ja said efforts were under way to secure the western axis and increase pressure on the RSF before what he described as a decisive battle for el-Geneina. Air strikes on a convoy travelling near the border with Chad have further isolated the RSF and struck a key supply route for the paramilitary group, Major General Othman Siraj said. Pressure on multiple fronts by the army was preventing the RSF from regrouping its forces and paving the way for what he believes will be the final battle for el-Geneina. Fadel Kaya, a leader and adviser with the Sudan Liberation Movement/Army – Transitional Council (SLM/TC), a Darfur rebel faction that split from the original Sudan Liberation Movement and signed the 2020 Juba Peace Agreement, told Al Jazeera that the Joint Force's victories in West Darfur indicated that the RSF had shifted away from trying to gain territory to retreating from key positions. Sudanese families displaced from el-Fasher, the capital of North Darfur state, which the RSF captured in October, receive food aid at a newly established camp in Sudan's Northern State on November 16, 2025 [Marwan Ali/AP] In North Kordofan state in central Sudan, the RSF had turned to drones to compensate for the loss of the strategic route linking Omdurman and el-Obeid. This had served as a major supply artery for the RSF before the armyrecapturedit on July 27. Amin Ishaq Zakaria, a SLM/TC spokesman, told Al Jazeera that the RSF's increased use of drones reflected "a predicament on the ground and an inability to engage in direct confrontations after losing vital positions". Sudanese armed forces had seized a number of attack drones along the Jabra al-Sheikh axis during the counteroffensive, he added. The International Organization for Migration reported on Saturday that the recent escalation in fighting has seen more than 6,650 people from 11 villages in the Sirba region displaced. More than 13 million people had already beendisplacedsince the war between the military and RSF began in April 2023, according toUnited Nationsestimates. The RSF and its allies have also established a rival administration, known as the Tasis government, in opposition to the Sudanese government based in Port Sudan. Al Jazeera reached out to the RSF and Tasis government about the fighting in the Bir Saliba area but received no response by the time the report was published.

headline: Australia to buy sophisticated US air-to-air missiles
body of the article: Australia will become the first export customer for the AIM-260A Joint Advanced Tactical Missile (JATM), an air-to-air missile that will be integrated onto the country's full fleet of fighter platforms. Defence Minister Richard Marles made the announcement on Aug. 6 while attending the multinational fighter exercise Pitch Black 2026 in Darwin. Marles said the JATM will allow the Royal Australian Air Force "to strike at a longer range, deter any adversary and protect our national interests." Australia and the U.S. are alarmed at growing threats from China, whose air force is fielding long-range missiles such as the PL-15 and the even larger PL-17. With aging missile types like the incumbent AIM-120 AMRAAM now outclassed by their Chinese equivalents, the AIM-260 is designed to restore order. Canberra will splash out A$736 million — around $520 million USD — on an unspecified quantity of AIM-260s through the Foreign Military Sales process. On March 17, the U.S. had approved the sale of up to 450 JATMs with an estimated price tag of $3.16 billion USD. Given that the recently announced order costs significantly less than this sum, Australia is presumably purchasing well under 100 missiles in this first tranche. The AIM-260 will be integrated first onto the RAAF's F/A-18F Super Hornet fleet, followed by the F-35A and then the EA-18G Growler. Another future Australian candidate is likely to be the MQ-28A Ghost Bat unmanned combat aircraft, which test-fired an AMRAAM last December. Lockheed Martin's secretive munition is a GPS-aided air superiority missile with increased range and effectiveness compared to existing U.S. air-to-air weapons. There have still been no official photos released of the missile. The JATM's capabilities — such as its range, propulsion and seeker — remain heavily classified. Its range is likely to be at least 120 miles — quite possibly more — which is far superior to the incumbent AIM-120 AMRAAM. Its form factor is similar to the AMRAAM's to ensure it fits inside the weapon bays of existing fighters. Australia said in a statement that the AIM-260 "will provide air force platforms with a credible deterrent against airborne targets, complementing existing air-to-air missile capabilities and other surface-based missile capabilities across the Australian Defence Force." Minister for Defence Industry Pat Conroy described JATMs as "some of the most sophisticated air-to-air weapons in the world, and Australia will be the first country to operate them outside the U.S." However, it will take years — not before 2033, according to some reports — until the JATM reaches Australian hands and is bolted onto RAAF Super Hornets. Australia's acquisition also opens the door for other Indo-Pacific air forces to procure the JATM in the future, especially given the widespread adoption of the F-35 by close U.S. allies in the region.

headline: Oslo court extends Høiby's house arrest by four weeks
body of the article: Marius Borg Høiby, the eldest son of Norwegian Crown Princess Mette-Marit, must remain in pre-trial detention for a further four weeks, an Oslo court ruled on Monday. The 29-year-old will continue to serve the detention under house arrest with an ankle tag, the news agency NTB reported. Høiby was sentenced to four years in prison in June, though the verdict has not yet become final. He was found guilty of two counts of rape and violence against a former girlfriend. A restraining order is in place to protect her, which Høiby has already violated on several occasions. Police argued there was a risk of Høiby committing further offences and requested an extension of the house arrest. The court agreed. Høiby sought release on condition that he stay away from certain areas, but the court rejected his application. Høiby intends to appeal the decision, NTB cited his defence lawyer, Petar Sekulic, as saying. The court's ruling remains in force pending a decision on the appeal. The extended pre-trial detention runs until September 7. Høiby is permitted to leave his residence for purposes such as medical appointments or visiting sick family members. He must also submit to regular drug tests.
